choosing a firm when you plan to use a passing service

not every evaluation is equally suitable for third-party execution, and the differences are structural rather than a matter of opinion. four criteria matter more than account size or marketing offers.

a static maximum loss is the most forgiving structure, because the failure level never moves. an end-of-day trailing drawdown is the next most workable: the floor follows closed profit, so intraday noise does not tighten it. an intraday trailing threshold is the hardest, because every unrealised gain drags the failure level upward and a normal pullback can end the account even while the day's net result is positive. if two firms are otherwise equal, the one with the static floor is the safer assignment.

some firms apply a consistency requirement during the evaluation, some only at payout, and some not at all. a rule that applies at payout is more forgiving, because the distribution of profit can be adjusted by adding additional winning days before requesting a withdrawal. a rule that applies during the evaluation shortens the time you have to fix a lopsided distribution.

no time limit is better than a thirty-day window, for an obvious reason: a flat week costs time rather than the account. minimum trading days cut the other way - they prevent a fast pass from being eligible for funding, which is why the log tracks days used as carefully as it tracks profit.

this is the criterion that decides whether the arrangement is appropriate at all. firms that explicitly require the account holder to place the trades make a passing service a poor bet regardless of how favourable the evaluation rules look. checking the current terms - not a review from two years ago - is part of the decision, not an afterthought.

how to read a prop firm rulebook in fifteen minutes

most of the questions on this page reduce to one skill: reading a firm's terms and extracting the four numbers that decide whether an evaluation is forgiving or brutal. once that skill is in place, the answers stop being firm-specific and start being arithmetic.
minute 1-3: find the loss limits and identify the measurement point

every rulebook states a daily loss limit and a maximum loss. the question that decides everything is what each is measured against. daily limits are usually measured on equity including floating positions, which makes them stricter than they appear; maximum loss may be measured from the starting balance, from current balance, or from peak equity on a trailing basis. a 10% maximum loss measured from a static starting balance and a 10% trailing maximum loss are not the same rule with different wording - they are two different challenges, and the trailing version is materially harder near the target.

where a maximum loss trails, the next question is when it updates. intradaily trailing moves with every tick of unrealised profit, which means a position that goes into profit and comes back can raise the failure level without the trader ever banking anything. end-of-day trailing updates once, at the close, on realised balance. the difference is dramatic on a volatile instrument and it is the single most under-read line in the entire document.

divide the target by your per-trade risk to get the target in r. a 10% target with 1.5% risk is roughly 6.7r; at 3% risk it is 3.3r. that single division tells you how much of the challenge is analysis and how much is patience, and it explains why traders who size aggressively report fast passes and frequent resets in the same breath.
minute 10-12: read the payout section as though it were the challenge

for most firms the payout terms contain more traps than the evaluation. minimum trading days, a profit threshold before the first withdrawal, a consistency requirement on the best day, a processing schedule, and sometimes a cap on how much can be withdrawn at once. a trader who passes cleanly and then discovers a 30% consistency rule on a 40% best day has not been funded in any useful sense - they have been given an account they must keep trading before they can be paid.

the last section lists what is banned: third-party trading, account sharing, certain strategies such as high-frequency arbitrage or latency exploitation, sometimes holding through specific news events. the important part is not the list but the enforcement clause - whether breaches are detected during the evaluation or after funding, and whether the remedy is a reset or a forfeit. a prohibition enforced after funding is the most expensive kind, because it arrives when the trader has the most to lose.

they often do. a marketing page will say "no time limit" while the terms say something narrower, or a headline will describe a static drawdown while a footnote describes a trailing one. the resolution is to ask the firm in writing and keep the reply. where no reply comes, or the reply is evasive, that is itself the answer: an unclear rulebook becomes a dispute at exactly the moment a trader cannot afford one.

the output of a fifteen-minute read should be a single index card, because a rulebook that lives in memory is a rulebook that gets misremembered on the day it matters. the card carries the daily loss budget in dollars, the current distance to the failure level, the target expressed as a number of r multiples at the chosen per-trade risk, and any constraint that applies at payout rather than during the evaluation. three of those four numbers change as equity moves, which is why the card is rewritten each morning rather than laminated once.

there is a second use for the card: it makes a rulebook comparison possible without reading two full documents side by side. two firms whose cards differ in only one line are comparable assignments; two whose cards differ in three are different puzzles, and picking between them on fee alone is picking between difficulties at random. that is the practical reason this site keeps returning to the same four variables - not because they are the only things in a rulebook, but because they are the only things that reliably change an outcome.

the card also settles arguments with yourself. when a session is going badly, the temptation is to renegotiate the plan - a slightly larger position, a slightly wider stop, one more trade to get back to flat. a written number removes the negotiation, because the budget was decided by someone calmer than the person currently looking at the chart.

one warning about the card, since it is a tool rather than a guarantee. firms revise terms, and a card written three months ago may describe a challenge that no longer exists. the card is dated for that reason, and the date is the first thing to check when a result seems to contradict the rules as remembered. a stale card is worse than no card, because it produces confident errors rather than cautious ones.

one last habit worth adding to the fifteen minutes: keep the firm's reply to your written question. rules that arrive by email are the only version of a rulebook that cannot be revised later without someone noticing, and the reply costs one message.

take profit trader sells futures evaluations on two different account models, and the difference between them is not cosmetic - it changes the arithmetic of every trade you take. this review works through the drawdown structure, the consistency gate at payout, the real cost of a failed attempt, and the specific kind of trader each model rewards. it is written from the rule mechanics outward, because the mechanics decide outcomes long before the market does.
tft runs two models - a cheaper one with an intraday trailing threshold and a costlier one with an end-of-day threshold. the second is materially easier to pass at equal skill.
a trailing threshold that responds to unrealised profit punishes a winning session that retraces. an end-of-day threshold does not, because it only looks at the closing balance.
cost per attempt, not headline fee, is the number to compare. two resets on a cheap account can cost more than one attempt on a better-structured one.
the consistency expectation binds at payout, not at evaluation. a fast pass built on one dominant day can produce a funded account that cannot withdraw.
futures firms restrict sizing, session hours and news windows. those rules fail more accounts quietly than the drawdown does.
terms change. every figure below describes a mechanism; confirm the current numbers on the firm's own pages before paying.

most prop firm reviews answer a question nobody asked. they list a fee, a target and a drawdown figure in a table and call the firm cheap or expensive, as though the three numbers were the whole product. they are not. the numbers that decide whether a trader passes are the ones that describe how the failure floor moves, what counts as a breach, how many sessions the target realistically takes, and what has to be true before a withdrawal is approved.

so this review measures five things, and it measures them in a fixed order. first, the structure of the loss limit: is the floor static, does it trail on closed profit, or does it trail on open profit? second, the target expressed as a percentage of the account, because that is the only form in which it can be compared across firms. third, the daily constraint, which on a trailing account is often the tighter of the two loss rules. fourth, the conditions attached to the funded stage, because a cheap evaluation leading to an unusable funded account is not cheap. fifth, the total cost of reaching a first payout, which includes resets, not just the initial purchase.

everything else - platform quality, dashboard design, the friendliness of support - matters to the experience and almost nothing to the outcome. a trader can be comfortable on a platform and still fail a rule, and the rule does not care about comfort. this is why the review leads with mechanism. if the mechanism is understood, the platform is a preference. if the mechanism is not understood, no amount of platform polish will save the account.
three drawdown structures, drawn as the same equity curve under each rule. the curve is identical; the survival outcome is not.

one structural note before the detail. tft is a futures firm, which means two things that do not apply to forex evaluations. accounts are denominated in dollars and traded in contracts, so a target is a dollar figure rather than a percentage you can halve or double freely. and futures firms enforce conduct rules - maximum contracts, permitted hours, news windows, holding restrictions - that forex firms usually leave unstated. a review that ignores conduct rules is reviewing perhaps half of the product.

the single most important fact about tft is that the firm sells two accounts with genuinely different failure mechanics. the cheaper model uses an intraday trailing threshold; the more expensive one uses an end-of-day threshold. calling them both "the tft evaluation" is the mistake most reviews make, and it produces advice that is wrong for half the readers.

the important insight is not that the pro model is better. it is that the two models reward different behaviour, and a trader who has practised on one will be miscalibrated on the other. a trader trained on the entry model has learned to take profit early and to cut size as the target approaches, because the floor punishes the alternative. put that trader on the pro model and nothing breaks: the habits are conservative, and conservative habits cost only a little pace. reverse the direction and it is expensive. a trader raised on end-of-day thresholds has never had to reduce size after a strong session, and the first strong session on an intraday account will feel like progress while it is quietly removing the cushion.

there is a second asymmetry worth noting. on an end-of-day structure, the account's risk profile is fixed each morning: you know the floor, you know the distance from equity to the floor, and that number cannot change during the session. that makes the sizing decision a single calculation made once. on an intraday structure, the distance shrinks and grows within a session, and the sizing decision is continuous. continuous decisions are harder to execute well, because they have to be made while the position is live and the trader is emotionally engaged.

choosing between them: if the two fees differ by less than the cost of one reset on the cheaper account, the more forgiving model is usually the better purchase. the calculation is in the cost section below, and it is the only comparison that matters when the choice is between these two.
a trailing drawdown is a failure floor that rises with account equity and never falls. the detail that decides everything is which equity it follows.

an intraday trailing floor follows the peak of unrealised equity, tick by tick. if a position runs $2,000 into profit, the floor has already risen by $2,000, even though nothing has been banked. close the trade at $600 after a retracement and the floor stays where the peak pushed it. the trader kept $600 of profit and lost $1,400 of room, permanently. on a $100,000 account with a $3,000 starting buffer, that single sequence can remove nearly half the remaining cushion on a day that ended in profit.

an end-of-day trailing floor follows the closing balance. nothing moves while the market is open. a position that runs to $2,000 and closes at $600 moves the floor by $600, because $600 is what the account actually holds. the unrealised excursion is invisible to the rule.

this is not a small difference in strictness; it is a difference in what the rule is measuring. the intraday version measures the best moment; the end-of-day version measures the result. a trader who is right about direction but poor at exits is punished severely by the first and barely at all by the second. a trader who is right about direction and disciplined at exits is punished only slightly by the first - which is why some traders genuinely do not need the more expensive model, and why the recommendation has to be conditional rather than universal.
the same winning trade, three rulebooks. only the intraday version keeps the room the peak consumed.

on a trailing account, a strong opening week is both an asset and a liability. the asset is obvious: you are closer to the target. the liability is that the floor has risen with you, so the remaining room is smaller than it was at the start, while the remaining distance to the target is also smaller. if the two shrink at the same rate, the evaluation never gets easier - it just gets shorter.

work the numbers. a $100,000 account, a $6,000 target, a $3,000 trailing buffer, all figures dollars. after $4,000 of profit the target is two thirds complete and the floor has risen $4,000; remaining room to the floor is $3,000, unchanged in absolute terms, but now the account is risking a $4,000 gain against a $3,000 buffer. in ratio terms the trade has become considerably worse. that is the arithmetic most traders never perform, and it is the reason a plan must reduce size as completion rises rather than hold it constant.

on an end-of-day structure the same sequence produces a different picture only because the peak cannot outrun the close. the trader who books $4,000 has genuinely moved the floor $4,000, so the ratio arithmetic is identical - but the trader who books $600 of a $4,000 excursion has moved the floor $600 and kept the other $3,400 of room. the end-of-day model converts exit discipline into structural advantage. the intraday model converts it into survival.

futures firms typically apply a daily loss limit alongside the trailing threshold, and the binding rule each morning is whichever sits closer to current equity. after a flat week the trailing floor is usually distant and the daily limit binds. after a strong session the floor can be closer than the daily limit permits, and then the floor binds first.

the practical consequence is that a single number is not enough. compute both each morning, take the smaller, and size from that. the arithmetic takes twenty seconds and prevents the most common self-inflicted failure on a trailing account, which is trading a normal-sized position on a morning when the floor had quietly moved within one trade of current equity.

passing an evaluation at tft produces a funded account with its own conditions, and on futures firms those conditions are usually stricter than the evaluation. three gates matter: a minimum number of trading days before a withdrawal can be requested, a profit threshold that has to be met again on the funded account, and a consistency expectation that caps how much of the total any single day may represent.

the consistency gate deserves its own arithmetic because it is the one that surprises traders. if a best day may not exceed a stated share of total profit, then required total profit equals the best day divided by that share. a $3,000 best day under a 30% rule requires $10,000 of total profit before the payout clears. a trader who reaches the funded threshold quickly on the back of one enormous session has not finished; they have created a requirement to keep trading until the ratio normalises, and that requirement arrives exactly when the trader believes the work is done.
at target but not at payout: a dominant session leaves the ratio unsatisfied and the withdrawal blocked.

the remedy is to cap daily profit during the evaluation at roughly a third of the eventual total. on a $6,000 target that is a $2,000 daily cap, which automatically satisfies a 30% best-day rule the moment the target is reached: the best day is $2,000 and the total is $6,000, a share of 33%. adjust the cap to the firm's stated threshold, and remember that the threshold can differ between the evaluation and the funded stage, so read both.

read the table from right to left. the cap is the decision; the total follows. a trader who sets the cap at a fifth of the target will satisfy even a strict rule, and will do so without ever thinking about the rule again. a trader who sets no cap is making a bet that no session will be unusually good, which is a strange bet for someone whose entire plan depends on sessions being good.

two further gates are administrative rather than mathematical, and they block more first payouts than either of the above. identity verification must be complete before a withdrawal is reviewed, and it is often left until the request is submitted. and the first payout is frequently subject to a waiting period measured from the first trade on the funded account. neither is a rule to plan around so much as a calendar to plan against: complete verification in week one, and request the first withdrawal on the earliest permitted date rather than at the largest possible size. the first payout exists to prove the pipe works.

prop firm pricing is quoted per attempt, and attempts fail. that makes the headline fee a poor measure of cost. the number that matters is the expected spend required to reach one funded account, which is the fee times the number of attempts a trader of that skill level typically needs.

the arithmetic is unforgiving. if a trader fails twice before passing, three fees is the cost of one funded account. at that ratio, a firm charging 60% more with a materially more forgiving drawdown structure is the cheaper purchase - and it is cheaper by a wide margin, because the second fee is not discounted by anything. this is the calculation that makes the entry-versus-pro decision, and it is also the calculation that most traders skip when they compare firms on a pricing page.
the cheap account stops being cheap the moment it needs a second attempt.

there is a third option that changes the arithmetic entirely, and it should be stated plainly because it is the service this site sells. a passing service trades the evaluation for a flat fee, once, and covers resets while the evaluation is running. under a flat $220 arrangement the expected cost is not fee times attempts; it is the flat fee, plus whatever the firm charges for a reset if one is needed. that is a different cost curve, and it is worth comparing against the fee-times-attempts figure rather than against a single fee.

two honesty conditions apply, and a service that does not state them is not worth using. first, many firms prohibit third-party trading of an evaluation; if the firm's terms forbid it, the service should decline the job rather than quietly accept the risk on the client's behalf. second, a passed evaluation is only worth paying for if the funded account is in the client's name and the payout history is genuine. the passing service review covers what to check, and the comparison of services sets out how the flat-fee model compares with doing it yourself.

for completeness, the do-it-yourself cost has three components that a fee comparison ignores: the fee, the time, and the opportunity cost of the capital. a trader spending six weeks on three failed attempts has spent more than three fees - they have spent six weeks during which a funded account could have been earning. that is not an argument for outsourcing; it is an argument for measuring the whole number before choosing. the profit calculator handles the payout side of the same question.
the two rulebooks need two plans, and the difference is concentrated in one decision: whether size falls as the target approaches.

for the intraday model, size must ladder down. a workable structure is full planned size to 40% of target, three quarters from 40% to 70%, and half beyond 70%. the reason is the ratio arithmetic above: as completion rises, the gain at risk grows while the buffer shrinks, so the trade that got you to 70% is not the trade you should take at 70%. traders who hold size constant through the last third are the population that fails from a winning position.

for the end-of-day model, size can stay flat - provided the daily loss limit is respected independently, because the daily limit still binds within a session even when the trailing floor does not move until the close. a flat size ladder is simpler to execute and produces a faster pass, which is part of what the higher fee buys.

in both cases the per-trade risk should be a third of the daily limit at most, and the session should stop at 80% of the daily limit realised. three consecutive losses at that size leave the account alive and the plan intact, which is the property that matters across a multi-week evaluation. a plan that survives two losses but not three is not a plan; it is a sequence of coin flips with a calendar attached.

the floor check: every morning, subtract the current failure floor from current equity. if the result is smaller than the risk of one planned trade, either cut size or do not trade. there is no scenario in which trading anyway is correct, because the evaluation can be finished tomorrow and cannot be recovered once failed.

the daily session count deserves the same treatment as the size. four or five planned sessions a week produces a slower pass and a materially lower breach rate than trading every available window. on a trailing account every session either moves the floor or consumes budget; a session with no specific plan does one or the other without adding profit. rest is not a cost. on this rulebook it is a control.
failures cluster. the same six behaviours account for the overwhelming majority, and none of them is a market-view error.

holding a runner through a retracement on the intraday model. the floor moved with the peak, so the retracement is measured from the peak rather than from the entry. this is the defining failure of any intraday trailing structure.
increasing size near the target. the instinct that feels like confidence and behaves like a liquidation order. progress is precisely when the buffer is thinnest.
one dominant day. efficient for reaching the target, fatal for the consistency ratio, and - on a trailing account - the same session that removes the cushion.

trading a news window. futures firms restrict trading around scheduled releases and enforce the restriction by pattern rather than by discussion. a position opened legitimately before the window can still breach if the rule requires it closed.

exceeding the contract cap. maximum position size is usually in the terms, not on the marketing page. trading a permitted instrument at twice the permitted size is a breach, and it is easy to do on a fast contract.

continuing after the target. reaching the target is not the same as satisfying the minimum day count, and a trader who keeps trading to fill days is adding risk to a completed evaluation. flat, qualified days satisfy a day count; they do not endanger it.

there is a seventh failure that is really a category: treating the funded account as a continuation of the evaluation. it is not. the evaluation asks whether a trader can reach a target without breaching; the funded stage asks whether a trader can extract money repeatedly under a consistency gate. the behaviours that answer the first question well are not identical to the ones that answer the second. the payout process guide walks through the sequence, and the scam checklist covers the firms for which the second question never gets asked.
a review that does not say who should walk away is a brochure. here is the honest split.

the entry model suits traders who exit well. if your edge includes taking profit at a target rather than riding, the intraday mechanic costs you comparatively little, and the lower fee is genuinely better value. it also suits traders who want to learn the strictest version of the rule first, on the theory that everything else will feel easy afterwards. that theory is sound, and it is expensive to test.

the pro model suits traders whose exits are discretionary. if you give back a third of your winners as a matter of habit - most discretionary intraday traders do - the end-of-day structure converts that habit from a structural threat into a cost. you still lose the giveback; you simply do not lose the room as well.

neither model suits a trader without a written plan. this is not a moral judgement, it is an arithmetic one. both accounts have a fixed dollar floor and a fixed dollar target. a trader who sizes by feel is running an uncontrolled process against a control system, and the control system wins on a long enough timeline regardless of skill. the fix is a page of numbers, not a different firm.

neither model suits a trader who cannot trade the permitted hours. futures rules are time-bound in a way forex rules are not. if your available hours fall outside the liquid window, or inside a restricted news window, the evaluation is not a fair test of your trading - it is a test of your schedule. choose a firm whose hours match your life rather than restructuring your life around a fee.
three comparisons do most of the work when choosing a futures firm, and they are all structural rather than financial.

against apex: both firms run trailing thresholds, and the useful question is which equity the threshold follows and whether the firm offers a non-trailing alternative. apex's rulebook is widely documented and its consistency treatment at payout is explicit; tft's distinguishing feature is the existence of two models, one of which removes the intraday mechanic entirely. a trader choosing between them is choosing between one rulebook and a menu. the apex guide covers that side in detail.

against topstep: topstep states a daily loss limit and a maximum loss limit separately, and applies a best-day expectation to the evaluation itself rather than only at payout. that makes its constraints more visible and its failure modes easier to plan around. tft's evaluation is less explicit about the consistency expectation during the pass, which is either freedom or a trap depending on whether you read the funded terms first. the topstep guide sets out the two-limit structure.

against a flat-fee pass: the comparison that matters most for anyone reading a review rather than a rulebook. a service trades the evaluation for a fixed fee and absorbs the reset risk; the firm still applies its rules to the resulting funded account. that means the service removes the evaluation risk and not the payout risk, which is the correct division of labour and is worth being clear about. the passed challenges page shows what a completed evaluation looks like when it is done this way.

the general principle across all three: compare the failure floor first, the target second, the daily constraint third, and the fee fourth. any review that inverts that order is selling rather than reviewing.
positioning firms by mechanism rather than by fee: the vertical axis is how fast the failure floor moves.

terms change, and a review written in october is a snapshot rather than a contract. before paying, confirm the following on the firm's own pages, in this order. each item takes under a minute and each one has invalidated a purchase decision at some point.
which equity the floor follows. starting balance, closed balance, or intraday peak including unrealised profit. the third is the strictest and the first is the most forgiving.
the distance from the starting balance to the floor, in dollars and as a percentage of the account. compare that percentage, not the dollar figure, across account sizes.
the target as a percentage of the account. a dollar target on a $150,000 account and the same dollar target on a $50,000 account are not the same evaluation.
whether a daily loss limit applies, whether it resets each session, and whether it is separate from the trailing floor.
the consistency rule, stated for the evaluation and for the funded stage separately, with the percentage and the measurement basis.
the minimum day count, for the evaluation and before each payout, and whether a scratch day counts.
conduct rules: contract caps, permitted hours, news windows, overnight and weekend holding.
the reset price and whether a reset preserves the account size or restarts the evaluation from scratch.
whether third-party trading is permitted. if it is not, no passing service should be engaged, and a service that does not ask is a service to avoid.
if any of those ten cannot be found in writing, that absence is itself the answer. a firm that does not state its failure mechanics clearly is not being modest; it is declining to be reviewed.

the pro model is reasonable for a first futures evaluation because its end-of-day threshold does not punish a winning session that retraces. the cheaper model is a harder first assignment, and the lower fee does not compensate for the extra attempts it typically takes.
what is the difference between the two tft account models?

the drawdown mechanic. one trails the failure floor intraday on unrealised equity, so a winner that retraces permanently reduces the cushion. the other trails only at the close, so unrealised excursions are invisible to the rule. everything downstream - sizing, pacing, expected number of attempts - follows from that difference.

on the entry model, yes. that is the single most consequential rule on the account, because it means a position that is $2,000 in profit has already moved the floor even if it closes at $600. on the pro model it does not, because the floor is only recalculated at the end of the day.

typically ten to eighteen trading days at a disciplined pace, depending on the model, the account size and the minimum day count. faster passes are possible, but a pass built on one dominant session creates a consistency problem at payout that takes longer to fix than the pass saved.

a third of the daily loss limit at most, with the session closed once 80% of the daily budget is realised. on the intraday model, reduce to three quarters and then half of that as completion passes 40% and 70% of the target.

because the floor trails the peak. profit raises the floor, so the distance from current equity to the floor does not grow with the gain - the account's remaining room is consumed by its own success. this is why size has to fall as the target approaches.

a cap on how much of total profit any single day may represent. required total profit equals the best day divided by the permitted share, so a $3,000 best day under a 30% rule requires $10,000 of total profit before the withdrawal clears.

policies differ by firm and by account type, and futures contracts carry rollover and gap risk that forex pairs do not. check the current terms; where holding is permitted, account for the weekend gap explicitly rather than assuming the stop will fill where it was placed.

a single fee comparison usually says yes for the entry model and no for the pro model. the meaningful comparison is fee multiplied by expected attempts, and on that measure the cheaper account often loses once it needs a second purchase.

the account is closed and the only recovery is a new purchase or a reset, priced by the firm. where a passing service is trading the evaluation, a reset on the same firm and size carries no additional service fee under the flat $220 arrangement - the firm's own reset charge is separate.

only if the firm's terms permit third-party trading, which many futures firms prohibit. the service should check the terms and decline the job where it is banned. passing an evaluation in breach of the terms produces a funded account that can be voided at payout, which is the worst possible outcome.

which equity the floor follows, the floor and target as percentages, whether a daily limit applies, the consistency rule at both stages, the minimum day counts, the conduct rules and the reset price. if the firm does not publish those, that absence is the answer.

a flat-fee service removes the evaluation risk and the reset cost while the firm's rules still govern the funded account. that is the correct division: the service solves the test, the trader keeps the payout. the service reviews cover how the model is priced and what to verify.

abstract rules are easy to agree with and hard to apply. here is the same plan executed on both models with identical trades, so the structural difference is visible in outcomes rather than in description.

the setup: a $100,000 account, a $6,000 target, a $3,000 starting buffer, a $1,000 daily loss limit, and a trader risking $350 per trade with a $1,000 daily profit cap. the trade sequence is fixed and deliberately unremarkable: +$520, +$1,180, −$410, flat, +$980, +$760, −$350, +$1,240, +$640, flat, +$940.

on the end-of-day model , the floor rises by each closed profit and never by an excursion. total realised profit after eleven sessions is $5,500, the best day is $1,240 - about 23% of the total - and the floor has risen $5,500 from its starting point. the account is $500 from target with $3,000 of room measured from the original balance and a best-day share comfortably inside a 30% rule.

on the intraday model , the same trades produce the same realised profit, but each winner's peak mattered. suppose the $1,240 day touched $1,900 before closing, the $980 day touched $1,450, and the $640 day touched $1,050. the floor rose to the peaks, not the closes. realised profit is still $5,500, but the floor is now $1,900 higher than the end-of-day case across those three sessions - and the remaining room is correspondingly smaller. the trader is closer to the target and closer to failure at the same time.

that is the whole difference between the models, expressed in one sequence. it does not say the intraday account is unfair, and it does not say the trader behaved badly. it says the rule measures a different quantity, and a plan calibrated to closed profit is miscalibrated for a rule that measures peaks. the correction is not more skill; it is a smaller size ladder and an earlier exit on the days that run.

note what the table makes obvious: the consistency ratio is identical on both accounts, because it is computed from realised profit, which the rule does not change. only the failure floor diverges. traders often assume the stricter model is stricter in every dimension; it is stricter in exactly one, and that one is the one that ends accounts.

the pacing lesson follows directly. on the intraday model, the eleven-session sequence above should have been twelve or thirteen sessions at a smaller size, with the winners cut earlier. on the end-of-day model the same sequence is unremarkable and can be repeated until the target is reached. neither is right or wrong; they are two different products, and the fee difference between them is the price of removing a single mechanic.
the funded phase, and why it feels easier and is not

two things change the day an evaluation passes. the trailing mechanic usually disappears, replaced by a static failure level measured from the starting balance of the funded account. and the consistency gate stops being a planning consideration and becomes a payment condition.

the first change is genuinely a relief: with a static floor, progress can no longer make the account more fragile, so a winning week is unambiguously good. the second change is the one that catches traders, because it arrives after the pressure has lifted. a trader who passed with a best day at 45% of total profit has a funded account that is technically active and practically unpayable until enough ordinary profit accumulates to bring the ratio down. the fix is to keep the daily cap in place during the funded phase, at the same fraction of the eventual payout threshold that satisfied the evaluation.

there is a third change that is rarely discussed and matters for planning: the funded account's minimum day count is usually counted separately for each payout cycle. a trader who reaches the profit threshold in five sessions but needs ten qualifying days has five sessions of nothing to do, and the temptation to fill them with size is the single most common way a funded account is lost. the correct approach is to land the threshold and the day count on the same date by pacing from the start, and to treat qualifying days as complete at the smallest closed trade that keeps the day positive.

finally, the exit itself. withdrawal processing on futures firms runs on a posted schedule, and the first request is usually the slowest because verification has not yet been completed. complete identity checks in the first week, request the first withdrawal on the earliest permitted date rather than at the largest available amount, and treat that first payment as a test of the pipe rather than as income. the payout guide sets out the sequence in full, including the verification steps that cause most first requests to be rejected.

none of this is unique to tft. it is the shape of the futures funded stage generally, and it is the part of the pipeline where a firm's reputation is actually made. an evaluation fee is small compared with a month of funded profit; the firm that pays reliably is worth a stricter rulebook, and the firm that does not is worth avoiding at any fee.
four decisions, in order, and each one narrows the next.

choose the model by exit behaviour, not by fee. if your journal shows winners routinely giving back more than a third of their peak, the end-of-day model is buying you room you are currently donating. if your exits are mechanical, the entry model is the better value and the stricter rules cost you little.

choose the size by payout ceiling, not by pass probability. the percentage rules are identical across sizes, so a larger account buys a bigger payout and a bigger fee, not an easier test. the smallest size that produces a meaningful payout is almost always the correct first purchase.

budget for two attempts. not because you will fail, but because the expected cost of the purchase includes the resets, and a trader who budgets for one attempt tends to take a second one in a hurry and a bad mood. the profit calculator makes the comparison against a flat-fee pass straightforward.

read the funded terms before paying the evaluation fee. the evaluation is the audition; the funded terms are the contract. a firm whose payout conditions are vague at the evaluation stage is telling you something about how the withdrawal will be reviewed.

the order matters because each decision constrains the next in a way that is invisible if you shop by price. a trader who begins with the cheapest account is choosing the strictest mechanic and then compounding it with the smallest payout ceiling, which is the worst combination available: maximum difficulty per dollar of upside.

for readers who would rather not run the evaluation at all, the flat-fee route exists and is priced at $220 for any firm and any account size, with resets covered while the evaluation is running. it is only available where the firm's terms permit third-party trading; where they do not, the service should say so before taking payment. the service comparison sets out the trade-offs honestly, and the rules matrix lets you check a firm's mechanics against the others before deciding whether to trade it yourself.

futures evaluations look simpler than forex challenges and are considerably harder to compare, because the two products do not measure risk the same way. a futures account is sized in contracts, its drawdown is often a dollar figure that trails a peak, and the daily loss limit rather than the profit target is what ends most attempts. this guide sets out the criteria that actually separate one futures firm from another, the arithmetic behind each one, and the questions to ask before paying a fee.
a futures evaluation is measured in contracts and dollars, so position size is quantised - you cannot halve a two-contract position without going to one.
the drawdown mechanism matters more than the headline number: a trailing threshold that follows intraday equity is far tighter than the same figure measured at end of day.
the daily loss limit ends more attempts than the profit target does, because it fires on normal variance rather than on a bad plan.
total cost is fee plus platform and market-data subscriptions plus any activation charge - a cheap evaluation on an expensive data feed is not cheap.
payout terms on the funded account, not the evaluation rules, decide whether a pass becomes income.
why futures firms are not forex firms in a different wrapper

the two product categories have converged in marketing language and diverged in mechanics. a forex evaluation usually states a percentage profit target, a percentage maximum loss, and a leverage cap on currency pairs. a futures evaluation states a dollar target, a dollar drawdown, and a contract limit per instrument. the first is scale-free; the second is not.

that difference has consequences that reach every decision a trader makes. on a percentage-based account, doubling the balance doubles both the target and the room, and the plan is unchanged. on a contract-based account, doubling the balance doubles the number of contracts permitted but does not double the number of contracts the market will tolerate at a given stop distance - a point that matters most on the index futures that dominate the category, where the contract's tick value is fixed and large.

there is also a structural difference in what the firm is selling. futures evaluations are generally cheaper to buy and shorter to complete than forex evaluations, and they typically carry a monthly or one-off fee rather than a subscription with an unlimited-tries clause. that changes the economics of failure: a reset on a cheap evaluation is a small purchase, which encourages a second attempt rather than a rethink. the traders who do well in this category are the ones who treat the first attempt as the only one, and size accordingly.

the instruments themselves impose a session. most futures contracts trade nearly around the clock but have a thin overnight book and a defined settlement. a plan built on the new york cash session behaves differently from a plan that holds through the asian session, and the drawdown mechanism will price that difference whether or not the trader has noticed it.
percentage rules and dollar rules are different products, not two labels on the same account.

none of that makes one category better. it makes them non-substitutable. a trader with a currency strategy and a part-time schedule is usually better served by a percentage evaluation with a static drawdown. a trader who already reads order flow on an index future, and who wants a fast, cheap evaluation with a clear dollar stop, is usually better served here.

the single most useful thing to understand before comparing futures firms is that a position is a whole number of contracts, and each contract has a fixed dollar value per tick. that makes risk per trade a multiplication problem rather than a percentage decision.

take a contract whose tick is worth a fixed dollar amount and whose stop is a fixed number of ticks. risk per trade is contracts multiplied by ticks multiplied by tick value. if the plan permits a maximum loss per trade, the number of contracts is that maximum divided by the tick cost of the stop. the result is rarely a round number, and it must be rounded down - always down, because rounding up converts a plan that fits the drawdown into one that does not.

three consequences follow. first, small accounts are effectively forced into one-contract positions on the larger index contracts, which means the stop distance, not the account size, determines risk. a one-contract position with a wide stop can risk more than a three-contract position with a tight one, so "one contract" is not a proxy for "small risk".

second, micro contracts change the arithmetic without changing the strategy. a micro version of the same instrument carries a fraction of the tick value, which allows a trader to take a stop of the same tick distance at a tenth of the dollar risk. for an evaluation, that is the difference between a plan that fits and a plan that does not - and it is the reason many experienced futures traders run micros during the evaluation and full-size contracts only after funding.

third, the contract limit in the rules is a ceiling, not a target. a firm that permits a large number of contracts is not inviting that size; it is setting the point at which the account is closed for breaching. the correct contract count is derived from the drawdown and the stop, and it is usually far below the ceiling.

write the number down before the first trade of the evaluation: instrument, tick value, stop in ticks, dollars at risk at one contract, and the maximum contracts the drawdown permits. that single line of arithmetic governs the entire attempt, and it does not change because the account is up or down.

drawdown is where futures firms differ most, and where the marketing is least informative. three mechanisms are in common use, and the same headline figure produces very different accounts under each.

an intraday trailing threshold is the harshest of the three because it converts unrealised profit into a liability. a trader who is up on the day and gives it back is not merely flat - the floor has risen behind them, and the retracement is measured against a peak that no longer exists. this is the mechanism that produces the familiar complaint about being stopped out of a profitable account.

end-of-day trailing is meaningfully gentler without being generous. the floor locks in at settlement, so a spike that reverses within the session costs the profit but not the account. the trader still cannot give back a completed day's gain, which imposes a real constraint on holding through the close.

a static threshold is the most forgiving and the least common in this category. the floor never moves, so the account's fragility is fixed at the start and profit cannot make it worse. the trade-off is that the initial buffer is usually smaller as a percentage, because the firm is carrying more risk on a structure that never tightens.

comparing two firms on the headline drawdown number alone is therefore meaningless. a large number attached to an intraday trailing mechanism can be tighter in practice than a smaller number attached to a static one, particularly for a strategy that holds winners through retracements. read the mechanism first, then the number, then the interaction with the daily limit.
the same profit path touches three different floors. the mechanism, not the headline number, decides survival.

there is one more clause worth locating in the terms: whether the threshold applies to realised or unrealised profit, and whether it applies during the overnight session. a mechanism described as end-of-day trailing but calculated on the highest unrealised equity of the day is, in practice, intraday trailing with a delay.

most attempts do not fail on the maximum loss. they fail on the daily limit, because the daily limit is calibrated to a normal bad day rather than to a catastrophic one, and normal bad days are common.

the arithmetic is unforgiving in a specific way. suppose the daily limit is a fraction of the maximum loss - the usual arrangement. that fraction defines how many losing trades a session can absorb at the plan's risk per trade. if risk per trade is a fifth of the daily limit, five consecutive losses close the session; if it is half, two do. both numbers sound survivable until the trader remembers that a 45% win rate produces five-loss runs regularly over a few hundred trades.

two design decisions follow. the first is that risk per trade should be derived from the daily limit as well as from the maximum loss, and the smaller of the two answers should govern. the second is that the session should have a hard trade cap independent of the dollar limit, because the dollar limit is measured by the firm's server and the trade cap is measured by the trader's discipline - and only one of those is under the trader's control.

there is also a definitional trap. daily loss limits are usually calculated from the day's starting balance or equity, and the day's start is defined by the firm's server time, not the trader's. a position opened late in the trader's evening may belong to the next trading day for the purposes of the limit. traders who trade the overnight session discover this the expensive way: two positions that feel like one day's risk are counted against two days' limits, and the second day starts with a deficit the trader did not know they had created.

the remedy is to establish the server's day boundary before the first trade and to build the trading day around it. if the boundary falls in the middle of the trader's session, the session should be split or shortened rather than run through it. this is not a detail; it is the difference between a limit that protects the account and a limit that surprises it.

a final point on the interaction with trailing drawdown: on an intraday trailing account, a day that begins after a strong previous day starts with a higher floor, so the same dollar loss is a larger fraction of the remaining room. the daily limit is static, the floor is not, and the two should be recomputed together each morning rather than assumed to be constants.
the profit target on a futures evaluation is usually expressed in dollars and is often modest relative to the drawdown - a ratio that looks generous until the contract arithmetic is applied.

take a target and a maximum loss where the target is a fraction of the loss limit. to reach the target at a given risk per trade, the trader needs a certain number of trades at positive expectation. if risk per trade is set by the drawdown survivability rule, that number of trades is large, and the calendar is long. if risk per trade is set by the target, the number is small and the account's survival probability falls sharply. the tension between those two calculations is the entire discipline of an evaluation.

minimum trading days are a separate constraint and usually a mild one. where they exist, they prevent a single-day pass, which is a sensible protection for the firm and a useful discipline for the trader. where they do not, a trader can pass in two sessions and then discover that the funded account's payout conditions assume a longer record - the minimum-day requirement has not disappeared, it has moved to the payout stage.

consistency rules appear in this category in two forms: a cap on the best day's share of total profit, and a cap on a single day's profit in absolute terms. the first is a ratio and constrains the shape of the profit; the second is a ceiling and constrains the size of any one day. a ratio of around a third means total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day before a full withdrawal is allowed, which is straightforward arithmetic and easy to violate with one good session.

the practical response is a daily profit cap set well below the consistency threshold, applied from the first day of the evaluation rather than at the payout request. a trader who reaches the target in one dominant day has passed the evaluation and created a payout problem at the same time, and the payout problem is the one that costs money.

where a firm publishes no consistency rule at all, the absence is worth verifying rather than celebrating. it sometimes means the rule lives in the funded terms rather than the evaluation terms, which is precisely where a trader is least likely to look before paying.
the headline fee is the smallest part of the cost of a futures evaluation, and comparing firms on that number alone produces reliably bad decisions.

the pattern that matters is the ratio of recurring cost to expected time. a monthly fee on an evaluation that takes four months costs four times the advertised figure, and a plan that takes four months is usually a plan that is being traded too conservatively for the target. the correct comparison is total cost to funding, not fee at signup.

commission per contract deserves separate attention because it is the one cost that scales with the strategy rather than the calendar. a plan that takes six trades a day at two contracts pays twelve round-turn commissions daily, and over sixty sessions that is 720 commissions - a number that can dwarf the evaluation fee. traders arriving from spot forex, where spreads are the only transaction cost, routinely underestimate this line.

data subscriptions are the quiet cost. exchange fees for real-time depth are usually passed through, and a trader who needs depth on two exchanges is paying for two feeds whether or not the evaluation is going well. before paying anything, establish which feeds the platform requires, whether the firm offers a bundled feed, and whether delayed data is sufficient for the strategy - for a swing plan it often is.

finally, price the retry. a firm with a generous retry policy is selling an option, and the option has value only if the second attempt is genuinely different from the first. a trader who resets with the same size and the same stop distance has bought the same outcome at a higher price. the retry should be budgeted as part of the plan, and the plan should change with it.

most published comparisons rank firms on account size and fee. those are the two numbers that matter least once an account is live. the following seven criteria are the ones that change outcomes, roughly in order of importance.

one: the drawdown mechanism, read precisely. intraday trailing, end-of-day trailing or static, measured on equity or balance, and applied during which sessions. this single clause dominates everything else, because it determines whether the plan's winners are permitted to breathe.

two: the daily limit relative to the maximum loss. a daily limit that is a small fraction of the total forces a low risk per trade and a long calendar. a large fraction permits more trades per session but raises the cost of one bad day. neither is wrong; the trader's plan has to match.

three: the funded account's drawdown. it is frequently tighter than the evaluation's, and it is the account where real money is at stake. a firm whose funded rules cannot accommodate the plan that passed the evaluation is selling a pass that cannot be used.

four: payout conditions and speed. minimum profitable days, profit threshold, consistency check, verification, and the interval between request and payment. a generous split paid in ninety days is worth less than a smaller split paid in five.

five: the third-party and automation clause. whether assistance is permitted on the evaluation and on the funded account are separate questions, and the funded answer is the one with money attached. where the terms are ambiguous, a written answer from support is the only reliable source.

six: platform and data routing. which platforms are supported, which exchanges are bundled, what a feed costs, and whether the trader's existing setup transfers without a new subscription. a firm that requires a platform the trader does not use has an unadvertised switching cost.

seven: the reproducibility of the terms. whether the current rules are published as a versioned document rather than a marketing page, and whether changes apply to existing accounts. a firm that revises terms mid-evaluation has transferred risk to the trader in a way the fee did not price.

ranking on those seven will usually produce a shorter list than ranking on fee and account size, and a list that is far more likely to survive contact with a funded account. the rules matrix lays out the comparison across firms, and the 2026 comparison covers the wider market including forex-side structures.
futures trading is platform-mediated in a way that spot forex is not, and the platform decision is effectively part of the firm decision.

the common arrangements are a dedicated futures platform with its own order engine, a retail multi-asset platform with a futures add-on, and a bridge into a charting and execution environment that many discretionary traders already use. each has a different cost structure and a different set of available order types, and the differences matter most for the stops.

order handling is where evaluations are quietly lost. a stop that is held on the platform's server behaves differently from a stop that is held locally on the trader's machine. if the connection drops - and it will - a local stop is not a stop. for an evaluation with a hard daily limit, that distinction is the difference between a planned loss and a breach, so the first question to ask about any platform is whether the protective orders sit on the server.

routing and fill quality are the second question. a firm that routes to a single liquidity provider during a thin session produces fills that a demonstration account on a different feed will not reproduce. a trader who has calibrated a stop distance on one feed and executes on another has calibrated against the wrong number, and the error appears as slippage on exactly the trades that matter.

the third question is the data. real-time exchange data usually carries a monthly fee, and the feed determines what the trader can see at the moments that count: the depth at the open, the book during a news release, the settlement print. a delayed feed is adequate for a plan with wide stops and inadequate for one that trades the first minutes of a session.

before paying for an evaluation, run the platform for a week on a demonstration account with the same feed and the same order types. measure the spread at the hours the plan trades, the average slippage on entry and exit, and whether the protective orders survive a deliberate disconnect. those three measurements are worth more than any comparison table, because they are the only ones taken on the trader's own setup.

one practical note: the platform subscription is often the same across firms, which means it is a constant rather than a differentiator. the differentiators are the feed bundle, the order handling, and whether the firm permits the platform's full order set during an evaluation. firms occasionally restrict bracket orders or automated exits on evaluation accounts, and a plan that depends on them should establish that before paying.
everything before funding is a qualifying round. the funded account is the product, and its payout mechanics are the specification.

the standard sequence is a minimum number of profitable trading days, a profit threshold before the first withdrawal, a consistency check on the profit being withdrawn, identity verification, and then a payment on a stated schedule. each step has a failure mode that has nothing to do with trading skill.

minimum profitable days are the most commonly missed condition, because they are satisfied by activity rather than by profit. a trader who reaches the threshold in nine sessions and needs fifteen has six sessions of obligation, and the temptation in those six is to trade for the sake of the count. the correct approach is to trade the plan at reduced size, accept whichever sessions produce a small profit, and treat the count as a calendar problem rather than a trading one.

the profit threshold before the first withdrawal is where the funded account's drawdown becomes relevant. profit that is not withdrawn sits in the account and can be given back, and on a trailing structure it also raises the floor behind the trader. a trader who builds a large unwithdrawn profit on an intraday trailing funded account has made the account more fragile, not less. the disciplined approach is to withdraw on the earliest permitted schedule at a size that keeps the account above its floor with room to spare.

cadence matters as much as size. a monthly cycle with a modest threshold produces a predictable income stream and a stable account; a quarterly cycle with a large threshold produces a larger single payment and a longer period of exposure. for a first funding, the monthly cycle is usually the better choice even where the split is less favourable, because the information gained from a completed payout cycle is worth more than the difference in percentage.

verification is administrative and should be finished before the first request rather than after it. identity documents, address confirmation, and any payment-method checks are routinely the cause of a delay that has nothing to do with the trading record. completing them in the first week of funding removes the only step in the sequence that the trader cannot influence later.
the arithmetic of a futures evaluation fits on one line, and it is worth deriving rather than copying from a table.

start from the drawdown. decide how many consecutive losses the plan should survive - for a discretionary plan with a win rate in the forties, eight to ten is a reasonable design target, because runs of that length occur within a few hundred trades. divide the available drawdown by that number to get the maximum dollar loss per trade.

then convert to contracts. divide the maximum dollar loss by the tick value of the stop distance. round down to a whole number, and if the answer is zero, the plan does not fit the contract at that account size - which is information worth having before paying a fee, not after.

then check the daily limit. multiply the dollar loss per trade by the number of losses the session should absorb, and compare it to the daily limit. if the session budget exceeds the limit, reduce the trade count or the size. if it is far below the limit, the plan is probably too conservative to finish inside a reasonable calendar, and the trader should consider a micro contract and a slightly larger size rather than a smaller one with the same stop.
the drawdown is a budget with three lines: per trade, per session, and a reserve that is never spent.

then check the target against the arithmetic. if risk per trade is fixed by survivability and the reward-to-risk ratio is known, expected value per trade follows, and the number of trades to reach the target follows from that. divide by the planned trades per week to get the calendar. if the calendar is longer than the trader is willing to fund - remembering the monthly data and platform costs - the plan needs a better ratio, not a bigger size.

the reserve is the part most plans omit. keeping a quarter of the drawdown untouched means the account can survive a sequence longer than the design case, which is exactly what a trailing mechanism punishes. it also means the trader has something to do after a bad week other than stop, which is a behavioural benefit as much as a financial one.

recalculate the whole line once a week, using the floor as it stands rather than the floor at the start. on a trailing account the floor moves, so the number of contracts that fitted at the beginning may not fit now. this is the single most common cause of a breach in the final third of an evaluation: a size chosen when the account had room, kept after the room had gone.
failures in this category cluster into five patterns, and each has a signature that can be recognised in advance.

breaching the daily limit on a normal day. the trader's risk per trade was set against the maximum loss and never checked against the daily limit, so a three-loss morning ends the attempt. the signature is a plan whose per-trade risk is a large fraction of the daily limit.

being stopped by a trailing floor after a good day. on an intraday trailing account, a winning session raises the floor and a normal retracement breaches it. the signature is a plan that holds positions through the afternoon after a strong morning.

oversizing after a drawdown. the trader is behind, the calendar is short, and the size goes up to recover. this converts a recoverable evaluation into a closed account, and it is the most reliably fatal of the five because it happens exactly when the account is least able to absorb it.

passing and then losing the funded account in the first fortnight. the evaluation's size is carried into a funded account with a tighter drawdown, and the first normal losing sequence ends it. the signature is no reduction in size at funding.

failing the payout conditions rather than the rules. the target was reached, but the minimum-day count, the consistency ratio or the verification step was not satisfied, so the profit cannot be withdrawn. the signature is a trader who read the evaluation page and not the funded terms.

all five share a common cause: a rule that was understood in principle and not converted into a number. the remedy is a written plan with the numbers filled in - contracts, stop in ticks, dollars at risk, session cap, weekly recalc - checked against the firm's actual terms rather than against a comparable firm's.
futures firms offer three routes to a larger position, and they are not equivalent.

the first is the scaling plan: the firm increases the account or the contract limit after a defined record of profitable payouts. this is the slowest and the most reliable, because it is judged on behaviour the firm can verify. it rewards a boring record of on-time withdrawals over a spectacular month, which is worth understanding before optimising for a single large result.

the second is combining accounts. many firms allow several evaluations to be run in parallel and their allocations to be combined for the purposes of size. this multiplies the fee and the data cost along with the size, and it multiplies the daily limit too, which is the part traders notice. what it does not multiply is the trader's attention, and a plan that requires monitoring four accounts at once is a different plan from the one that passed a single evaluation.

the third is copy trading between accounts, either across the trader's own accounts or through a third-party system. where the firm permits it, copying is an efficient way to apply one decision to several allocations. where the terms are silent, it is a compliance risk: a firm that later classifies copied positions as account management can void a payout, and the trader will have no route to appeal.

the prudent sequence is one account, one payout cycle, then a decision. a first funding that produces a completed withdrawal is worth more than three parallel evaluations, because it establishes the entire chain - trading, rules, verification, payment - rather than only the first link. traders who combine before completing a cycle are scaling an unverified process.

one structural note on scaling plans: they usually reward consistency of profit rather than size of profit, so the fastest route to a larger allocation is a smaller, steadier result repeated. a trader who produces one month at triple the threshold and then a breach has produced nothing the firm can scale, and has probably also broken a consistency ratio in the process.
thirty days is a realistic horizon for a futures evaluation at survivable size, and it divides into four weeks with different jobs.

week one: calibrate, do not perform. trade the plan at half the eventual size, cap the session at two trades, and record three numbers per trade: planned risk, realised risk including slippage, and the time in the trade. the purpose is to establish whether the stop distance the plan assumes is the stop distance the market delivers at the hours being traded. most plans are wrong about this by a meaningful margin, and week one is the cheapest place to find out.

week two: full size, tight session cap. if week one's realised risk matched the plan, move to the full contract count and keep the trade cap. if it did not, adjust the tick distance rather than the size, because the slippage is a property of the instrument and the session, not of the account.

week three: protect the buffer. by now the account is either ahead or behind. ahead, reduce size by a quarter and keep the target in sight; the risk of the final third is giving back a good evaluation, not failing to finish. behind, keep the size and move the calendar, and do not touch the daily limit to catch up.

week four: finish or extend deliberately. review the four numbers - trades, expectation per trade, worst drawdown, distance to target - and decide. a plan on pace continues. a plan behind on pace with a healthy expectation extends. a plan with negative expectation stops, because another fortnight of the same process produces the same result at a higher cost.

two rules make the plan robust across all four weeks. the first is that size is recalculated from the current floor every monday, not inherited from the start. the second is that no position is opened in the final hour of the trading day defined by the firm's server, because that is where the day-boundary and trailing-floor traps live.

if the evaluation is being traded on the trader's behalf by a passing service, the same four weeks apply with one addition: confirm in writing that the firm's terms permit third-party trading on both the evaluation and the funded account. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, and declines firms whose terms forbid it - the passing services guide explains what to check, and the scam guide covers the failure modes on the other side of that market.

there is no single answer, because the best firm is the one whose drawdown mechanism and funded terms match the plan being traded. a static or end-of-day structure suits a plan that holds winners; an intraday trailing structure does not. rank candidates on the drawdown mechanism, the daily limit relative to the maximum loss, and the funded account's conditions before comparing fees.

it is tighter, not automatically worse. a trailing floor follows peak equity, so open profit raises the failure point and a retracement can breach from a winning position. a static floor never moves, which is more forgiving but usually comes with a smaller starting buffer as a percentage of the account.

derive it: divide the maximum dollar loss per trade by the tick value of the stop distance, then round down. check the result against the daily limit and against the firm's contract ceiling. if the answer is zero, the plan does not fit that contract at that account size - use a micro contract or a smaller account.
why do most futures evaluations fail on the daily limit?

because the daily limit is calibrated to a normal bad day and normal bad days are common. if risk per trade is a large fraction of the daily limit, three ordinary losses close the session. setting risk per trade from the daily limit as well as the maximum loss, and capping trades per session, removes most of that failure mode.

fee plus platform subscription plus market data plus commission per round turn, plus any activation charge on funding. a monthly fee on a four-month attempt costs four times the headline figure, and commission on an active plan can exceed the fee entirely. compare total cost to funding rather than cost at signup.

most permit it, with conditions: reduced size over the settlement window, no holding through certain news events, and a daily limit that resets on the firm's server time rather than the trader's. the weekend holding guide covers the gap arithmetic for positions held across a close.

a cap on how much of the total profit can come from one day, usually expressed as a share of around a third. it means total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day before a full withdrawal. cap daily profit well below the threshold from day one rather than discovering the ratio at the payout request.

often yes. a micro carries a fraction of the tick value, which lets a trader keep the stop distance the strategy needs while risking a fraction of the dollars. many experienced futures traders run micros during evaluation and full-size contracts only after funding.

usually permitted, and usually a mistake before the first payout cycle is complete. parallel accounts multiply the fee, the data cost and the daily limit, but not the trader's attention. complete one funding and one withdrawal before combining allocations.
what happens if i pass and then breach the funded account?

the allocation is typically closed and the fee is not refunded. funded drawdowns are frequently tighter than evaluation drawdowns, so the correct response at funding is to halve the evaluation's size for the first fortnight, complete verification, and only then scale back toward the evaluation plan.

only where the firm's terms permit third-party trading, and that must be checked separately for the evaluation and the funded account. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation regardless of stage or size, covers retries, and declines firms whose terms prohibit it.

four to eight weeks at survivable size is realistic for most plans. faster passes are possible with larger size and a correspondingly lower survival probability. on a monthly-fee structure, the calendar is a real cost, so a plan that needs four months is usually a plan that needs a better reward-to-risk ratio rather than more time.
