a funded certificate is the only evidence in this market that is hard to fake and easy to check, which is why it is the claim worth building a page around. it is also narrower than it looks, and a client who understands the limits of the evidence makes a better decision than one who takes the page at face value.

what a certificate proves: that an evaluation on that firm, at that account size, reached its target and completed its verification stage on the date shown. that is a genuine achievement and it is not something a screenshot of a profitable trading account can substitute for - a trading account shows outcomes, a certificate shows that a specific rulebook was satisfied, including the loss limits that a profitable account history may have breached repeatedly.

what it does not prove: that the same result will repeat next month, that the funded account was traded profitably afterwards, or that the trader behind it has an edge that survives a change of market regime. a certificate is evidence of a process applied successfully once. anyone claiming more than that from a certificate is overstating, including this page.
ask for the certificate, not a testimonial. a screenshot of a dashboard with the account number visible and the firm's branding is a start; a pdf certificate issued by the firm is better.

match the account size and date. a certificate for a $25,000 account is not evidence of work on a $200,000 one, and a certificate from two years ago predates at least one rulebook revision at most firms.
check the firm's rules on third-party trading. a pass obtained in a way the firm prohibits is a liability, not an asset, because the funded account can be withdrawn afterwards.
ask what happens on failure, in writing. the retry terms matter more than the pass count, since the failure case is the one where a client has no leverage.
look for absent claims. no guaranteed pass, no "proprietary algorithm", no profit-share arrangement that depends on the client never reading the small print.

every number on a results page depends on the denominator, and providers choose it. a rate calculated against evaluations started will always look worse than one calculated against enquiries received, and a provider can move between the two definitions without saying so. the honest framing is to state the definition alongside the number, which is why the figures here name the period and the base.

there is a second distortion worth naming: survivorship in the sample. a service that quietly stops counting clients who abandoned an attempt, or who passed on a second firm after failing the first, reports a rate that describes a filtered population rather than its own work. asking directly how abandoned attempts are counted is a better use of a question than asking for the headline rate, and the answer is usually more informative.

they were all obtained by trading a plan rather than by pressing for a fast finish, and most took between two and four weeks. the account sizes vary because clients choose sizes they can afford rather than sizes that look impressive, and the firms vary because the rulebook, not the brand, determines which assignment is sensible at a given moment.

the common thread worth taking from the page is not any single result but the shape of the process behind them: a rulebook read carefully, four numbers written on a card, constant risk per trade, and a hard stop at eighty percent of the daily budget. that process is repeatable by a disciplined trader working alone, and this page exists partly to show what it produces rather than to suggest it cannot be done without help.

apply the same five checks to every provider you consider, including this one, and prefer the provider that answers the awkward questions plainly. the awkward questions are always the same: what happens when an evaluation fails, what the refund and retry terms really cover, whether the firm permits the arrangement, and what evidence exists beyond a testimonial. a provider that answers all four in a single reply is rare enough to be worth shortlisting, and a provider that answers none of them has told you something useful too.

it is also worth asking what happens to a certificate if the firm later revokes the account. firms do close accounts after the fact for rule breaches discovered in review, and a results page that has never removed an entry has probably never checked. the honest position is that a certificate proves a pass on a date, and that later events at the firm are outside anyone's control.

one further check that costs nothing: ask which firms the provider will not trade, and why. a provider with no refusals either has not read the rulebooks or is willing to accept terms its clients will bear the cost of. the refusals are usually the most informative sentence in the entire reply.

treat that answer as the shortlist filter it is. a provider that names the firms it will not touch, and gives a rulebook reason, has demonstrated the one thing a results page cannot: that it reads the terms before accepting money.
ask it of this page too. the firms not traded here are named where the reason is a rulebook position, and the reason is given in a sentence rather than a slogan.

a prop firm evaluation is a rules problem wearing the costume of a trading problem. this guide takes it apart: the four constraints that end most attempts, the sizing arithmetic that keeps an account alive, how to pace a two-phase structure, and what changes at payout.
almost every failed evaluation breaches the daily loss limit or a trailing floor in a single session.
size against the loss limit, not the profit target - a third of the daily budget per trade is the workable ceiling.
drawdown type matters more than target size: static beats end-of-day trailing, which beats intraday trailing.
a pass is not a payout; funded accounts have a second rulebook covering consistency, minimum days and kyc.

the marketing framing is that a prop firm evaluation tests whether you can trade. the operational reality is narrower: it tests whether you can produce a specific return, inside a specific window, without ever breaching a loss threshold. those are related skills, but they are not the same skill, and the difference explains why experienced traders fail evaluations that beginners occasionally pass.

a trader with ten years of discretionary experience typically has a feel for position size built on personal accounts, where the consequence of a bad week is a smaller balance and time to recover. an evaluation removes that recovery option. a $100,000 account with a 5% daily loss limit and a 10% maximum loss is a machine with two independent failure conditions, and a style built on surviving drawdowns by waiting is structurally incompatible with a floor that moves.

what the evaluation is genuinely testing is constraint management. can you calculate the risk that the rulebook permits? can you take that risk repeatedly without escalating after a loss? can you stop for the day when the budget is spent, even when an obvious setup appears ten minutes later? can you resist accelerating as the target approaches? those questions are mechanical, and they have mechanical answers, which is why a structured process outperforms a good market view inside an evaluation and underperforms it outside one.

two consequences follow, and they are worth internalising before reading the rest of this guide. first, the strategy that passes an evaluation is usually not the strategy a trader wants to run on a funded account - it is more conservative, more patient and less profitable per unit of risk. second, the constraint set itself is the biggest variable: two firms with identical headline targets produce very different pass rates depending on how their loss limits behave. choosing the firm is a risk decision, not an administrative one.
across thousands of evaluations, failures cluster around four rules. everything else - instrument restrictions, time windows, platform quirks - matters, but these four do the damage.

the maximum loss permitted in a single trading day, resetting each morning. on forex evaluations it is usually 5%, on futures evaluations it is a dollar threshold. the number that matters is not the percentage but the basis : a limit measured on equity including floating positions is breached by an open trade that is temporarily deep in the red, even if it recovers before the close. a limit measured on closed balance only counts realised losses. the first is roughly twice as strict in practice, at the same headline figure.

why it ends so many attempts: a loss is emotionally uncomfortable, and the natural response is to take a slightly larger position to recover it before the day ends. that single decision converts a manageable −1% day into a −5% day. the rule does not fail traders; it catches the response to a small failure.
the total drawdown permitted before the account fails. there are three behaviours and they are not interchangeable.

static. the failure level never moves. on a $100,000 account with a 10% limit, it stays at $90,000 whether the balance is $100,000 or $115,000. every dollar of profit is real progress with no side effect.
end-of-day trailing. the failure level rises with profit closed at the end of each session. bank $4,000 and the floor becomes $94,000. intraday noise does not move it.

intraday trailing. the failure level follows unrealised equity. a position that is $4,000 in profit and then retraces to $1,000 has already moved the floor, leaving the account $3,000 above failure with only $1,000 of realised profit on the books.

the third behaviour produces failures that look inexplicable when a trader reviews their own p l: no losing trade was taken, and the account still ended. the floor simply outran the balance. any plan built for an intraday trailing account must reduce size as profit accumulates, which is the opposite of the instinct that develops on a static account.
the same equity curve under three drawdown models - only one of them leaves the buffer intact at the top.

typically four to ten days before an evaluation can be verified. this rule rarely ends an account but routinely delays funding, and it has a second-order effect that catches traders out: having reached the target on day three of a ten-day requirement, the account must survive seven more days of trading to qualify. seven days at target is more exposure than most plans budget for, and a common failure is giving back enough profit to drop below target while waiting.
the right approach is to reach the target later than the minimum and finish on the final required day, so there is no waiting period at all. the plan's pace is set by the day count, not by ambition.

a cap on how much of total profit can come from a single day, usually 30%. it is applied at payout by most firms and during the evaluation by a few. the arithmetic is unforgiving: a $6,000 best day under a 30% rule requires $20,000 of total profit, so an account that looks finished can still be unable to withdraw.
consistency is covered in more depth below and in the dedicated consistency rule guide , because it is the rule most likely to turn a pass into a disappointment.

firm selection is where most of the outcome is decided, and it is usually made on the wrong criteria - account size and split percentage, both of which matter far less than the structure of the loss limits.

first, the drawdown type. a static floor gives a plan room; an intraday trailing floor takes it away as profit accumulates. if two firms offer the same target and the same daily limit, the static one is the easier assignment, and it is not close.
second, the daily limit basis. equity-based limits are stricter than balance-based ones. this detail is rarely in a comparison table and almost always in the client agreement.
third, consistency. a payout-stage rule can be managed by adding ordinary winning days before a withdrawal. an evaluation-stage rule constrains the pace from the first session.
fourth, time limits. no overall window is better than thirty days, because a flat week costs time rather than the account.

fifth, payout reliability. a firm that pays slowly is a worse home for a funded account than a firm with a slightly less generous split that pays weekly. no firm publishes a withdrawal-reliability column, which is why community reporting matters here more than marketing.

the 2026 comparison and the rules matrix cover these criteria firm by firm. the practical summary is that the easiest structures to pass have a single phase, a static floor, no consistency rule and no time limit - and that the hardest are intraday trailing futures evaluations with a payout-stage consistency rule and a thirty-day window.

sizing is where the evaluation is won or lost, and the rule is simpler than most traders expect: risk a third of the daily loss budget per trade at most, and stop for the day once roughly 80% of the budget has been spent.

on a $100,000 account with a 5% daily limit, the budget is $5,000. a third is $1,650. three consecutive losses at that size cost $4,950 - enough to make the day uncomfortable, not enough to end the account. on a $25,000 account the same calculation gives a budget of $1,250 and a per-trade ceiling of about $410, which is small enough that a normal losing streak is survivable and large enough that reaching the target is possible.
dividing the daily limit into thirds keeps an ordinary losing streak from becoming a failure.

two refinements matter. first, the 80% stop exists to absorb slippage on the closing trade of a losing day; it is not headroom for another setup. second, the profit target should never determine size. a trader who calculates the position needed to reach the target fastest is solving for variance, not for survival, and the daily limit will find them.
target and drawdown are one equation: the second constrains the first.

a useful sanity check before starting: at the planned risk per trade and an average reward-to-risk of about 1.8:1, how many net winning trades does the target require? on the $100,000 example, each win at $1,650 risk produces roughly $2,970, so a $10,000 target needs about nine more wins than losses. if that number implies more trading days than the firm's window allows, the plan is wrong for that firm - not the trader.
two-phase forex evaluations have a particular rhythm, and following it removes most of the risk that comes from impatience.

week one: build distance from the floor. the objective is not progress toward the target but a cushion that makes the second week survivable. one or two setups per session, no averaging into losers, no trading in the first thirty minutes if spreads are wide. a realistic outcome is $2,000 to $3,500 of profit on a $100,000 account, or a small loss with the daily budget barely touched. both are acceptable.

week two: convert the cushion. with a cushion in place, the same per-trade risk produces a larger share of the target because a losing sequence no longer threatens the maximum loss. sessions can lengthen slightly. this is the phase where the target is actually reached, in increments rather than in one decision.

phase two: smaller target, tighter discipline. verification phases usually have a smaller target and the same limits, which sounds like relief and behaves like a trap. one oversized attempt erases the work of the previous two weeks. risk per trade is typically reduced by a quarter for phase two and the profit is taken in smaller pieces.

the last 20%: reduce, do not accelerate. the instinct near the finish is to add size and close the gap quickly. the opposite is correct. size comes down, sessions shorten, and the remaining ground is covered in increments that cannot breach anything. this is especially true on trailing structures, where a late drawdown is fatal in a way it would not have been at the start.

if a firm enforces a 30% best-day rule, your largest profitable day must be no more than 30% of total profit at the time of the payout request. that means total profit must be at least 3.33 times your best day.
one dominant day can fail a consistency check even when the profit target is met.

the practical response is to cap individual days during the evaluation at roughly a third of the target, even when the firm only enforces consistency at payout. that habit makes the funded phase mechanical instead of a scramble to add ordinary days after the fact. the full arithmetic, including worked examples with real numbers, is in the dedicated guide .
oversizing after a losing morning. the recovery trade is the single most expensive habit in evaluation trading.
not recalculating the trailing floor. on a trailing account, the failure level after a strong session is not the level from yesterday.
sprinting to the target. the fastest route to the target is also the fastest route to the daily limit.
waiting on a minimum day requirement at target. reaching the target early creates exposure you did not budget.
trading restricted instruments. a permitted list is a rule, not a suggestion, and a breach voids the pass.
holding through a news window. firms define these differently and enforce them strictly.
treating floating profit as banked. targets require closed profit on almost every platform.
day-trading the platform, not the plan. checking equity every few minutes produces decisions the plan did not authorise.
choosing the firm by split percentage. a generous split on a structure you cannot pass is worth nothing.
funding is the end of the evaluation and the start of a second rulebook. most firms relax the daily limit on a funded account but add conditions around withdrawals.
six checkpoints stand between a passed evaluation and a first withdrawal.

the sequence is consistent across firms: funded credentials, a minimum number of trading days, a profit threshold, a consistency check, kyc, then the withdrawal itself. each is a separate gate. a trader who meets the profit threshold but has a dominant best day will not be paid until the distribution changes; a trader who meets both but has not completed kyc will wait.
the payout process guide covers the sequence step by step, including the delays that account for most first-withdrawal frustration.

numbers in a guide are easier to trust when they are attached to a sequence. here is how a $100,000 two-phase forex evaluation is paced under a standard 10% target, 5% daily limit (measured on equity), 10% static maximum loss and four-day minimum, with risk capped at $1,600 per trade.
session 1 - +$820. two setups, one winner, one scratch. the failure floor is 8.2% away. nothing notable, which is the objective: the first session exists to establish the routine, not the profit.

session 2 - −$430. one loss taken at the planned size, then the day is closed early because the second setup did not meet the plan's conditions. the log records a losing day inside the budget, which is a normal and expected outcome.
session 3 - +$1,540. the best session so far, and deliberately not repeated at larger size the next day. on a 5% daily limit this day used under a third of the budget.

sessions 4-6 - +$2,180 combined. three ordinary winning sessions, each capped so no single day becomes an outsized share of total profit. target completion reaches 45%. the failure floor has not moved because the drawdown is static.

session 7 - flat. three trades, two small wins, one small loss. logged as flat. the temptation at this point is to force a result because progress stalled; the plan does not permit it, and the next session is treated as a fresh budget rather than a correction.
sessions 8-9 - +$3,150 combined. two stronger sessions taking the total to $7,260, or 73% of target. risk per trade is reduced by a quarter from this point.

sessions 10-12 - +$3,020 combined. the target is cleared on session 12 at $10,280. because the firm requires four minimum trading days and none of the sessions breached the daily limit, verification completes immediately and phase two begins.

phase two. target $5,000 with the same limits. risk per trade is cut to $1,200 and the pace is intentionally slower: nine sessions rather than five. total elapsed time across both phases: twenty-one trading days. total daily-budget utilisation never exceeded 42% of the limit on any single session.

what the sequence demonstrates: no session was remarkable, one was flat, two were losing, and the evaluation still completed in three weeks with the maximum-loss floor never closer than 6% away. pace, not performance, is what produced the pass.

the mechanics in this guide are stable; the numbers attached to them are not. a target of 8% with a 5% daily limit and a static floor behaves almost identically across firms. the same target with an intraday trailing floor, a payout-stage consistency rule and a thirty-day window behaves like a different product entirely, and no amount of pacing adjusts for it. that is why the firm decision precedes the plan.
there are three honest options, and which is right depends on where your failures actually come from.

do it yourself if your problem is strategy rather than constraint management, or if you want to build the skill of passing evaluations. the guides here are written to make that possible, and many readers never contact us.
use a signal service or course only if the gap is market selection. it will not help with a daily limit, and it will not take responsibility for the outcome of the evaluation.

use a passing service if you can trade but keep breaching one specific rule. the trade is money for execution: a flat $220 fee with retries covered, a funded login in your name, and no profit split. that is what elitepropx sells, and the passed challenges page shows the documentation behind it.

one check before you buy anything: read your firm's terms on third-party trading. some prohibit it, some restrict account sharing, and enforcement can arrive after funding. that risk belongs to the account holder, and no service can remove it.
the questions below are the ones that come up most often in relation to this guide. each answer is written to be useful on its own, without requiring the rest of the article.
how long does it take to pass a prop firm challenge?

on a two-phase forex evaluation with a 10% target and a 5% daily limit, roughly sixteen to twenty trading days is a realistic pace. futures evaluations with trailing thresholds and minimum day requirements typically run two to four weeks. anything promising a fixed calendar date is guessing.

breaching the daily loss limit on a single oversized position, usually after an earlier loss. it is a behavioural failure rather than a market failure, and it is why a fixed per-trade risk cap matters more than any trading edge.

a static floor never moves. a trailing floor follows profit upward and shrinks the cushion. end-of-day trailing updates on closed profit; intraday trailing follows unrealised equity, which makes it the strictest of the three.

only if the firm's rules support it. a 10% target with a 5% daily limit cannot be reached in five days without gambling, and many firms require a minimum number of trading days regardless. where a fast pass is claimed, the firm is usually one with generous rules or the result is luck.
should i take a larger account or a safer firm?

safer firm first. a $50,000 evaluation at a firm with a static floor and no consistency rule is more likely to produce a funded account than a $200,000 evaluation with an intraday trailing threshold, and the funded account can be scaled later.

you need a positive-expectancy approach and disciplined sizing. a modest edge executed at a third of the daily budget passes comfortably; a large edge executed at the full budget often fails, because the variance that comes with size hits the limit before the edge shows up.
the firm's reset policy applies, which varies from a free reset to a full new challenge fee. with a passing service, the retry is covered by the flat fee, though the firm's own charge is separate.
how much should i risk per trade in an evaluation?

no more than a third of the daily loss limit, and stop for the day once about 80% of the budget has been spent. that ceiling keeps three consecutive losses survivable, which is the property that matters most across a multi-week evaluation.

it depends on the firm. some prohibit third-party trading explicitly, others restrict account sharing, and some are silent. check your firm's current terms and understand that enforcement can happen after funding.

the first week of an evaluation is where the attempt is usually won or lost, and almost none of it involves trading. a trader who spends the first week building the arithmetic and the routine starts the second week with an advantage that compound interest cannot buy: they know exactly how much room they have at every moment.

read it once for the numbers and once for the exceptions. the numbers are the target, the daily loss, the maximum loss and the minimum days. the exceptions are what make the challenge hard: what counts as a trading day, whether a position held into the next session counts twice, whether the daily limit resets at midnight server time or at the broker's close, and whether the maximum loss trails. almost every dispute between a trader and a firm traces back to an exception read only once.

the card carries the four numbers, dated. the sheet is a simple table with a row per session: date, starting equity, daily budget remaining, number of trades, realised result, and whether any rule was broken. the sheet is not a diary; it is an instrument panel, and it takes ninety seconds a day to maintain. traders who keep it can answer questions about their own behaviour that traders who do not can only guess at.

place three or four trades on a demo account on the same platform, purely to confirm that position sizing, stop placement and the platform's equity display behave as expected. this is not strategy testing; it is checking that the instrument panel reads correctly. a trader who discovers on day nine that their platform shows balance rather than equity has been flying on the wrong gauge.

write the closing conditions in advance: a profit threshold at which you stop, a loss threshold at which you stop, and a time at which you stop regardless of either. the third condition is the one traders omit, and it is the one that prevents a session drifting into an unplanned third trade at the wrong hour. a session with a defined end is a session that can be reviewed.

the first live session should be at half the planned risk, with the explicit purpose of confirming that the process works when money is involved rather than of making progress toward the target. half-size sessions rarely make the difference between passing and failing, and they frequently reveal the small frictions - order entry, spread widening at the open, a stop that sits one tick from a round number - that cost far more later.
once a week, twenty minutes, five questions. the audit is not a performance review; it is a check that the challenge is still being solved as a rules problem rather than as a trading problem.
is risk per trade within 10% of the plan? a drift here invalidates every other calculation, including the daily budget.
how many rule violations, and which rules? zero is the target. one is a coaching note. two of the same is a structural problem.
what is the current distance to the failure level? if it has shrunk for two consecutive weeks, size must come down before the next session.
did any session end without a defined closing condition being met? that is the signature of drift, and it usually precedes a breach by about a week.
is the pace still deliberate? if the target is close and the temptation to press is strong, the answer is to halve risk rather than to maintain it.

the value of the audit is that it converts a vague sense of how the attempt is going into five numbers, and numbers can be acted on. a trader who cannot answer question three without opening the platform is already relying on memory for the one figure that decides whether the next trade is affordable.

it is also worth writing down what a good week looks like before it happens, in numbers: so many sessions, so many trades, a defined result range and zero violations. a week judged against a written standard is reviewable; a week judged against how it felt is not, and feeling is the variable that rules are meant to replace.

the response is always the same, and it is always reduction rather than effort: cut size, shorten sessions, narrow the instrument set, and remove the setups that produced the violations. nothing in a prop firm evaluation is improved by trying harder. the rules are fixed, the target is fixed, and the only variables the trader controls are exposure and frequency - both of which should move down when the evidence says the process has slipped.

two reductions cover most situations. halving risk per trade doubles the number of consecutive losses required to reach the daily limit, and cutting the session in half removes the tired trades that produce violations without removing the setups that produce the target. neither change requires a new strategy, which is exactly why both are usable mid-attempt, when changing strategy is the worst available option.

both changes are reversible. if the audit shows three clean weeks and a stable risk figure, risk can go back to plan and sessions can lengthen again. the asymmetry is deliberate: the cost of a smaller position is a slightly slower pass, and the cost of a larger one is the attempt itself, so the error to make is always in the same direction.

applied consistently, those two levers turn an evaluation from a test of conviction into a test of bookkeeping, which is a far easier thing to pass and a far more useful thing to be good at once the account is funded.

the best firm for a beginner is almost never the one with the largest advertised payout. it is the one whose rules you can actually satisfy on the worst week of your first month, at a fee you can afford to lose twice. this guide sets out the four rules that end most beginner accounts, how to choose an account size that gives the plan room to work, and a ninety-day path that gets to a first payout without pretending the first evaluation will go smoothly.
beginner accounts fail on rules, not on analysis: the daily loss limit, the trailing threshold, consistency at payout and the news window account for most closures.
choose the smallest account that produces a meaningful payout, not the largest you can finance. the percentage rules are the same at every size.
total cost is fee times expected attempts. a firm with a generous reset policy is cheaper than a firm with a lower fee and no resets.
instant funding and one-phase evaluations look simpler and are usually stricter on the rules that actually matter.
budget for two evaluations, treat the first as tuition, and plan the funded phase before you start.

search results for this topic are dominated by lists that rank firms on profit target and payout ceiling. both numbers are chosen by the firm's marketing department, and both are close to irrelevant for a trader in their first year.

what actually determines whether a beginner gets funded is the interaction between three variables: the difficulty of the rulebook, the size of the account relative to the trader's risk model, and the cost of a failed attempt. a firm with a modest target and a static drawdown is easier for a beginner than a firm with a larger target and a trailing threshold, even though the second firm's marketing is more impressive. a $100,000 account is harder to pass than a $25,000 account at the same discipline, because fixed trading costs consume a larger share of a smaller target - but the opposite is also true if the smaller account forces position sizes so small that the plan cannot express its edge.

the honest framing is that a first evaluation is a paid test of a process, not an investment. the buyer is purchasing information: does this plan survive a rulebook for a few weeks without breaking a limit? framed that way, the criteria for a first firm change completely. the cheapest useful test wins, provided the firm pays out reliably and its rules are documented well enough to plan around.

that reframing also kills the most common beginner mistake, which is financing the largest account the budget allows because "the payout is bigger". the payout is bigger, the fee is bigger, and the probability of passing is not - the percentage rules are identical. the efficient path is to prove the plan on a small account, then scale with the firm's own terms once a payout history exists.
across firms, closures cluster around four rules. learning them properly is worth more than any indicator.

the daily limit caps what a session can cost. its purpose is to stop a bad day becoming a closed account, and it fails at that job whenever the trader treats it as a target to be spent rather than a wall to be respected. the useful habit is to convert it into a number of trades: if risk per trade is a third of the daily budget, the day ends after three losses, before the limit is reached rather than at it.

one detail beginners miss is how the limit is measured. where it is measured on floating equity, an open losing position counts against the budget the moment it moves, which means the account can breach while the trade is still running. where it is measured on closed balance, only realised losses count. those are different games, and a plan written for the second will breach the first.

this is the rule that closes accounts permanently. on a static structure, the failure point is a fixed distance below the starting balance and never moves, so progress makes the account safer. on a trailing structure, the failure point follows peak equity upward - including unrealised profit - so progress makes the account more fragile.

for a beginner, the static structure is the more forgiving introduction, because it removes the specific behaviour that kills trailing accounts: giving back a winner and discovering the cushion went with it. a trader who wants to learn on a trailing account should size at a third of what feels natural in the final third of the evaluation, when the remaining room is smallest.
same trades, three floors: the trailing structures leave less room at the end than at the beginning.

consistency rules are usually applied at the payout stage rather than the evaluation stage, which is why beginners discover them late. the mechanic is simple: no single day should dominate total profit, and the common threshold is around thirty per cent of the total. in arithmetic, total profit must reach roughly 3.3 times the largest day before withdrawal.

the practical implication is a daily profit cap well below half the target, ideally around a third, so that the ratio is satisfied the moment the target is reached. a trader who hits the target with one dominant session has passed the evaluation and cannot withdraw the profit until they keep trading and dilute the ratio - which is a stressful way to discover a rule you could have read.
one dominant day can leave an account at target but unable to withdraw.

scheduled economic releases create slippage that can exceed a stop, so firms restrict trading around them. the rule is stated, but the definition matters: windows are usually expressed in minutes either side of a release, and a position opened legitimately before the window can still breach if the terms require it to be flat. the safe reading is the strict one - treat the window as closed regardless of the instrument's behaviour inside it.

beginners break this rule in a specific way: they avoid the release but trade the immediate aftermath, when spreads are still wide and the first move has already happened. that is the worst of both - the volatility without the opportunity.
two structures dominate. the difference is not cosmetic; it changes how a plan is written.

a percentage rulebook - typical of forex and cfd firms - states target and loss limits as a fraction of the starting balance. it scales cleanly, so a plan tested on a small account transfers to a large one unchanged, and risk per trade is easy to express. it also runs around the clock, which suits traders whose available hours are unusual.

a dollar rulebook - typical of futures firms - states limits as fixed amounts and positions as contracts. risk per trade becomes a tick calculation, and the minimum position is one contract, so small accounts lose precision when converting a percentage intention into a position. the trade-off is a cash-settled market with no swap and a defined session, which suits traders who keep a fixed routine.

for a beginner, the decisive question is availability, not arithmetic. a trader who is only free in the evening cannot run a futures evaluation properly, because the liquid part of the session has already happened. a trader who is at a desk every morning has no reason to accept overnight gap risk on a 24-hour market. the fundednext versus topstep comparison works through that decision in detail, and the rules matrix lists the structures side by side.
account size is where beginners overspend most often. four considerations, in order, produce a sensible answer.

start from the risk unit. decide the smallest amount of money per trade that still represents a real decision. if a 1% risk on a $25,000 account is $250, and that is the number the plan was designed around, a $25,000 account is the right size. buying a $100,000 account changes the risk unit to $1,000, which is a different plan and an untested one.

check that the position is expressible. on futures, a risk budget that rounds to a fraction of one contract means the plan cannot trade at its intended size. on forex, a risk budget below the minimum lot size has the same effect. both produce a plan that looks valid on paper and cannot be executed.

price the fee as a percentage of income. if a payout at the target would be a meaningful month, the fee is reasonable. if the fee is a large multiple of what the first payout would produce, the economics are inverted and the trader should start smaller.

assume a second attempt. budget for two evaluations from the beginning. traders who can only afford one attempt trade the first one defensively in a way that makes it more likely to fail - the daily budget gets spent on the last trade of the day because there is no tomorrow.
risk per trade as a third of the daily budget: three losses end the day, not the account.
the market has settled into four product shapes. none is universally better; each solves a different problem.

two-phase forex evaluations are the traditional product: a profit target in phase one, a smaller target in phase two, a drawdown limit, and a funded account on completion. they are slower and more forgiving per phase, which makes them the natural first evaluation for a forex trader. the two-phase structure also gives a beginner two chances to observe the rulebook before real payouts depend on the plan.

one-phase evaluations collapse the process into a single target, usually with a tighter drawdown and an explicit consistency requirement. they are faster and less forgiving. a beginner should read the consistency clause carefully here, because single-phase products often apply it during the evaluation rather than at payout.

futures evaluations run on exchange-traded contracts with dollar-based rules and a session structure. they suit traders with a fixed daily window and a preference for cash settlement. the trailing threshold is the rule to understand first, and the daily limit is the one that ends afternoons.

instant funding products skip the evaluation and issue a funded account with stricter constraints: a smaller drawdown, a lower profit split, sometimes a reduced position cap. for a beginner they are usually a poor first purchase, because they replace a paid test with real risk on day one. the instant funding guide sets out the trade-offs.

two categories deserve caution rather than enthusiasm. firms advertising no time limit are often stricter on drawdown to compensate, and firms with unusually generous headline terms tend to change them once the cohort of traders on those terms is large enough. both are reasons to read the current rules rather than a review from last year.

ranking lists answer a question no beginner is actually asking. what a beginner needs is a scorecard that can be filled in from a firm's own documentation in about twenty minutes, and that produces a defensible answer without depending on anyone's opinion.
six lines, each scored simply, cover almost everything that determines the outcome:
is the drawdown static or trailing? static scores better for a first attempt, because it removes the specific behaviour - giving back a winner - that ends trailing accounts.
how is the daily limit measured? closed balance scores better than floating equity, because an open position cannot breach a balance rule while it is still running.
when does the consistency rule apply? at payout only scores better than during the evaluation, because it leaves room to finish the target before the ratio has to be managed.
what is the reset policy? a discounted or free reset on the same size scores better than a full repurchase. this single line changes the expected cost of a first year more than the headline fee does.
how long is the first-payout delay? shorter scores better, not because the amount is large but because the delay is when newly funded traders do the most damage.
can the terms change retroactively? no scores better than yes. a firm that reserves the right to apply new rules to existing accounts is a firm whose rules cannot be planned around.

that scorecard produces uncomfortable answers. several of the firms with the most aggressive marketing score badly on lines one, three and six. several quiet firms with modest targets score well on every line. for a first evaluation, the quiet firm is the better purchase - its rules are more likely to still be true in three weeks, and the trader is buying a test of a process rather than a story about a payout.

two practical notes on using it. first, fill it in from the firm's terms document, not from its landing page; where the two disagree, the terms are what will be enforced. second, write the answers down and keep them. when an evaluation is going badly in week three, the reason will be traceable to one of those six lines, and having the original answers makes the post-mortem honest instead of emotional.

there is a final line worth adding for beginners specifically: does the firm's smallest account satisfy your risk unit? a firm whose entry tier is too small to trade the plan at its intended size is not a cheap option - it is a slower, more frustrating version of the same purchase. size the account to the plan, then find the firm that offers it.
the advertised fee is one line in a longer budget. a realistic first-evaluation budget has four components.
the evaluation fee , paid to the firm, at the account size chosen.
the reset or repurchase cost on a failure, which is often close to the original fee.

trading costs - commissions and spread - which are small per trade and material across a two-phase evaluation. on futures, commissions are a fixed dollar figure per contract and do not scale with account size, so they weigh more on smaller accounts.
time , which is only a cost where the product is a subscription. on a one-off fee, a slow pass is free; on a monthly charge, every week is a line item.

multiply the first three by the expected number of attempts and a ranking emerges that has little to do with the advertised price. a firm with a modest fee, a generous reset policy and tight spreads beats a cheaper firm with no resets and wide spreads, usually by a wide margin.

that arithmetic is also the honest case for a passing service, where the firm's terms permit one. a flat $220 per evaluation, at any account size, with retries covered and no profit split, replaces the labour and the retry cost but not the firm's fee. for a trader whose failure mode is behavioural rather than analytical - losing the same rule every attempt - that is the variable worth pricing, and the service guide covers how to vet a provider.
the funded account has its own rulebook, and it is stricter than most beginners expect.

minimum trading days. a profit threshold is rarely enough on its own. firms typically require a number of profitable sessions before a withdrawal, so a trader who reaches the profit target in six days may still wait a fortnight. the efficient plan lands both conditions on the same date.

first-payout waiting periods. many firms hold the first payout for a fixed period after funding, which is disclosed but easy to miss. it matters because the first payout is usually the smallest, and the waiting period is when newly funded traders do the damage - trading larger to make the wait worthwhile.

consistency at withdrawal. the best-day ratio applies again, and it applies to the funded account's profit, not the evaluation's. a trader who passed with a dominant day often starts the funded phase already close to the limit.

documentation. identity verification sits between a profit and a payment. a trader who has not completed kyc before the first withdrawal request adds days to the process at the worst moment. the payout process guide walks through each step in order.
ninety days is enough to pass an evaluation and take a first payout, if the sequence is respected.

trade the plan on a demo account for fifteen sessions and record three numbers: average loss per trade, average win per trade, and the longest losing streak. those numbers determine whether the plan can survive a daily limit of any meaningful size. a plan with a nine-trade losing streak cannot pass a firm whose daily limit is three losses deep, regardless of its win rate.
most beginners skip this and buy immediately, then discover the plan's streak length in week two of a paid evaluation. fifteen sessions of demo is cheaper than a reset.

choose the smallest size that expresses the plan, with a static drawdown if the firm offers it. trade four or five sessions a week rather than every session, and treat the daily limit as a wall rather than a budget. the goal is not speed; it is to finish inside the rules with a routine that can be repeated.

if the evaluation fails, stop. do not buy a reset in the same hour. read the journal and identify which rule came closest to breach. if it is the same rule twice, the plan is wrong; if it is a different rule, the execution slipped and a retry is reasonable.

the funded phase is not the evaluation with a bigger balance. trade at half the evaluation's risk for the first two weeks, satisfy the minimum day count, keep the best-day ratio intact, and complete documentation before requesting a payout. the first payout's purpose is to prove the pipe works, not to change the month.

a beginner who reaches a first payout inside ninety days has done something most funded traders never do, and has done it without needing a large account or a spectacular month. that is the whole strategy: small, repeatable, and finished inside the rules.
almost every beginner sizes an account from the payout rather than from the streak, and the streak is what decides whether the account survives.

take a plan with a 45% win rate and a 1.8 reward-to-risk ratio. it is profitable on paper, and it will produce a run of seven or eight consecutive losses roughly once every few hundred trades. on an account risking 1% per trade with a 5% daily limit, a seven-loss streak spread across three days breaches the daily limit twice before it ends. the plan is not broken; the sizing is.

the arithmetic that prevents this is straightforward. write down the longest losing streak the plan has produced in testing, then size so that the entire streak costs less than the maximum loss. if the longest observed streak is eight and the maximum loss is 10%, risk per trade must be 1.25% or less - and that leaves nothing for the streak being longer than the sample showed, which it will be. halve it. half a per cent per trade against an eight-loss streak costs 4% of the account and leaves the plan intact.

beginners resist this because half a per cent feels like it cannot produce a meaningful month. run the numbers before rejecting it. at 0.5% risk with a 1.8 reward-to-risk ratio and a 45% win rate, the expected value per trade is roughly 0.13% of the account. forty trades a month is about 5% - which, on a funded account with a profit split, is a real month. the plan that survives is the plan that compounds; the plan that gets aggressive is the plan that gets a reset.

there is a second reason to size from the streak: it makes the evaluation's pace predictable. a trader risking 0.5% per trade needs a specific number of trades to reach a target, and that number can be checked against the firm's minimum day count. if the arithmetic says the target needs sixty trades and the minimum day count is five, the plan is comfortably inside the rules. if it says the target needs eight trades on a good week, the consistency rule will bite at payout.
firm selection deserves at least as much scrutiny as the trading plan, because the plan cannot protect against a firm that does not pay.
terms that can change unilaterally with immediate effect, especially on drawdown measurement or payout timing. read the amendment clause before you read the payout table.
payout complaints in volume , particularly complaints about verification after a profitable month rather than before. a firm that verifies slowly on the way out is a firm with a cash-flow problem.
rules that exist only in an faq. if a restriction is not in the terms, it can be invented later. what matters is what is written and enforceable.
no named legal entity or jurisdiction. anonymous operators can vanish with a cohort of fees, and the buyer has no remedy.
aggressive affiliate marketing in place of documentation. the louder the review site, the more likely the recommendation is paid for.
the scam guide covers the specific patterns in more depth, and the passed challenges page shows what a completed evaluation actually looks like on a firm's own dashboard.
everything in the evaluation was a rehearsal for this, and the rules are different in three ways.

the drawdown is usually tighter as a percentage, because the firm is now exposed to real payouts. the profit split is applied to what you withdraw, not to what you earn, so an unwithdrawn profit is not income. and the consistency check reappears at every payout rather than once.

the practical approach is to run the funded account at a lower risk than the evaluation, target small regular withdrawals rather than large irregular ones, and keep a written record of the running totals for both the profit threshold and the day count. firms scale accounts on the basis of completed payouts, so the fastest route to a larger allocation is a boring record of small, on-time withdrawals.
the complete passing guide covers the funded stage in more depth, and the 2026 edition tracks the rule changes worth knowing about.
what is the best prop firm for a complete beginner?

the one with the simplest, most static rulebook at the smallest account size that still expresses your plan - typically a two-phase forex evaluation with a static drawdown and a clear reset policy. the "best" firm is a function of your hours and your risk unit, not a universal ranking.

an amount you can afford to lose twice, because the realistic plan budgets for two attempts. if the fee is painful to lose once, the account size is too large for a first attempt and the pressure will change how you trade.
should i start with a small account or a large one?

small. the percentage rules are identical at every size, so a larger account buys a larger payout and a larger fee without improving the odds. prove the plan at a size that matches your risk unit, then scale on the firm's terms once you have a payout history.

usually not as a first purchase. they replace a paid test with live risk on day one, and they typically carry tighter drawdown, a lower split and sometimes a position cap. they suit traders who already have a proven plan and want to skip the evaluation, not traders still learning the rulebook.
how many days does it take to pass a first evaluation?

around two to four weeks at disciplined sizing, depending on the firm's minimum day count. attempts finished in a handful of days tend to create a consistency problem at payout, which makes the apparent speed expensive.

a third of the daily loss limit at most, with a hard stop at eighty per cent of the day's budget spent. three consecutive losses at that size leave the account alive and the plan intact, which is the property that matters across a multi-week evaluation.

because the funded phase is traded at evaluation size. the drawdown is typically tighter, the consistency check applies at withdrawal, and the first payout is small and delayed - a combination that tempts traders into larger positions at exactly the wrong moment. halve the risk for the first fortnight.
do i need a trading course before buying an evaluation?

no. you need a written plan with three measured numbers - average loss, average win, longest losing streak - and the discipline to size to the daily limit. a course that does not produce those three numbers is not preparation for an evaluation, it is preparation for a different activity.

practically, no. firms increasingly require stops, and even where they do not, an unstopped position on a fixed drawdown account converts a controlled risk into an uncontrolled one. a position without a stop is a position whose maximum loss is set by the market rather than by the plan.
what should i check in the firm's terms before paying?

how the daily limit is measured (equity or balance), whether the maximum loss trails and on what basis, the consistency rule and when it applies, the minimum day count, the payout schedule and first-payout delay, the news-window definition, and the amendment clause. those seven answers cover most of what closes accounts.
is it better to pass one big account or several small ones?

several small ones, eventually. correlated positions across accounts count as a single exposure at most firms, so running two simultaneously splits attention without diversifying risk. passing one, trading it, and adding a second after a payout is slower to start and faster to a first withdrawal.
how does a passing service fit into a beginner's plan?

it does not replace the learning. a flat $220 per evaluation with retries covered can clear an evaluation a trader has failed repeatedly for the same behavioural reason, but the funded account still has to be traded by its owner. buyers who expect the service to teach them the funded phase are buying the wrong product.

there is no independent authority ranking passing services, so the only useful comparison page is one that gives you the criteria and the arithmetic to judge them yourself. this is that page: four criteria, a worked cost comparison, and the questions that separate a provider who has read the rulebooks from one who has read the testimonials.
four criteria decide quality: rulebook competence, fee structure, failure terms, and whose name the funded account is in.
a percentage-of-payout model pays the provider for duration; a flat fee pays for a clean pass. the incentives are different and so is the behaviour.
the failure case is where every client has the least leverage, so the retry terms matter more than the pass count.
price is the last variable to compare, not the first, because a cheap attempt on the wrong rulebook is the most expensive option available.

a passing service sells labour and discipline, not a signal. the deliverable is an evaluation traded to target or failure under a specific firm's rules, with the funded account issued in the client's name. everything else in the category - the dashboards, the "algorithms", the community channels - is packaging around that one transaction.

understanding that changes what a buyer should value. if the product were a signal, track record would be the main criterion. since the product is execution against a rulebook, the main criteria are rulebook competence and the terms that apply when the execution fails. a provider with an ordinary edge and a perfect rulebook process beats a provider with a better edge who misreads a trailing drawdown.

no regulator, no audited body, and no independent sample exists. review sites are mostly affiliate operations paid per lead, which means the ranking reflects commission rather than quality. provider testimonials are self-selected, and forum threads are dominated by whichever outcome the last poster had.

the practical consequence is that any page claiming to rank services should be read as a page selling something. the alternative - and the approach taken here - is to give a buyer a method that works on providers the author has never heard of, and then apply it in public to one provider, including its weaknesses.

it cannot remove variance, guarantee a pass, or change a firm's rules. it cannot make an unsuitable rulebook suitable: a trader with a swing strategy who buys a trailing-drawdown futures evaluation has bought a problem, and no amount of competent execution fixes that. the most valuable thing a good provider does in the first conversation is occasionally decline.
a provider who cannot explain your rulebook cannot execute it.

the test is whether the provider volunteers a distinction you had not considered. a provider who says "trailing drawdown" has read the marketing page; one who says "intraday trailing, so an unrealised gain that comes back to entry still leaves your floor higher" has read the terms. that difference is the whole product.

a second test costs the same: ask which firms they will not trade, and why. providers with no refusals either have not read the rulebooks or are willing to accept terms their clients will pay for. the refusals are usually the most informative sentence in the reply.

percentage-of-payout arrangements sound aligned and behave differently. a provider paid from withdrawals has an interest in the account continuing to trade and in the payout being large; a provider paid a fixed fee has an interest in the pass being clean and the client returning for a second account. neither is dishonest, and the second is easier to verify, because a certificate exists or it does not.

most of the value in a service is in what it does when the attempt fails. a retry covered on the same firm and size is a real term with a real cost to the provider, which is why it is stated precisely when it exists and hedged when it does not. read the wording: "retries covered" and "discounted resets" are different products.

the funded account must be in the client's name, with payouts arriving in the client's account. a provider that wants to hold the login or receive the money is asking the client to take counterparty risk in exchange for convenience. that arrangement also creates an obvious incentive to delay, which is the last thing a trader needs at the payout stage.
flat fee and profit split reward different behaviour from the provider.
the models can be compared, and the comparison is less favourable to the split model than its marketing suggests once the expected number of attempts is included.

consider a trader who passes a $50,000 account and withdraws $4,000 a month for six months - $24,000 in total. a 20% split costs $4,800. the flat fee costs $220. on that arithmetic the flat model is cheaper by an order of magnitude for anyone who intends to keep trading, and the split model is only competitive for a client who passes and never withdraws, which is not a client anyone should be optimising for.

there is a counter-argument worth stating honestly: a split model costs nothing if the provider fails. a flat fee is paid whether or not the evaluation passes. that is why the retry clause carries the weight it does - with retries covered, the flat model's failure case is bounded at $220, and without it the fee is a bet.

a fee should cover the work: reading the rulebook, writing the plan, trading the evaluation, and the retry if a rule is breached. it should not be presented as covering the firm's challenge fee - that is paid to the firm and is usually separate - and it should not be presented as an investment in a profit share that may never materialise.

three hypothetical providers, each competent, differing only in structure. the point is not that one is dishonest; it is that the same client gets a different product and a different cost depending on which structure they choose.

$220 for any firm and size, retries on rule breaches covered at the same firm and size, no profit split, funded account in the client's name. a client who passes on the first attempt pays $220 and keeps every dollar of the funded account. a client who breaches a daily limit twice pays $220 and, if the third attempt passes, still keeps everything.

the risk to the client is capped and the risk to the provider is real: two failures on a $540 challenge cost more than the fee. that is the structure working as intended - the provider's own margin is what disciplines the execution.

no up-front fee, 20% of every withdrawal, funded account held by the provider. the client's cash outlay is zero, which is why the model sells. over six months at $4,000 a month, the provider collects $4,800. the client also carries the risk that the provider delays or disputes a payout, and has no certificate to point to if the arrangement sours.

$99, no retries, no split. on the surface this is the cheapest option and it frequently ends up the most expensive: at a realistic 50% pass rate the expected cost is $198 plus the firm's own reset charges, and the client bears the full cost of every failure. providers of this kind are usually reselling an attempt rather than executing a plan.

the table makes the argument better than prose can. the client who intends to withdraw more than a few thousand dollars is paying a large premium for the illusion of a free service, and the client who intends to withdraw nothing is not a client a provider should be building a business around.
most of these are visible in the first reply, and any one of them is sufficient reason to stop.
requests for platform passwords. a service needs the account to trade it, not the client's bank login, email password or identity documents. anything beyond the trading account is a security problem.
no answer on third-party trading policy. the answer determines whether the funded account survives; a provider who has not asked the firm has not read the terms.
guaranteed passes. variance exists, so the claim is either false or the definition of "pass" has been quietly narrowed.
funded login held by the provider. counterparty risk at the exact moment the client has the most to lose.
payment only in crypto, only by transfer, no receipt. not automatically dishonest, but it removes the client's ability to prove what was paid for.
screenshots instead of certificates. evidence that cannot be checked is marketing.
pressure to buy today. rulebooks do not expire overnight, and a provider whose pricing depends on urgency has priced it that way deliberately.
the criteria should be applied to this provider as readily as to any other, so here is the assessment in the same terms.

the service reads each firm's terms before quoting, distinguishes trailing from static drawdowns and equity from balance measurement, and declines assignments where a firm's position on third-party trading makes the arrangement unsafe for the client. the articles on this site exist for the same reason: they are the long version of the rulebook translation.
one flat $220 for any prop firm and any account size. no profit split, no performance fee, no charge at withdrawal. the firm's own challenge fee is separate and paid to the firm.

retries on rule breaches at the same firm and size are covered under the flat fee; the firm's own reset charge, where it applies, is separate. a client who abandons an evaluation mid-way does not receive a refund, which is stated before purchase rather than argued about afterwards.
the funded account is issued in the client's name and payouts are paid directly to the client. the service does not hold the login after handover and takes nothing from withdrawals.

it is a small operation, which means capacity is limited and scheduling depends on how many evaluations are running at once. verification evidence is provided on request rather than published as a live tracker for every account, because several firms' platforms do not support external linking. and the flat fee is paid whether or not an evaluation passes, which is why the retry clause is load-bearing rather than decorative.
the order of the decision matters more than the criteria, because each step eliminates work in the next.
read your firm's rulebook. two minutes, and it decides whether the rest of the conversation can produce anything useful.
confirm the firm permits third-party trading. in writing, to the firm, before any provider is paid.
choose the structure. flat fee if you intend to keep the account and withdraw repeatedly; a split only if you genuinely expect one small payout.
ask the four criterion questions. rulebook mechanic, fee, failure terms, account ownership.
ask for evidence. a certificate for a comparable firm and size, dated, plus a verification link where the platform allows one.
only then compare price. a $220 pass on a suitable rulebook beats a $99 attempt on one your strategy cannot survive.
six steps, one afternoon, and the result is a decision that can be explained in three sentences. that is the standard this page holds itself to, and the standard a buyer should hold against it.
buyers often know what to ask and not how to ask it, which matters because vague questions get marketing answers. the wording below is designed to produce answers that can be checked.

"on my firm, is the maximum loss static or trailing - and if trailing, does it update intraday or at the close?" a provider who answers with a percentage has not read the terms. a provider who answers with a mechanic, and then explains what it implies for exit discipline, has.

"is the daily loss measured on equity including floating positions, or on closed balance?" this is the single most consequential line in most rulebooks and the one most often glossed over. the answer changes how a session has to be managed, not just how it is sized.

"what has to be true before my first withdrawal - profit threshold, trading days, consistency ratio?" a provider who names all three without being prompted has read the payout section, which is where most surprises live.

"if a daily limit is breached in week two, what happens and what does it cost me?" the answer should be specific: covered retry at the same firm and size, or a stated fee, or a refusal. "we'll work something out" is not a term.
"whose name is on the funded account, and who receives the payout?" if the answer is not "yours", the arrangement has a counterparty problem that no amount of competence resolves.
when a provider says they "read the rulebook", the output should be a short document, not an assurance. here is what a competent translation contains for a typical $100,000 futures evaluation.

six lines, one page, and every one of them can be checked against the firm's own terms in ten minutes. a provider who cannot produce something like this before taking money is asking the client to fund an experiment.

two traders with identical skill and identical firms can produce different outcomes purely on how they convert the rulebook into a plan. one sizes at the daily budget and loses the account in a fortnight; the other sizes at a third of it and reaches the target in three weeks. the difference is not analysis - it is arithmetic done at the right moment, and the translation is where that arithmetic happens.
expected cost is the fee divided by the pass rate, plus everything a failed attempt consumes.
failure is the outcome a buyer should price first, because it is the one with the least negotiating room afterwards. it has three components and buyers usually count only the first.

the service fee, plus the firm's challenge fee, plus any reset charge the firm levies. on a $540 challenge with a $220 service fee, a failed attempt without retries costs $760 before anything else. with retries covered, the second attempt costs nothing beyond the firm's own reset, which is often discounted.

two to four weeks per attempt. a trader who takes three attempts has spent two to three months on the same puzzle, which is a meaningful share of a trading year and, more importantly, of the period during which a track record is being built.

a failed attempt that is not analysed is a purchase of nothing. a failed attempt that is analysed produces the sentence that prevents the next failure - which rule was broken, in which session, under what conditions. that sentence is worth more than the fee, and it only exists if someone writes it down.

a provider whose fee covers retries has priced the first two components into a fixed number. a provider who charges per attempt has left the variance with the client. neither is automatically better, but the first is easier to budget and the second is easier to sell, which explains which one is advertised more heavily.

two firms offer a 10% target on a $100,000 account. firm one charges $540 with a static 10% maximum loss and no consistency rule. firm two charges $450 with a trailing maximum loss updated intraday and a 30% best-day consistency rule at payout. the cheaper option looks obvious until the mechanics are applied.

at 1.5% risk, firm one tolerates six and a half full-risk losses from the starting balance and allows a trader to hold size constant throughout. firm two's floor follows equity, so at 4% profit the available room is roughly 6% and shrinking, and the consistency rule means the payout depends on the distribution of the gain rather than its total.

the realistic pass probability on firm one, for a trader with a modest edge, is materially higher than on firm two, and the expected cost per funded account is lower despite the higher headline fee. that is the whole argument for comparing mechanics rather than prices, and it is the argument most buyers never run.
reviews of passing services are a narrow sample, but they do contain information when read by category rather than by score. five patterns recur often enough to be useful.
pattern one: complaints about firm rules mistaken for service failures

the most common negative review describes a payout refused by the firm, not a service failure. that is a rulebook problem: a consistency ratio, a day count, or a position held over a weekend. it matters to a buyer because it predicts the next complaint, and it is preventable by reading the payout section before purchase.

the second most common complaint is communication dropping once the fee is paid. it is also the easiest to test in advance: ask a question before buying and time the reply. a provider who answers within hours before payment and within days after has a staffing problem that will show up at the worst moment.

positive reviews that mention a rule being explained - rather than a pass being achieved - are the most reliable signal in the category, because they describe the product doing its actual job. a buyer who reads five of those has learned more than from fifty reviews about results.
where results are shown but dates are missing, the sample is probably older than it appears. rulebooks change, and a pass from eighteen months ago was obtained under terms that may no longer exist.
twenty reviews in a week on a service that had none for a year is solicitation, not evidence. it is not dishonest, and it is not information either.

a fair comparison has to include doing nothing, because a disciplined trader with three weeks and a routine does not need the service. the checklist below is the entire method in one place, and it is deliberately short.
read the rulebook twice - numbers, then exceptions - and write the date on it.
convert to four numbers: daily budget, distance to failure, target in r, payout constraint.
risk one third of the daily budget per trade and hold it constant within 10%.
stop at 80% of the daily limit , not 100%, because floating equity is measured.
pace for sixteen to twenty-two days and remove any invented deadline.
halve risk above 70% of target ; stop entirely once the target is banked.
journal five fields and review weekly for risk drift and rule violations.
check payout conditions before requesting , especially any best-day ratio.

eight steps, no proprietary knowledge, and they are the same steps a service executes. the reason to pay someone is time and enforcement, not secret information - and any provider who implies otherwise is selling mystique rather than a method.

if you have passed an evaluation before, have a written plan you have followed for a month, and can commit to a fixed session each day, the marginal value of a service is small. the service is most valuable when the rulebook is unfamiliar, the pacing is hard to sustain without accountability, or the account size is large enough that the fee is trivial relative to the payout.

when a service is the better decision when the trader's constraint is time rather than knowledge: a full-time job, a business, or a period in which screen hours are simply unavailable. the service converts a three-week task into a fee, and for a trader whose alternative is an abandoned attempt in week two, that conversion is rational. three questions buyers forget to ask what happens if my firm changes its rules mid-evaluation?

firms revise terms, and an evaluation that started under one rulebook may finish under another. a competent provider will notice a change to a target, a limit or a payout condition and say so rather than continuing silently. ask directly: "if my firm changes its drawdown mechanic next week, what happens to my assignment?" the answer should be a sentence about the plan being re-run against the new terms, not a shrug.
what happens to the funded account if i stop trading it?

several firms close accounts that are inactive for a set period, which matters to a trader who wants to bank a payout and pause. it also matters at handover: a funded account issued in your name may have an inactivity clause that no one mentioned, and discovering it after a month of silence is expensive.

an enquiry requires an email address, and a purchase requires a payment record. beyond that, nothing is needed - no identity documents, no broker login, no platform password. a provider who asks for more than the trading account has given no thought to the security of the person paying them.

none of those three questions appears in most comparison articles, and each of them has been the cause of a real dispute. a buyer who asks them signals that the conversation is being recorded, which tends to improve the answers to everything else.

the general principle is that the questions which cost a provider something to answer are the ones worth asking. a provider with good answers is not merely polite; it has done the reading, priced the risk, and decided what it will refuse - and all three of those are visible before a fee is paid.

that is why this page is structured as a method rather than a ranking: a method keeps working when the provider you are considering is not the one being written about, and it keeps costing nothing to apply. six questions, one afternoon, and a decision that survives being explained out loud to someone who is not selling you anything at all.

most ftmo guides explain the rules. this one is a sequence: the four things to audit before paying, the arithmetic that fixes account size and risk, a twenty-day calendar with decision gates at each milestone, and the exact steps between the moment the target is hit and the moment a funded account pays. it is written as a procedure to follow in order, because the order is where attempts are won and lost.
the sequence matters more than the strategy: size comes from the drawdown, risk comes from the daily limit, and the calendar comes from both.
