every step here assumes the firm's terms permit the way you trade. confirm that in writing before the first fee, especially if anyone else is trading the account.

two traders can run the same strategy on the same evaluation and produce opposite results, purely because they made their decisions in a different order. the first picks an account size they can afford, then works out risk from the target, then discovers the daily limit is too small for the schedule. the second works backwards from the rules: the drawdown fixes the size, the daily limit fixes the risk, and the target fixes the calendar.

the second order is the only one that produces a plan which cannot breach by construction. it is also slower to set up and considerably faster to complete, because time spent on arithmetic before the fee is time not spent recovering from an avoidable breach.

there is a second reason to think in sequence. an evaluation is a chain of conditions, and a chain is only as strong as its weakest link. the trading rules are one link. verification is another. the funded account's tighter drawdown is a third. the payout conditions are a fourth. traders who fail rarely fail at the link they were watching, which is why the procedure below continues past the pass instead of stopping there.

finally, a note on expectations. ftmo's structure is well documented and widely copied, which means the mechanics are not the hard part - the hard part is executing a boring plan for four weeks without inventing a reason to deviate. this guide is therefore as much a schedule as a strategy. the strategy is the trader's; the schedule is what makes it survive a rulebook.
four questions, answered in writing, before any fee is paid. each one has ended someone's attempt before it began.

one: which account stage and size? the smallest account whose rules can be satisfied is usually a better purchase than the largest that can be financed. a large account with a risk plan that is too conservative to finish inside a reasonable calendar is a slow loss; a small account with a plan that fits is a fast pass and a funded login.

two: does the firm's terms permit the way you trade? the relevant clauses are the news-trading restriction, the weekend and overnight policy, any prohibition on high-frequency or latency-dependent strategies, and - separately - whether third-party trading or account management is allowed on the evaluation and on the funded account. those are two different answers and the funded one is the one with money attached.

three: what is the total cost to funding? fee, platform, data, and any activation charge on the funded account. a one-off fee makes a slow pass cheap; a monthly fee makes it expensive. the ftmo mechanics guide covers the structure and the ftmo tips guide covers the practical filters; this page assumes both are read and moves straight to the procedure.

four: what is the server's day boundary? the daily loss limit is measured from a defined start of day, and that start is set by the firm's server, not the trader's clock. establish it before the first trade, because a session that straddles the boundary can put two positions' risk against two different days, and the second day begins with a deficit the trader did not plan.

write the four answers on one page. if any of them is unclear, the correct next action is a support ticket rather than a payment, and the reply should be kept. a written answer from the firm is the only version of the terms that survives a dispute.

the maximum loss, not the fee, should choose the account size. the reason is that the maximum loss defines the per-trade risk, and the per-trade risk defines whether the strategy can be traded at all.

take the firm's stated maximum loss as a percentage of the starting balance. decide how many consecutive losses the plan should survive - for a discretionary plan with a win rate in the forties, eight to ten is a sensible design case, because runs of that length occur within a few hundred trades and are not anomalies. divide the maximum loss by that number to get the maximum loss per trade as a percentage.

now convert it into money. on a smaller account, that percentage produces a dollar figure that may be too small to place the stop the strategy needs on the instrument being traded. that is not a reason to widen the risk; it is a reason either to trade a smaller contract size or to choose a larger account.

the same calculation run on several account sizes produces an obvious answer surprisingly often: the middle size fits the strategy, the smallest does not permit the stop distance, and the largest is unnecessary because the plan's return is percentage-based and scale-free. buying the largest affordable account is a common error with a specific cost - the daily limit scales with the account, so the trader ends up with more room than the plan can use, and a larger fee for the privilege.

one adjustment is worth making at this stage. if the plan's stop distance produces a per-trade risk that is more than about a tenth of the daily limit, the plan will spend the session on two or three ordinary losses. either the stop is too wide for the timeframe or the size is too large; both are fixable before the fee rather than after it.
target and drawdown are one equation. sizing for the loss limit is what keeps the account alive long enough to reach the target.

scale is the reason this step is worth doing properly. a percentage target is identical on every account size, so the plan that passes a small account passes a large one with no changes at all - the only difference is the dollars per trade. that makes the small account a legitimate training ground rather than a consolation prize, and it makes the first pass the cheapest information a trader can buy.
the risk line is a single written sentence with four numbers in it, and it governs every trade of the evaluation. write it before the first session and read it at the start of every one.

risk per trade as a percentage. derived in step one from the maximum loss and the streak the plan must survive. it does not change because the account is up, and it does not change because the account is down.

maximum trades per session. a hard cap, chosen so that the worst session the plan permits cannot breach the daily limit. if risk per trade is a tenth of the daily limit, ten losses would exactly exhaust it - so the cap should be five or six, leaving room for the trade that goes wrong differently from the plan.
maximum daily loss in money. the firm's limit, restated as an amount the trader can see on the platform without doing arithmetic in the moment. the moment is the worst time to calculate.

the stop rule. every position has a protective order placed at entry, on the server rather than locally, at a distance the plan specifies. no position is held without one, for any reason, including a high-conviction view.

the line only works if it is checked against both limits. a risk per trade that survives the maximum loss but consumes half the daily limit is a line that fails on a normal tuesday. the correct number is the smaller of the two constraints, and it is usually the daily constraint that binds.

two habits make the line stick. the first is to compute the position size before the session, not during it, and to write the size on the same page. the second is to stop trading when the trade cap or the daily loss is reached, whichever comes first, and to close the platform rather than watch it. watching is how a stopped session becomes an unstopped one.

there is a version of the risk line for traders who are already funded, and it has one extra clause: the funded account's drawdown is frequently tighter than the evaluation's, so the percentage in the line goes down, not up, on the day the funded login arrives. traders who carry the evaluation's number into the funded account lose it in the first fortnight more often than at any other time.

once the risk line is fixed, the calendar follows from arithmetic rather than optimism. this is the part most plans skip, and it is the part that determines whether the trader spends one fee or three.

expected value per trade is a function of the win rate, the reward-to-risk ratio and the risk per trade. with a risk of a fraction of a percent and a ratio of two, a plan with a win rate in the forties produces a small positive expectation per trade. dividing the profit target by that expectation gives the number of trades required at expectation, and dividing by the trades per week the schedule allows gives the calendar.

running that calculation usually produces a number between fifteen and thirty trading days for a conservative plan. that is the honest pace. a twenty-day target is achievable because it is roughly what the arithmetic produces, not because it is a round number that sounds good in marketing.

the important consequence is what to do when the plan is behind. if the calendar was derived rather than assumed, being behind on day twelve is information: either the expectation is lower than designed or the trade count is lower than planned. neither is fixed by increasing size. the correct responses are to increase the trade count within the cap, to accept a longer calendar, or to conclude that the plan's ratio is not good enough and stop - in that order.

two calendar rules make the plan robust. first, trade a fixed number of sessions per week, not every available session; a schedule with rest days produces a lower breach rate over a month than one without. second, put the calendar in the diary with a review every friday, so the decision to extend is made deliberately rather than discovered in week six.

a word on minimum trading days, where the firm imposes them. they are satisfied by activity, not profit, and they are almost never the binding constraint on a twenty-day plan. the trap is the reverse: a trader reaches the target in five sessions, then has to trade for ten more days to satisfy a count, and gives back a fifth of the target in the process. if the count is longer than the plan, slow the plan down from the start so the target and the count finish together.
the checklist exists because the rules are simple and the moment is not. it runs in the same order every session.

before the session. confirm the account's distance to the maximum loss and the daily limit as they stand this morning, not as they stood at the start of the evaluation. on a static drawdown those numbers are fixed; on anything that trails, they have moved, and the position size computed three weeks ago may no longer fit.

before the first trade. name the setup being waited for. if the plan's setup has not appeared, the session has no trades in it, and that is a completed session rather than a missed opportunity. the trade taken without a named setup is the one that consumes the daily limit.

at entry. place the protective order at the same time as the position, at the planned distance, on the server. size comes from the risk line, not from the chart. if the chart suggests a size larger than the line permits, the chart is not in charge of the size.

during the trade. no stop widening, no adding to a loser, no partial close that leaves the remainder without a protective order. each of those three is a rule breach in a different costume, and each is more likely on the trade the trader feels most strongly about.

at the close. record the trade: setup, size, planned risk, realised risk, result. realised risk is the number that matters, because slippage and spread are part of the strategy's cost and are usually underestimated. a month of records turns a guess about the plan's expectation into a measurement.

at the session end. compare the day's loss to the daily limit and the day's trade count to the cap. if either is at the limit, the session is over regardless of how the market looks. then close the platform.

the checklist is deliberately dull. its value is that it removes the two decisions that cost the most: whether to take a trade that does not match the plan, and whether to stop after a loss. both are decided in advance, when the trader is calm and the arithmetic is checkable.

one addition for traders who work full time: compress the checklist rather than skip it. a single session per day with a two-trade cap and a pre-written size satisfies every item on this list in under ten minutes. what cannot be compressed is the pre-session check of the remaining room, because that is the number every other decision depends on.
a one-month evaluation is too long to hold in working memory, so it is worth splitting into four short ones at fixed points of progress. each gate has one question and one action.

the first gate is the most informative and the most often skipped. traders plan risk in percentage terms and measure results in money, and the difference between the two is the cost of executing the plan - spread, commission, slippage on entry and exit. on a plan with a small expectation per trade, a cost that is a fifth of the planned risk can turn a positive expectation into a flat one. gate one exists to catch that before it compounds over a month.

the second gate is where patience is either granted or refused. being at half the target with half the calendar gone is on pace and requires no change. being at a quarter of the target with half the calendar gone is behind, and the arithmetic from step three says what to do: raise the trade count, extend the date, or stop. the one forbidden response is to raise the size, because that changes the plan's survival probability rather than its speed.

the third gate is a diagnostic. a daily limit touched once in a month is variance. touched three times, it is a risk line that is too heavy for the session count, and the account is one ordinary bad day from ending. cutting size at three-quarters of the target feels like giving up progress; it is in fact the cheapest insurance available at that point.

the fourth gate is about the shape of the profit, not the amount. nearly there, the temptation is a large position to finish the job. that single trade creates two risks at once: a breach of the daily limit if it goes wrong, and a consistency problem at the payout stage if it goes right. halving the size and adding sessions costs a few days and preserves both.
the moment the target is reached, the objective changes from making money to keeping a record clean. four steps, in this order.

stop trading the account. not reduce, stop. a target reached on tuesday and a position opened on wednesday is a target that can be lost before the firm processes it. the evaluation is complete; there is nothing left to gain and a fee to lose.

check the day count. if the firm requires a minimum number of trading days and the target arrived early, the remaining days must be traded. do it at a fraction of the risk line, with a daily profit cap, and accept flat sessions. the purpose is activity, not profit.

check the consistency position. establish the share of total profit contributed by the best day. if one session dominates, a funded payout may later be constrained by that ratio, and the constraint cannot be fixed retroactively. where the firm applies consistency at the evaluation stage, this is the moment to verify the number rather than assume it.

read the funded terms properly. the evaluation page is marketing; the funded terms are the contract. look specifically at the funded drawdown, the minimum profitable days before a withdrawal, the profit threshold, the consistency rule and whether it applies at every payout or only the first, and the third-party clause. each of those changes how the funded account should be traded from the first session.
a pass starts a second sequence. verification and the funded rules sit between the target and any income.

one practical detail that costs people a week: begin identity and address verification on the day the funded account is issued, not the day the first withdrawal is requested. verification is administrative, has nothing to do with the trading record, and is routinely the step that delays a first payment. completing it early removes the only part of the chain the trader cannot influence afterwards.

then, before the first funded trade, rewrite the risk line for the funded account. the drawdown is usually tighter as a percentage, the payout conditions constrain how much profit should be taken per day, and the objective is no longer to hit a target but to complete a payout cycle. those are three different numbers from the evaluation's, and carrying the old line across is the single most common way a fresh funding is lost.
a two-phase evaluation is not the same task repeated. the second phase has a different cost of failure, a different psychological position and, usually, a slightly different target.

the cost of failure is higher because a breach in phase two wastes the phase-one work as well as the fee, and any retry usually restarts the sequence. the psychological position is worse for the same reason: the trader is close, and closeness is the condition under which discipline erodes. the target is often smaller, which is a trap - a smaller target invites a larger size to finish quickly, at exactly the point where the account is most expensive to lose.

the correct response is to run phase two at a lower risk per trade than phase one, not the same. a reduction of a quarter to a third is enough to change the survival probability meaningfully while adding only a few days to the calendar, and the few days are cheap relative to a restart. the trade cap stays, the checklist stays, and the four gates move to the new target's fractions.

there is one structural advantage worth using. phase one produced a month of records. those records are the best available estimate of the plan's expectation, its realised cost per trade and its true win rate. running phase two without reading them is choosing to repeat the first phase's mistakes with less room for error. if the records show the expectation is thin, phase two should be slower and smaller, not faster and larger.

if the firm offers a single-phase route at a higher fee, it is worth costing honestly rather than reflexively choosing the cheaper two-phase path. two phases at a lower fee is cheaper only if both are completed; a breach in phase two usually costs the whole sequence. the comparison is expected cost, not sticker price, and the expected cost depends on the trader's own breach rate - which the first month's records will now estimate.
the funded account has conditions of its own, and the first payout cycle is a sequence rather than a single request.

halve the risk for the first fortnight. the funded drawdown is frequently tighter than the evaluation's, and the account is now the thing that produces income. half the evaluation's risk per trade for the first ten sessions is enough to establish that the funded rules behave as expected without putting the allocation at risk of a normal losing sequence.

satisfy the day count deliberately. minimum profitable days are usually the most commonly missed condition, because they are satisfied by activity rather than by profit. plan for them: a smaller size, a fixed session count, and a daily profit cap that keeps the consistency ratio intact while the count is accumulated.

keep the consistency ratio intact from day one. under a best-day share of around a third, total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day before a full withdrawal. a trader whose best day is a fifth of the threshold needs five times that day in total profit. setting a daily profit cap well below the ratio from the first session makes the condition automatically satisfied by the time the threshold is reached.

withdraw on the earliest permitted schedule. profit left in the account is profit the market can take back, and on a trailing structure it also raises the floor behind the trader. the first withdrawal is worth taking at the smallest permitted size rather than waiting for a larger one, because a completed cycle establishes the payment route, the timing and the tax treatment - three things that are otherwise guesses.

do not scale before the first payout completes. scaling plans are judged on completed withdrawals, not on a good month. a trader who increases size after a strong fortnight and then breaches has produced nothing the firm can scale, and has usually broken a consistency ratio on the way.

the payout process guide walks through the sequence in detail, and the consistency guide covers the arithmetic for the common thresholds. both are worth reading before the funded account is traded rather than after the first withdrawal request.
a breach is a decision point, not an ending, and the decision should be made with the records rather than with the feeling.

the first question is which limit was breached. a maximum-loss breach means the plan's survival arithmetic was wrong: the risk line permitted a sequence the account could not absorb. a daily-limit breach usually means the session cap was too generous or the trade count too high. a rule breach - news trading, holding over a restricted period, exceeding a lot cap - means the plan did not account for the terms, which is a reading failure rather than a trading one. each has a different fix, and none of them is "try harder".

the second question is whether the plan's expectation was positive over the attempt. the records answer it: trades, average result, realised cost per trade. a plan with a positive expectation and a breached limit needs a smaller size, not a different strategy. a plan with a negative expectation needs to stop being traded for money until it is fixed, because a reset buys another sample of the same distribution.

the third question is whether the retry is a new attempt or the same one at a higher price. a reset that keeps the size, the stop distance and the session cap is the same attempt. a reset that changes one of the three numbers is a genuine second data point. budget the retry deliberately, and change something measurable.

there is also a version of the reset decision that involves help. where the firm's terms permit third-party trading, a passing service converts an uncertain attempt into a fixed cost, which is a legitimate trade for a trader whose own breach rate is high. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid it. that last point is not a formality: a pass produced in breach of a third-party clause is a pass that can be voided at the payout request. the passing services guide sets out the checks, and the scam guide covers the failure modes.
if the account is going to be traded by someone else, the questions change from trading questions to contract questions. six of them, in order.

is third-party trading permitted on the evaluation? and, separately, on the funded account? a firm can permit one and prohibit the other, and the funded answer is the one that decides whether a pass produces money.

what exactly is the flat fee, and what does it cover? a per-evaluation price that is independent of account size and stage is a price that can be compared. a percentage of the target is a price that scales with the thing the service is being paid to achieve, which aligns incentives in the wrong direction.
what happens if the attempt fails? retries covered at no additional cost is the only answer that makes a fixed fee meaningful. a retry fee converts the fixed cost back into a per-attempt gamble.

who holds the login? the funded account should be issued in the trader's name, with credentials in the trader's control, and the service should have access only for the duration of the work. any arrangement where the service owns the account is a different product.

what is the profit split? a passing service should take none: the payment is for the pass, and the funded account's profit belongs to the account holder. a service that takes a share of payouts has an incentive to keep trading the account after the pass.

what is the refund or decline policy? a service that refunds when the firm's terms turn out to forbid the work is a service that has read the terms. one that does not is transferring that risk to the buyer.

the wider point is that a flat fee changes the arithmetic of an evaluation from a repeated cost to a single one. for a trader whose own breach rate is high, that conversion is worth more than the difference between the fee and a reset, because it removes the variance as well as the cost.
how long does it take to pass an ftmo challenge?

fifteen to thirty trading days at a conservative size, derived from the plan's expectation per trade rather than chosen in advance. faster is possible with larger size and a correspondingly lower survival probability. a twenty-day calendar is a reasonable target because it is roughly what the arithmetic produces at survivable risk.
what is the first thing to do before paying the fee?

audit four things: the account size whose rules the plan can satisfy, whether the terms permit the way you trade, the total cost to funding including platform and data, and the firm's server day boundary. any unclear answer should become a support ticket with the reply kept.

from the maximum loss, not the fee. divide the maximum loss by the number of consecutive losses the plan should survive to get risk per trade, then check that the resulting dollar risk permits the stop distance the strategy needs. the smallest account that fits is usually the better purchase.
why does the daily limit end more attempts than the target?

because it fires on normal variance rather than on a bad plan. if risk per trade is a large fraction of the daily limit, two or three ordinary losses close the session. setting risk from the daily limit as well as the maximum loss, and capping trades per session, removes most of that failure mode.
what should i do the moment i hit the target?

stop trading the account. then check the minimum day count, the consistency position, and the funded terms - particularly the funded drawdown, the payout conditions and the third-party clause. start identity verification on the day the funded login is issued.
should phase two be traded at the same size as phase one?

lower, not the same. a breach in phase two wastes both phases, and the temptation to accelerate is strongest when the target is closest. a quarter to a third less risk per trade adds a few days to the calendar and removes most of the restart risk.

half the evaluation's risk per trade for the first ten sessions, then reassess. funded drawdowns are frequently tighter as a percentage, and the funded account is where the income comes from - the cost of being slow is small, the cost of a breach is the allocation.

check the firm's policy for the instrument and account type, since swing accounts and standard accounts usually differ. where holding is permitted, price the gap as a multiple of the stop and cut the size accordingly - the weekend holding guide covers the arithmetic.

not the headline limits but the secondary clauses: news trading inside a restricted window, holding through a restricted period, exceeding a lot cap, or breaching the daily limit because the server's day boundary differed from the trader's. all four are reading failures, and all four are avoidable before the fee.

only if the firm's terms permit third-party trading, which must be confirmed for the evaluation and the funded account separately. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid it.

identify which limit was breached - maximum loss, daily limit, or a rule clause - because each has a different fix. then check whether the plan's expectation was actually positive over the attempt. a positive expectation with a breached limit needs smaller size; a negative expectation needs a fixed plan before another fee.

different rather than harder. two phases mean two targets and two chances to breach, but each target is smaller. the honest comparison is expected cost, which depends on your own breach rate - and the first month's records will estimate that better than any guide.

passing an evaluation produces a funded account. getting money out of it is a separate sequence of conditions - minimum trading days, a profit threshold, a consistency check, identity verification and the withdrawal itself. this guide covers each one and the errors that delay them.
five conditions usually sit between a pass and a first withdrawal, and they are checked independently.
completed kyc before the profit threshold is reached removes the most common avoidable delay.
a consistency rule at payout is the most frequent reason a profitable account cannot withdraw.
withdrawal methods and processing windows matter more than a few points of profit split.
a payout is the last step of a sequence that begins before the funded login arrives.
a funded account is not a bank account. withdrawals are governed by conditions that differ from firm to firm but follow the same order almost everywhere.
the typical funded-account payout sequence: funded login, minimum days, profit threshold, consistency, kyc, withdrawal.
funded credentials issued. the evaluation is verified and the live account is opened in your name.
minimum trading days completed. usually five to ten days of qualifying activity.
profit threshold met. often 5-10% on forex accounts, or a dollar figure on futures accounts.
consistency satisfied. no single day should dominate total profit - commonly a 30% best-day cap.
kyc completed. identity and address documents matched to the account holder.
withdrawal processed. typically one to seven business days after approval, depending on the method.

two properties of this sequence cause most of the frustration traders experience. first, the conditions are cumulative but independent: satisfying four of the five produces nothing. second, the threshold usually resets after each withdrawal, so the sequence repeats for every payout rather than being a one-time gate.
firms require a minimum number of qualifying days before a payout can be requested, and the definition of a qualifying day varies in ways that matter.
a closed trade. the most common definition: at least one position opened and closed on the day.
a day meeting a minimum activity level. a few firms require a minimum number of trades or a minimum holding period.
a calendar day with platform activity. rare, but occasionally used for accounts that must show continuous engagement.

the practical implication is that day count cannot be accelerated. a trader who reaches the profit threshold in three sessions still waits for the remaining days, and during that wait the account must stay profitable - which is why reaching the threshold early is not an advantage. the efficient approach is to pace the profit to arrive on or just after the minimum day, so there is no idle period at target.

our own recorded pass timelines cluster around fourteen trading days for two-phase forex evaluations, which comfortably exceeds most minimum-day requirements - the pacing arithmetic naturally produces enough sessions without any deliberate pad.
after funding, most firms require a fresh profit threshold before the first withdrawal. on forex accounts this is commonly 5-10% of the account; on futures accounts it is usually stated in dollars.
three details are worth confirming in the firm's terms rather than assuming.
whether the threshold resets after each payout. many firms apply the same threshold to every withdrawal, which means the sequence repeats monthly or bi-weekly for as long as the account is traded.
whether floating profit counts. almost universally, the threshold is measured on closed profit. a trader sitting on a large unrealised gain has not met it.
whether the threshold scales with the account. on firms with scaling plans, the threshold may rise as the account grows, which changes the arithmetic for subsequent payouts.
this is the gate that blocks the most withdrawals, and it is entirely an arithmetic problem.

a consistency rule at payout limits how much of total profit may come from one day. the common shape is 30%, which means total profit must reach at least 3.33× the best day. a trader with a $6,000 best day needs $20,000 in total before the withdrawal is approved, regardless of the firm's profit threshold being met.
consistency is measured on the distribution of profit, not the total - one dominant day can block a withdrawal.

the remedy is additive rather than surgical: more ordinary winning days, with each of them small. a trader with a dominant day who repairs the ratio with a second large day has simply raised the bar, because the required total scales with the new best day. the full arithmetic, including worked examples at 30%, 40% and 50%, is in the consistency rule guide .
identity verification is handled by the firm, not by any passing service, and it is the most common source of avoidable delay in a first withdrawal.

what firms typically require: a government-issued photo identity document, a proof of address dated within the last three months, and in some cases a payment method in the same name as the account. requirements differ by jurisdiction and by firm, and a document accepted by one firm can be rejected by another for reasons such as a name mismatch, an expired date or an address that does not match the account details exactly.

complete kyc before reaching the profit threshold. verification queues are not instant, and a trader who reaches the threshold first waits at the gate rather than at the desk. doing it in the first week of the funded phase converts a delay into a formality.

use the same name, spelling and address everywhere. account registration, identity document, address document and payment method should match character for character. most kyc rejections are clerical rather than substantive.
photograph documents properly. glare, crop, angle and file size cause a surprising share of rejections. a flat, well-lit phone photo with all four corners visible is usually sufficient.

one clarification that matters for anyone using a third-party service during the evaluation: kyc is tied to the account holder, and it should be. the account is registered in your name, funded in your name and paid out to you. no passing service should ever request your identity documents, and any that does should be avoided.
with the conditions met, the withdrawal request enters the firm's processing queue. three variables determine how long it takes and how much arrives.

processing windows. some firms process payout requests on a fixed schedule - weekly, bi-weekly or monthly - rather than on demand. a request submitted the day after a processing run waits for the next one, which can add three weeks to a withdrawal that appeared to take two days.

method. bank transfer, cryptocurrency and e-wallet transfers have different speeds and different fee structures. firms differ on which are available and whether the method must match the payment method used to purchase the evaluation.

split and fees. the firm pays your share of the profit - typically 80-90% - and may deduct transfer fees. on a $10,000 payout at an 85% split, the arriving amount is $8,500 before any transfer costs, and the split percentage is worth less attention than the processing window.

a useful comparison habit: an 85% split paid weekly delivers cash more often than a 92% split paid monthly, and for a trader withdrawing regularly the difference over a year is larger than the headline percentage suggests. where a firm's split is unusually generous and its payout cycle unusually slow, that combination is usually deliberate.
the sequence is the same for both, but the practical experience differs in four ways that matter to how you plan the funded phase.

the consequence of the second row is underrated. on a futures account with a ten-day minimum, the funded phase is effectively an extension of the evaluation, and the rules that got you through the evaluation are the rules that get you through the waiting period. traders who treat funding as permission to change their approach tend to lose the account during the wait, before the first payout is ever requested.

a second difference is how the threshold interacts with consistency on futures accounts. because the threshold is a dollar figure and consistency is a ratio, a trader can meet the threshold and fail the ratio simultaneously - for example, reaching a $6,000 threshold with a $5,000 best day, which requires $16,667 of total profit under a 30% rule. reaching the threshold in that situation is not progress; it is a request that will be refused.
first payouts are usually about clearing the gate rather than maximizing income, and the reason is that most firms tie account growth to a demonstrated payout record.

scaling plans generally work in one of two ways. the first increases the profit split as payout milestones are met - 80% rising to 85% or 90% after a defined number of withdrawals. the second increases the account size, either by allocating additional accounts or by raising the balance on the existing one, sometimes conditioned on consistent monthly payouts rather than on a single large one.

both structures reward regularity over size. a trader who withdraws a moderate amount every month for six months accumulates a stronger record than one who withdraws a large amount once and then breaches a rule. that is not a moral point; it is how the plans are written, and it means the payout discipline described in this guide - small, evenly distributed daily profit, repeated - compounds into a larger funded account.

a practical sequencing note for traders intending to scale: pass one account, take one or two payouts on it, then add a second account rather than running two evaluations simultaneously. two funded accounts at once split attention, create correlated-position risks that firms treat as a single exposure, and delay the point at which either account produces income.
these are the causes we see most often, in roughly the order they occur.
one dominant day, total profit below the required multiple, withdrawal refused until the distribution changes. this is arithmetic rather than discretion, and no negotiation alters it.
the threshold is met, the request is submitted, and verification is requested for the first time. add several days to a week depending on the firm's queue.
an unrealised gain does not satisfy a threshold measured on closed profit. traders watching an open position that would push them over the line have not yet met the condition.
monthly payout windows are common and often buried in the terms. a firm advertising "fast payouts" may mean fast processing inside a fixed window rather than on-demand payment.

a day with no closed trade may not count, which quietly extends the requirement beyond what the trader expected. the fix is to close at least one small position on each intended day rather than holding positions open across sessions.
6. a rule interaction with the funded account's own limits

funded accounts have their own daily limits and drawdown conditions. a trader who spends the wait to the payout threshold trading aggressively can breach one of them, which ends the account and the pending withdrawal with it. the waiting period is the worst possible time to increase size, and it is exactly when many traders do.

the one-line summary: treat the funded phase as a second evaluation with different rules, complete kyc early, keep daily profit small and evenly distributed, and the first payout becomes a formality rather than a negotiation.
the sequence is easier to plan with dates attached. here is a realistic first payout on a $100,000 funded forex account with a 5% payout threshold, a ten-day minimum and a 30% consistency rule.
day 1 - funded credentials received. kyc is submitted the same day rather than at the payout request. the funded-phase rules are read: threshold, minimum days, consistency, payout window.

days 1-4 - small, capped sessions. daily profit is deliberately limited to roughly 0.4% of balance, which paces the 5% threshold across ten sessions and keeps every day comfortably under the consistency ratio. nothing dramatic; the objective during this phase is a clean record rather than a fast finish.

days 5-8 - kyc clears, progress continues. verification completes in the background while trading continues. by day 8 the account is at 3.1% of the threshold, with a best day of 0.6% - about 19% of total profit, well inside a 30% rule.

day 10 - minimum days satisfied. the threshold is reached on the same day the day count completes, which is the ideal outcome and the reason the pace was planned backwards from the minimum-day requirement rather than forwards from ambition.
day 11 - payout requested. the request is submitted with the day count complete, the threshold met on closed profit, the consistency ratio at 19% and kyc already approved. no gate is left open.

days 12-14 - processing. the withdrawal clears inside the firm's processing window and the trader's share of $5,000 arrives after the split is applied. on an 85% split that is $4,250 before transfer costs.

afterwards - the cycle repeats. the threshold resets, so the same disciplined pace is required for the next withdrawal. traders who maintain it find the second payout easier, because both the ratio history and the kyc requirement are already established.

what made that sequence smooth: kyc before the threshold, pacing planned backwards from the minimum-day requirement, daily profit capped well inside the consistency rule, and no attempt to accelerate once the finish was in sight. each of those is a scheduling decision made before the funded phase began.
traders often assume the funded account is the evaluation with a bigger target. it is a different rulebook, and knowing which conditions change prevents the most common funded-phase losses.

the pattern in that table explains a widely reported frustration - that the evaluation was easier than the funded account. evaluations punish risk: a trader who takes modest, consistent positions passes. funded accounts punish concentration: a trader who banks one large day cannot withdraw until the distribution changes. a trader who passes by grinding and then switches to a larger, more directional style on the funded account has adopted the one behaviour the funded rules penalise.

keep the evaluation's risk discipline on the funded account. the daily limit may be relaxed, but the consistency rule is not, and the threshold resets with every payout. trading the funded account at double the evaluation's risk converts a relaxed limit into an unused safety margin and a concentrated profit history into a delayed withdrawal.

write the funded plan before the handover. most traders arrive at the funded phase with a detailed evaluation plan and no plan at all for what comes next. the four numbers that matter are the same as before - risk per trade, maximum daily risk, daily profit cap and the day on which the payout will be requested - plus the kyc deadline. writing them down takes ten minutes and removes the improvisation that funded accounts punish.

almost every question about payouts is really a question about timing, and timing is a planning problem rather than a performance one. three numbers determine when money actually arrives: the first day on which the payout can be requested, the firm's processing window, and the speed of the withdrawal method.

the first number is the one traders control. it is the later of two dates: the day the minimum-day requirement completes, and the day the profit threshold is met on closed trades. planning backwards from that date - dividing the threshold by the number of available sessions and checking the result against the daily profit cap - produces a schedule in which the two dates coincide. improvising forwards usually means one of them is reached weeks before the other, and the interim period is spent holding an account at target with a consistency ratio at risk.

the processing window is the number traders most often discover late. a firm that processes withdrawals weekly has a worst-case wait of seven days on top of the day count; a firm with a monthly window can add three weeks to a request submitted the day after a run. where two firms are otherwise comparable, the shorter window is worth more than a couple of percentage points of split for a trader who withdraws regularly rather than compounding inside the account.

the third number - method speed - rarely changes the picture on its own, because method options are usually available to all traders at a firm. its practical relevance is administrative: the method used to purchase the evaluation sometimes has to match the method used for the payout, and confirming that early avoids a rejected request at the last step.

most firms require five to ten trading days of qualifying activity plus a profit threshold before the first payout request, then one to seven business days of processing. in practice the first withdrawal arrives three to six weeks after funding, with the biggest variable being whether kyc was completed in advance.
almost never. thresholds are measured on closed profit, so a large unrealised gain does not satisfy the condition. closing the position converts it into qualifying profit.

yes, most commonly for a consistency failure, incomplete kyc or a rule interaction on the funded account. the account is not usually closed - the withdrawal is deferred until the condition is met, or the request is resubmitted after verification.

on most firms, yes: the threshold applies to every withdrawal rather than being a one-time gate. some firms reduce the requirement after a number of payouts or tie it to a scaling plan, so the specific answer belongs to the firm's funded-account terms.

usually a day with at least one position opened and closed. holding a position across sessions without closing anything may not count, which is why the plan opens and closes something small on each intended day during the minimum-day period.

it varies by firm and jurisdiction, and the processing window matters more than the method itself. cryptocurrency and e-wallet transfers are typically faster where offered, but the firm's schedule - weekly, bi-weekly or monthly - usually dominates the timeline.

some firms allow it, and where they do it can be useful: a smaller requested amount may satisfy a consistency ratio measured against the withdrawal rather than against total profit. confirm the measurement basis in writing before relying on it.
what happens if the account breaches a rule during the payout wait?

the account ends and any pending payout goes with it. funded accounts carry their own daily limits and drawdown conditions, and the waiting period to a payout is the worst time to increase size - which is statistically when many traders do.

they usually drive it. most scaling plans increase the split percentage or the account size based on a record of completed payouts, which rewards regularity over a single large withdrawal. a steady monthly record compounds into a larger funded account over time.

elitepropx does not. the fee is a flat $220 paid before the evaluation; the funded account and 100% of what it earns belong to the account holder. any service taking a share of payouts should be treated with the same scrutiny as a copy-trading arrangement.
when a payout is refused, and what the refusal usually means

a refused withdrawal is the moment the rules stop being abstract, and the reason is almost never the one the trader assumes. refusals cluster into five causes, and four of them were knowable before the request was made.

the most common refusal is distribution, not profitability. the firm measures the best day as a share of total profit at the moment of the request, and a single outsized session can push that ratio above the threshold even when the account is comfortably in profit. the fix is to add ordinary profit rather than to argue: required total equals best day divided by the consistency percentage, and the difference is the amount of quiet trading still to do.

many funded accounts require a set number of trading days before the first withdrawal, and a day only counts if a position was opened. a trader who reaches a profit threshold in four sessions may be waiting another fortnight for the calendar, not the market. requests submitted before both conditions are met are usually refused without prejudice, which is better than a rejection but still costs a processing cycle.

some firms require a flat book at the moment of the request, and a request submitted with a position open can be refused or queued. this is a small thing that becomes large at a month end when the processing window closes: a trader who submits at 23:50 with a position open may wait another cycle for a technicality.

firms audit funded accounts, sometimes after the fact, and a payout can be held while a review is open - a position held over a weekend on an account type that does not allow it, a news event that was restricted, a strategy that the terms describe as prohibited. this is the refusal that hurts most and the one where the trader has the least recourse, because the enforcement clause was in the rulebook from day one.

name mismatches, an unverified wallet, a bank account in a different name from the trading account. these are administrative and usually fixable in a day, but they can consume a processing cycle if discovered at the request stage rather than at the start. setting up and verifying payment details on day one is the cheapest insurance in the entire process.

the last row deserves a note. some firms offer to credit a payout to a new account at a favourable rate instead of paying it out. that can be a good deal for a trader who intends to keep trading and understands that the money is now a claim on the firm rather than a balance in a bank. it is a poor deal for anyone who wanted the money in the first place.

payouts are income and are treated as such in most jurisdictions, though the exact classification - trading income, self-employment, other income - varies and is worth confirming with an accountant in the country where the trader is resident. two practical points are worth more than a general disclaimer.

first, keep a record of every payout with its date, amount, currency and the firm that paid it, alongside the fee paid to enter the evaluation. the fee is usually a deductible expense against the income, and reconstructing that record a year later is far more expensive than keeping it as it arrives. second, treat crypto payouts as valued at receipt rather than at withdrawal, because the taxable event is normally the receipt of value, not the moment the coins are sold.

most firms describe the relationship as a simulated account with performance-based remuneration, not a brokerage account with client funds. that distinction matters practically: there is no segregated client money, no investor protection scheme, and the payout is a contractual payment rather than a withdrawal of owned assets. reading the agreement once, before the first request, removes a category of expectation that no amount of forum reading repairs.

it also clarifies what a funded account is worth. the account is a licence to earn a share of simulated profits under a specific rulebook, and the licence can be revoked under that rulebook. that is not a reason to avoid the model; it is a reason to keep the payout cycle short and not to treat an unpaid balance with the firm as savings.

the practical consequence is a rule of thumb: request the first payout as soon as the rules allow it, even if the amount is small. a payout that has arrived is real; a balance that has not been requested is a number on a dashboard that the next bad week can reduce.

small, frequent withdrawals also make the accounting simpler: each payout is a dated, documented event, and a series of them is a better record than one large transfer whose origin is harder to explain.

fundednext sells evaluations in two shapes - a staged two-phase model and a faster one-phase model - and the failure mechanics differ between them in ways that change how a plan should be sized. this guide works through the two drawdown figures, the target arithmetic that decides pace, the consistency gate at payout, and the specific behaviours that end attempts. everything is written as mechanism rather than as quoted numbers, because the numbers change and the mechanics do not.
two drawdown figures apply at once: a daily limit that resets each session and a maximum limit that does not. the binding one is whichever is closer to current equity that morning.
the one-phase model asks for one larger target instead of two smaller ones, which concentrates risk into a single arc rather than splitting it. for most traders that is harder, not easier.
pace is a decision, not a discovery. working backwards from a target date produces a required daily profit, which can be checked against the daily limit before the first trade.
a consistency rule applied at payout means the largest day must stay well under the permitted share of total profit - so a fast pass built on one dominant session can produce an unpayable account.
most breaches are conduct breaches: news windows, sizing caps and weekend holding, not drawdown.
terms change. confirm the current figures on the firm's own pages; this guide describes the structure, not a contract.
the first decision is not the account size. it is the model, because the model determines how many separate targets must be cleared and how long the account is exposed to the rules.

a two-phase evaluation splits the work. the first phase asks for a profit target while holding inside the drawdown limits; clearing it moves the account to a second phase with its own target and its own minimum day count. the advantage is that each phase is smaller and the trader gets a genuine checkpoint at the halfway mark. the disadvantage is duration: twice the calendar means twice the exposure to the daily limit, and the number of sessions in which something can go wrong roughly doubles.

a one-phase evaluation asks for the whole target in a single arc. there is one checkpoint - the end - and the calendar is shorter. this is usually marketed as easier, and in one narrow sense it is: there is no second phase to fail. in every other sense it is harder, because the target is larger relative to the starting balance, the daily limit has to survive the entire distance without a reset in the middle, and a single bad session costs proportionally more of the evaluation.
two checkpoints versus one: the one-phase model is shorter and less forgiving of a single bad session.

which is better depends on a single trader characteristic: how much a losing week costs you psychologically. a trader who can absorb a bad week and continue at planned size is better served by the two-phase model, because the smaller per-phase target means the plan's risk per trade can be lower and the account has more room for ordinary variance. a trader who abandons a plan after two bad days is better served by the shorter model, not because it is easier but because the exposure is shorter. that is a statement about behaviour, not about the rulebook.

the test: look at your last twenty sessions. if the maximum losing streak was three and you kept size constant, the two-phase model is the better purchase. if a three-loss streak made you double the next position, fix that before buying either.

there is a second structural difference that matters more than it appears. on a two-phase account, the second phase begins after a passing moment, and the natural instinct is to trade the second phase as a continuation of the first - same instruments, same size, same expectations. but the drawdown has reset to the new balance, which means the account starts the second phase with a full buffer and an empty record. traders who carry the first phase's aggression into the second are carrying the wrong lesson: the first phase proved that the plan works at that size, not that the size should now increase.
two loss limits apply, and they measure different things. confusing them is the most expensive mistake available on this kind of account.

the daily drawdown governs the session. it resets each trading day, so a loss that reaches it ends the day and leaves the account intact. its purpose is to prevent a single session from destroying a multi-week evaluation, and it is the limit that most failures actually hit.

the maximum drawdown governs the account. it does not reset, and reaching it closes the evaluation. its purpose is to cap the total damage a plan can do, and it is the limit that traders plan for and then breach while thinking about the other one.

both figures may be expressed either as a percentage of the starting balance or as a percentage of current equity, and the choice changes the account's behaviour as it moves. a limit measured from the starting balance is static in dollars: it does not move when you profit, so a winning account's cushion grows in absolute terms. a limit measured from current equity moves with the balance, so a profitable account has proportionally more room but a losing account has absolutely less - the floor rises toward the price.

the distinction matters because most traders assume the more forgiving structure. check which basis applies before doing any arithmetic, and if the terms state a percentage without saying which balance it is a percentage of, treat that as an unresolved question rather than as a detail. the difference is large enough to change whether a given risk per trade is survivable.
one limit resets every morning; the other is spent once. size from the smaller, and count losses against the larger.

the working method is a two-line calculation each morning. line one: current equity minus the maximum drawdown floor equals the total room left on the account. line two: current equity minus the daily limit equals the room available today. the smaller of the two is the number the plan must respect, and neither is a suggestion.

early in an evaluation the maximum floor is usually distant and the daily limit binds. late in an evaluation, after a drawdown has been spent, the maximum floor can be closer than the daily limit permits, and then the daily limit is a fiction - you cannot lose the daily maximum without closing the account. a trader who computes only the daily number will be surprised by exactly one session, and it will be the last one.
a profit target is only meaningful as a percentage of the account, and pace is only meaningful as a rate relative to the daily limit. both conversions are simple and both are routinely skipped.

convert first. a dollar target on a $200,000 account is a different evaluation from the same dollar target on a $50,000 account, even though the marketing page shows the dollar figure in both places. divide the target by the balance to get the percentage, then compare that percentage across firms and across account sizes. this is the only figure that transfers.

then pace. choose a target date - not the firm's deadline, your own - and divide the target by the number of sessions you intend to work. on a target of 8% over twenty sessions, the required average is 0.4% per session. compare that with the daily limit: if the daily limit is 5%, the required pace uses under a tenth of the daily budget, which tells you that a disciplined plan has enormous room for ordinary losing days. if the required pace is a third of the daily limit, the plan has almost no tolerance for variance, and the target date is the thing that should change.
target as a percentage, then pace as a fraction of the daily budget. two divisions that decide whether a plan is achievable.

read the last column as a measure of fragility. a plan whose required pace consumes 5% of the daily budget per session can absorb twenty losing sessions of a fifth of the daily limit and still be alive; a plan at 20% can absorb five. both may pass, but the second depends on the market cooperating within a narrow window, and the first depends on the plan being executed. only one of those is under the trader's control.

the practical recommendation is a pace that consumes under a tenth of the daily budget per session on average. that sounds slow, and it is - twenty sessions at 0.4% is eight percent, which is a realistic evaluation. the reason traders resist it is that the fee is paid up front and the calendar feels like a cost. it is; it is just a smaller cost than a second fee.
consistency rules vary in where they apply and how they are measured, and the difference decides whether a fast pass is an achievement or a liability.

where a rule applies at payout, the arithmetic is a single division. total profit must reach the largest day divided by the permitted share. a $2,500 best day under a 30% rule needs $8,334 of total profit. a $5,000 best day under the same rule needs $16,667. the larger the best day, the more total profit is required, which means the fastest route to a large profit is also the slowest route to a withdrawal.

where a rule applies during the evaluation itself, it constrains the pass rather than the payout, and the effect is more direct: a trader who reaches the target on one dominant session may not have completed the evaluation at all. either way, the correct planning response is the same, and it is a daily profit cap set at roughly a third of the target. on an 8% target, that is about 2.7% per session - comfortably inside a 30% best-day share by construction, because the largest day is a third of the total and the total is the target.
at target, not at payout. the consistency ratio is computed from realised profit, so one large session can block a withdrawal indefinitely.

there is a subtlety about measurement that trips traders even when they know the rule exists. some firms measure the best day against total profit, others against the payout amount, and some measure the share of total profit at the moment of the request rather than at the target. if the rule is measured at the request, then a trader at exactly the threshold with a best day at exactly the permitted share is in a knife-edge position: one ordinary session improves the ratio, one unusually good session makes it worse. in that situation, the right move is to keep trading at reduced size until the ratio has clear headroom, not to submit and hope.

set the cap before the first trade. a daily profit cap converts a payout rule into a habit. a trader who caps the day at a third of the target never has to compute the consistency ratio at all - the arithmetic is satisfied in advance, every time.
five numbers define a workable plan, and each follows from one of the rules above. write them down; a plan held in memory is a plan that changes under pressure.
risk per trade: a third of the daily limit at most. this makes three consecutive losses survivable within the session, which is the property that decides whether a plan can be executed at all.
daily stop: stop opening positions once 80% of the daily budget is realised. the last fifth exists to absorb slippage on the closing trade, not to be spent on a recovery attempt.
daily profit cap: about a third of the target, which satisfies a 30% consistency rule by construction and protects the ratio without further arithmetic.

loss count against the maximum: divide the total room by the risk per trade to get the number of losing trades the account can absorb. if that number is under six, the account size is too small for the risk, or the risk is too large for the account.

weekly loss pause: a hard stop at two losing sessions in a week. the pause costs nothing on a static drawdown structure and prevents the sequence that ends most accounts - three losses, a size increase, and a fourth.
one budget, three consumers. per-trade risk, the daily stop and an untouched reserve that the plan never reaches.

the fifth number is the one traders argue with, and it is the one that produces the largest change in outcomes. a trader who stops for the week after two losing sessions turns a bad week into a two-session event. a trader who continues turns it into a series, because the losses compound in both directions: the balance falls and the emotional pressure to recover rises, which is precisely when size grows.

there is an honest objection to the pause: on a one-phase model with a self-imposed deadline, stopping costs calendar. that is true, and it is still correct. the calendar cost of two days off is a few sessions; the calendar cost of a failed evaluation is the whole thing, plus a new fee, plus the time to re-earn the confidence. the pause is cheap by comparison.

drawdown limits are the rules everyone reads. conduct rules are the ones that actually end a large share of attempts, because they are easy to breach by accident and almost impossible to argue about afterwards.

news windows. trading around scheduled economic releases is usually restricted, with the window defined in minutes either side of the release. the detail that matters is whether a position must be closed before the window or merely not opened inside it. if the rule requires closure and you hold through, the breach is not the profit or loss; it is the position itself.

sizing caps. maximum lots or contracts per position are frequently stated in the terms rather than on the evaluation page. trading a permitted instrument at twice the permitted size is a breach even if the risk in dollars is identical, because the cap is about position size rather than exposure.

prohibited strategies. latency arbitrage, exploiting demo or price-feed errors, group hedging and copy-trading between accounts are prohibited nearly everywhere. the last one catches traders who run a personal account and an evaluation account with mirrored positions, which can be read as hedging against the firm.

weekend and overnight holding. forex positions held over a weekend carry gap risk that a fixed drawdown may not survive. where holding is permitted, the position needs to be sized for the gap rather than for the stop, because a gap can open beyond the stop and the loss is then the gap, not the stop.

account sharing. logins are personal and location checks are routine. a service that trades an evaluation must do so under the terms the firm permits; where third-party trading is banned, a flat-fee pass is not available and a provider that accepts the job anyway is putting the client's funded account at risk of being voided at payout.
failure is patterned. these six account for the great majority of lost evaluations on a two-limit forex account.
hitting the daily limit on the first trade. almost always a sizing problem rather than an analysis problem: the position was too large for the budget, so a normal adverse move consumed the session.
recovering after the daily limit. the limit ends the day, not the evaluation. traders who reopen a position after the limit has been hit convert a recoverable day into a breach.
spending the maximum drawdown in one week. three bad sessions at full risk, followed by a doubled position to recover, is the classic sequence. the weekly pause exists to break it.
one dominant day. efficient to reach the target, expensive at the payout gate, and usually the product of a position that should have been closed earlier.
trading the news window. a rule breach that has nothing to do with profit and everything to do with conduct, and it is checked automatically.
continuing after the target. reaching the target is not the same as satisfying the minimum day count, and a trader filling days with size is adding risk to a finished evaluation.

the unifying cause is not a lack of market skill. it is a plan that was never written down, executed under pressure by a trader who was improvising. every one of the six is prevented by a number on a page: risk per trade, daily stop, daily cap, weekly pause, a news calendar and a minimum day count. that is the entire countermeasure, and it costs a page.
passing produces a funded account, and the funded account is a different product with different conditions. three gates apply, and they are usually stricter than the evaluation.

minimum day count. a payout typically requires a number of qualifying trading days, and a qualifying day is often one with a closed profit rather than merely a closed position. that changes pacing: a trader who reaches the profit threshold in a week may need another two weeks of small positive sessions, and the efficient plan lands both conditions on the same date.

the consistency check. applied at the payout request in most cases. as above, the required total is the best day divided by the permitted share, and the correct response when the ratio is tight is smaller size and ordinary profit rather than another strong session.

verification and timing. identity checks should be complete before the first request, and the first withdrawal is usually the slowest. requesting the first payout at the earliest permitted date rather than at the largest available amount is the correct strategy, because the purpose of the first payment is to prove the pipe works.
the funded stage is a calendar with two mathematical gates attached, not a continuation of the evaluation.

the funded phase also usually introduces a scaling path: a record of completed payouts unlocks larger balances or additional accounts. that changes the calculus of the first few months. a trader choosing between maximising the first payout and building a clean record is choosing between a small amount of money now and a larger balance later, and the second is nearly always worth more. the payout process guide covers the sequence in detail.
four comparisons cover most of the decision, and all four are structural.

against ftmo: both are staged forex evaluations with a daily and a maximum limit, and the useful question is which balance each limit is measured from and how the consistency rule is applied. ftmo's rulebook is the most widely documented in the industry, which makes it easier to verify and harder to misread. the ftmo guide sets out the structure, and the passing walkthrough covers execution.

against topstep: a futures firm with an explicit daily limit, a trailing threshold and a best-day expectation applied to the evaluation. the instruments differ, the mechanics rhyme. if you trade both asset classes, compare the percentage targets and the drawdown bases rather than the dollar figures. the fundednext versus topstep comparison does that directly.

against e8 markets: a comparison usually framed as which is easier, which is really a question about drawdown basis and target percentage. the e8 versus fundednext comparison works the arithmetic rather than quoting a verdict.

against a flat-fee pass: the option that removes evaluation risk entirely for a fixed fee. the trade-off is explicit - the service absorbs the reset cost, the firm's rules still govern the funded account, and the arrangement is only available where third-party trading is permitted. the 2026 service review sets out what to verify before paying anyone.
compare firms on how the failure floor is measured, then on target percentage, then on fee - in that order.

the general rule for all four comparisons: a lower fee on a stricter structure is not cheaper, because it is bought more than once. multiply the fee by the number of attempts a trader of your discipline typically needs, and the ranking usually reverses.
an 8% target on a $100,000 account, a 5% daily limit, a 10% maximum drawdown, risk of 1.5% per trade and a daily profit cap of 2.7%. the plan runs four sessions a week for five weeks.
week one - +2.1%. three sessions, one small loss. nothing remarkable, which is the point: the first week exists to prove the plan executes, not to make progress.
week two - +3.4%. two strong sessions, one capped at 2.7% and closed early, one ordinary, one flat. cumulative 5.5%, which is 69% of the target with three weeks of calendar left.

week three - −1.8%. two losing sessions and a pause. the pause is the important line in this record: the plan stopped at two losses rather than continuing to a third, and the week closed 1.8% down with the daily limit and the maximum both intact.
week four - +2.9%. four ordinary sessions. cumulative 6.6%, target 83% complete. the daily cap is now doing the work: every session that reaches it is closed rather than extended.
week five - +1.5%. two sessions at reduced size complete the target, and the minimum day count is satisfied on the same day because the pace was planned backwards from the requirement.

the record contains one losing week, one capped strong session and no dominant day. the largest day is 2.7% against a total of 8.1%, a share of 33% - which satisfies a 30% rule only marginally, and this is exactly where a plan should be tightened rather than celebrated. a cap at a quarter of the target would have produced a largest day of 2.0% and a share of 25%, with more headroom at the payout gate.

the lesson from the table is not the total. it is that the plan never used more than 54% of the daily limit on any day, never spent more than 1.8% of a 10% maximum in a week, and finished with the best-day share inside tolerance. a trader could run this plan four times in a year and only need one to pass; a trader running a 20% per session pace would need the market to cooperate in a specific fortnight.
the funded account has three jobs, in order: satisfy verification, complete the minimum day count, and produce a first withdrawal small enough to be unremarkable. everything else is a distraction.

verification first, because it is the one task with a fixed external dependency and the longest tail. complete it in week one, including any address or source-of-funds documentation, and keep the confirmation. a payout request blocked on an unverified document can delay the first payment by weeks, and the delay is entirely self-inflicted.

then the day count, which is a calendar problem rather than a trading problem. a qualifying day usually needs a closed profit, so the plan should produce small positive days deliberately rather than waiting for a good session to count. a single closed trade that keeps the day green satisfies the count without adding meaningful risk, and it is a perfectly legitimate way to finish the requirement.

then the withdrawal, requested at the earliest permitted date and at a modest size. the first payout's purpose is to prove the pipe: that the request is accepted, the review clears, the payment arrives and the account continues afterwards. a trader who maximises the first withdrawal is optimising a number before testing the process that delivers it.

what not to do in month one is equally specific. do not increase size because the evaluation is over. do not take a position through a news window because the rule felt like an evaluation formality. do not hold a weekend gap on a position sized for a stop. and do not treat a funded account with a static floor as an invitation to trade bigger - the floor is static, but the consistency gate is not, and the payout is the thing being protected.

for readers weighing the do-it-yourself route against a flat-fee pass, the arithmetic is in the profit calculator and the honest trade-offs are in the service comparison . the short version: a flat $220 pass removes evaluation risk and reset cost, the firm's rules still apply to the funded account, and the arrangement is only legitimate where the firm permits third-party trading. where it does not, the service should decline before payment rather than after.

the two-phase model is easier for most traders, because each phase has a smaller target and the account gets a genuine checkpoint. the one-phase model is shorter, so it is better for a trader whose discipline breaks down over a long calendar - but the single larger target makes it less tolerant of one bad session.

whichever is closer to current equity on the morning you are trading. early in an evaluation the daily limit usually binds; after a drawdown has been spent, the maximum limit can sit closer than the daily limit permits. compute both and use the smaller.
is the drawdown measured from the starting balance or current equity?

it varies by model and can change between the evaluation and the funded account, so check the current terms rather than assuming. a limit measured from the starting balance is static in dollars; one measured from current equity moves with the balance and gives a profitable account proportionally more room.

fifteen to twenty-five trading days at a pace that consumes under a tenth of the daily budget per session. faster passes are possible but tend to create a consistency problem at the payout gate that takes longer to resolve than the pass saved.

a third of the daily limit at most, with the session closed once 80% of the budget is realised. on a 5% daily limit that is roughly 1.7% per trade, which survives three consecutive losses and leaves the account alive.
what is the consistency rule and when does it apply?

a cap on how much of total profit any single day may represent, applied at the payout request in most cases and during the evaluation in some. required total profit equals the best day divided by the permitted share, so a $2,500 best day under a 30% rule needs about $8,334 of total profit.

usually only outside defined windows around scheduled releases, and the rule may require positions to be closed before the window rather than merely not opened inside it. treat the window as closed regardless of what the market is doing.

policies differ by model. where holding is allowed, size for the gap rather than for the stop, because a weekend gap can open beyond the stop and the loss becomes the gap. where it is not allowed, be flat before the close rather than leaving it to chance.

the session ends and the account continues with a fresh daily budget against the same maximum floor. reopening a position after the limit is a breach in itself, and it is the most common way a recoverable day becomes a failed evaluation.

no. the funded account has its own minimum day count, consistency check, verification requirements and sometimes a first-payout waiting period. a pass is the audition; the payout conditions are the contract.

no. correlated positions across accounts can be read as hedging, and split attention produces worse execution on both. sequential funding - pass one, trade it, then add a second - is slower to start and faster to reach a first payout.

only if the firm's terms permit third-party trading. many firms prohibit it, and a funded account passed in breach of the terms can be voided at payout. the flat $220 arrangement is offered where it is permitted, and declined where it is not - the service reviews explain how to check.
