there is no single best prop firm, only a best fit for a style, a budget and a rulebook tolerance. this guide explains what "best" has to mean for you, how to compare firms whose marketing looks identical, and how to run the comparison in an afternoon.
difficulty is set by three mechanics: whether the maximum loss trails, how the daily limit is measured, and what happens at payout.
for a first account, a static drawdown and no payout consistency rule beat a lower fee every time.
payout reliability matters as much as difficulty and is judged separately - from the terms, not the testimonials.
account size is the last decision, not the first: percentage rules are identical at every size.

any page ranking prop firms is doing one of two things: selling referrals, or describing its own preferences. neither is a ranking, because there is nothing to rank on. firms differ in rulebooks, payout speed and reliability, and those three dimensions point in different directions for different traders.

the useful reframing is that a firm is a set of constraints, and the best firm is the one whose constraints your trading style can satisfy repeatedly without changing what you do. a scalper with tight exits can survive an intraday trailing drawdown that would ruin a swing trader. a swing trader can thrive on a static drawdown that bores a scalper to the point of over-trading. neither firm is better; one of them fits.

first, can i reach the target on this rulebook without breaching a limit? second, will the payout arrive when the rules say it should? third, can i afford to fail here, including the firm's own reset terms? a firm that answers yes, yes and yes is the best firm for that trader, whatever any comparison table says.

firms advertise account size and fee, because those are the two numbers that can be compared without reading anything. they under-emphasise drawdown mechanics and payout conditions, which are the two numbers that decide outcomes. a buyer who has learned to look at the second pair can compare firms that market themselves as incomparable.
the drawdown mechanism is the first of the three mechanics, and the one most often misread in a comparison table.

a static maximum loss sits at a fixed level - on a $100,000 account with a 10% limit, the failure line is $90,000 and never moves. a trailing maximum loss follows peak equity, so profit reduces the room available rather than increasing it. on an intraday trailing model, an unrealised gain that comes back to entry still leaves the failure line higher than it was, which charges the trader twice for the same movement.

this single difference changes what a trader can do. on a static account, size can stay constant from the first trade to the last. on a trailing account, size must shrink as equity rises, because the room for a normal losing sequence is shrinking at the same time as confidence is rising. traders who fail trailing accounts almost always fail by ignoring that second half.

a daily limit measured on closed balance allows a position to move against you intraday without a breach, as long as it recovers or is closed inside the limit. a limit measured on equity including floating positions counts the worst moment of the day, which is a stricter and more common rule. the practical effect is on stop placement and position size, not on strategy: a trader on the equity version needs the eighty-percent stop, and a trader on the balance version can afford to be less precise.

consistency rules live at payout rather than at evaluation at most firms, and they are the most common reason a profitable account cannot withdraw. a 30% best-day rule means the best session cannot exceed 30% of total profit at the moment of the request. an account at target with one dominant day is not a failed evaluation; it is a delayed payout, and the delay is planned for or suffered.
firms cluster into recognisable types once mechanics are used as the organising principle rather than brand.

usually forex and cfd firms. the most forgiving structure available: a trader can hold size constant, can give back an unrealised gain without the floor moving, and can reach a payout without worrying about the distribution of profit. this is the correct first firm for almost everyone, at a slightly higher fee than the alternatives.

usually futures firms. harder in two ways at once, and popular because account sizes and payout ceilings are attractive. suited to traders with tight exits and genuinely small best days - scalpers, mostly - and to traders who can plan a distribution deliberately rather than accidentally.

skips the evaluation and charges more for it, with a first-payout condition that is often heavier than the evaluation it replaced. sensible for a trader who has already passed evaluations and whose constraint is time; a poor first purchase, because the evaluation phase is where the routine is built.

cheap per month and expensive over a year, with terms that reward duration. the payout schedule decides whether it is worth it: a firm that pays frequently on a subscription model can be good value, and one that pays monthly on a slow process usually is not.
evaluation rules decide whether you pass; funded rules decide whether the pass is worth anything.
difficulty decides whether an account is passable. payout terms decide whether passing it was worth anything. three conditions do most of the work.

most funded programs require a profit threshold plus a minimum number of trading days before the first withdrawal. the efficient plan lands both on the same date; the inefficient plan reaches the threshold in week one and waits three weeks for the calendar, trading the whole time with a live floor.

where it exists, compute the gap before requesting: required total profit equals best day divided by the threshold percentage. if the account shows less than that, the request will be refused, and the fix is small ordinary profit rather than a second large session.

on-demand withdrawals are worth more than a marginally higher profit split, because money that can be requested is money that can be banked. monthly windows, name-matching requirements and slow processing all delay the only event that proves the arrangement works.

ask for the last three payout dates the firm processed for accounts of the size you are considering. a firm that cannot answer is not necessarily unreliable; a firm that answers with a specific pattern has told you something concrete about how it operates when money is due.
the comparison below uses two fictionalised firms with realistic structures. the point is the method, which works on any pair.

firm a offers a $100,000 account for $540 with a 10% target, a 5% daily limit measured on equity, a static 10% maximum loss and no consistency rule. firm b offers $100,000 for $450 with an 8% target, a 5% daily limit, an intraday trailing maximum loss and a 30% best-day rule at payout.

at 1.5% risk per trade - $1,500 - firm a's daily limit allows three losses and its maximum loss allows six and a half. firm b's daily limit is identical, and its maximum loss starts at six and a half losses but shrinks with every new equity high: at 3% profit the room is closer to five losses, at 6% profit it is closer to four.

firm a needs 6.7 full-risk wins; firm b needs 5.3. on paper b is faster. combined with the shrinking tolerance, b is also the account where a normal losing sequence near the target is most likely to end the attempt, which is precisely when a trader is most tempted to hold size.

a payout requires a distribution under b's 30% rule. a trader with one strong session - common on a small target - must keep trading to dilute it before withdrawing. a has no such condition, so the pass converts to cash sooner even though the target is larger.

b is $90 cheaper and harder. expected cost is fee divided by pass probability: at 55% on a and 40% on b, that is roughly $980 against $1,125, before counting the reset terms and the extra weeks. a wins on expected cost despite the higher headline price, and it wins by more once the wasted time is priced.
for a first evaluation the objective is not the best payout ceiling; it is the highest probability of a clean pass followed by a payout. that rules out the harder structures on purpose.

intraday trailing is a mechanic to learn later, ideally once the daily routine is established. a first account should not punish a trader for giving back an unrealised gain, because that is the behaviour every new trader has to unlearn anyway.
consistency rules are manageable and they add a second puzzle to the first. for a first attempt, choose a firm where passing is enough.
step three: an explicit daily limit that can be tracked
a daily limit measured on equity is fine, and it must be explicit - firms that express the daily limit only through the trailing floor leave a trader guessing about the number that ends a session.

on-demand or frequent payouts matter for a first funded account because the first withdrawal is where the arrangement is proved. waiting a month to learn whether the pipe works is a slow way to learn it.

percentage rules are identical at every size, so a larger account buys a bigger ceiling and a bigger bill. sequence instead: pass one, trade it to a payout, then decide whether a second account adds anything beyond administration.
step six: read the reset terms before buying, not after failing

the cost of a second attempt is part of the price of the first. where a service covers retries at the same firm and size - as this one does under a flat $220 - the failure case is bounded and the comparison between two firms becomes a comparison of difficulty rather than of exposure.
when the evaluation is not going to be traded by the person paying for it, the selection criteria shift. difficulty still matters, and two additional questions become decisive.

policies vary and some firms enforce them after funding rather than during the evaluation, which is the worst possible moment for a client. any provider that treats this as a technicality is transferring its own risk. the honest approach is to ask the firm in writing, keep the reply, and decline assignments where the position is prohibition with credible enforcement.

the account should be issued to the client, with payouts paid directly and no profit split. a provider holding the login or receiving the money introduces counterparty risk at the point where the client has the most to lose, and it creates an incentive to delay that no amount of goodwill fixes.

firms with static or end-of-day drawdowns, clear daily limits and on-request payouts are the best fit, because the plan does not need to change shape as equity moves. firms with intraday trailing floors are workable but demand a stricter exit discipline, and firms whose terms are ambiguous should be avoided entirely: an unclear rulebook becomes a dispute, and a dispute is the one outcome that costs the client more than a failed attempt.
a headline drawdown with a footnote that changes it. "10% drawdown" plus a trailing clause is a different product from a static 10%.
no stated daily limit. expressing the daily limit only through a trailing floor leaves the most important number unstated.
payout terms that require a support request to read. terms that are not published are terms that can change quietly.
account sizes that scale faster than payouts. very large accounts with monthly payout windows and high thresholds are marketing assets, not income.
reviews that all appear in one week. not fraudulent, and not information.
no published answer on third-party trading. silence on the question that decides whether a funded account survives.

it states the target, the daily limit and its measurement point, the maximum loss mechanic and whether it trails, the minimum trading days, the payout conditions and the prohibitions - on one page, without a support ticket. firms that publish all of that are not automatically better traders' firms, and they are far easier to plan around, which is most of what a trader needs.

firms revise terms. targets move, drawdown mechanics change, payout windows tighten, and a rulebook read in march can describe a challenge that no longer exists in june. that reality belongs in the selection process rather than in a complaint afterwards.

date the rulebook when you read it, and re-read the objectives and payout pages before starting an attempt rather than before buying one. two minutes of re-reading catches the most expensive category of surprise: an evaluation planned against mechanics that have moved.

if a target rises or a drawdown becomes stricter mid-evaluation, the plan's arithmetic changes and size must be recalculated rather than assumed. where the change makes the target unreachable within the original risk budget, the decision is between accepting a longer timeline at reduced size and abandoning the attempt. both are legitimate; continuing at the old size while hoping the old rules apply is not.

a firm that publishes its terms and updates them visibly is easier to plan around than one whose conditions surface in support tickets. it is also a reason to prefer firms that state mechanics on the objectives page rather than relying on a help centre article written two years earlier.

most firms offer a scaling path - either larger accounts as a trader proves consistent, or the ability to hold several accounts at once. both are worth reading carefully, because scaling terms determine what a funded account becomes after six months.

where scaling depends on "consistent performance" without stating a period, a profit level or a maximum drawdown, it is not a criterion; it is a possibility. ask for the specifics in writing. a firm that can state them has a policy; a firm that cannot has a marketing line.

three accounts traded with the same setup are one position at three times the size, with three failure thresholds that trip together. if several accounts are running, halve the per-account risk for each additional one so the combined exposure stays near the original figure. sequencing - pass one, fund it, trade it to a payout, then add - produces a funded portfolio faster than running several evaluations in parallel and splitting attention.

most traders imagine that a bigger account or more accounts will increase income, and discover that the constraint is the size of the edge rather than the size of the account. a single $50,000 account traded carefully to a monthly payout produces more than five accounts traded carelessly to a single reset.
list your style's requirements: static or trailing drawdown, holding period, instrument set.
read the payout section and compute the first-withdrawal condition in dollars.
convert target and limits into wins required and losses tolerated at your risk per trade.
check the reset and retry terms, including any firm charge.
confirm the third-party trading policy in writing if the evaluation will be traded for you.
choose the smallest size with a meaningful payout, and plan two attempts' worth of budget.

week one is spent establishing the four numbers and trading small - often at half the planned risk - while the routine settles. week two builds toward the target without letting any single day dominate, which protects the payout ratio later. week three is where size comes down as the target approaches, because progress reduces the room available for a normal losing sequence on any trailing account. week four converts the pass into a funded login and, if the dates align, into the first withdrawal request.

that sequence is unglamorous, repeatable and boring, which is exactly why it works and why it is rarely advertised. a firm chosen well and traded this way produces a funded account in three to five weeks. a firm chosen on price and traded on instinct produces a drawer of receipts and an opinion about the industry.
firms differ less by brand than by rulebook model and asset class.
ten firms is too many to evaluate and three is a shortlist. categories make the pruning mechanical.

decide which category your style fits, then shortlist only within it. a trader who does this before reading any review has already made the decision that most buyers spend a month failing to make, and the remaining questions - which firm in the category, at which size - are comparatively small.

a prop firm review is only useful if it tells you what will fail an account and what will delay a payout. this one works through alpha capital group's evaluation mechanics - the drawdown type, the daily limit, the trading clauses and the funded-stage conditions - then sets out which trader profile the structure suits and which six things to verify in the current terms before paying a fee. figures are described by mechanism rather than quoted as current, because terms in this industry change faster than any review.
the structure is a staged evaluation with a percentage target and a maximum loss, followed by a funded account with its own withdrawal conditions.
the drawdown mechanism, not the headline percentage, decides how much room the account actually has - read whether it trails or stays fixed before anything else.
the daily limit is the constraint most attempts touch first, so risk per trade has to be derived from it as well as from the maximum loss.

this is a mechanics review. it explains how the evaluation is built, what each clause does to a trading plan, and where the structure is generous or tight relative to alternatives. it is not a ranking, it is not sponsored, and it is not a substitute for the firm's own terms.

the reason for the restraint is straightforward. prop firm terms change: targets move, drawdown mechanisms are revised, payout schedules are adjusted, and account sizes are added or withdrawn. a review that quotes a specific fee or a specific percentage is accurate for a few months at best, and misleading afterwards - usually at exactly the moment someone is deciding whether to pay. describing the mechanism instead means the analysis stays useful even when the numbers move.

there is a second reason. the published marketing page and the contract are different documents, and the contract is the one that governs. a review built on the marketing page repeats the marketing. the sections below therefore focus on the clauses a trader can check in the actual terms, and on what each one implies for position size, calendar and payout timing.

where a figure is described as a mechanism - a staged evaluation, a percentage target, a maximum loss measured from the starting balance - that description is structural and stable. where a specific number would be needed to trade the account, read it from the firm's current documentation on the day you pay. that is not a hedge; it is the only accurate way to write about this industry.

one disclosure: elitepropx is an independent challenge-passing service and is not affiliated with alpha capital group or any other proprietary trading firm. firm names appear for identification only. if the firm's terms prohibit third-party trading, this service declines the work - and that check is described in the last section, because it is the single most consequential clause in any review like this one.

the offer follows the standard architecture of the category: a paid evaluation with one or more stages, each carrying a percentage profit target and governed by a percentage maximum loss, followed by a funded account with a profit split and withdrawal conditions.

three properties of that architecture are worth absorbing before the detail. percentage targets mean the challenge is scale-free, so a trader who has passed one stage knows exactly what the next requires in relative terms - only the fee and the payout change. a staged structure means the cost of a late breach is high, because completing stage one and failing stage two usually restarts the sequence. and a stated time limit means the calendar is not the trader's to choose, which changes the pace calculation from a preference into a constraint.

the practical consequence of the third point is underrated. on an evaluation with a deadline, the required weekly return is fixed by arithmetic: target divided by weeks available. that number sets the minimum risk per trade, and the minimum risk per trade has to be checked against the maximum loss and the daily limit. if the required pace does not fit the rules, the evaluation is not passable at a survivable size - which is information worth having before the fee rather than after the second reset.
every comparison of prop firms begins and ends with the drawdown, and almost every published comparison gets it wrong by quoting the headline percentage without the mechanism attached.

three mechanisms are in common use. a static maximum loss is fixed at the starting balance and never moves, so profit cannot make the account more fragile. an end-of-day trailing loss resets to the day's closing balance, so intraday spikes are forgiven but completed gains are locked in. an intraday trailing loss follows peak unrealised equity, which means open profit raises the failure point behind the trader and an ordinary retracement can breach from a winning position.

the same percentage produces three different accounts under those three mechanisms. a generous-looking static figure with a large buffer is more forgiving than a smaller trailing figure in almost every strategy that holds winners through pullbacks. conversely, a static figure with a tight buffer can be harsher than it looks, because the account has no room to absorb an early losing sequence before the plan has produced anything.
the same profit path touches three different floors. read the mechanism before comparing the number.

two further clauses belong to the same paragraph and are frequently missed. the first is whether the threshold is measured on balance or equity - equity includes open positions, which makes the limit tighter in practice for a trader who holds through drawdowns. the second is when the threshold is sampled: continuously, at the end of the trading day, or at the end of the firm's server day. a mechanism described as end-of-day that samples the highest unrealised equity of the session is intraday trailing with extra steps.

for planning purposes, the mechanism should be converted into one number: the distance from the current balance to the floor, in money, right now. that number, not the headline percentage, is what the position size must be built from. it changes daily on a trailing structure and never on a static one, and the difference is the reason a plan calibrated at the start of an evaluation can be oversized by the final third.
the daily limit is the constraint that ends the most attempts, because it fires on ordinary variance rather than on a catastrophic error.

the arithmetic is simple and unforgiving. if risk per trade is a large fraction of the daily limit, two or three consecutive losses close the session. with a win rate in the forties, three consecutive losses are a routine event - they occur several times within a few hundred trades. a plan whose risk line permits only two losses per session is therefore not a conservative plan; it is a plan that will spend a meaningful number of sessions on the sideline after a bad start.

two derivations follow, and the smaller one governs. risk per trade from the maximum loss: divide the maximum loss by the number of consecutive losses the plan must survive, typically eight to ten. risk per trade from the daily limit: divide the daily limit by the number of losses a session should absorb, typically four to six. the second number is usually the smaller, which is why the daily limit and not the maximum loss is the real constraint.

there is a definitional trap that costs traders an attempt. daily limits are measured from a defined start of day, and that start is the firm's server day, not the trader's local midnight. a trader in one time zone trading the overnight session can unintentionally spread what feels like one day's risk across two server days, or compress two days into one. either way, the limit behaves differently from the plan's assumption, and the discovery is expensive.

the remedy is to establish the boundary before the first trade and to build the session around it. if the boundary falls mid-session, split the session or shorten it. then write the daily loss in money, not percentage, at the top of the trading page - the moment of maximum loss is the worst possible time to do arithmetic.
the daily limit is a session budget. once it is spent, the only correct action is to stop.

a related clause worth locating: whether an open position that is losing counts against the daily limit as its unrealised loss grows, or only when it is closed. on an equity-based limit it counts continuously, which means a trader can breach without closing a trade. on a balance-based limit the loss is only recognised at exit, which permits a position to be held through a drawdown the plan did not authorise. neither is necessarily better, but the plan's stop rule has to match the one in force.
beyond the two headline limits, a rulebook contains a set of clauses that are individually reasonable and collectively capable of voiding an otherwise successful attempt.

news restrictions. many firms restrict opening or closing positions within a window around high-impact releases. the trap is not the restriction itself but the definition: which calendar, which tier of event, and whether the window applies to the trade or to the position. a trader who holds through a release rather than opening during it can breach a clause they believed applied only to entries.

weekend and overnight holding. standard accounts frequently restrict holding across the weekend or over specific periods, while swing accounts permit it at a different fee or a different leverage. on a standard account, a position left open on friday is not merely exposed to gap risk; it may be a rule breach regardless of the result. the weekend holding guide covers the gap arithmetic and the clauses to look for.

lot and contract caps. a maximum position size is usually stated per instrument or as a total. it is a ceiling, not a target, and it is checked at the moment of the trade rather than at the end of the day. a plan that scales into a position can breach a cap that the initial entry satisfied.

prohibited strategies. latency arbitrage, gap trading on stale quotes, and certain forms of copy trading are commonly excluded. the important question is not whether the strategy is named but whether it is described - a clause that prohibits "exploiting platform errors" is broad enough to cover behaviour a trader considers ordinary.

third-party trading and account management. this is the clause with the largest financial consequence, because a pass produced in breach of it can be voided at the payout request. crucially, the evaluation terms and the funded terms are separate documents and can answer differently. where either is ambiguous, the only reliable evidence is a written reply from support, kept on file.

each of these clauses has the same remedy: read the current terms before the fee, write the restrictions into the risk line as explicit no-go conditions, and where a clause is unclear, ask. a support ticket costs a day; a voided payout costs the evaluation, the pass and the funded account.
sizing on a percentage-based evaluation is arithmetic, and it fits on one line: distance to floor, streak tolerance, dollars per trade, lot size, session cap.

start from the money, not the percentage. convert the maximum loss into the current distance between balance and floor, which on a static structure is the same number every day and on a trailing structure is not. divide by the number of consecutive losses the plan should survive. the result is the maximum dollar loss per trade.

convert that into position size using the instrument's value per pip or point and the stop distance the strategy requires. if the resulting size is below the platform's minimum, the account is too small for the strategy at that stop distance - a genuine finding, and one that should change the account size rather than the stop.

then check the daily limit. multiply the per-trade loss by the number of losses the session should absorb and compare with the daily limit. if the budget exceeds the limit, cut the trade count or the size. if it is far below, the plan is probably too conservative to finish inside the deadline, and the correct adjustment is a tighter stop or a better reward-to-risk ratio rather than a larger position at the same stop.
three lines in one budget: per trade, per session, and a reserve that is never spent.

keep a quarter of the drawdown untouched. on a static structure the reserve is psychological; on a trailing structure it is arithmetic, because the floor moves and a sequence longer than the design case is exactly what the mechanism punishes. a reserve also gives the trader something to do after a bad week other than stop, which is a behavioural benefit with a financial value.

recalculate the line every monday, using the floor as it stands. this single habit prevents the most common late-evaluation breach: a size chosen when the account had room, retained after the room had gone. if the recalculated size is smaller than last week's, trade the smaller size - the plan's job is to finish, not to maintain a position.
the funded account is a different product with the same name, and the differences are where a pass either becomes income or becomes a story.

the first difference is the drawdown. funded accounts frequently carry a tighter limit as a percentage, because the firm is now exposed to real payouts rather than to a fee. a plan that ran at a given risk per trade during the evaluation may be twice as aggressive as the funded account permits, which is how newly funded accounts are lost in the first fortnight.

the second difference is that profit only becomes income when it is withdrawn. unwithdrawn profit sits in the account, contributes to the drawdown calculation, and on a trailing structure raises the floor behind the trader - making the account more fragile rather than less. the disciplined approach is to withdraw on the earliest permitted schedule at a size that leaves room above the floor, rather than accumulating a large balance and hoping to withdraw it later.

the third difference is the payout gate, which typically consists of a minimum number of profitable days, a profit threshold, a consistency check, identity verification, and a payment interval. each has a failure mode unrelated to trading skill.
the first payout is a sequence of conditions. trading is only the first of them.

minimum profitable days are satisfied by activity rather than by profit, and are the most commonly missed condition. a trader who reaches the threshold in six sessions and needs fifteen faces nine sessions of obligation, and the temptation in those nine is to trade for the count. the correct approach is a reduced size, a daily profit cap and an acceptance of flat sessions.

the consistency check is where a good month can become a constrained payout. applied to the profit being withdrawn, a best-day share of around a third means total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day. a single dominant session therefore constrains the first withdrawal even though it helped reach the evaluation target - the consistency guide covers the arithmetic for the common thresholds.

verification is administrative and should be completed in the first week of funding rather than at the first request. documents and payment-method checks are routinely the cause of a delay that has nothing to do with the trading record, and they are the one step in the chain a trader can finish early at no cost.
the advertised fee is the least informative number in a prop firm comparison. what matters is the total cost of reaching a funded account, and that number depends on how long the attempt takes.

the time line is the one traders omit and the one that often dominates. a three-month evaluation that could have been completed in five weeks does not lose money on fees; it loses seven weeks of funded trading, which is usually the larger figure. that is an argument for a plan efficient enough to finish reasonably and conservative enough to survive, not for a plan that grinds indefinitely.

retry structure deserves separate attention. a one-off fee with a paid reset is a per-attempt model, and it rewards getting the plan right before the second payment. a monthly subscription with unlimited retries is a different product: it lowers the marginal cost of a failed attempt and raises the cost of a slow one, which changes the optimal strategy toward more attempts and more risk. neither model is better in itself; a trader whose breach rate is high benefits from the subscription, and a trader whose plan is sound benefits from the one-off.

finally, price the funded stage. an activation charge on funding, a data subscription that continues, and the profit split together determine the economics of the thing the evaluation is for. a cheap evaluation attached to an expensive funded stage is a cheap entry to an expensive product.
a staged, percentage-based evaluation with a deadline suits a specific trader, and being honest about the fit is more useful than a rating out of five.

it suits traders with a defined setup and a measured win rate, because the pace calculation depends on expectation per trade and a trader who has not measured theirs cannot compute it. it suits traders who can trade a fixed number of sessions a week, since the deadline converts the calendar into a requirement. it suits traders who prefer a scale-free plan, where the same percentage risk and the same percentage target apply unchanged at every account size. and it suits traders who want the discipline of a deadline, because the deadline does the work that a self-imposed schedule would otherwise have to do.

it also suits traders who are prepared to read the funded terms before paying, because the evaluation's rules are only half the rulebook and the funded half determines the payout. a trader who treats the evaluation page as the contract is buying a qualification without checking what it qualifies them for.

the structural advantage worth naming is the staged target. two smaller targets are easier to complete than one large one, because the plan resets its psychology between stages and because the second stage begins with a funded account in view rather than an abstract target. the structural disadvantage is that a late breach costs both stages, which raises the value of reducing risk in the final third - a rule most plans state and few follow.

if a passing service is being considered, the fit question becomes a terms question: whether third-party trading is permitted on the evaluation and on the funded account. that is answered below, and it should be answered before any fee is paid to anyone.
the same honesty applies in the other direction. three profiles are usually better served by a different structure.

traders whose strategy needs to hold winners for weeks. a deadline plus a daily limit is a poor fit for a position that needs a month to work. a swing or static-drawdown structure, or a firm with an explicit swing account, is the better match - the instant funding guide covers the alternative of skipping the evaluation entirely.

traders who accelerate under a deadline. if the historical pattern is a good first fortnight followed by an oversized final week, a timed evaluation amplifies the flaw rather than correcting it. a no-deadline structure such as the one in the the5ers guide does not fix the behaviour either, but it removes the external trigger, which is a start.

traders who want futures contracts. percentage-based forex rules and contract-based futures rules are different products. a trader whose edge is in index futures is better served by a futures evaluation, where the stop is measured in ticks and the daily limit is a dollar figure - the futures firm guide sets out the criteria, and the fundednext versus topstep comparison explains the two rulebook models side by side.

a fourth, less obvious group: traders who have not yet measured their own expectation per trade. an evaluation is an expensive way to discover that a strategy is flat after costs. a demonstration account with the same feed and the same order types produces the same information for nothing, and the scam guide explains what a genuine firm will and will not ask for while that measurement is being taken.
six checks, each answerable from the firm's own documentation in under an hour. together they replace every review, including this one.

one: the drawdown mechanism and its sampling. static, end-of-day trailing or intraday trailing, measured on balance or equity, sampled continuously or at a defined time. convert the answer into the current distance to the floor in money.

two: the daily limit and the server day boundary. the percentage, the reference point, and the exact time the trading day starts and ends in the firm's server time zone. then check how that interacts with the hours you actually trade.

three: the funded account's drawdown and payout conditions. not the evaluation's - the funded one. minimum profitable days, profit threshold, consistency clause and whether it applies at every payout or only the first, verification requirements and the payment interval.

four: the restricted-behaviour clauses. news windows, weekend and overnight holding, lot caps, prohibited strategies, and the definition of each. where a definition is broad, ask for a specific example in writing.

five: the third-party and account-management clause, on both stages. evaluation terms and funded terms separately, in writing. this is the clause that decides whether a paid pass survives a payout request.

six: the total cost to funding. fee, platform, data, activation, and the cost of a reset. then divide by the realistic number of weeks the plan needs, remembering that a monthly data subscription is a cost per month, not per attempt.

keep the answers. terms change, and a trader who has the version they agreed to is in a materially better position than one relying on memory. where a firm publishes a versioned terms document, save the version in force on the day of purchase.

comparisons are only meaningful within a category. the two categories that matter are the rulebook model and the drawdown mechanism, and a firm's position on both explains most of the difference between accounts that feel similar.

on the rulebook model, percentage-based forex rules and dollar-based futures rules are not interchangeable. the first is scale-free and permits fractional position sizes; the second is quantised in contracts and priced in ticks. a plan built for one behaves badly in the other, regardless of the trader's skill. the rules matrix sets the structures side by side and is the fastest way to see where a given firm sits.

on the drawdown mechanism, the ranking from most to least forgiving is usually static, then end-of-day trailing, then intraday trailing - with the caveat that the size of the initial buffer can invert that ranking for a given account. a static floor with a small buffer and a tight daily limit can be harsher than a trailing structure with generous room, which is why the mechanism has to be converted into money before it is compared.

the third axis is the funded stage. two firms with near-identical evaluations can differ sharply in what a pass is worth, because the funded drawdown, the payout cadence and the consistency conditions are set independently of the evaluation rules. a firm that is generous during the evaluation and strict afterwards has priced the strictness into the payout, and that is where the revenue is.

the 2026 comparison covers the wider market including the firms most often shortlisted alongside this one, and the beginners guide covers the criteria that matter when there is no track record to compare against.
assuming the six checks are satisfactory and the fee is paid, the first month divides into four weeks with distinct jobs.

week one: calibrate at half size. two trades a session maximum, half the eventual risk, and three measurements per trade: planned risk, realised risk including spread and slippage, and time in the trade. the purpose is to establish whether the cost of execution matches the plan's assumption. most plans are wrong about this by a meaningful margin, and week one is the cheapest place to find out.

week two: full size, fixed session cap. if week one's realised risk matched the plan, move to the full size and keep the cap. if it did not, shorten the stop distance rather than increasing the size - slippage is a property of the instrument and the session, not of the account.

week three: protect the buffer. ahead, reduce size by a quarter and keep the target in view. behind, keep the size and move the calendar; the daily limit is not increased to catch up. this is the week where most evaluations are either secured or lost, and it is lost by the same mechanism in both directions: a change in size that was not in the plan.

week four: decide, do not drift. review four numbers - trades taken, expectation per trade, worst drawdown so far, distance to target. a plan on pace continues. a plan behind on pace with a healthy expectation extends the calendar. a plan with negative expectation stops, because another fortnight of the same process produces the same result at a higher cost.

two habits hold the month together. recalculate the risk line from the current floor every monday, and never open a position in the final hour of the firm's trading day, where the day-boundary and trailing-floor traps live. if a passing service is doing the work, the same month applies with one addition: a written confirmation that third-party trading is permitted on both stages, kept before the first payment rather than after the pass.

legitimacy is not something a review can certify, and it is not the useful question. the useful questions are whether the terms are published clearly, whether the funded-stage conditions are stated before purchase, and whether support answers clause questions in writing. a firm that does all three is one you can evaluate; a firm that does not is one you cannot.

read this from the current terms rather than from any review, and read three details: whether the threshold trails or stays fixed, whether it is measured on balance or equity, and when it is sampled. convert the answer into the current distance to the floor in money, because that number - not the headline percentage - is what position size must be built from.
why does the daily limit matter more than the maximum loss?

because it fires on ordinary variance. if risk per trade is a large fraction of the daily limit, two or three consecutive losses close the session, and runs of that length are routine at a win rate in the forties. risk per trade should be derived from both limits and the smaller result used.
how much can i risk per trade on the evaluation?

divide the maximum loss by the number of consecutive losses the plan should survive, typically eight to ten, then check the result against the daily limit divided by the losses a session should absorb. the smaller of the two is the correct number. keep a quarter of the drawdown untouched as a reserve.

usually a minimum number of profitable days, a profit threshold before withdrawal, a consistency check on the profit being withdrawn, identity verification and a payment interval. the funded drawdown is frequently tighter than the evaluation's, so the correct first move after funding is to halve the risk for the first ten sessions.

depends on the account type: standard accounts often restrict it while swing accounts permit it on different terms. where holding is allowed, price the gap as a multiple of the stop and cut the size accordingly - the weekend holding guide covers the arithmetic.

only if the terms permit third-party trading, and the evaluation and funded documents answer separately. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid third-party trading. confirm the clause in writing before paying anyone.

neither is better in the abstract; the rulebook has to match the strategy. percentage rules suit plans with fractional sizing and a percentage edge. contract rules suit traders whose stop is measured in ticks on an index future. the futures guide sets out the criteria for that side.

derive it from expectation: divide the target by expected value per trade to get the trade count, then divide by planned trades per week. a conservative plan usually lands between fifteen and thirty trading days. if the derived calendar exceeds the firm's deadline, the size is too small to pass within the rules and the account is the wrong purchase.

a risk line that was derived from the maximum loss and never checked against the daily limit, followed by an increase in size in the final third to finish on time. both are arithmetic failures rather than strategy failures, and both are fixed before the fee rather than during the attempt.

six checks: drawdown mechanism and sampling, the daily limit and server day boundary, the funded-stage drawdown and payout conditions, the restricted-behaviour clauses, the third-party clause on both stages, and total cost to funding. where a definition is broad, ask for a specific written example and keep the reply.
should i read the funded terms before or after passing?

before paying the evaluation fee. the funded terms determine whether a pass produces income, and they frequently include a tighter drawdown and a consistency condition that changes how the evaluation should be traded. a trader who reads them first often chooses a different account size.

passing an apex evaluation is the audition, not the job. the funded account has its own activation condition, its own payout threshold, its own consistency cap and a scaling path that decides what the account is worth in a year. this guide covers that whole arc - activation, the first payout, the second, the transition from trailing to static behaviour, and the ninety days that turn a funded login into recurring income. rules are described by mechanism, because the numbers change and the mechanics are what you actually trade.
a funded account is a different product: the failure floor usually becomes static, and a consistency cap becomes a payment condition rather than a planning consideration.
the first payout exists to prove the process. sizing it modestly is the correct strategy, not a timid one.
activation and minimum-day conditions are calendar problems. plan them alongside the profit threshold so both complete on the same date.
a 30% best-day rule means required total profit equals the best day divided by 0.30. cap the day at a fifth of the payout target and the gate is satisfied by construction.
scaling is granted on a record of completed payouts, not on a single large month. the fastest route to a bigger account is boring consistency.
terms change. confirm the current figures on the firm's own pages; this guide describes structure, not a contract.

an evaluation asks one question: can this trader reach a target without breaching a rule? a funded account asks a different one: can this trader extract money repeatedly, under a consistency condition, without losing the account? the behaviours that answer the first are close to the behaviours that answer the second, but not identical, and the gap is where most funded accounts die.

three things change the day the evaluation passes. the failure floor usually stops trailing and becomes static, measured from the funded account's starting balance. a consistency condition stops being advice and becomes a gate on the withdrawal. and the target stops being a single number to reach and becomes a recurring threshold that has to be cleared again before every payout.

the first change is unambiguously good. on a trailing account, profit makes the account more fragile: the floor rises with the peak, so the remaining cushion shrinks as the target approaches. on a static account, profit makes the account safer, because the floor does not move. that is a genuine relief, and it is the reason some traders find the funded stage easier to trade than the evaluation.

the second change is the opposite. a consistency cap that was a planning consideration becomes a payment condition, and it is applied to realised profit rather than to the plan. a trader who passed with one dominant session has a funded account that is technically active and practically unpayable until enough ordinary profit accumulates to bring the ratio down. that is not a punishment; it is arithmetic, and it is avoidable.

the third change is the one that surprises on timing. a funded account's profit threshold is usually paired with a minimum day count, and the two rarely complete on the same day unless the plan is built to make them. a trader who reaches the threshold in five sessions but needs ten qualifying days has five sessions of doing nothing useful, and the temptation to fill them with size is the single most common way a funded account is lost before it pays.
evaluation, activation, day count, consistency gate, payment - and then the same cycle again.

futures firms commonly require an activation step before the funded account is live, and it is a cost that traders forget when they budget for the evaluation. the evaluation fee is paid at purchase; the activation condition arrives after a pass, when the trader is committed and less price-sensitive. budget for it from the beginning, because a pass you cannot activate is not a funded account.

the activation condition is usually one of two shapes: a fee, or a profit threshold that has to be met on the funded account before anything is withdrawable. some programs combine them. the practical effect is the same - the first money earned on the funded account belongs to the firm until the condition is cleared - and the planning consequence is that the first payout is farther away than the evaluation's marketing implies.

then the calendar. three clocks start at roughly the same moment: the minimum day count before a withdrawal can be requested, the profit threshold that has to be reached, and any waiting period measured from the first trade on the funded account. the efficient plan finishes all three on the same date, which means working backwards from the longest clock rather than forwards from today.

two mistakes recur here. the first is trading the funded account at maximum size on day one to "get the threshold out of the way", which converts a calendar problem into a drawdown problem. the second is treating the day count as a formality and then discovering that a scratch day does not count, which pushes the date back a fortnight. both are solved by the same decision: decide the payout date first, then work out how many sessions and how much profit per session it requires, and check that the answer is compatible with the daily loss limit.

do the activation arithmetic before the evaluation. evaluation fee plus activation condition is the true entry cost. if that total is uncomfortable, the account size is too large or the firm is the wrong purchase - not something to discover after a pass.

a funded account's profit threshold is a dollar figure, and dollar figures hide the two things that decide difficulty: what fraction of the account it represents, and how the consistency cap interacts with it.

convert first. a threshold of a few thousand dollars on a $50,000 account is a materially different requirement from the same dollar threshold on a $150,000 account, even though the marketing page shows the same number in both places. divide the threshold by the balance to get the percentage, and compare that percentage across tiers. on futures accounts the threshold usually scales with size, which means difficulty per dollar is roughly constant and the smaller tiers are not proportionally easier - commissions and slippage are identical in dollars, so they consume a larger share of a smaller target.

then check the interaction with the cap. if the threshold is $3,000 and the consistency rule permits a best day of 30% of total profit, then a single $3,000 day would require $10,000 of total profit before the withdrawal clears - three times the threshold. that is the trap: reaching the threshold quickly with one large session creates a requirement that is far larger than the threshold itself. a daily profit cap set at a fifth of the threshold prevents it entirely.
at threshold, not at payout. the cap is computed from realised profit, so one large session can triple the requirement.

read the table from right to left again. the cap is the decision; everything else follows. a trader who caps the day at $900 against a $3,000 threshold has a best-day share of at most 30% at the moment the threshold is reached, and can request a withdrawal without further arithmetic. a trader who caps nothing is running a lottery on their own behaviour.
the consistency rule is the only condition on a funded account that can block a payment while the account is profitable, so it deserves more than a sentence.

the mechanics are a single division. required total profit equals the largest day divided by the permitted share. a $2,400 best day under a 30% rule needs $8,000 of total profit. a $1,200 best day under the same rule needs $4,000. the larger the best day, the more total profit is needed, which means the fastest route to a large number is the slowest route to a payment.

three measurement details decide whether a trader is inside the rule, and they differ by firm and by program. is the share computed against total profit, against the payout amount, or against the threshold? is it measured at the request or at some later review? and does a day count from realised profit only, or from the day's peak equity? read the clause for the exact basis, because a 30% rule measured against total profit and a 30% rule measured against the payout amount are not the same rule at all.

where the rule is measured at the request, a trader at exactly the threshold with a best day at exactly the permitted share is in a knife-edge position: one ordinary session improves the ratio, one unusually good session makes it worse. in that position the correct move is to keep trading at reduced size until the ratio has clear headroom rather than to submit and hope. a request that is refused costs time; a request that is never marginal costs nothing.

there is a second-order effect that catches traders who know the rule well. the best day is a fixed historical fact. once a $2,400 day exists in the record, the total profit requirement is $8,000 forever, regardless of how the remaining profit is earned. a trader cannot reduce the best day; they can only raise the total. that is why the cap has to be applied from the first funded session rather than discovered at the request: after the fact, the only remedy is more profit, and more profit means more exposure to the drawdown that ends accounts.

the first withdrawal is not an income event. it is a test of the pipe: that the request is accepted, the review clears, the payment arrives and the account continues afterwards. treating it as a test changes every decision around it.

size it modestly. a first payout that is small relative to the account is less likely to run into a consistency problem, less likely to be held for review, and less likely to leave the account in a fragile position afterwards. a trader who withdraws the maximum available on the first request is optimising a number before verifying the process that delivers it, which is the wrong order.

complete verification first. identity checks, address documentation and any source-of-funds request should be finished in the first week of the funded account, not at the moment of the request. a document request is the single most common cause of a delayed first payment, and the delay is entirely self-inflicted.

then keep the record. screenshot the request confirmation, save the statement for the period, and note the date the payment lands. those three artefacts make the second request faster and give you something to point at if the process stalls. the payout process guide walks through the sequence step by step.
four gates, one of which is about trading. verification is the one traders leave until it delays them.
the shift from a trailing to a static floor is a genuine change in the maths, and traders who do not adjust leave value on the table in one direction and take unnecessary risk in the other.

on a trailing account, the correct response to profit is to reduce size, because the floor has risen and the remaining cushion is thinner. on a static account, that response is unnecessary: profit does not move the floor, so the cushion grows with the balance. a trader who keeps shrinking size after the pass is being needlessly conservative and will take far longer to reach the payout threshold.

the correct response on a static account is to keep size constant in dollar risk terms and let the cushion grow. if risk per trade was a fixed dollar amount during the evaluation, keep it. if it was a percentage, a larger balance produces a larger dollar risk, which is also defensible - but be deliberate about which of the two you are doing rather than drifting between them.

what does not change is the daily limit. a static floor does not remove the daily loss limit if the firm applies one, and on a funded account the daily limit is often the constraint that actually ends accounts. the morning calculation is the same as during the evaluation: current equity minus the floor is total room, current equity minus the daily limit is today's room, and the smaller number governs.

the one rule that survives the transition: a static floor makes the account safer as you win, but it does not make a single trade safer. risk per trade should be set by the daily limit, not by the cushion - otherwise a comfortable account is used to justify an uncomfortable position.

there is a further subtlety on futures accounts specifically: once the floor is static, the funded account's threshold and the floor define a band. the account is only dangerous at the bottom of the band and only paid at the top. that framing makes the mid-band the place to do ordinary work at ordinary size, which is exactly what the ninety-day plan below is designed to produce.

the second payout is where a funded account becomes a process rather than an event. it is also where most traders break the discipline that produced the first one, because the fear that motivated the evaluation has gone.

the efficient rhythm is a repeating cycle with four parts: reach the profit threshold, satisfy the day count, keep the best day in proportion, request. once the cycle has run twice, the trader knows the actual dates and amounts, and can plan three months rather than one payout.

two adjustments make the rhythm cheaper. first, spread the profit across sessions rather than compressing it: a threshold reached in fifteen ordinary sessions produces a better consistency ratio than the same threshold reached in six, and the daily limit is never stressed. second, keep the daily profit cap in place permanently, at a fraction of the threshold that satisfies the consistency rule at every point in the cycle - not just at the first request.

the rhythm also changes how a losing week is experienced. during an evaluation, a losing week consumes calendar that cannot be recovered. on a funded account with no deadline, a losing week is a smaller drawdown against a static floor and an unchanged threshold, so the correct response is to trade the next ordinary session at ordinary size. traders who respond by increasing size to "get back on schedule" are applying an evaluation instinct to a funded account, and it is the instinct that ends accounts.

futures firms scale on a record, not on a month. the path to a larger balance or an additional account usually runs through a completed payout history, so the fastest way to a bigger account is a boring sequence of small, on-time withdrawals.

that has a counter-intuitive implication for the first quarter: a trader optimising for income should withdraw modestly and consistently, and a trader optimising for account size should do the same thing. the two objectives point in the same direction for once, because both are served by a clean record rather than by a large single payment.

running multiple accounts is where the record gets complicated. firms generally treat correlated positions across accounts as a single exposure, and some prohibit the practice explicitly. two accounts trading the same instrument in the same direction at the same time is not diversification; it is one position with two sets of fees. the legitimate version of a portfolio is several accounts traded at different times, in different instruments, or with genuinely different plans - and even then the firm's terms come first.

the practical sequencing advice is unglamorous and correct: pass one account, trade it for a full quarter, complete two or three payouts, and only then consider a second. a trader running three funded accounts in month one has three times the conduct-rule exposure and no payout history to show for it.
the failure modes on a funded account are different from those on an evaluation, and they are more expensive because the thing being lost produces income.

size inflation after the pass. the single largest cause. the pressure that produced discipline disappears once the fee is earned, and the first position after the pass is often the largest of the trader's career.
filling the day count with size. waiting for qualifying days and using them to make money is the second largest. a qualifying day can be completed with one small closed trade.
one dominant session near the request. converts a compliant account into one that needs three times the profit before it can pay.
treating the static floor as unlimited room. a larger cushion is not a licence for a larger position, because the daily limit still applies and the threshold is still the objective.
conduct breaches after the pass. news windows and size caps do not disappear at funding, and a breach on a funded account costs the account and the pending payout together.
withdrawing the maximum immediately. maximising the first request leaves no room for a review query and no cushion if the payment is delayed.

every one of those is a decision rather than an accident, and every one is prevented by a number written down: risk per trade as a fixed dollar amount, a daily stop at 80% of the limit, a daily profit cap at a fraction of the threshold, and a first payout sized to be unremarkable. the failure recovery guide covers what to do if the account is lost anyway.
a funded account generates income, and income generates obligations. the paperwork is not difficult, but it has to be assembled as it happens rather than reconstructed in april.

keep three records. a trade log with entry, exit, size and result for every position, exported monthly. a payout log with the request date, the amount, the fee withheld and the date the payment landed. and a copy of the firm's terms as they stood when each payout was requested, because the basis for the payment can change and the version that applies is the version in force at the time.

on tax, the treatment differs by country and by whether the activity is classified as trading, self-employment or something else. that classification is a question for a local accountant rather than for a blog, and it is worth asking early - the answer affects whether the income is reported gross or net, what expenses are deductible, and how the firm's payment documentation should be read. what can be said generally is that a payout log makes any of those conversations shorter.

keep payment documentation as well. firms typically issue some form of payment statement or invoice, and a trader who relies on bank deposits alone will find the reconciliation harder than it needs to be. save the statements alongside the payout log, and keep them for as long as your jurisdiction requires.
here is the arc that turns a pass into a track record, expressed as three months rather than as a list of rules.

days 1-10 - activate and verify. clear the activation condition, complete identity checks, and set the daily and per-trade numbers in writing. trade small. the objective of this period is a verified account and a recorded baseline, not profit.

days 11-30 - reach the first threshold at a controlled pace. cap the daily profit at a fifth of the threshold, spread the work across ordinary sessions, and complete qualifying days deliberately. request the first payout on the earliest permitted date, at a modest amount, with the record attached.
days 31-60 - repeat the cycle twice. by the second payout the dates and amounts are known, so the plan becomes a calendar rather than a hope. keep the cap in place. do not add an account yet.

days 61-90 - build the record that scaling depends on. three completed payouts, no conduct breaches, no dominant session, and a documented plan that produced them. that record is the asset. a larger balance is usually granted against it, and it is worth more than any single month's profit.

the plan is deliberately unambitious per week, because the objective is a record rather than a number. a trader who completes three modest payouts in ninety days has something a firm will scale and a trader can budget against. a trader who makes one large withdrawal and loses the account has a story.

for the evaluation side of the same journey, the apex challenge guide covers the rulebook and the trailing drawdown maths works the floor arithmetic line by line. readers who would rather not run the evaluation at all can have it traded for a flat $220 where the firm's terms permit third-party trading; the service review sets out what to verify, and the passed challenges page shows completed evaluations.

take a funded account with a $3,000 payout threshold, a 30% best-day rule, a $1,000 daily loss limit and a ten-day minimum before a request. the plan: 1.5% risk per trade, a daily stop at 80% of the limit, a daily profit cap of $600 and four sessions a week.
week one. activation cleared on day one, verification submitted on day two, three ordinary sessions producing $1,100 in total with a best day of $450. two qualifying days.
week two. four sessions, $1,050, best day $600 at the cap. five qualifying days, total $2,150, threshold 72% complete.

week three. a losing session of $400, then three ordinary sessions of $260, $330 and $290. total $3,030 - threshold reached on the tenth counted day, which is also the earliest permitted request date. the best day is $600, which is 20% of total profit, comfortably inside a 30% rule.
the request. $2,000 withdrawn rather than the full balance above the threshold. the account continues with just over $1,000 of profit above the starting balance and the full daily limit intact.

notice what the numbers did not require: no dominant session, no day near the daily limit, and no session in which size was increased. the threshold was reached in ten counted days at an average of $303 per session against a $600 cap, which means the cap was never the binding constraint on progress - it was the binding constraint on the consistency ratio, doing its job by remaining unused.

the pattern is the point. three weeks of unremarkable sessions produced a compliant payout, and the same plan can run again immediately. a trader who reached the same threshold in four sessions with one $2,000 day would have needed $6,667 of total profit before a request, and would still be trading three weeks later with the daily limit as the only thing standing between them and a reset.
a short list, in the order it should be completed. each item takes minutes and each one has delayed a first payout for someone.
failure floor recorded as a dollar figure, with the basis noted (static or trailing, from starting balance or from equity).
daily loss limit recorded and the per-trade risk set at a third of it.
payout threshold, minimum day count and consistency share recorded from the current terms, with the date the terms were read.
daily profit cap set at a fraction of the threshold that satisfies the consistency share.
calendar marked for the earliest request date, the verification follow-up and any payout window.
conduct rules re-read - news windows, size caps, holding restrictions - because they are unchanged by the pass.

that list is the whole of the difference between a funded account that pays and one that does not. it is not a trading edge; it is the administrative layer that lets a trading edge reach a bank account.

three things. the failure floor usually becomes static instead of trailing, so profit stops making the account more fragile. a consistency cap becomes a payment condition rather than planning advice. and the target becomes a recurring threshold with a minimum day count attached before each withdrawal.

that depends on the activation condition, the minimum day count and any first-payout waiting period, all of which are in the current terms. plan backwards from the longest of the three rather than forwards from the pass date, and complete verification in week one so it is never the thing that delays you.
why does my best day matter so much at payout?

because a consistency rule caps the largest day as a share of total profit. required total equals the best day divided by the permitted share, so a $3,000 best day under a 30% rule needs $10,000 of total profit - three times a $3,000 threshold. cap the daily profit at a fraction of the threshold and the problem never arises.

no. the first payout's purpose is to prove the process: request, review, payment, account continues. a modest amount is less likely to run into a consistency query, less likely to be held for review and leaves a healthier account afterwards.

you can, and it is the most common way funded accounts are lost. a static floor makes the account safer as you win; it does not make a single trade safer. set risk per trade from the daily limit and keep it there for at least a quarter.
does the daily loss limit still apply on a funded account?

usually yes, in some form. the static floor caps total damage and the daily limit caps session damage, and the binding rule each morning is whichever is closer to current equity. compute both before the first trade.

through a record of completed payouts, not a single large month. firms typically scale on a payout history, so the fastest route to a bigger balance is a sequence of modest, on-time withdrawals with no conduct breaches. two or three clean cycles is usually the currency.

check the terms first: correlated positions across accounts are often treated as a single exposure, and some programs prohibit it outright. the legitimate version is several accounts traded at different times or in different instruments, and even then the rules come before the strategy.
what if i hit the daily limit on a funded account?

the session ends and the account continues with a fresh daily budget against the same floor. reopening a position after the limit is a breach in itself, and it is the most common way a recoverable day becomes a closed account.

yes, and the treatment varies by country and by how the activity is classified. keep a trade log, a payout log with fees withheld and payment dates, and a dated copy of the terms. ask a local accountant about the classification early rather than reconstructing everything later.

the trading is often easier because the floor stops trailing, and the pressure is different because there is no deadline. the consistency gate and the day count make the payout harder to reach than a target, which is why the first withdrawal often takes longer than expected.

most services, including ours, cover the evaluation. the funded account should be in your name with payouts to you, and the firm's rules govern it from then on. anything else puts the account at risk at the exact moment it starts producing income.

the daily profit cap, expressed as a fraction of the payout threshold that satisfies the consistency share. it is the only number that protects both the payout gate and the account, and every other figure can be derived from it.

audacity capital runs a capital allocation programme rather than a conventional challenge with a plan-specific loss floor, a daily rule that varies with the plan and one-off or profit-share based depending on programme billing. this guide works through the rulebook in the order that decides an attempt: the loss floor first, then sizing, then the calendar, then the payout conditions that decide what a pass is actually worth. the numbers are illustrative and the mechanics are the firm's; confirm the current schedule on the plan page before you buy.
the loss floor is firm-specific, often a fixed loss allowance. that single sentence decides how every trade must be sized.
daily stop: programme-specific. on most evaluations it is measured on equity, so open positions count.
billing is one-off or profit-share based depending on programme, so a slow attempt costs more each month, which rewards a fast pass.

the audacity capital evaluation is best understood as a set of constraints that interact, not as a headline profit target with some footnotes. the target decides how much you have to make. the loss floor decides how much room you have to make it. the daily stop, if there is one, decides how quickly a bad session ends. the minimum-day rule decides how long the attempt takes even when the target is reached early. change any one of those and the same trading strategy produces a different outcome.

for audacity capital, the published structure is a capital allocation programme rather than a conventional challenge. the loss floor is firm-specific, often a fixed loss allowance, the daily stop is programme-specific, and the consistency condition is yes, a minimum trading period. billing is one-off or profit-share based depending on programme, payouts follow profit split on a fixed schedule, and the supported platforms are mt4, mt5. those are the rows that matter. marketing pages tend to foreground the profit target and the profit split because both are easy to compare; neither tells you whether a given trade is survivable.

there is a test that separates a trader who understands a audacity capital rulebook from one who has only read the sales page: ask what happens to the failure point after a winning trade. on a static floor the answer is "nothing". on a trailing threshold the answer is "it moves up, and it does not move back down". everything else in the risk plan follows from that answer.

the table is the whole argument. the same two scratch trades leave a static-floor account untouched and a trailing-threshold account with significantly less room than it started with. the balance is identical in both cases; only the rule is different. a trader who measures risk as a percentage of the balance will not notice the change until a normal losing trade breaches a floor they believed was still $10,000 away.
one floor is anchored to the starting balance; the other follows the high-water mark.

there is a second-order consequence for the plan. on a trailing threshold, the largest risk of the attempt is in the middle: the account has accumulated some profit, the floor has moved up, and the cushion is thinner than it looks while the target is still some distance away. that is the moment to reduce size, not to press. many failed attempts breach in this middle phase, after a good start and before the target, which is why the trailing rule is often described as punishing success.

practical rule: keep a note of the current high-water mark and recompute the room before every trade. if the room divided by your normal risk is fewer than five, cut the size. if it is fewer than three, stop for the day. on a static floor the same check is cheap insurance against the daily stop; on a trailing one it is the difference between finishing and failing.

sizing is not a judgement call; it is arithmetic with one fixed input and two measured ones. the fixed input is the dollar risk, which comes from the plan. the measured inputs are the stop distance, which comes from the chart, and the value of one pip per lot, which comes from the instrument's specification. change either measured input and the size changes, even if the dollar risk does not.

the trap in the table is the tight-stop column. a tight stop with a large position looks efficient because the dollar risk is unchanged, but it moves the failure point of the trade into the market's ordinary noise. on an evaluation the consequence is a loss that was not a loss of the idea, only a loss of the stop. wide stops are slower but they fail for the right reason, and a journal full of right-reason failures is a journal that can be improved.
fixed risk, variable size: the stop decides the position, not the other way round.

on forex the numbers depend on the pair. a standard lot of a dollar-quoted pair moves $10 per pip, so a 20-pip stop is $200 per lot; a $500 risk budget therefore supports 2.5 lots. on a cross or a metal the pip value is different, and on gold the contract specification changes the calculation entirely. read the platform's specification window once, write the number down, and reuse it rather than estimating from memory.

two checks close the loop. before entry, confirm the ticket's estimated loss equals the intended dollar risk; after entry, confirm the position's value per pip or point matches what the size calculation assumed. both take seconds, and together they catch the two most common sizing errors: a fat-fingered size and a stop placed in the wrong unit.

a profit target is a distance, and the only useful question is how many trades it takes to cover that distance at a given risk-reward. on an illustrative $100,000 audacity capital account with an 8% target, the account needs $8,000 of net profit. at a 1:2 risk-reward and 0.5% risk per trade, a winning trade makes $1,000 and a losing trade loses $500. a 50% win rate over 20 trades produces ten winners and ten losers: $10,000 gained, $5,000 lost, $5,000 net. that is short of the target. the same win rate over 32 trades produces $8,000 net, which is the target.

the table explains why most challenge failures are not caused by a bad strategy but by an expectancy that is too thin relative to the calendar. at a 50% win rate and 1:1, the strategy has zero expectancy before costs; no amount of discipline turns it into a pass. at 1:2 it works, but it needs 32 trades, and 32 trades at two per day is sixteen sessions - longer than many traders plan for and longer than many subscription budgets allow.
