the other side of the equation is the loss allowance. a strategy with a 60% win rate and 1:2 risk-reward will still produce losing streaks. the probability of four consecutive losses at a 40% loss rate is roughly 2.6%; over 32 trades, the chance of seeing at least one four-loss streak is high enough to plan for. at 0.5% risk, four losses cost 2% - survivable. at 2% risk, the same streak costs 8%, which is most of a typical total loss allowance. the target is not the hard part; surviving the distribution on the way to it is.

there is also a minimum-days interaction. if the rulebook requires ten trading days and the strategy needs sixteen sessions, the calendar is set by the strategy. if the strategy needs eight sessions, the rulebook adds two idle days that must not be used to "speed things up" with oversized trades. the correct behaviour on a required idle day is no trade, or a trade at the normal size with the normal stop. the requirement is a floor on time, not an invitation to fill it.

finally, subtract costs before comparing any of this to a backtest. spread, commission, swap and slippage are charged whether the trade wins or loses. on a forex account, a one-pip spread on a 20-pip stop is a 5% tax on every trade. a backtest that ignores costs overstates expectancy, and an overestimated expectancy produces a plan that is too fast for the target and too large for the drawdown.

a plan is not a prediction. it is a set of rules that decides what you do on each of the twenty sessions an evaluation typically takes, including the sessions where nothing happens. the plan below is built around a 0.5% risk unit, a 1:2 minimum risk-reward and a hard stop at two losses per session. it assumes a forex and cfd account and a rulebook with a plan-specific loss floor. adjust the numbers to your own account, but keep the structure.

the reductions in the final week are the part most traders skip. on a static floor they are optional; on a trailing one they are close to mandatory, because the remaining room is measured from the high-water mark. if the account is $7,000 into an $8,000 target and the trailing cushion has compressed to $2,500, a 0.5% risk is $500 - one fifth of the entire remaining cushion. halving the size at that point is not cowardice; it is the only sizing that keeps a normal losing streak survivable.
the plan reduces risk as the target approaches; the target does not justify increasing it.

each session has a pre-trade checklist: the economic calendar, the session's key levels, the maximum loss for the day, and the one or two setups that are allowed. if a setup is not on the list, it is not taken. the checklist is not there to improve win rate; it is there to prevent the improvisation that turns a planned 0.5% loss into an unplanned 2% loss at the worst moment of the attempt.

the journal is part of the plan, not an optional extra. record the setup, the reason for entry, the planned stop, the realised result, the remaining room before and after, and one sentence on execution. twenty entries produce a dataset that can answer the only question that matters at the end of the attempt: was the loss caused by the strategy, the sizing, or a rules breach? without the journal, every failure looks like bad luck and every pass looks like skill.

finally, define the abort condition in advance. if the account reaches 60% of the total loss allowance, stop for the day and review. if it reaches 80%, stop for the week. the rulebook will not stop you; it will let the account run to the floor. the abort condition is the only part of the plan that protects the fee, and it has to be written before the first trade, when it is still a decision rather than a reaction.

most failed attempts share a small number of causes, and almost none of them are "the market moved". the causes are structural: a position sized against the balance rather than the remaining room, a stop moved to avoid a loss, a session traded because the trader was at the screen rather than because a setup existed, a consistency rule discovered at payout. each is preventable with a rule written before the attempt.

sizing against the starting balance. on a trailing threshold, the room shrinks as profit accumulates. a fixed 1% risk becomes a growing share of the cushion, and a normal losing streak ends the account even though the strategy is unchanged.

moving the stop. the stop is the trade's definition of failure. moving it converts a planned 0.5% loss into an unplanned 2% loss and, on a daily-stop rulebook, can breach the daily limit in a single trade.

trading the calendar instead of the setup. minimum-day rules create idle days. filling them with lower-quality trades is the most common way a profitable strategy fails an evaluation it would otherwise pass.

ignoring the news window. a position held through a scheduled release can gap past the stop. where the rulebook restricts news trading, the breach is a rules failure; where it does not, the gap is still a risk failure.
discovering the consistency rule late. a concentrated profit distribution can pass the target and fail the payout. the limit has to be part of the sizing plan from day one.
increasing size after a winner. the account is closest to the target when the remaining room is smallest. increasing size at that moment is the opposite of what the arithmetic requires.
not reading the plan name. multi-plan firms sell different rulebooks under one brand. buying the plan whose marketing page you read is not the same as buying the rulebook you planned for.

treating the funded account as a second challenge. the funded rules are usually stricter and the payout conditions are where the money is decided. a pass is the start of a new compliance period, not the end of one.
one oversized loss does more damage than several planned ones; the floor does not care about intent.

the list is short because the causes are few. a trader who writes these eight items on a card and checks them before each session has removed most of the ways an evaluation fails. the remaining failures are strategy failures - a genuinely negative expectancy - and those are the only ones that require a new method rather than a new rule.

there is one more mistake that deserves its own line: failing to stop. a rulebook will let an account run to the floor. it has no interest in protecting the fee. the trader has to define an abort condition - 60% of the loss allowance, three losses in a day, two breaches of the checklist in a week - and honour it before the account is gone. the abort is not a failure of the attempt; it is the only thing that makes the next attempt affordable.

scheduled economic releases are the most predictable source of unpredictable loss. a position held through a central-bank decision or a payrolls print can gap past its stop, and a stop that is jumped does not limit the loss to the planned amount. for an evaluation account, that is a double problem: the loss can breach a daily stop, and where the rulebook restricts news trading, the trade can also be a rules breach independent of the result.

the audacity capital position on news trading is: plan-specific, so confirm it for the exact plan before trading. read that as a constraint on the calendar, not as a suggestion. if the rule prohibits opening or holding positions in a window around a release, the correct behaviour is to be flat before the window and to stay flat until it closes. a stop is not a substitute for being flat, because the gap can be larger than the stop.

the mechanics of a gap are worth spelling out. a stop is an instruction to close at the market once a price is touched. if the market opens beyond the stop, the fill is at the opening price, not at the stop. on a $100,000 account risking 0.5%, a 40-pip stop that gaps 120 pips loses three times the planned amount, which on a tight daily stop can end the day before the trader has made a single decision. the only protection is position size small enough that a multiple of the stop is still survivable, or no position at all.

news also changes the shape of the session. the best setups often occur after the initial spike, when the market has chosen a direction and the spread has normalised. trading the spike itself is a coin flip with a wide spread and a high chance of a stop on both sides. waiting thirty minutes costs nothing in a twenty-session plan and removes the most expensive form of variance.

if the rulebook permits news trading, the risk is still real. the permission is not a recommendation, and the firms that allow it usually still apply a general market-conduct clause that can be used against a trader who appears to be exploiting a pricing error. the safe interpretation is: trade the setup, not the release. if the setup requires the release to work, it is a news trade and should be sized as one.

no rulebook is best for every trader, and the useful comparison is between structures rather than brands. audacity capital fits a trader whose constraints match a plan-specific loss floor, a daily rule that varies with the plan and one-off or profit-share based depending on programme billing. a trader with a different constraint - a swing strategy, a session that does not overlap the market, a budget that cannot absorb a retry - will get a better expected outcome from a different structure, even if the other firm is less famous.

the first mismatch to check is session availability. a forex and cfd evaluation whose opportunity set sits in a session you cannot trade is not a difficulty problem; it is a scheduling problem. the second is the drawdown mechanic: a strategy that holds positions through retracements needs a static floor, while a strategy that takes quick profits and re-enters can live with a trailing one. the third is billing: a one-off fee rewards patience, a subscription punishes it.

the fourth is the payout rhythm. a firm that pays on demand after a short seasoning period is worth more to a trader who needs cash flow than a firm with a higher split and a ninety-day cycle. compare the first-year cash, not the headline percentage. the fifth is platform access: if your strategy depends on a specific order type or chart, a firm that does not support it is not a candidate, whatever its target.

it is also worth distinguishing between switching firms and switching rulebook models. a trader who keeps failing a trailing threshold will keep failing it at every firm that uses one. moving to a static floor is a structural change; moving from one trailing firm to another is a change of logo. the comparison table is useful only if it changes the mechanic, not just the name.

finally, price the switch honestly. a new evaluation fee, a new data subscription and a new learning curve are real costs. if the current rulebook is a reasonable fit and the failures are execution failures, the cheaper fix is a rule, not a new firm. if the failures are structural - the mechanic fights the strategy - the switch is the cheaper fix even at a higher fee.

the cost of a audacity capital attempt is not the entry fee. it is the entry fee multiplied by the expected number of attempts, plus the value of the time spent, plus the cost of the mistakes the attempt teaches. a $100 fee that takes four attempts costs $400; a $250 fee that takes one attempt costs $250. firms compete on the first number because it is visible at checkout, and traders compare on it because it is easy, but the second number is the one that leaves the bank account.

the comparison is not an argument that one route is always cheaper. a trader with a tested edge and a $100 fee may pass first time, in which case self-trading is obviously cheaper. a trader who has failed the same rulebook three times has already spent more than the flat fee in cash alone, before counting the months. the honest way to compare is to estimate your own pass probability from your record, not from the marketing claim that "most traders fail".
repeated attempts cross the flat fee quickly; the exact crossover depends on the entry price.

there is also a hidden cost in the retry model: the rulebook does not change between attempts, so a trader who fails for a structural reason - position sizing, session timing, a trailing threshold - tends to fail again for the same reason. paying for a third attempt without changing the cause is not a strategy; it is a subscription to the same mistake. the fee is only worth paying when the cause has been identified and fixed.

if you use a passing service, the relevant cost is the flat fee plus the firm's own rules on third-party trading. some firms permit it explicitly, some prohibit it, and some are silent. a service that does not ask which firm you are using, or that guarantees a pass without reading the terms, is a risk to the account and to the fee. the $220 figure on this site is flat across firms and account sizes, includes retries, and is refunded or declined where the firm's terms do not allow it.

whatever route you choose, keep the cost in the same units as the payoff. a $10,000 funded account that pays an 80% split on $2,000 of profit is worth $1,600 before fees. spending $1,000 of fees and three months to reach that payoff is a poor trade unless the process also produces a repeatable skill or a second account. the evaluation is a means; the funded account's cash flow is the end. judging the means by its sticker price rather than by the end it produces is the most common financial mistake in this market.

a passing service trades the evaluation on your behalf for a flat fee, then hands back a funded account in your name. the model only works if three conditions hold: the firm permits third-party trading on the plan you bought, the service trades the actual rulebook rather than a generic strategy, and the fee is flat enough that a difficult account does not change the economics. remove any one and the arrangement is either a rules breach or a bad deal.

the first condition is a documentation question, not a marketing one. some firms prohibit account sharing and third-party trading explicitly; others restrict it to the evaluation but allow it on the funded account, or the reverse. the service should ask for the firm and plan before quoting, read the terms, and decline the work if the terms forbid it. a blanket "we can pass any firm" claim is a red flag, because the firms do not share one rulebook.

the second condition is about process. an evaluation is a constrained optimisation: reach a target without touching a loss floor, inside a calendar, under a daily stop and a consistency condition. the trading that satisfies those constraints is not the same as the trading that maximises long-run return. a service that treats the account like a personal trading account, with full-size positions and no regard for the floor, is not passing the evaluation; it is gambling with your fee.

the third condition is pricing. a percentage-of-profit or profit-split model aligns the service with the funded account, but it also gives the service a claim on the account after the pass. a flat fee is simpler and leaves the funded account entirely yours. the trade-off is that a flat fee is paid whether or not the attempt succeeds, which is why the retry policy matters more than the headline number. elitepropx charges $220 per evaluation, covers retries, and takes no share of the funded account.

before buying any service, ask five questions in writing: which firm and plan, whether the terms permit third-party trading, who holds the login during the evaluation, what happens if the account breaches, and what the retry policy is. a service that answers all five consistently is worth considering. a service that answers with a guarantee and a countdown timer is not. the guarantee is the part that cannot be enforced; the terms are the part that can.

finally, the account remains yours. the pass certificate, the funded login and the payout details should be in your name, with your email and your identity verification. a service that needs to hold the funded account, or that pays out through its own account, has changed the product from a service into an investment. that may be a legitimate arrangement, but it is a different one, with different counterparty risk, and it should be priced and documented accordingly.

every number in this guide describes the published shape of the audacity capital rulebook, not a guarantee of the terms on the day you buy. firms revise targets, loss limits and payout conditions between cohorts, and the dashboard you see after checkout is the only version that binds. the verification routine below takes ten minutes and is worth more than any comparison table, including this one.
open the plan page and the terms page side by side. the plan page carries the marketing numbers; the terms page carries the definitions. where they differ, the terms page wins.
screenshot the loss-floor definition and the daily-stop definition. the words "balance" and "equity" mean different things, and the difference decides whether open positions count.
find the consistency clause. note whether it applies to the evaluation, the funded account or both, and what the threshold is.
find the payout section. note the first-payout restriction, the payment cycle, the minimum withdrawal and the processor fees.
find the prohibited-conduct list. note the rules on news trading, hedging, copy trading, account sharing, eas and maximum lot size.
check the refund and retry policy. a fee is only cheap if a failed attempt can be repeated without paying the full price again.
save the pages as pdfs with the date in the filename. if a dispute arises, the dated copy is the only evidence that the terms were different when you bought.

the most common source of dispute is not a hidden rule; it is a rule the trader read on a comparison site instead of the firm's own page. comparison content, including this page, is a map of the questions to ask. it is not the contract. treating it as the contract is how a trader ends up surprised by a consistency clause that was published all along.

a second source of dispute is the plan name. a firm with three models can publish three different loss definitions under one brand, and a search result for the brand will mix them. when you compare two firms, compare the exact plan names and the exact account sizes. a $100,000 two-phase plan and a $100,000 one-step plan from the same firm are different products with different probabilities of passing.

finally, ask support the question you cannot answer from the page. "is the trailing threshold calculated on equity including open profit, or on closed balance?" is a question with a specific answer, and the reply is worth keeping. if support cannot answer a mechanics question, that is itself information about the firm's operational depth.

the pass email is the midpoint, not the finish. between the pass and the first payout there is a verification step, a contract, a funded login and a compliance period. each has its own failure mode, and none of them is about trading skill. the first week after a audacity capital pass is mostly administrative, and treating it that way prevents the most avoidable loss of the whole process.

complete identity verification with the same documents and the same name as the evaluation account. a mismatch between the account name and the payout method is the most common reason a first withdrawal is held.
read the funded contract before signing. the loss floor, the consistency condition and the conduct rules can differ from the evaluation, and the signature is the point at which they bind.
log in to the funded account and confirm the balance, the platform and the rulebook shown on the dashboard. if anything differs from the contract, raise it before the first trade.
trade the first week at the same or smaller size than the evaluation. the target is gone, but the loss floor is not, and the funded account is the asset that produces the payouts.

request the first payout as soon as it is eligible. the first payout is the proof that the process works end to end; delaying it to grow the balance increases the risk without increasing the evidence.

the psychological shift is harder than the administrative one. during the evaluation, the target gave every trade a purpose. after the pass, there is no target, and the absence of one can produce either over-trading or paralysis. the replacement is a payout plan: a monthly profit goal expressed as a percentage, a maximum risk per trade, and a withdrawal schedule. the goal is cash flow, not a certificate.

most traders who pass and then lose the funded account do so in the first month, by increasing size because "the account is already funded". the account is funded, which means it is now the thing that pays. treating it as a victory lap is how the payout that justified the fee never arrives. the correct size after a pass is the size that survived the evaluation, not the size that feels deserved.

keep the records. the pass certificate, the signed contract, the first payout statement and the trade history are the evidence base for a second account, a scaling application or a dispute. a trader who can show a funded account, a payout and a clean rulebook history has a much easier time with the next firm than one who can only show a screenshot of a target reached.
how long does it take to pass a audacity capital evaluation?

at disciplined sizing, most attempts land in the two-to-four-week range, with the lower bound set by the minimum-day rule (undefined) and the upper bound by the strategy's expectancy. a pass attempted in a handful of days usually relies on oversized trades, which is why it tends to create a consistency problem at payout or a thin cushion in the funded account.

position sizing against the starting balance instead of the remaining room. on a plan-specific loss floor, the room changes as profit accumulates, so a fixed percentage risk becomes a growing share of the cushion. the second most common cause is a stop moved to avoid a loss, which converts a planned small loss into an unplanned large one.

the rule is plan-specific. check the funded terms as well as the evaluation terms, because the two can differ. where holding is restricted, close well before the session ends rather than at the bell, and size any permitted overnight position so that a two-times-stop gap is still survivable.
can i pass a audacity capital evaluation in one day?

only where the plan has no minimum-day rule and the target is reachable inside a single session without breaching the daily stop. this plan applies a minimum-day rule (undefined), so the calendar cannot be compressed below it. a one-day pass built on one oversized trade often fails a consistency test at payout, which makes the speed expensive.

legitimacy is a question about payout evidence, not about the size of the marketing budget. look for published terms, a documented payout process, a support channel that answers mechanics questions in writing, and a track record you can verify independently. no comparison page can substitute for the firm's own contract, and no firm is risk-free.
how much does a audacity capital evaluation cost in total?

the entry fee multiplied by your expected number of attempts, plus platform or data costs. because billing is one-off, a slow pass costs the same as a fast one, which rewards patience. the flat $220 service fee on this site covers retries and does not depend on account size.

you complete identity verification, sign the funded agreement, receive a funded login and trade under the funded rulebook, which can be stricter than the evaluation. audacity capital pays profit split on a fixed schedule. the first payout is the point at which the process is proven; until then, the evaluation fee is a bet on the firm as well as on the strategy.

only if the plan explicitly allows it. where it is restricted, being flat before the window is safer than relying on a stop, because a release can gap past the stop and the resulting loss can breach the daily limit. where it is allowed, the permission is not a recommendation; size the event like an event.

only if the firm's terms permit third-party trading on the exact plan. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any account size, covers retries, takes no profit split and declines work where the terms forbid it. the service fee is separate from the firm's own evaluation or reset charge.

start from the remaining loss room, not the starting balance. risk 0.25-0.5% per trade while the room is intact and reduce that as the target approaches, especially on a trailing threshold. the stop belongs where the trade idea is invalidated; the position size is whatever makes that stop equal the chosen dollar risk.

usually yes, because most firms measure it on equity rather than balance. that means an open position in profit can still breach the limit if it reverses far enough. confirm the definition on the firm's terms page and treat the daily stop as a hard cut-off rather than a target to approach.
what is a consistency rule and does it apply here?

a consistency rule caps how much of total profit may come from one trading day, often 30-50%. it can pass the evaluation target and still reduce or deny a payout, so it has to be part of the sizing plan from day one. check whether it applies to the evaluation, the funded account or both.

topstep combines a trailing maximum loss limit with an optional daily loss limit chosen at checkout, plus a best-day consistency target of 55% of the profit target during the combine. this guide covers each rule as it is published, the sizing that survives them, and the mistakes that end attempts. the rules were checked against topstep's own help centre on 19 october 2026.
two loss rules apply at once - a trailing threshold and a daily loss limit - so the binding constraint is whichever is tighter that day.
the best-day target is 55% of the profit target during the combine, and 40% at payout. exceeding 55% raises the profit target rather than failing the account.
progress makes a trailing account more fragile, so risk per trade falls as the target approaches.
typical pass time with disciplined pacing is ten to eighteen trading days.
topstep's combine is a futures evaluation with dollar-based figures. the headline numbers scale with account size, but the mechanics do not.

the distinctive feature of this rulebook is that the daily limit is a choice rather than a fixed rule. if it is bought at checkout, it caps the session and triggering it is not a breach; if it is not bought, the trailing maximum loss limit is the only failure condition. on a day when the trailing floor sits far beneath current equity, the optional daily limit binds first. on a day after a strong session - when the floor has risen close to the balance - the trailing limit binds first. a plan that assumes both rules always apply will overstate the constraint on an account that never bought the daily limit.

two comparisons are worth having in mind before choosing a futures firm. against apex , the difference is the shape of the floor: topstep's maximum loss limit trails the end-of-day balance, while apex's intraday threshold follows unrealised profit. the second is stricter during a winning session, because a retracement has already moved it. topstep's end-of-day method is closer to a static floor early in the account, and the limit locks permanently once it reaches the starting balance.
the trailing limit is the rule traders underestimate, and the optional daily limit is the rule they misread. both deserve precise treatment.

topstep sets the limit at $2,000 on a $50,000 account, $3,000 on $100,000 and $4,500 on $150,000. it is a trailing limit that rises with the end-of-day balance , never moves down, and locks permanently once it reaches the starting balance. suppose a $100,000 account opens with a $3,000 limit at $97,000. if the balance closes the day at $102,000, the limit rises to $99,000; a $500 loss the next day leaves it at $99,000, and the room is now $2,500 rather than $3,000.

the critical detail is the measurement point. because the floor follows the closing balance rather than unrealised profit, an open position that moves $3,000 in the money does not move the limit until the session closes. that makes the rule gentler than an intraday threshold during a winning day, and stricter in one specific case: a position held into the close that gives back its gain still sets the higher floor if it closed profitably.
intraday trailing responds to unrealised profit, so a retracement on a winning day still reduces the cushion.
the daily limit resets each session and is measured on the day's loss, which means a losing day is capped independently of the trailing floor. three consequences follow.

first, a losing day is cheap on a trailing account. the floor only ever rises, so a session that ends down does not move it - the loss consumes the daily budget and nothing else. that asymmetry means the expensive behaviour is not losing; it is giving back a peak.

second, the effective daily room is not the daily limit on every day. after a strong session the trailing floor may sit closer than the daily limit allows, in which case the floor binds first. a plan should compute both numbers each morning and use the smaller.

third, because the daily limit is a dollar figure while the trailing distance is also a dollar figure, both scale with account size - but the ratios between them differ by plan. on some account tiers the trailing distance is the tighter constraint; on others the daily limit is. this is exactly the kind of detail that is invisible in a headline comparison and decisive in practice.

consistency is treated differently here than at firms where it appears only as a payout gate. the expectation is that no single session dominates total profit, and it is applied with enough weight that a trader who reaches the target on the back of one large day can find the evaluation incomplete or the payout delayed.

the arithmetic is different from a 30% payout rule, and it is worth restating in dollars. in the combine the best day must stay at or below 55% of the profit target: under $1,650 on a $3,000 target, under $3,300 on a $6,000 target and under $4,950 on a $9,000 target. exceeding the line does not fail the account; it raises the target to best day ÷ 0.55. a $2,000 best day on a $3,000 target therefore turns the target into $3,636, and the extra profit has to be earned on a later session. at payout the limit tightens to 40% of total profit.
a dominant session can leave an account at target but unable to complete or withdraw.

on a futures evaluation this restraint is doubly important, because the same session that produces a dominant day also lifts the trailing floor. a trader who finishes a strong day has both a consistency problem and a thinner cushion - the two worst outcomes in the same session, produced by the behaviour that felt most successful.
two loss rules and an end-of-day threshold consume one budget, so they must be sized together.
five numbers define a workable combine plan, and each derives from one of the rules above.
maximum risk per trade: a third of the daily loss limit. this keeps three consecutive losses survivable, which is the property that matters across a multi-week evaluation.
daily stop: stop opening positions once 80% of the daily limit is realised. the remaining 20% exists to absorb slippage on the closing trade.
daily profit cap: well below 55% of the target. on a $6,000 target the hard line is $3,300; a self-imposed cap of $2,000 leaves room for an ordinary day to be the best day.
size ladder: full planned size to 40% of target, three quarters from 40% to 70%, half beyond 70%. this is the response to the trailing threshold, and it is mandatory rather than optional.

floor check: recalculate the trailing failure level every morning and compare it with current equity. if the remaining buffer is smaller than the risk of a single planned trade, the session does not start.

the fifth item is the one traders skip, and it is the one that prevents the defining failure mode of a trailing account. the check takes twenty seconds: current equity minus trailing threshold equals available room; if that number is under the planned per-trade risk, either reduce size or do not trade that session. there is no scenario in which trading anyway is correct, because the evaluation can always be finished tomorrow and cannot be recovered once failed.

the counter-intuitive rule: on a combine, a strong start is a liability as well as an asset. it raises the floor and raises the consistency bar. the correct response to a large winning session is not to press, but to reduce.
a realistic pace on a $100,000 account with a dollar target and a trailing threshold is ten to eighteen trading days, structured as follows.

sessions 1-3 - establish the plan. half of planned size while the plan is tested against real conditions. one or two setups per session, a hard daily cap and an explicit decision to stop at the cap rather than extend a good day. expected outcome: 15-25% of target with the floor moved modestly.

sessions 4-7 - the working middle. full planned size, which on a six-day-a-week futures schedule is three or four sessions a week. daily profit capped at roughly a third of the target. target completion should reach 55-70% by the end of this phase, with no single day exceeding the cap.

sessions 8-12 - reduce and protect. size falls to three quarters and then to half as completion passes 70%. the trailing floor is now close enough that a retracement from the peak is a genuine risk, so sessions get shorter and the remaining ground is covered in small increments. any session that reaches the cap is closed rather than extended.

completion. once the target is reached and the minimum day count is satisfied, trading stops. on a trailing structure there is nothing to gain from continuing: the account cannot improve its standing, and every tick in either direction moves the floor or consumes budget.

the single most useful habit during pacing is to write the daily cap and the floor check into the plan as rules rather than intentions. traders who track their ratio and their buffer informally tend to abandon both in the session where they matter most - which is the session after a large winner.
holding a runner through a retracement. the floor moved with the peak; the retracement is measured from the peak, not from the entry. this is the most common failure on any trailing structure.
increasing size as completion approaches. the instinct that fails trailing accounts, because progress is precisely when the buffer is thinnest.
one dominant day. efficient for reaching the target and expensive for consistency, in the same session that raises the floor.
reading only one of the two loss rules. a plan built around the daily limit alone assumes the trailing floor is distant. after a good session it is not.
trading through the daily cap to "stay active". activity is not a requirement; the minimum day count is. on a qualified day, the smallest possible closed trade satisfies it.

treating a flat day as lost ground. flat sessions cost nothing on a trailing account, because a losing day does not move the floor. the recovery trade after a flat day is a bigger risk than the flat day itself.
ignoring news and session restrictions. futures firms restrict trading windows around scheduled releases and enforce them by pattern detection rather than manual review.
rule sources (checked 19 october 2026). maximum loss limit , optional daily loss limit and consistency targets . figures apply to the trading combine and can change; confirm the plan at purchase.
passing the combine produces a funded account with its own conditions, and on a futures firm they are usually more demanding than the evaluation itself.

the good news is that the trailing behaviour usually disappears at funding, replaced by a static failure level. that removes the mechanic that made the evaluation hardest. the less good news is that the consistency check becomes strictly binding, so a trader who passed with one dominant day can be funded and still unable to withdraw.

the remedy is the same discipline applied one step earlier: cap daily profit at about a third of the eventual total during the funded phase too, complete kyc in the first week rather than at the payout request, and plan the threshold and the minimum day count to complete together. the payout process guide walks through the sequence and the delays that block first withdrawals.
a $100,000 account, a dollar target of $6,000, an end-of-day trailing maximum loss limit of $3,000 and the optional $2,000 daily limit, traded on the size ladder described above.
session 1 - +$520. half size while the plan is tested. the floor rises modestly with the peak. nothing notable, which is the objective of a first session.

session 2 - +$1,180. full size. the session is closed at $1,180 rather than extended toward the daily cap of $2,000, because the cap exists to protect the consistency ratio and extending a good session spends that protection for no additional benefit.

session 3 - −$410. one loss at planned size, then closed. note what this session did not cost: on a trailing account a losing day does not move the failure floor, so the day consumed budget and nothing else.
session 4 - flat. three scratch trades. logged as flat and treated as a normal outcome rather than a reason to increase size the next morning.

sessions 5-8 - +$2,940 combined. the working middle. completion reaches 74%, so risk per trade drops to three quarters of planned size and then to half. the daily cap of $2,000 means no session can threaten the consistency ratio even if it finishes at the cap.

sessions 9-11 - +$1,760 combined. the final 26% at half size, in three short sessions. the floor is checked each morning before trading; on one of those mornings the remaining buffer was smaller than the planned per-trade risk, so size was cut again for that session rather than trading the standard plan.

completion. the target is reached on session 11 with a best day of $1,180 - 19.7% of the $6,000 target, comfortably inside the 55% consistency line. the minimum day count is satisfied on the same session because the pace was planned backwards from the requirement. trading stops.

what the sequence demonstrates: two losing-or-flat sessions, no dominant day, a floor check that changed the plan once, and a completed evaluation in eleven sessions. none of it required a better market view than the plan already assumed.
topstep's account tiers run from $50,000 to $150,000, and the target and the trailing distance both scale with size. two practical observations follow from that.

the smaller tiers are not proportionally easier. because both the target and the threshold distance scale with the account, the evaluation difficulty is roughly constant across tiers - a $50,000 account needs a smaller dollar target and has less dollar room. what does not scale is the fixed cost per contract: commissions and slippage are identical in dollars, so on a smaller account they consume a larger share of the target. in practice, small accounts are marginally harder to pass than large ones at identical discipline, which is worth knowing before buying the cheapest tier and expecting a higher pass rate.

the funded phase is where size pays. a funded account at a mid-tier size with a satisfied consistency record produces real income; a failed evaluation at the largest tier produces nothing. the efficient path for a trader new to futures is to prove the plan at a mid-tier size, then scale on the firm's own terms once a payout history exists. firms increasingly tie additional accounts or larger balances to a record of completed payouts rather than to a single large profit month.

a related point about sequencing: running two combine attempts at the same time splits attention and creates correlated positions across accounts, which firms treat as a single exposure. sequential funding - pass one, trade it, add a second - is slower to start and considerably faster to reach a first payout.
the rules that surround the loss limits matter as much as the limits themselves, because they determine which opportunities are legitimate in the first place.

permitted hours. futures trading is confined to session windows defined by the firm and by the exchange's own trading hours. the practical effect is that the plan must choose its windows in advance rather than reacting to an instrument that looks interesting at an unusual hour. for most evaluations, the liquid part of the session is where the plan operates, and the thin overnight hours are avoided - not because they are prohibited, but because slippage on a thin book is the most expensive kind of loss on an account with a fixed dollar threshold.

news windows. firms restrict trading around scheduled economic releases, and the futures firms are generally strict about it. the definition matters more than the existence of the rule: windows are usually specified in minutes either side of the release, and a position opened legitimately before the window can still breach if the rule requires it to be closed. the safe reading is the strict one, and the plan treats the window as closed regardless of what any instrument is doing inside it.

contract caps. maximum position size per instrument is often stated in the terms rather than on the evaluation page. trading a permitted instrument at twice the permitted size is a breach, and it is one of the most common accidental ones because the cap is easy to exceed on a fast-moving contract.

daily session count. a plan that trades four or five sessions a week rather than every available session produces a slower pass and a materially lower breach rate. rest is not a cost on a trailing account; it is a control, because every session moves the floor or consumes budget, and sessions with no clear plan do one or the other without adding profit.

holding overnight and over weekends. policies differ and the fees or restrictions attached to them can convert a technically valid position into a rule breach. where the plan permits holding, it accounts for the gap risk explicitly; where the firm restricts it, the position is flat before the close rather than left to chance.
what is the single most important rule in the combine?

the trailing threshold, because it changes every other decision. it sets how much room remains, how size must fall as progress accumulates, and why a flat day costs far less than a day that gives back a peak. read the daily limit second.
how long does it take to pass a topstep combine?

ten to eighteen trading days with disciplined pacing, depending on the account size, the target and the minimum day count. faster passes are possible but usually create a consistency problem at payout.

no. the maximum loss limit trails the end-of-day balance, not unrealised profit, and it never moves back down. once it reaches the starting balance it locks there permanently. that makes it gentler than an intraday threshold during a winning session, though a strong closing day still raises the floor for the next session.

in the trading combine the best day must stay at or below 55% of the profit target. if it exceeds that, the target rises rather than the account failing: on a $50,000 account, a $1,800 best day raises the target to about $3,273. at payout the stricter 40% limit applies, so the largest day cannot exceed 40% of total profit.
which rule binds first, the daily limit or the trailing floor?

it depends on the day. early in an evaluation the daily limit usually binds because the floor is distant; after a strong session the trailing floor can sit closer to current equity than the daily limit allows. calculate both each morning and use the smaller number.
a third of the daily loss limit at most, with a hard stop at 80% of the day's budget spent. three consecutive losses at that size leave the account alive, and the plan intact.

they use different floors. apex's threshold follows unrealised profit, so a retracement on a winning day has already tightened the account. topstep's follows the end-of-day balance and locks at the starting balance. topstep also publishes a 55% best-day target during the combine and 40% at payout, while apex applies a 30% best-day rule at payout. the harder firm depends on whether your method gives back open profit or closes it.

the firm's reset and purchase options apply. where a passing service trades the evaluation, a reset on the same firm and account size carries no additional service fee under the flat $220 arrangement - the firm's own reset charge is separate.

a funded account is issued with a minimum day count, a profit threshold, a consistency check and kyc requirements. most futures firms also apply a first-payout waiting period. the payout guide covers each step.
the two loss rules, and why they are not the same rule

topstep states a daily loss limit and a maximum loss limit separately, and the distinction matters more than it appears. one governs what can happen in a session, the other governs what can happen to the account. traders who treat them as one number usually discover the difference on a day that starts badly.

the daily limit ends the session. reach it and the day is over; the account survives, and tomorrow starts with a fresh budget against the same floor. the maximum loss ends the account. there is no tomorrow, and the only recovery is a new purchase.

in practice almost every failure arrives through the daily limit first, because reaching the maximum loss requires either a single enormous position or a run of days that each came close to the daily cap. both are preventable, and the second is entirely visible in a journal two weeks before it happens.

the useful habit is to compute both numbers each morning and to treat the smaller of the two as the binding constraint. on a $50,000 account with a $1,000 daily limit and a $2,000 maximum loss, the daily limit is a fifth of the total room - which means the account can only survive two bad days before the maximum loss becomes the live number.

the funded stage on topstep has its own conditions, and they are the ones that decide whether a pass becomes income. the variables are familiar: a minimum number of winning days, a profit threshold, a consistency expectation on the best day, and a processing schedule. what differs is how they combine.

where a firm counts winning days, a day with a small loss does not count and a scratch does not count. that changes pacing: a trader who reaches the profit threshold in a week may still need another fortnight of positive sessions to satisfy the day count, and the efficient plan lands both conditions on the same date rather than treating the second as a formality.

where a best-day expectation applies, the same arithmetic as every other firm applies: required total profit equals best day divided by the threshold. a trader with one very strong session and a thin remainder will be asked to keep trading until the ratio normalises, and the correct response is smaller size and ordinary profit rather than a second strong session.
what to do between the pass and the first withdrawal

trade small, close the day early, and keep a written record of the running totals for both conditions. the temptation during this period is to make the first payout worth having, which is the single most common way a funded account is lost before it pays anything. the first payout's purpose is to prove the pipe works, not to change a trader's month.
topstep is a reasonable first assignment because the rules are documented and the day count is forgiving, but three things are worth doing before the fee is paid.
trade the platform on demo for a week. futures mechanics - tick value, contract sizing, session hours, the difference between es and mes - are learned cheaply before money is involved.
choose the smallest size that permits a meaningful payout. the percentage rules are identical at every size, so the only thing a larger account buys is a bigger payout ceiling and a bigger fee.
write the daily budget on paper. in dollars, in ticks, and in contracts. a trader who has to calculate the budget mid-session has already lost the discipline the budget was meant to enforce.

none of that is novel advice; all of it is routinely skipped. the traders who pass futures evaluations on the first attempt are not usually better analysts than the ones who fail - they are the ones who did the arithmetic before the market asked them a question.

one further suggestion, drawn from the pattern of failures rather than from best practice: choose the session before the instrument. a trader who knows they will be at the screen from the new york open until 11:30 has a fixed window, a fixed set of instruments that behave well in it, and a natural end to the day. a trader who trades "whenever there is a setup" has no end to the day, and the session that never ends is the one that spends the last dollars of the daily budget on a trade nobody needed.

the complementary rule is to decide the day's maximum trade count before the open and to treat the third trade as a decision rather than a continuation. futures traders on a five-contract limit reach three trades remarkably quickly in a volatile session, and the third trade is where sizing discipline usually slips.

both rules - a fixed session and a fixed trade count - are ways of putting an end to the day before the account puts one there. on a firm with a separate daily limit and maximum loss, that end is the only thing standing between a bad session and a closed account.

neither rule is difficult to follow on a good day. both are almost impossible to follow on a bad one, which is why they are written down in advance and checked before the first trade rather than remembered in the middle of the third.

most prop firms do not refund an evaluation fee when an attempt fails, and the ones that do attach conditions that are narrower than the marketing suggests. there is also a second policy - the fee credit - that is routinely confused with a refund and behaves quite differently. this page sets out the four things a "refund" can mean, the exclusions that void most claims, the arithmetic of a refund guarantee against a lower fee, and how to escalate a refusal in an order that preserves your options.
most firms refund nothing on a failed attempt; the fee buys an attempt, not a guaranteed outcome.
a refund, a fee credit and a free reset are three different policies. only one returns money.
refund conditions almost always exclude conduct breaches - conduct rules void a refund even when the loss was inside limits.
a refund guarantee raises the headline fee. the question is whether the expected refund is worth the premium, and for most traders it is not.
a chargeback is a last resort and can cost you the account and future access; use the firm's process first and keep records.
consumer-protection rights vary by country and cannot be waived by a terms-of-service clause. check your local rules rather than assuming.
the word is used loosely across the industry, and the looseness costs traders money because they hear one meaning and sign another. four distinct policies hide behind it.

a cash refund. the fee is returned to the payment method. this is rare on a failed attempt and occasionally available within a short window after purchase if the account has not been traded. it is the only policy that returns money.

a fee credit. the fee is applied to a future purchase - a reset, a larger account, or a second attempt. no money moves. a credit is worth the face value only if you intend to buy again, and its real value is the fee minus the discount you would have negotiated anyway.

a free reset. the account is reissued at no charge after a failure, usually once and usually within a time limit. this is the most common concession in the industry, and it is genuinely valuable: a reset at no charge is a refund of the next attempt's cost rather than this one's.

a pass guarantee. the firm promises a refund or a free retry if you pass and are not paid, or if the firm changes terms mid-evaluation. this is a different product entirely, and it is the one worth reading most carefully, because a guarantee that triggers only on conditions the firm controls is close to worthless.

the practical consequence is that a firm advertising "refundable fee" and a firm advertising "free reset" may be offering the same economic thing, and a firm advertising neither may still return money if you ask within the purchase window. read the clause, not the badge.
a free reset is a refund of the next attempt, which is worth more than a partial cash refund of this one.
across the industry, refund language clusters into a small number of shapes. knowing the shapes makes a terms page readable in two minutes.

"fees are non-refundable." the default. the fee buys the attempt; the outcome is the trader's risk. almost every firm states this somewhere, and it survives the marketing badge because the badge refers to a separate, narrower program.

"refundable within 24 hours if untraded." a short cooling-off window. it is a genuine consumer-friendly term and it is also easy to lose: logging in and placing a trade usually ends it, and some firms treat any login as use.

"one free reset if the first attempt fails." common, and usually automatic rather than requested. the reset is often time-limited, and it may not apply if the failure was a conduct breach rather than a drawdown breach.

"refund if the firm fails to pay after a pass." a pass guarantee. the trigger is firm-side non-payment, which is exactly the scenario a trader actually fears, and the clause is only worth what the firm's dispute process is worth.
"no refunds after a payout has been made." a clause that appears in funded-account terms. it exists because the fee is effectively earned once the firm has paid out, and it is reasonable on its face.

none of these is unusual, and none is inherently unfair. the problem is a marketing page that says "refund guaranteed" while the terms say "non-refundable except as set out in the reset policy". both statements can be simultaneously true, and only one of them is binding.

the two-minute test: search the terms for the word "refund" and read every hit, including the ones in the funded-account section. a policy that appears only in marketing and not in the terms does not exist.
exclusions, not conditions, are where refund claims die. five recur across nearly every firm.

conduct breaches. a failure caused by trading a news window, exceeding a size cap, hedging between accounts, or using prohibited strategies voids a refund even if the account was well inside its drawdown limits. this is the exclusion that surprises traders most, because the loss was not reckless - it was rule-shaped.

multiple accounts or shared logins. terms usually prohibit running several accounts in a coordinated way and prohibit sharing access. a breach of either is treated as fraud-adjacent, and refund claims in that category are refused as a matter of policy.

expired windows. a refund window measured in days after purchase, or a reset window measured in days after failure, is enforced to the day. traders who discover the failure a fortnight later have usually missed it.

third-party trading. where a firm prohibits someone else trading the evaluation, a failure in breach of that rule is not refundable - and a pass in breach of it can be voided, which is a much worse outcome than a lost fee.

chargeback-first behaviour. some terms void the account and any pending payout if a payment dispute is opened before the firm's own process is used. that converts a fee dispute into a funded-account loss, which is an expensive way to recover a fee.

the pattern is consistent: a refund is available for outcomes the firm considers ordinary, and unavailable for behaviours it considers a breach of contract. that is a defensible policy. it is also a reason to read the conduct rules before paying, because they are the rules that decide whether the refund exists at all.
a refund guarantee has a price, and the price is embedded in a higher fee. whether it is worth paying is a calculation, not an opinion.

suppose firm a charges a lower fee with no refund, and firm b charges a premium of roughly a third with a full refund on failure. if you fail, b returns the premium. if you pass, b keeps it. so the refund is worth the premium multiplied by the probability of failure - and nothing more. at a 60% failure rate, a premium of a third of the fee is worth about a fifth of the fee in expectation. at a 30% failure rate, it is worth a tenth.

that is a poor trade in most cases, because the same money spent on a more forgiving rulebook has a larger effect on the failure rate than the refund has on the cost of failing. a static drawdown instead of a trailing one, a longer deadline, a lower target percentage - each of those reduces the probability of failure directly, and a lower probability of failure is worth more than a partial rebate after it.
the refund reduces the cost of failing; the rulebook reduces the chance of it. only one of those compounds.

there is an exception worth naming. a refund guarantee is valuable to a trader who is confident of passing and wants protection against firm-side risk - a firm that changes terms mid-evaluation, refuses a payout, or becomes unreachable. that is a different guarantee (the pass guarantee above), and it is worth a premium because the underlying risk is large and not under the trader's control. a refund on a failed attempt protects against a risk the trader controls, and that is the cheaper risk to manage with discipline.
credits and resets are the industry's real refund mechanism, and they are more generous than they are usually given credit for.

a free reset is worth the full price of the next attempt. on a 2-attempt path, that is a 50% discount on the total cost of a funded account, which is materially better than a partial cash refund of the first fee. the conditions to check are the count, the window, and whether a conduct breach consumes the reset.

a fee credit is worth the face value only if you were going to buy again at that firm. if the credit is only applicable to a larger account, its value is the difference between the larger account's fee and the credit - which may still be substantial, but is not the number on the badge.

both mechanisms share a trap: they encourage a second attempt at a firm whose rulebook may be the reason for the first failure. a credit is not a reason to repeat a structure that does not suit you. if the failure came from a trailing drawdown you cannot trade well, a credit at the same firm buys another failure at a discount. the failure recovery guide covers how to decide whether to retry the same firm or change the rulebook.
a chargeback is a dispute raised with the card issuer or payment provider. it exists for fraud and for goods not delivered, and it is the wrong first move for a fee disagreement.

three reasons. first, terms commonly void the account and any pending payout when a dispute is opened before the firm's own process is used, so a fee dispute can cost a funded account. second, a chargeback on a digital service that was delivered - an evaluation account that was issued and traded - is frequently decided in the firm's favour, because the service was provided even though the outcome was not. third, payment processors share dispute history, and a pattern of disputes can affect access to services well beyond one firm.

there is a legitimate case for a chargeback: the firm took payment and never issued an account, or issued an account that did not match the purchased terms, or became unreachable after a pass. those are delivery failures, and a chargeback is designed for them. the distinction is whether you received the product and disliked the result, or did not receive the product at all.

before any dispute, assemble the record: the purchase confirmation, the terms as they stood on the purchase date, the account statement showing the failure or the pass, and the support correspondence. a claim with those four documents is a different conversation from a claim without them, in either direction.
disputes are resolved in order, and skipping a rung usually costs the higher ones. here is the order that preserves the most options.

check the terms against the claim. establish which policy applies, whether the window is open, and whether an exclusion is triggered. if an exclusion applies, stop: the claim will fail and the effort is better spent on the next purchase decision.

write to support, once, with the record attached. state the policy you are relying on, quote the clause, and ask for a specific outcome. a specific ask produces a specific answer; a general complaint produces a template.
escalate to a named contact or a complaints address. many firms publish one in their terms. a second-level request is treated differently from a first-level ticket, and it creates a dated record.
ask for the decision in writing. a written refusal is useful evidence for the next rung and occasionally reverses itself once someone has to put it in a document.

use the payment provider's dispute process - only for a delivery failure. as above, this is the right tool for non-delivery or a materially different product, not for a rule outcome you disagree with.

use a consumer-protection route where one exists. a regulator, an ombudsman or a small-claims process, depending on the jurisdiction and the amount. these routes are slow and their availability varies enormously by country.

two practical notes. keep everything in writing; a phone call that resolves a dispute leaves no record if it later does not. and keep the tone factual - a claim that quotes the clause and states the requested outcome is handled by a different team than an angry message, and the difference in outcome is larger than it should be.

nothing here is legal advice, and the rules differ by country. what can be said generally is that consumer-protection law sits above a firm's terms, and a clause that purports to remove a statutory right does not automatically do so.

in the european union and the united kingdom, distance-selling rules give consumers a cancellation right for many online purchases, with an exception for digital content supplied immediately with consent. whether a trading evaluation falls inside or outside that exception is not obvious, and firms rely on the exception. a consumer who believes the exception does not apply should seek local advice rather than assume either way.

in the united states, there is no general federal cooling-off right for online service purchases; protections come from state law, from card-network chargeback rules, and from whether the firm's representations were deceptive. a misrepresentation - advertising a refund the terms do not provide - is a stronger claim than disliking the rulebook.

elsewhere, the pattern is usually some combination of a statutory cancellation window, a misleading-advertising rule and a payment-dispute mechanism. the practical implication is the same everywhere: the most useful fact in a dispute is what the firm said at the moment of purchase, which is why the terms should be saved on the purchase date rather than read afterwards.

one general point that is safe to state: if a firm advertises a refund on its marketing page and the terms exclude it, the advertising itself may be the strongest part of the claim. screenshots taken before purchase matter more than arguments made after.
five minutes of record-keeping converts a dispute from an argument into a process. do it before the first trade, not after the failure.
save the terms as a pdf, dated. terms change, and the version that applies is the one in force when you paid. a saved copy is the difference between quoting a clause and remembering one.
screenshot the pricing page and any refund badge. marketing claims are evidence, and they are edited frequently.
record the purchase confirmation and the account number. obvious, and routinely missing from support tickets.
keep the daily statements. if the dispute is about a failure, the statement shows whether the failure was a drawdown breach or a conduct breach, which decides whether a refund clause applies.
note the reset and refund windows in a calendar. a window that expires unused is the most common reason a valid claim is lost.

the same discipline applies to choosing a service rather than a firm. a flat-fee provider should state in writing what happens if the evaluation fails, what happens if the firm changes its terms, and whether resets are covered. a provider that answers those three questions in writing is a provider worth using, and the answers are checkable. the service comparison sets out how the models differ, and the 2026 review covers what to verify before paying anyone.
a refund badge is a pricing feature. the rulebook is the product. compare firms on the second, then on the first.
the refund question changes shape when someone else trades the evaluation, and it is worth being precise about how.

a flat-fee passing service at $220 for any firm and any account size does not refund the firm's evaluation fee - that fee is paid to the firm and is not recoverable by anyone if the attempt fails. what the service changes is the number of attempts: resets are covered while the evaluation is running, so a failed attempt costs the service nothing additional rather than costing a second fee. that is economically similar to a free reset, which is the industry's real refund mechanism.

three conditions make the arrangement honest, and a provider that does not state all three is not worth using. the firm's terms must permit third-party trading; where they do not, the service should decline the job rather than accept the risk of a voided funded account. the funded account must be in the client's name, with payouts to the client. and the firm's own reset charge, where a reset is needed, remains the client's cost - a flat-fee service covers its own work, not the firm's fees.

on the refund question specifically: a service that promises to refund the firm's evaluation fee is promising something it does not control. a service that promises to keep working until the evaluation passes, at no additional fee, is promising something it does control. the second is the arrangement worth having, and it is the one described on the passed challenges page and priced on the home page .
for readers comparing the do-it-yourself path, the arithmetic is in the profit calculator , and the rules matrix sets out which firms' structures suit which strategies before any fee is paid.
abstract policy is easier to apply with examples. these three cover the outcomes a trader is most likely to face.

claim one: failed on the drawdown, no conduct breach, first attempt. the refund clause is "fees non-refundable, one free reset on failure". the trader is entitled to the reset, not the fee. the correct request is a reset within the stated window, in writing, quoting the account number and the failure date. if the firm offers a credit instead, its value is the next attempt's price minus the credit - check whether the credit applies to the same account size, because a credit restricted to a larger account is worth less than face value.

claim two: failed after trading a news window. the loss was inside the drawdown limits, so the trader believes the failure was ordinary. it was not: the conduct rule ends the account independently of profit and loss. the refund clause excludes conduct breaches, and therefore the reset does too. the claim will fail, and the useful response is to read the conduct rules before the next purchase rather than to escalate. this is the single most common refund dispute in the industry, and it is lost before it starts.

claim three: paid, never received an account. this is a delivery failure, not a rule outcome. the record is the purchase confirmation and the absence of any account credentials. this is the one category where a payment dispute is the right tool, and it is worth opening immediately rather than after a fortnight of support tickets, because card-network windows are short.

notice how much of the outcome is decided by which category the failure falls into, and how little by how the trader feels about it. that is the practical lesson of the whole subject: the refund question is answered at purchase, by the clause you saved and the conduct rules you read, not at failure by the argument you make.
the best refund policy is the one you never invoke. four habits reduce the probability of a failed attempt more than any refund clause reduces its cost.

read the conduct rules first, the numbers second. most disputes are conduct disputes. news windows, size caps, weekend holding and third-party trading are the clauses that void a refund, and they are the clauses least likely to be on the marketing page.

budget for two attempts in the decision. a trader who has budgeted for one buys the second in a hurry and a bad mood, which is when sizing discipline slips. a trader who has budgeted for two chooses the second attempt deliberately, possibly at a different firm with a structure that suits better.

choose the structure that matches your equity curve. if your good months are strong and your bad months are shallow, a static floor and unlimited calendar is close to ideal. if you need a deadline to finish anything, buy the deadline. a refund does not fix a mismatch; it discounts the second failure.

write the numbers down. risk per trade, daily stop, daily profit cap, weekly pause, minimum day count. every one of those is a rule that prevents the failure the refund was meant to soften, and a page of numbers costs nothing.

none of that is novel, and all of it is what the firms' own terms are implicitly assuming when they price a refund badge. a trader who plans to fail is buying insurance; a trader who plans to pass is buying a rulebook. the second is cheaper, and the difference is a page of arithmetic rather than a clause in a contract.
do prop firms refund the challenge fee if i fail?

most do not. the fee buys an attempt, not a guaranteed outcome, and the standard clause is that fees are non-refundable. what many firms do offer is a single free reset, which is worth the price of the next attempt rather than a return of this one.
what is the difference between a refund and a reset?

a refund returns money. a reset reissues the account at no charge, so no money moves but the next attempt costs nothing. on a two-attempt path, a free reset is worth roughly half the total cost of reaching a funded account, which is usually more valuable than a partial cash refund.
can i get a refund if i breach a conduct rule?

usually not. conduct breaches - trading a news window, exceeding a size cap, hedging across accounts, sharing a login - void refund clauses even when the account was well inside its drawdown limits. this is the most common refund dispute and the most commonly lost one.

rarely. the refund is worth the premium multiplied by the probability of failure, so at a 30% failure rate a third-of-a-fee premium returns about a tenth of the fee in expectation. the same money spent on a more forgiving rulebook reduces the failure probability directly, which compounds.

only for a delivery failure - no account issued, a materially different product, or an unreachable firm after a pass. for a rule outcome you disagree with, a payment dispute is usually decided in the firm's favour, can void the account and any pending payout, and can affect access to other services.
what if the firm changes its terms after i buy?

you are generally governed by the terms in force when you paid, which is why a dated copy matters. if the change materially affects the evaluation you purchased, escalate in writing and cite the version you agreed to. some firms publish a pass guarantee that covers exactly this.

statutory rights sit above a contract in most jurisdictions, but what they cover varies enormously. the eu and uk have distance-selling cancellation rights with an exception for immediately supplied digital content, and the us relies on state law and card-network rules. this is general information, not legal advice - check your local rules or ask a local adviser.
how long do i have to claim a refund or reset?

windows are short and are enforced to the day - commonly measured in days after purchase for a cancellation and days after failure for a reset. put both dates in a calendar at purchase; an expired window is the most common reason a valid claim is lost.

a dated copy of the terms, a screenshot of the pricing page and any refund badge, the purchase confirmation and account number, the daily statements, and all support correspondence in writing. those five items turn a dispute into a process.

no, and a service claiming to is promising something it does not control. the fee is paid to the firm and is not recoverable if the attempt fails. what a flat-fee service can offer is to keep working until the evaluation passes at no additional service fee, which is a promise it can keep.

the arrangement is a flat $220 per evaluation at any firm and any size, with resets covered while the evaluation is running and no profit split. because retries are covered rather than charged, the practical outcome of a failed attempt is a reset at no additional service fee rather than a refund claim. it is offered only where the firm's terms permit third-party trading.

buying on a marketing badge without saving the terms. by the time a claim arises, the pricing page has changed and the version you agreed to is not the version on the site. a dated pdf taken at purchase is the whole defence.

every provider in this category sells the same sentence: we will pass your evaluation. almost nothing else is standardised - not the price, not what happens on a failed attempt, not who owns the account afterwards, and not whether the firm you bought permits the arrangement at all. this guide treats the category as what it is: a purchase with unusual risk, where the difference between a good provider and a bad one is measured in what happens after something goes wrong.
the service you are buying is trading labour plus risk transfer , not a guarantee. any provider describing it as a guarantee is describing something it cannot deliver.
pricing falls into four shapes: percentage of account size, per-phase fee, retainer, and flat fee. the shape tells you more about the provider's incentives than the number does.
the single biggest hidden risk is the prop firm's own terms. some prohibit third-party trading outright, and the penalty is account removal - after you have paid.
proof of past passes is only worth reading if it is timestamped, attributable and shows the firm's own dashboard rather than a screenshot of a balance.
elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any account size, retries covered, no profit split - and declines firms whose terms forbid the arrangement.

strip the marketing away and a passing service sells two things at once. the first is labour: someone else sits through the evaluation sessions, applies a rule-aware trading plan, and produces the pass. the second is risk transfer: if the attempt fails, the provider absorbs the cost of the retry rather than the buyer paying for another evaluation.

neither of those is a guarantee. the evaluation is still run by the prop firm, under the firm's rules, on the firm's platform, and the firm can void an account for a rule breach regardless of who placed the trades. a provider that promises a guaranteed funded account is either describing a different product - selling access to an account they already own - or is not being precise about the risks.
the scope of work is worth pinning down in writing before payment, because providers interpret it differently. the questions that matter are unglamorous:
which phases are covered? a single-phase evaluation and a two-phase evaluation are different jobs with different failure surfaces.
what account sizes? many providers scale their fee with the account, which means the largest account is not necessarily available at the advertised price.

what happens at the funded stage? some providers hand over the login and stop. others trade the funded account for a share of payouts. the second is a materially different commercial relationship, and on some firms it is explicitly prohibited.
who pays the firm? the evaluation fee is normally the buyer's. confirm that, because a provider who "includes" the fee is really marking it up.
what is the failure policy? retry at no cost, retry at a discount, or no retry - this is the term that decides whether the price is good value.

a provider that answers all five without hedging is a provider that has thought about the job. one that answers in slogans has not, and the gap will show up at the worst possible moment: when an account fails and the buyer discovers the retry policy was never as broad as the sales page implied.

there is a more fundamental question underneath all of this, and it is the one the industry prefers not to raise. if a provider can pass any evaluation reliably, the economics of doing so for $220 are strange - the same skill applied to a funded account would earn far more without the compliance risk. the honest resolution is that the service is a volume business with modest margins, and that most providers are trading a specific style of plan rather than possessing an edge that prints money. that does not make the service worthless; it makes it a labour purchase rather than an investment in superior skill. buyers who understand that price the service correctly and are rarely disappointed.
once you start collecting quotes, patterns appear quickly. there are four shapes in the market, and each one encodes a different assumption about where the provider expects to make its money.
pricing shapes diverge sharply once a retry is involved, which is the case the sales page usually omits.

the percentage model is the most common and the most misunderstood. because it is payable on success, it looks risk-free to the buyer - no pass, no fee. the catch is that the fee scales with the thing the buyer most wants, and on a large account the percentage can exceed the evaluation fee several times over. it also creates an incentive for the provider to prefer accounts it is confident about, which in practice means refusing the difficult firms and the difficult sizes. that is rational for the provider and frustrating for the buyer who came for exactly those.

the per-phase model is the most transparent and the least forgiving. the provider is paid for work performed, so a failure is the buyer's cost. where the provider offers a discounted retry, this model becomes reasonable; where it does not, the buyer is financing the provider's variance.

the retainer is the model that hides the most. a monthly charge sounds modest next to a large percentage, but it has no ceiling. an evaluation that takes twelve weeks can easily cost more than a percentage-based quote on the same account, and the buyer has no way to cap the spend once they have started.
