the flat fee is the least common, because it requires the provider to be confident in a repeatable process and to absorb the cost of its own failures. it is also the model buyers understand instantly: one price, any size, retries included. elitepropx uses it at $220 for that reason - it makes the buyer's decision simple and puts the cost of a failed attempt on the party that controls the trading.
the scope of work is narrow and finite: pick the firm, pay once, the evaluation is traded, the login is handed over.

price shapes behaviour, and the behaviour you should care about is what happens when the evaluation starts going badly. on a flat fee, a failed attempt is a pure cost to the provider, so the incentive is to trade conservatively enough to finish inside the rules. on a percentage, a failed attempt costs the provider only its time, and a pass on a large account is worth far more than a pass on a small one - which pushes the provider towards cherry-picking easy assignments.

the per-phase model aligns incentives reasonably well for phase one and poorly for phase two, because the second fee is small relative to the first and the second phase is where most evaluations die. a provider optimising for phase one revenue may take risks that make phase two fragile.

the retainer is the weakest alignment of the four. the provider is paid for elapsed time, so a fast pass is a short invoice. that is not an accusation - most providers in this category are honest and simply prefer predictable revenue - but a buyer should read the structure rather than the intentions.

one practical consequence follows for anyone comparing quotes. a percentage quote and a flat-fee quote are not comparable at face value, because they load risk in different places. convert every quote into a single number: expected total cost across three attempts , including the firm's own evaluation fees and reset charges. that number is what the decision actually hinges on, and it is almost never the number on the sales page.

there is a second-order effect worth mentioning because it changes behaviour in the funded phase. providers who take a share of payouts have an interest in the funded account performing, which sounds like alignment until you notice that the buyer may prefer a cautious funded account and the provider may prefer an aggressive one. flat-fee providers have no position in the funded account at all, which is cleaner, provided the buyer is equipped to run it. that trade-off is covered in the service review and in the payout process walkthrough .

this is the section that decides whether the purchase is sensible, and it is the section most buyers skip. proprietary trading firms write their own terms, and those terms govern whether someone else may trade the evaluation.

three positions exist in the market. some firms prohibit third-party trading explicitly, with account closure and forfeiture as the stated remedy. some firms are silent on the question, which is not permission - it is an unresolved ambiguity that a firm can resolve against the trader later. a smaller number of firms permit it, sometimes with conditions such as disclosure or a limit on shared access.

the consequences are asymmetric. if a firm voids a funded account after a payout request, the buyer loses the account and anything owed on it, and has no recourse against the firm because the firm's terms were clear. a provider cannot indemnify that risk, because the relationship it breached is between the trader and the firm. the buyer carries it either way.

that is why the terms check belongs before payment, not after. the practical process is short: open the firm's terms of service, search for "third party", "authorised user", "account sharing" and "proxy", and read the surrounding paragraph rather than the heading. where the answer is unclear, email the firm's support and keep the reply. it is not a guarantee, but a written answer is better than an inference.

a provider worth using will raise this itself and decline assignments it believes are prohibited. that refusal is a useful signal: it means the provider has read the terms, understands the downside, and is not optimising for the sale. elitepropx states the position on every service page and will not take a job on a firm whose terms forbid it, even where the buyer is willing to accept the risk.

there is a second terms issue that nobody advertises, and it concerns the funded account rather than the evaluation. several firms allow a trader to use assistance during an evaluation but require the funded account to be traded by the account holder personally, on the reasoning that payouts are the firm's real exposure. a buyer who has read the evaluation clause and stopped there has read half the contract. the question to ask support, in writing, is not "can someone trade the evaluation" but "who may trade the funded account after it is issued". the answers differ more often than the marketing implies, and the funded clause is the one with money attached.

there is a related trap that catches buyers who do check. some firms permit third-party trading on the evaluation but prohibit it on the funded account , or vice versa. a provider covering only the evaluation has not solved the second problem, and the buyer inherits it at the moment of maximum value. read the clause twice, once for each stage.

pricing a retry is the clearest way to compare providers, because the retry is the event the buyer is actually buying insurance against. an evaluation that passes first time makes every provider look identical; an evaluation that fails twice separates them completely.

start with the arithmetic of the firm's side. a failed evaluation must be replaced, and most firms charge a reset or a new purchase fee. that cost is the buyer's regardless of provider. what the provider can cover is the service fee for the next attempt - the labour - and that is the part worth comparing.

three policies exist. the strongest is unlimited retries on the same firm and account size at no additional service fee. the middle is a discounted retry, usually a fraction of the original price. the weakest is a new full fee, which is simply another purchase.

read the qualifying conditions even on the strongest policy. "same firm and account size" excludes switching firms, which is exactly what a buyer wants to do after a strategical mismatch. "same strategy" can exclude the buyer from a retry if the provider decides the plan was the problem. "subject to availability" is a soft cap disguised as a promise. none of these is unreasonable; all of them narrow the headline.

then value it honestly. a retry is worth the price of the alternative, which is a fresh service fee, multiplied by the probability of needing one. for a provider with a genuine completion rate near the top of the market, that is a small expected value. for a provider whose advertised rate is aspirational, the retry cover is the entire product. which is why the number that matters is not the success rate on the page but the failure policy in the contract.
every provider shows passes. the question is whether the evidence establishes what it claims, and most of it does not.

a screenshot of a balance is close to worthless: it shows a number, not an account, not a firm, not a date, and not whether the account was funded or evaluated. a screenshot of a firm's dashboard is better, because the interface identifies the firm and usually the account status. a third-party verified track record - a public myfxbook or similar linked account - is better again, because the history is timestamped and the equity curve cannot be edited after the fact.

even a verified track record has limits worth understanding. a verified account proves that trading happened, not that it happened on a prop firm evaluation, and not that the same plan can be repeated on a firm with different rules. it also shows drawdown, which is the part providers rarely discuss and the part that decides whether the plan survives a trailing threshold. read the maximum drawdown before the return.

the test that separates the serious from the theatrical is simple: ask for a pass on the exact firm and account size you are buying, dated within the last month, with the firm's own dashboard visible. a provider that can produce it is operating at volume. a provider that deflects to a general track record is telling you something useful about its coverage.

reviews deserve the same scepticism and a different technique. look for reviews that describe a failure, because the failure handling is the only part of the service a happy customer cannot evaluate. a wall of five-star reviews with no negative detail and no dates is a marketing asset, not a customer record. the client reviews page collects both directions for that reason.
the commercial relationship requires access to a trading account. it does not require access to your identity.

never hand over the email address registered to your prop firm account unless the provider needs it for the platform login, and never hand over the password for that mailbox. never provide identity documents, bank statements or payment-method details for kyc - those are between you and the firm, and a provider asking for them is either confused about the process or building a profile it does not need.

what a legitimate provider needs is narrow: the firm name, the account size and phase, the platform credentials for the evaluation account, and a way to reach you. some providers ask for the platform investor password rather than the master password, which is a reasonable precaution on platforms that support it. on platforms that do not, the master password is unavoidable during the evaluation and should be changed the moment the login is returned.

two habits reduce the residual risk. use a unique password for the trading account, not one reused elsewhere. and screenshot the account settings before handing anything over, so that a later dispute about what was changed has a baseline. both take a minute and neither is standard practice in this category, which is precisely why they are worth adopting.
none of these is decisive alone. together they produce a clear picture quickly.
they raise the terms issue before you do. a provider that never mentions the firm's position on third-party trading has either not read the terms or is hoping you will not.
they quote one price. providers that add a platform fee, a management fee or a success fee on top of the headline number are pricing in stages to make the first number look small.
they describe the failure case without being asked. what happens on a breach, who pays the reset, how long a retry takes - a provider with a process answers immediately.
they refuse some firms. a provider that will take any firm is not screening; it is selling. screening is the expensive part of the service.
they have a completion time, not a completion guarantee. "fourteen days on average" is a measurement. "funded in seven days guaranteed" is a sales script.
they do not ask for your email password or kyc documents. the account credentials are the job. everything else is overreach.

they publish a business identity. a domain, an email address and a payment processor that resolves to a real merchant account. anonymous providers are not automatically fraudulent, but a buyer has no remedy against one.

two failures against that list is a warning; four is a decision. the category attracts operators who disappear after a bad month, and the tests above are mostly tests of whether the provider expects to be around next quarter.
provider coverage matters more than the headline price: a flat fee is only flat for the firms the provider actually trades.
a passing service is a labour and risk-transfer product, and it is the wrong product in several common situations.

it is wrong if your reason for buying is to learn. the evaluation is the cheapest trading education available - a defined risk, a defined target, and a clear verdict on whether the plan survives rules. outsourcing it removes the feedback loop and leaves the funded account in the hands of someone who has never traded under those rules.

it is wrong if the funded account is the point. a trader who cannot run the funded account has bought a login, not an income. the funded stage has its own rules - minimum days, consistency checks, payout schedules - and the failure rate there is high precisely among traders who did not do the evaluation themselves.

it is wrong where the firm prohibits it, obviously, and it is wrong where the economics do not work. if the evaluation fee is small relative to the service fee, and the trader has a plan that passes most of the time, the service is expensive insurance against a loss that is already affordable.

it is right in a narrower set of cases: the trader has a funded-account plan but no time to execute an evaluation; the firm requires a pace of trading that does not fit a day job; the trader has failed the same rule repeatedly and wants the evaluation cleared while they work on the behaviour. those are rational purchases. "i want to be funded" is not, on its own, a reason to buy labour.
clarity about the exclusions is half of a good purchase. four things are almost never included, and a buyer who assumes otherwise will be disappointed at the worst moment.

you are not buying the firm's fee. the evaluation, the reset and any platform charges belong to the firm. a provider quoting a single all-in figure is either bundling the firm's charge into its own price or being vague about who pays what. ask for the split explicitly.

you are not buying the funded account's performance. the login is handed over and the account is the trader's from that point. a provider that continues to trade it is selling a different product - a profit-share arrangement - which is usually prohibited and always a different risk profile.

you are not buying a guarantee against a rule breach. if the firm decides a trade breached its terms - a news window, a position cap, a hedging clause - the account can be voided regardless of the provider's intentions. good providers trade defensively around those rules, but no provider can underwrite the firm's discretion.

you are not buying anonymity from the firm. the account is opened in the trader's name, verified with the trader's documents, and paid to the trader's payment method. any arrangement that asks the trader to hide the relationship from the firm is both a terms risk and a sign that the provider knows it.

those four exclusions explain most of the complaints in this category. they are also easy to state up front, which is why a provider that states them is worth more than one that leaves them to be discovered.
ten items, all answerable in under an hour, and all worth more than another review thread.
i have read the firm's terms on third-party trading, for both the evaluation and the funded account.
i have the provider's answer in writing on that specific firm.
i know the total price, including the firm's fee, and whether a retry costs anything.
i know which phases and which account sizes the price covers.
i know what the provider does at the funded stage, and whether it takes a share of payouts.
i have seen a pass on my firm and size, dated recently, on the firm's own dashboard.
i know the expected completion time and what happens if it slips.
i have a unique password on the trading account and a screenshot of its settings.
i have not been asked for identity documents, bank details or mailbox access.
i have compared this quote to the alternative - trading it myself - using expected total cost.

that list is deliberately unexciting. the category's problems are rarely exotic; they are the ordinary ones - an unread clause, an unpriced retry, a provider that stops answering. a buyer who works through ten boring questions is already in the top decile of customers this industry serves.

there is no single market price. percentage-of-account providers can charge several hundred dollars on a large evaluation, per-phase providers charge per stage, and flat-fee providers like elitepropx charge $220 regardless of size. the number that matters is the expected total across attempts, including the firm's own fees and resets.

it depends on the firm and it is written in the terms, not the marketing. some prohibit third-party trading with account closure as the remedy, some are silent, and a few permit it with conditions. silence is not permission - ask the firm's support and keep the reply.

on the $220 flat fee, a retry on the same firm and account size carries no additional service fee; the firm's own reset charge is separate and paid to the firm. check any provider's retry policy for qualifying conditions such as switching firms or changing strategy, because those narrow the cover considerably.

no. the funded account is opened in the trader's name and payouts are paid to the trader's own verified payment method. a provider that asks to receive payouts on your behalf - or asks for bank details to "process" them - is describing something the firms do not do.

around two weeks on average across managed evaluations, with two-phase forex evaluations usually taking longer than single-phase ones and futures evaluations bounded below by a minimum session count. be sceptical of any promise expressed as a guarantee rather than an average.

you cannot verify a rate directly; you can verify individual passes. ask for a recent pass on your specific firm and size, shown on the firm's dashboard with a visible date, and look at a third-party verified track record for drawdown rather than for return. a provider that cannot produce a specific example is quoting a number it does not measure.

it is unusual rather than suspicious. flat fees are viable for providers running a repeatable plan at volume, and they are unattractive to providers who prefer pricing on upside. what deserves scrutiny is not the price but the coverage: which firms, which phases, which sizes, and what happens on a failure.

buy the evaluation. a service that sells a ready-funded account is either reselling an account it already passed, which may breach the firm's transfer rules, or describing a profit-share arrangement on an account you do not control. the evaluation is the clean, documented product.

a dated pass on your exact firm and account size, visible on the firm's own dashboard. add a third-party verified track record if one exists, and read its maximum drawdown before its return. screenshots of a balance chart prove nothing on their own.

the firm name, account size and phase, the platform credentials for the evaluation account, and a way to contact you. nothing else. identity documents, bank details and mailbox access are outside the scope of the job and should be refused.
can i use a service and then trade the funded account myself?

yes, and that is the standard arrangement on a flat-fee model: the login is handed over and the funded account is entirely the trader's. it is also the harder half of the job - the funded rules on minimum days, consistency and payout schedules are covered in the payout guide .

buying before reading the firm's terms. every other risk in the category is priced and disclosed; the terms risk is neither. a funded account removed for third-party trading is the one outcome that costs the buyer everything and is entirely avoidable with ten minutes of reading.

a passing service trades a prop firm evaluation on a client's behalf for a fixed fee. the model is simple to describe and easy to misrepresent, so this page sets out exactly what is delivered, what is excluded, how the pricing works, where the arrangement is legitimate, and the seven checks that separate a provider from a reseller with a telegram channel. elitepropx charges one flat $220 for any firm, any account size, with retries covered and no profit split.
a passing service removes evaluation risk, not trading risk. the funded account is still governed by the firm's rules and still has to be traded.
the flat-fee model prices the evaluation, not the outcome: one fee, retries covered, no share of profit.
third-party trading is prohibited by many firms. a provider that does not check the terms is putting the client's funded account at risk of being voided at payout.
delivery is a sequence - terms check, fee, trading, pass, handover - and every step should be documented.
percentage-of-profit and profit-split models create a different incentive: the provider is paid to keep trading your account.
verify the provider's identity, the fee structure and the reset policy in writing before paying anything.

a passing service takes responsibility for one thing: producing a completed evaluation that meets a firm's profit target without breaching its rules. the client buys the evaluation from the firm, supplies the account or the credentials as the provider requires, and receives a funded account that satisfies the firm's conditions.

the deliverable is narrow and worth being precise about. it is not a trading strategy, it is not a signal service, it is not a managed account, and it is not a guarantee of income. it is a completed test. everything that happens after the pass - the funded account's profit threshold, its consistency rule, its payout schedule, its conduct restrictions - belongs to the client and to the firm.

that narrowness is the reason the model can be priced flat. a provider that trades evaluations repeatedly is running a process rather than a view: the target, the drawdown and the daily limit are known in advance, and the work is to reach a fixed objective inside fixed constraints. it is closer to project delivery than to trading advice, which is why a fixed fee is a coherent price and a percentage of future profit is not.
five stages, one of which is a refusal: if the firm's terms forbid third-party trading, the job does not start.
the industry prices this work in three ways, and the differences matter more than the headline numbers because each model rewards different provider behaviour.

flat fee per evaluation. one price for any firm, any account size, often with retries covered. the incentive is to pass efficiently, because the provider absorbs the cost of a retry. the trade-off is that the fee has to be high enough to cover the failure rate across all clients, so a flat fee is priced for the average rather than for one client's rulebook.

percentage of the funded account or of the payout. the provider is paid a share of what the account earns. the incentive is aligned in theory and dangerous in practice: a provider paid a share of profit has a reason to keep trading the account after the pass, which extends the exposure and can lose the account in pursuit of a larger fee.

per-attempt fee with a reset charge. the provider charges for each evaluation attempt. the incentive is the opposite of the flat model: every failure is billable, so the provider is paid more when the client needs more attempts. that is a structural conflict, and it is worth noticing even when the provider is honest.

elitepropx uses the first model: a flat $220 for any firm and any account size, with resets covered while the evaluation is running and no profit split. the consequence is stated openly - the fee is the same whether the account is a $10,000 forex evaluation or a $150,000 futures account, because the work is the same process applied to different numbers.
this is the part most providers skip, and it is the part that decides whether a funded account survives.

proprietary trading firms are not uniform on third-party trading. some permit it explicitly. some prohibit it. some permit it on the evaluation and prohibit it on the funded account, or the reverse. and some are silent, which in practice means the firm can decide at payout time that the account was not traded by the named holder.

the consequence of getting it wrong is asymmetric. a prohibited evaluation that is passed can produce a funded account that is voided at the first withdrawal, which is a worse outcome than a failed evaluation, because the client has paid the firm, paid the service, and earned nothing. a provider that does not check the terms before accepting the job is transferring that risk to the client without saying so.

our rule: if the firm's terms forbid third-party trading, we tell the client before payment and decline the job. there is no version of this where quietly accepting is acceptable, because the loss lands on the funded account rather than on the fee.

two related points belong here. first, the funded account must be in the client's name with payouts to the client - anything else turns a service into an unauthorised managed account, which most firms prohibit outright. second, the client must complete identity verification personally; a provider cannot and should not do that on someone else's behalf.

where the terms are ambiguous, the honest answer is to ask the firm in writing before buying the evaluation. a support response that permits third-party trading on the evaluation is worth having, and it is worth saving. the scam checklist covers the firms and providers where that question is never answered.
a provider should be able to describe the sequence in advance, in order, without hedging. here is ours.

terms check. the client names the firm and account size. we read the current terms for third-party trading, on the evaluation and on the funded account, and confirm in writing that the job can proceed. if it cannot, the process stops here at no cost.

purchase. the client buys the evaluation directly from the firm, in their own name, with their own payment method. the fee for the evaluation is never routed through us - that keeps ownership unambiguous and keeps the client's identity where the firm expects it.

handover. the client supplies what the firm's model requires for the account to be traded. the scope of that access is agreed in writing before it is granted, and it is limited to the evaluation account.

trading. the evaluation is traded to the firm's target and within its rules. progress is reported at agreed checkpoints, and the client is told immediately if an attempt fails rather than at the end of a reporting period.

pass and return. the evaluation is completed, credentials are returned or removed, and the client takes control of the funded account. the pass is documented with the firm's own confirmation, not a screenshot of a dashboard.

two details in that sequence are worth emphasising because they are the usual points of failure in the industry. the first is step one: a provider that accepts any firm without checking is a provider that has not read the terms, which means the client is relying on luck at payout. the second is step five: credentials should be returned or removed at handover, and the client should change the password afterwards regardless. a service that keeps access after the pass is keeping access to a funded account.

the reporting cadence matters too. an evaluation can take one to three weeks depending on the firm's rules and the minimum day count. a provider that goes quiet for that period leaves the client unable to distinguish a slow pass from a failed attempt. checkpoints - even a weekly line - are part of the product.
scope is where expectations are set, and a vague scope is the most common source of dispute. ours is explicit.

the line that matters most is the third row. a passing service solves the evaluation; it does not solve the funded account's payout conditions. those conditions - a profit threshold, a minimum day count, a consistency cap, a verification step - are unchanged by who traded the evaluation, and a client who passes and then loses the funded account to a daily limit has lost the account for the same reason anyone else would.
the payout guide covers what happens after handover, and the profit calculator models what a given account is worth once the payout conditions are met.
these apply to any provider, including this one. a provider that cannot answer all seven in writing is not ready to be paid.
who is the provider? a named business, a verifiable contact address and a payment method that can be traced. an anonymous telegram handle with a wallet address fails this check.
is the fee structure unambiguous? flat, per attempt, or profit share - and what happens on a retry. "contact for pricing" usually means the price depends on how much the provider thinks you will pay.
does the provider check the firm's terms? ask directly: "will you confirm in writing that my firm permits third-party trading before i pay?" a hesitation is the answer.
who owns the funded account? it must be in the client's name, with the client's identity and payment details on it. anything else is a managed account in disguise.
what is the reset policy? whether retries are covered, how many, and whether the firm's reset charge is separate.
what is the reporting cadence? weekly updates at minimum, and immediate notice of a failure.
what happens if the provider cannot complete the job? a refund policy for service failure - distinct from the firm's refund policy - stated before payment.
run those seven against any provider, including the ones ranked highly in search results. the 2026 service review applies them to the market, and the review index collects the individual assessments.
the comparison is not "easy versus hard". it is a comparison of three costs: the fee, the calendar, and the probability of needing a second attempt.

doing it yourself costs the firm's fee per attempt and whatever calendar the evaluation takes. it also costs attention, which is the input most traders under-price: an evaluation traded badly consumes the same weeks as one traded well, and a trader running three failed attempts has spent six weeks that could have produced a funded account.

a flat-fee service converts that into a known number. the client pays the firm's fee once, pays the service's fee once, and does not pay for retries while the evaluation runs. what the client gives up is control of the evaluation and the learning that comes from trading it - which is a real cost for a trader who wants to build the skill and a negligible one for a trader who wants the account.
the comparison is fee times expected attempts. a flat fee removes the multiplication; it does not remove the firm's charge.

there is a third option that is often overlooked: buy the evaluation yourself, trade it yourself, and use a passing service only after a failure. that hybrid keeps the learning on the first attempt and caps the downside after it. it is a reasonable strategy, and it is worth saying that the flat fee does not change based on how many attempts have already failed.
a page that lists only advantages is marketing. five risks are real, and a client should weigh all of them.

terms risk. the firm may prohibit third-party trading, or may change its terms between the pass and the payout. the first is checkable in advance; the second is not fully, which is why the funded account should be treated as a separate risk from the evaluation.

provider risk. the fee is paid before the work is done. a provider that disappears, or that quietly stops reporting, leaves the client with a failed attempt and no recourse unless the payment method is traceable.

concentration risk. the provider is trading several evaluations, possibly the same firm and instrument and direction. firms that treat correlated positions across accounts as one exposure may treat that as a breach, which is another reason the terms check comes first.

skill risk. a trader who passes by service has not practised the evaluation. the funded account still requires a plan, and the first month of a funded account is not the place to learn one. the complete passing guide covers the plan; it is worth reading even if someone else trades the test.

expectation risk. the service produces a funded account, not income. a client who expects the fee to convert directly into withdrawals has misunderstood the product, and that misunderstanding is the industry's most common complaint.

every one of those is manageable with the checks above, and none of them is eliminated by a cheap price. the correct question is not "which provider is cheapest" but "which provider will tell me, in writing, when the answer is no".
whether a flat fee is worth paying is a calculation, and it can be done with four numbers: the firm's fee, the service's fee, the expected number of attempts, and the value of the calendar.

take a firm fee of $500, a service fee of $220, and a trader whose discipline suggests two attempts on their own. doing it themselves costs about $1,000 in fees over six weeks. using a service costs $500 plus $220 - $720 - over the same period, with retries covered while the evaluation runs. the saving is $280, and the calendar is equal.

now take a trader who passes first time. doing it themselves costs $500. using a service costs $720. the service is $220 worse, and the trader has also given up the evaluation experience. that is the honest case against the model, and it is not small: for a disciplined trader with a suitable firm, doing it yourself is cheaper.

the break-even is a single failure. if there is any meaningful chance the first attempt fails, the flat fee is priced competitively against the expected cost - and the chance is meaningful for most traders, which is why the market exists. what the table cannot price is the value of the calendar and the attention, which for a trader with a full-time job is usually the deciding factor.

two honest caveats. the service fee does not include the firm's reset charge where one is needed, and it does not cover the funded account. and the comparison assumes the service passes - a provider with a poor record is worse than doing it yourself at any price, which is why the checks above matter more than the arithmetic.
preparation is short and it materially improves the outcome, because the provider can only trade the account it is given.
choose the firm and the size deliberately. the cheapest account is usually the strictest rulebook. the smallest size that produces a meaningful payout is almost always the right first purchase.
confirm the terms in writing. ask the firm whether third-party trading is permitted on the evaluation and on the funded account, and save the answer.
have a plan for the funded account before it arrives. risk per trade, daily stop, daily profit cap, minimum day count. writing it after the pass is how funded accounts are lost in week one.
complete verification immediately. identity checks can be started before the first trade, and doing so removes the most common cause of a delayed first payout.
decide what happens after handover. change the password, confirm the account is in your name, and check the funded terms yourself rather than relying on a summary.
four of those five take under an hour in total. the fifth - a plan for the funded account - is the one that decides whether the fee produces income or a screenshotted pass.
every provider claims a high pass rate. almost none of them publish something that can be checked, and the difference between a claim and a record is the whole of the decision.

ask what a pass looks like as evidence. the useful artefact is the firm's own confirmation that an evaluation was completed - an account-stage change, a dashboard state, or a funded login that the client controls. a screenshot of a profit number is not evidence of a pass; it is evidence of a profit number. the distinction matters because a trader can be up 9% on a 10% target and be nowhere near finished.

ask for the sample size. a provider advertising a handful of passes is describing a small sample, and small samples are dominated by luck: a single good week can produce an impressive-looking record. ask how many evaluations were attempted in the last quarter alongside how many passed, because the ratio that matters is pass rate, not pass count.

ask about failures honestly. a provider that claims no failures is either new or lying. the informative question is not whether attempts fail but what happens when they do: how quickly the client is told, whether the retry is covered, and whether the failure was a drawdown breach or a conduct breach. a provider that cannot classify its own failures has not read the rules closely enough to trade them.

ask which firms the record covers. a provider that only works with one or two firms is not necessarily worse - specialisation is a reasonable strategy - but the fee advertised as "any firm" should be tested. a rulebook the provider has never traded is a rulebook the provider will learn on a client's account.

check whether the record is verifiable independently. the strongest version of a track record is a reviews page where clients can be contacted, or a public archive of completed evaluations. the weakest is a collage of green numbers with no dates and no account identifiers. where the evidence sits between those two, ask what a client whose evaluation failed would say, and expect a specific answer rather than a deflection.

the standard for this site is deliberately unglamorous: passes are described as a count of completed evaluations, the public record is on the passed challenges page, and the review articles describe both what works and where a provider is weak. a track record that cannot survive that level of description is not a track record.

due diligence runs in both directions, and the questions a provider asks are a reliable signal of how carefully it works. a provider that takes payment without asking any of the following is trading blind.

which firm, and at which account size? the rulebook is decided by the firm and the difficulty is decided by the size. a provider that does not ask cannot price the work accurately, which means it is pricing an average and absorbing the variance somewhere - usually by being slow or selective.

has this evaluation been attempted before? a second attempt on an account the client has already traded is a different job from a clean purchase: the firm's reset terms apply, the account may carry a reduced balance, and the minimum day count restarts. those are all visible in the terms and all relevant to the price.

is the client's identity verification complete? not because a provider needs it, but because an unverified account that is passed produces a funded account that cannot pay. raising it before the work starts is the only point at which it is easy to fix.

what does the client intend to do with the funded account? a client who intends to trade it has to satisfy the funded conditions personally, and a provider that knows this can flag the ones that matter - a tight consistency share, an unusual minimum day count, a first-payout waiting period. a client who does not intend to trade it should be told plainly that the funded account is not income.

does the client understand the firm's conduct rules? news windows, size caps and holding restrictions are unchanged by who trades the evaluation. if the client is planning to trade the funded account immediately, those rules are about to apply to them, and the first week after handover is a poor time to read them.

what is the client's refund expectation? the service fee and the firm's fee are different things with different policies, and the most common post-purchase dispute is a client who expects the service to refund an evaluation fee it never received. setting that expectation before payment costs one paragraph and prevents the argument entirely.

the pattern across all six questions is that a careful provider is really asking whether the client's plan survives the funded stage. that is the part of the transaction the fee does not buy, and it is the part most likely to decide whether the money was well spent.

it depends entirely on the firm's terms. some permit third-party trading, many prohibit it, and some permit it on the evaluation while prohibiting it on the funded account. a provider should check and confirm in writing before taking payment, and decline the job where it is banned.

one evaluation at any firm and any account size, traded to the firm's target within its rules, with retries covered while the evaluation is running and no profit split on the funded account. the firm's own evaluation and reset fees are paid by the client directly to the firm.
do you take a share of the funded account's profit?

no. the funded account and its payouts belong to the client. a profit share creates a reason to keep trading someone else's account after the job is done, which is a conflict of interest we choose not to have.

the attempt is retried at no additional service fee while the evaluation is running. the firm's own reset charge, where it applies, remains the client's cost, and the client is told about the failure immediately rather than at the end of a reporting period.

the client, always. the evaluation is purchased in the client's name with the client's payment method, identity verification is completed personally, and credentials are returned or removed at handover. anything else is a managed account in disguise and is prohibited by most firms.
do i need to give you my trading account password?

the mechanics depend on the firm's platform, and the scope of any access is agreed in writing before it is granted and limited to the evaluation account. after handover, change the password regardless of how access was provided.

typically one to three weeks, driven mainly by the firm's minimum day count and target rather than by trading speed. a provider that promises a fixed number of days without knowing the firm's day count has not read the rulebook.
at agreed checkpoints, at minimum weekly, plus immediate notice if an attempt fails. silence during an evaluation is indistinguishable from a failure, so a reporting cadence is part of the product.

the evaluation is traded to the terms in force when it started, and any material change is raised with the client immediately. firms that change payout conditions retroactively are a risk that no service can remove, which is why the review process matters.

it should not. the funded account belongs to the client and is governed by the firm's rules; keeping a provider on it converts a completed job into an ongoing arrangement that most firms prohibit and that puts the payout at risk.

only if you would have needed more than one attempt. at a $500 firm fee, one attempt costs $500 and a service costs $720, so the service is worse if you pass first time. from the second attempt onward the arithmetic reverses.

a named business, a clear fee structure, a written terms check, client ownership of the funded account, a reset policy, a reporting cadence and a refund policy for service failure. a provider that cannot answer all seven in writing is not ready to be paid.

reviews of passing services are the strangest evidence in retail trading: written by a self-selected sample, about a binary outcome, on platforms where competitors can post freely. this page sets out what the reviews actually show, which patterns carry information, and how to test a provider in an afternoon without relying on any of it.
most negative reviews describe a firm's rule, not a provider's failure - a distinction that changes what you should check.
the most useful positive reviews mention a rule being explained, not a pass being achieved.
review volume is a marketing metric; review specificity is an evidence metric.
any provider - including elitepropx, at a flat $220 for any firm and size - can be tested with five questions before payment.

a review section is normally a sample of customers. in this category it is a sample of outcomes, because the product is binary: an evaluation either reaches its target or it does not. that single feature distorts everything downstream.

a trader who was funded and paid writes while the experience is fresh, usually within a fortnight of the payout. a trader whose evaluation failed writes immediately, often the same evening. a trader whose evaluation is still running writes nothing, and that group is the largest of the three. the published sample is therefore dominated by the two extremes and barely represents the median experience.

first, selection: unhappy people write more often than contented ones, except in this category where a successful payout is exciting enough to produce a review. the two effects partly cancel, which is why review scores in this market cluster around extremes rather than the middle.

second, attribution: a client cannot easily tell whether a refused payout was the provider's error or the firm's rule. reviews frequently attribute a rulebook outcome to the service, and the reader has no way to check unless the reviewer names the rule.

third, solicitation: reviews can be requested, and requested reviews are warmer than unsolicited ones. a cluster of five-star entries in a single week is not evidence of fraud; it is evidence of a campaign, which is a different thing and equally uninformative.

ideally: every client, pass or fail, reviewing within a month, naming the firm, the account size and the fee. that sample does not exist anywhere in this market, and the absence is not a conspiracy - it would require a provider to publish its own failures, which no commercial operation volunteers.
the practical substitute is to read reviews for categories rather than scores, and to test the provider directly on the things reviews cannot establish. the rest of this page is that method.
positive reviews fall into four groups, and they are not equally informative.

"passed in 16 days" is the most common positive review and the least informative. it establishes that the service can produce a pass, which is the minimum viable claim for a business that sells passes. it says nothing about the failure case, which is where the risk sits.

"answered every question before i paid" is useful, and it has a limitation: communication before payment is the cheapest thing a provider can do well. the test is communication after payment, and specifically after a problem, which is rarely reviewed because it rarely happens to a reviewer.

"they explained why my payout would be blocked before i even asked" is the most valuable sentence in the category. it describes the product doing its actual job - translating a rulebook into a plan - and it is hard to write convincingly without having experienced it.

fast passes read well and should be treated with mild suspicion. a pass in six days on a 10% target implies risk high enough that the account had little margin, and the same approach that produced the pass would have produced a reset in a different week. speed is a property of the risk taken, not of the service's skill.
negative reviews cluster into six causes. reading them by cause tells you what to check before buying; reading them by score tells you nothing.

four of the six are rulebook questions that a buyer can settle before paying anything. one is a communication question answerable with a single test email. only the last is a genuine disagreement about method, and even that is resolvable by asking for a timeline.

a funded account closed after review is the worst outcome in the category, because it arrives after the work is done and the client has the least recourse. it is also the most preventable: firms that prohibit third-party trading tend to say so, and a provider that checks the policy before accepting an assignment removes the risk entirely. a provider that treats the prohibition as a technicality is transferring its risk to the client.
across review pages, five patterns repeat and each maps to a question a buyer can ask.
specifics predict reliability. reviews naming the firm, size, dates and fee are checkable; reviews with adjectives are not.
answered negatives predict conduct. a provider who replies to a one-star review with a reason behaves differently from one who replies with a reassurance.
deleted negatives predict everything. a page with no negative reviews in a market where payouts are routinely refused is a page that has been curated.
clusters predict campaigns. twenty reviews in a week on a service that had none for a year is solicitation, not evidence.

rule mentions predict competence. reviews that mention a trailing floor, a consistency threshold or a payout window were written by clients who understood what they bought, usually because someone explained it.
five questions, one email, and the answers either hold together or they do not. this is the substitute for a reliable review sample, and it takes less time than reading fifty entries.

"on my firm, is the maximum loss static or trailing, and if trailing does it update intraday or at the close?" the answer distinguishes a provider who has read the terms from one who has read the pricing page. it also produces a useful side effect: if the answer is wrong, everything else in the reply becomes suspect.

"what has to be true before my first withdrawal?" a complete answer names a profit threshold, a trading-day minimum and any consistency ratio. an incomplete answer names the threshold only, which is the one on the marketing page.

"if a daily limit is breached in week two, what happens and what does it cost?" this is the question that matters most and is asked least. a provider who says "retries covered at the same firm and size, the firm's own reset separate" has priced the risk. a provider who says "we'll sort it out" has not.
"whose name is on the funded account, and who receives the payout?" the only acceptable answer for a client who intends to keep the account is their own name and their own bank account.

"which firms will you not trade, and why?" a provider with no refusals has not read enough rulebooks. the refusals are the most informative sentence in any reply, because they show where the provider has decided to lose a sale rather than take a risk.
any page reviewing the category should review its own operator in the same terms, including the parts that are not flattering.

one flat $220 for any prop firm and any account size, with retries on rule breaches at the same firm and size covered, no profit split, and the funded account issued in the client's name. the rulebook is read before quoting, and assignments are declined where a firm's third-party policy makes the arrangement unsafe for the client.

the fee structure is the part that is genuinely different from most of the market. a flat fee removes the incentive to keep a client trading longer than the rules require, and it removes the argument at payout about who is owed what.

it is a small operation with limited capacity, so scheduling depends on how many evaluations are running at once. verification is provided on request rather than published as a live tracker for every account, partly because several firms' platforms do not support external linking. and the fee is paid whether or not an evaluation passes, which is why the retry clause carries so much weight - without it the fee would be a bet rather than a purchase.

the honest summary is that this is a service for a trader who wants the rulebook handled and the account in their own name, and who is willing to check the terms before paying. it is not a service for someone who wants a guarantee, and it will not pretend otherwise.

most reviews in this market are written from inside an emotion rather than from inside a file. a review that helps contains five things: the firm, the account size, the dates, the fee, and whether the payout arrived. add one sentence on what went wrong, if anything, and one on how the provider responded.

that is about sixty words, and it is worth more than any rating. it also protects the reviewer: a specific review is harder to dispute than a general complaint, and it can be checked by anyone reading it a year later when the rulebook has changed.

providers are entitled to reply, and a reply should state the rule and the date rather than question the reviewer's competence. where a review is factually wrong - a fee misquoted, a firm's rule attributed to the service - the correction belongs beside the original, not in place of it. deleting a review is the one action that makes every remaining review suspect.
rulebooks shape behaviour, and behaviour shapes the reviews a firm collects.

the reviews a provider receives are partly a function of the firms it trades, because some rulebooks generate complaints no matter how well they are explained. understanding that relationship explains why a service can look excellent on one firm and dreadful on another in the same month.

a 30% best-day rule means a profitable account can be refused a withdrawal, and the client experiences that as a service failure. the rule is disclosed, the client agreed to it, and the emotion is real. a provider trading only firms of that type will accumulate negative reviews that describe the industry rather than the service.
the defence is on the first page of the plan: a client who is told at purchase that the first payout may need more ordinary profit than the evaluation target is not surprised three weeks later.

a trailing floor makes a profitable session more fragile, and traders who give back an unrealised gain often believe the account was mishandled. on an end-of-day model the give-back is free intraday; on an intraday model it is charged. a service that does not explain the difference before trading will be blamed for the mechanic.

monthly payout windows and multi-day processing produce a gap between "i earned it" and "i have it". that gap is where trust is tested, and it is the one thing a provider can manage by setting expectations rather than by promising speed.

ambiguity is the real problem. when a rulebook contradicts itself, the outcome depends on who reads it, and disputes become unanswerable. that is why the assignments worth refusing are the ones where the terms are unclear, not the ones where they are strict.
a flat fee and a share of profit diverge sharply once the outcome is uncertain.

prices in this category range from nothing to several hundred dollars per attempt, and the spread is only partly explained by quality. it is mostly explained by the model, and the model determines what the client pays over a year rather than per attempt.

the subscription model deserves a note because it is the one that quietly costs the most. its economics reward a client who pays for months without withdrawing, which is the opposite of what a funded trader should be doing. where a subscription is the only option, the payout schedule should be aggressive enough to make the duration short.

the percentage split is the most advertised and the least examined. it is genuinely free if the service fails and genuinely expensive if the client succeeds, which means the provider's revenue is highest for the clients who need it least. that is not fraudulent, and it is a strange thing to call alignment.

every model leaves the firm's own challenge fee with the client, and every model treats reset charges differently. a buyer should ask for the total outlay in the failure case - service fee plus challenge fee plus reset - as a single number, because that is the number that decides whether a second attempt is affordable.
fit is answered by the rulebook, not by the review score.
a buyer can construct a defensible shortlist in an hour without reading a single review, using four inputs that are all publicly available.

list two or three firms whose rules suit your style. for most discretionary traders that means a static or end-of-day drawdown and a daily limit measured in a way that can be tracked. this list determines which providers are even relevant.

decide in advance whether you will accept a percentage split. if you intend to withdraw repeatedly, the arithmetic in the table above makes the answer obvious. if you genuinely expect one small payout, a split can be cheaper.
ask each candidate which firms they will not trade. a provider whose refusals include the firms on your list has saved you both an afternoon.
ask for a dated certificate on a comparable firm and size. where a live verification link exists, follow it and run the four checks: sync status, age, worst drawdown, distribution of winning days.

with those four inputs, the shortlist is usually two names, and the decision between them turns on communication and price rather than on reputation. that is a better ordering than starting from a review page and working backwards, because reputation is the one input that cannot be checked.
marketing language in this category is consistent enough to translate. six phrases appear constantly and each means something narrower than it appears.

almost always calculated on a denominator that flatters: enquiries, or clients who agreed to proceed, or passes counted against the accounts that were traded to completion. a meaningful rate needs the denominator named and the period. where it is not named, the number is decoration.

possible, and it describes a risk level. a 10% target reached in ten trading days at 2% risk has a plausible mechanism; reached in four days it required 2.5% a day with no losing days, which is a direction rather than a process. the phrase describes the best case, not the median.

more often a percentage split with a delayed payment than a free service. the money comes from withdrawals instead of a card, and the total is usually larger. that is not a deception as long as the split is stated in the same sentence, which it rarely is.

prop firm evaluations are not an algorithmic problem. they are a budgeting problem with a rulebook attached, and the disciplines that pass them are arithmetic and consistency. a provider selling an algorithm is selling mystique; a provider selling a plan is selling the thing that works.

meaningful only if the verification is checkable. a certificate naming firm, size and date is checkable; a screenshot is not; a claim of verification without a link is a claim about the provider's own honesty, which is the thing being tested.

this one is also the offer here, so it deserves a straight answer: it means the fee does not change with the firm or the size, because the work does not. it does not mean every firm is acceptable - firms that prohibit third-party trading are declined - and any provider using the phrase should be asked which firms it excludes and why.
a trader with a $50,000 futures evaluation in mind, a modest edge, and roughly three weeks available. four candidates, all found through search results rather than reviews.

$220, retries on rule breaches at the same firm and size, funded account in the client's name. the reply to the first email names the firm's drawdown mechanic correctly and explains why the trailing floor makes exits important. the refusal list includes two firms the trader had considered, with rulebook reasons.

free to start, 25% of each withdrawal, funded account held by the provider. over five $3,000 withdrawals the cost is $3,750 against $220. the email does not mention the payout conditions and answers the drawdown question with a percentage.

$99, no retries, client holds everything else. on a first attempt the arithmetic is acceptable; on an expected two attempts it is $198 plus the firm's reset charge, and neither attempt is informed by the first, because there is no process to improve.

$150 a month while the evaluation is live. a three-week evaluation costs about $115, which looks like the cheapest option until the payout phase extends the subscription by another two months. the model's incentives point at duration, which points away from the client's interest.

candidate one wins on three of four criteria and is the only one that answered the rulebook question without prompting. candidate four is the interesting case: its pricing looks competitive per month and becomes expensive because the payout phase is slow, which is a rulebook fact the buyer has to know in advance.

the decision did not require any reviews. it required the firm's rulebook, four questions, and a multiplication. reviews would have added colour and no new information, which is the correct role for them in this category: colour, notes, and questions to ask - not a verdict.
the first week with a provider, and what to expect
reviews rarely describe the first week, and it is where most of the avoidable friction lives. six things should happen, and their absence is a signal rather than a delay.

before a single order, the client should receive the firm's numbers in writing: daily budget, failure distance, target, payout conditions and the firm's position on third-party trading. this document is the reference point for every later conversation, and a provider who does not produce one is improvising.

two to four weeks is the honest range for most evaluations. a provider quoting four days is describing the best case, and a provider quoting six weeks should explain which constraint is binding. either is fine as long as the number is checkable against the plan.
a date, ideally with an account identifier. vague reassurance that "we're on it" costs nothing to give and nothing to verify, which is exactly why specificity matters here.
