an account with 1:100 leverage sounds dangerous and an account with 1:10 sounds conservative. on a prop firm evaluation that impression is almost exactly backwards, because neither number sets how much money is at risk on a trade. leverage sets how much margin a position requires; it does not set the size of the loss if the trade goes wrong.

consider two traders with a $100,000 account and a 1% risk rule - $1,000 per trade. one has 1:100 leverage and the other 1:10. both risk $1,000. the first needs $1,000 of margin for a position that would otherwise require $100,000 of capital; the second needs $10,000. their expected losses, their daily budgets and their distance to a failure level are identical. only the amount of equity sitting in margin differs.

what the ratio does change is how large a position can be opened before the platform refuses. that is a permission, not an instruction, and treating permission as instruction is the actual hazard in this topic.

retail marketing uses leverage as a proxy for opportunity - "trade 100 times your capital" - which implies that the account's risk scales with the multiple. it does not. a trader who risks 1% per trade at 1:500 leverage risks 1% per trade. a trader who risks 20% per trade at 1:5 leverage risks 20%.

the one place the confusion has teeth is margin calls. on a live account, a position too large for the available margin is closed by the broker at the worst possible price. on a prop firm evaluation the same mechanic exists in a different form: the failure level is reached and the account ends, whether the trader intended the size or not.
the three figures below are the whole topic. anything else is commentary.

read the table in that order and the logic is unavoidable. risk is chosen first. stop distance is chosen second, from the chart. position size is derived third. margin is the last and least important figure - a consequence of the position, not an input to it.

a trader who starts from leverage - "i can open 20 lots, so i will" - has inverted the order. the size no longer follows from the stop, so the loss when the stop is hit is whatever the stop distance happens to imply, which is usually far more than the plan allowed.
the same trade, three leverage ratios: identical risk, different margin. leverage permits size; it does not create risk.

two traders opening 2 lots of eurusd are not taking the same risk. one has a 20-pip stop, the other a 100-pip stop. the first risks $400, the second $2,000. position size without stop distance is an incomplete statement, and this is the sentence that explains most failed evaluations: the size looked normal and the stop was wide.

on an evaluation there is a third constraint the live trader does not have: the daily loss limit. sizing should therefore be derived from the smaller of two numbers - the per-trade risk the plan allows, and the share of the daily budget that a single trade may consume. a daily limit of 5% divided into three trade slots means each trade risks no more than 1.67% even if the plan would allow 2%.

on a 1:100 account that ceiling is reached long before margin is. the 2 lots in the example above require $2,200 of margin on a $100,000 account - 2.2% of equity, nowhere near a constraint. the binding number is the $1,000 of risk, not the $2,200 of margin, and it will keep being the binding number at every leverage ratio a firm offers.
every account has four limits, and only one of them is usually close to being hit. knowing which one is live on a given account is the difference between sizing from a plan and sizing from a feeling.

margin is the slackest constraint on a typical prop account. on a $100,000 account with 1:100 leverage, the maximum position size permitted by margin is roughly 45 lots of eurusd - which, with a 50-pip stop, would risk $22,500 per trade and end the account on the first loss. the leverage allows a position the rules do not, and the rules always win.

this is why experienced prop traders ignore the leverage ratio entirely after checking it once. it tells them what the platform will let them do, not what the plan permits, and the two numbers differ by a factor of twenty.

there is a genuine case where a low ratio becomes binding: heavily correlated or overnight positions with wide stops, on an account where the daily budget is large relative to equity. a trader holding four positions of 1% risk each with wide stops can find the margin requirement consuming 20% or more of equity, which reduces the room available for further positions and can trigger platform-level forced reduction.

the remedy is not more leverage; it is fewer simultaneous positions. a prop firm evaluation is not a portfolio exercise, and the traders who pass are not the ones holding six correlated positions at once.

since leverage does not create risk, why do accounts with generous leverage fail more often? the answer is behavioural rather than mathematical, and it is worth being precise about because it is the honest version of the warning.

on a low-leverage account, an oversized position may simply be impossible: the platform rejects it or requires more margin than exists. that is a mechanical brake on a decision the trader was about to make badly. remove the brake and the decision stands on the trader's discipline alone.

most people are less disciplined than they believe under pressure, which is why the brake had value. on a 1:500 account there is no brake at all - only the daily limit, which arrives after the position is open rather than before.

high leverage makes very small stop distances look attractive, because a tight stop on a large position produces a small risk figure. a 5-pip stop on 20 lots risks $1,000 - the same as a 50-pip stop on 2 lots. the risk is identical; the probability of being stopped out by noise is not. tight stops on large size convert a normal losing sequence into a long series of small losses that eventually breach the daily limit without a single trade being "wrong".

the permission to open large positions across several pairs invites what looks like diversification and behaves like one position. long eurusd, long gbpusd and long audusd are three expressions of one view on the dollar. on a leveraged account the three can be opened at full size before the trader notices that the daily budget is already committed.

firms set leverage where they do for commercial rather than educational reasons - generous ratios are a marketing feature - and they rely on the daily and maximum loss limits to contain the risk. those limits are generous in percentage terms and unforgiving in practice, which is exactly why the discipline has to come from the plan rather than from the platform.
on a leveraged account the daily budget, not the margin requirement, is the number that stops a session.
leverage changes the margin required, not the risk the account can carry.
the procedure below works on any instrument and any leverage ratio, and it takes about thirty seconds once it is familiar.

take the smaller of the plan's per-trade risk and the daily limit divided by three. on a $100,000 account with a 5% daily limit and a 1.5% plan, both come to $1,500. write it down. every later step reads from this number.

pips for forex, points or ticks for indices and futures, dollars for a fixed-range instrument. the measurement has to be taken from the chart before the position is opened, not adjusted afterwards. placing an order and then moving the stop to fit the loss is the most common way a 1.5% trade becomes a 3% trade.

risk divided by stop distance gives the value per unit. on eurusd, $1,500 divided by a 30-pip stop gives $50 per pip, which is 5 standard lots. on the es futures contract, $1,500 divided by a 6-point stop and $50 per point gives 5 contracts. on a gold cfd, $1,500 divided by a $6.00 stop gives $250 per dollar of movement, which is 2.5 lots at $100 per lot per dollar.

three positions of that size must fit inside the daily limit. if they do not, the per-trade risk comes down rather than the number of trades going up. this is the step where prop firm sizing differs from live-account sizing, and it is the step most often skipped.

multiply the position value by the margin requirement and confirm the platform accepts it. on a leveraged prop account this check almost always passes, which is the point: it is a formality rather than a constraint.

two observations from that table. first, the sizes look large, which is what leverage does - a 5-lot eurusd position on a $100,000 account is unremarkable at 1:100 and impossible at 1:5. second, the risk is identical in every row, which is the whole point of doing the arithmetic in this order.
prop firms do not usually publish leverage as a headline feature, because it is not the constraint their rules use. where it is published, it varies for three reasons.

forex and cfd firms typically offer 1:30 to 1:200, with the lowest ratios on indices and commodities. futures firms do not use a leverage ratio at all: intraday margin is set per contract by the clearing broker, and the effective ratio depends on the contract's notional value. a trader comparing a futures account's "leverage" with a forex account's is comparing two different systems.

where a firm operates under a regulatory umbrella, the maximum retail leverage may be capped. where it does not, the ratio is a commercial decision. neither implies anything about the difficulty of the evaluation, because the loss limits do the containing.

some firms reduce leverage around major news releases or over weekends, which can force a position reduction on an account that was compliant an hour earlier. this is worth checking before holding a large position through a release: the rule change can be as consequential as the price move.

three things, all quick: the margin requirement per instrument, whether it changes over weekends or news, and whether the platform supports partial position closures. the last one matters most in practice, because reducing size on a winning position is how a trader cuts risk near a failure level without closing the trade entirely.
the same procedure applied to three markets, with the leverage ratio varied to show that it does not enter the calculation.

a $100,000 evaluation, 1% per-trade risk, a 40-pip stop. risk is $1,000, so the size is $25 per pip - 2.5 standard lots. at 1:30 the margin required is roughly $16,600; at 1:200 it is about $2,500. the trade, the risk and the outcome are identical. the difference is that at 1:30 the trader can only hold four or five such positions before margin becomes a factor, while at 1:200 they can hold twenty - and holding twenty correlated positions is a failure mode, not a feature.

that is the honest case against generous leverage: not that it increases the risk of any single trade, but that it removes the arithmetic that would otherwise have stopped a trader from taking too many.

gold moves $1.50 in a quiet minute and $4.00 around a release. a stop of $6.00 is reasonable; a stop of $1.50 is noise. with $1,000 of risk, the $6.00 stop permits 1.67 lots at $100 per lot per dollar. the $1.50 stop permits 6.67 lots for the same $1,000.

the second position is four times larger and carries a far higher probability of being stopped out by a routine fluctuation. both respect the 1% rule on paper. only one of them respects it in the sense that matters, which is that the stop should be placed where the analysis is wrong rather than where the loss is acceptable.

on a $50,000 futures evaluation with a $1,000 per-trade risk limit, the micro es contract at $5 per point and a 10-point stop risks $50 per contract. that allows 20 micros, which is equivalent to 2 full-size contracts. with a 5-point stop the risk is $25 per contract and the allowance is 40 micros - the same 2 full-size contracts, expressed in smaller units.

micros are the useful instrument for a first futures account precisely because they break the coarse granularity of contracts into fifty-dollar steps. they do not change the arithmetic; they make it possible to follow it.
"high leverage is high risk." risk is size times stop distance. leverage only sets margin.
"low leverage is safer." it constrains how much you can open, which helps some traders and is irrelevant to others. both can lose the account on one bad decision.
"use maximum leverage to pass faster." the target is a percentage, not a function of position size. larger size shortens the path only by increasing the chance of a failure that costs the fee.
"1% risk at 1:500 is 500% risk." it is 1%. the multiplication is done by people selling courses.
"margin is the same as risk." margin is capital locked; risk is capital lost if the stop fills. a trade can require $10,000 of margin and risk $500.
"leverage does not matter at all." it matters as a behavioural factor - it removes the last mechanical brake on size - and not at all as an arithmetic one.

the defensible claim is narrow: a firm offering 1:500 while requiring 1% risk discipline is creating an environment in which the constraint comes entirely from the trader. that is fine for someone with a written plan and a daily budget, and it is a trap for anyone who treats the available margin as a target.

if that distinction is understood, the leverage ratio can be ignored after the initial check. it never appears again in the sizing arithmetic, the daily budget or the distance to a failure level - the three numbers that decide whether an evaluation is passed.

when the evaluation is traded on someone else's behalf, leverage becomes an execution detail rather than a client decision - and it is one of the better ways to judge whether the process is disciplined.

"what risk per trade do you use on a 10% target, and does the size change near the end?" a process answer names a percentage, a pacing estimate and a reduction near the target. a marketing answer mentions the firm's leverage, the instrument with the highest ratio, or how fast the evaluation usually passes.

the second kind of answer is a warning. on a leveraged account, the fastest way to pass is also the fastest way to fail, and a provider whose pitch emphasises speed is describing a risk profile rather than a method.

position size derived from the daily budget rather than the margin ratio; risk constant within ten percent across the evaluation; size halved above seventy percent of target; sessions closed at eighty percent of the daily limit. none of those depend on leverage, and all of them are visible in the plan a provider sends before trading starts.

elitepropx charges one flat $220 for any prop firm and any account size. a percentage-of-payouts arrangement would give a provider an interest in larger positions and larger accounts, because the fee scales with the outcome - the same incentive that makes generous leverage attractive to a retail broker. a flat fee removes that incentive, which is why it is worth stating in an article about position sizing.
a written policy takes ten minutes and removes the topic from the decisions made under pressure.
fix the per-trade risk figure at one third of the daily budget, in dollars.
require a stop distance before any order: if the chart does not define where the analysis is wrong, there is no trade.
derive size from risk divided by stop distance, never from the margin available.
cap simultaneous positions at two, and treat correlated pairs as one position.
never widen a stop to avoid a loss; reduce size instead.
reduce size by half once the evaluation is seventy percent complete.
re-check the margin requirement before holding through a weekend or a major release.

seven lines, one page, and every one of them is a defence against a specific failure that leverage makes easier. traders who write this down and keep to it treat the leverage ratio as what it is - a platform setting - rather than as a strategy input.

if nothing else on this page is read, this is the substance of it. write the dollar risk first. measure the stop second. divide to get size. confirm three positions fit inside the daily limit. check margin last, and only to confirm the platform accepts the order.

every sizing failure in prop trading is a violation of that order. the trader who starts from the lot size, or from the margin available, or from the leverage ratio, has skipped the two decisions that determine the outcome and made the third one a consequence of nothing.
on a leveraged account, that order is the entire discipline. the platform will never stop you; the calculation has to.

on a leveraged account, partial closes are the most underused tool available. most platforms allow a position to be reduced in steps, which converts "do i keep this trade?" into "how much of this trade do i keep?" - a much easier question to answer well.

first, when a trade has moved in your favour by more than the original risk and the stop is being moved to break-even: closing a third converts an uncertain outcome into a banked result. second, when the evaluation is above seventy percent of target and the remaining room for a normal losing sequence is thin. third, when a correlated second position is opened, because the exposure has doubled without the analysis changing.

they do not repair an oversized entry. if the position was opened at twice the plan's risk, reducing it to plan size still leaves the loss already incurred on the excess. the lesson belongs in the entry, and the daily limit does not distinguish between an intentional and an accidental oversize.

on a prop account, the platform-level margin call is rare and the evaluation-level failure is common, which inverts the retail experience. a trader used to a broker closing positions will look for a margin warning that never comes, while the number that actually ends accounts - distance to the failure level - goes unmonitored. the two numbers worth checking each morning are the daily budget and the distance to the failure level, not the margin available.

that single substitution is the practical difference between retail intuition and prop discipline: the account is not at risk from a broker's margin policy, it is at risk from a percentage that a rulebook defines and a trader has to track.

two figures, updated each morning: the daily budget in dollars, and the distance from current equity to the failure level. add the maximum position size for the day, derived from the smaller of the two constraints. nothing about margin, and nothing about leverage, because neither changes between today and yesterday unless the firm amends its terms - and if it does, it will say so on the objectives page rather than in a margin notification.

that card is the whole interface between a trader and a leveraged account. it takes ninety seconds to write and it removes the two failure modes that leverage makes possible: an oversized position taken because margin permitted it, and a losing sequence continued because the distance to failure was misjudged.

one last observation from the arithmetic rather than from theory: across every leverage ratio a firm might offer, the four numbers that decide an evaluation are identical - daily budget, per-trade risk, distance to failure, and target in r. leverage does not appear in that list, and a trader whose plan is written entirely from those four figures has made the ratio irrelevant to their outcome, which is exactly where it belongs. that is the whole of the leverage question, and it is answerable before the first trade with a calculator and a rulebook - no platform access required, and no leverage ratio involved in the answer. write the four numbers down, date the page, and the ratio becomes a setting you check once and forget.

if you take one habit from this page into the next evaluation, make it the order of operations rather than the formula: risk first, stop second, size third, margin last. traders who keep that order pass leveraged accounts at the same rate as unleveraged ones, because the account's settings never enter the arithmetic that decides the outcome. present it that way to yourself each morning and the rest of the plan follows from four numbers rather than from a feeling about how much the account will allow.
no. risk is position size multiplied by stop distance. leverage sets how much margin a position requires, so a 1:100 account and a 1:10 account can carry identical risk on the same trade.
forex and cfd firms typically offer 1:30 to 1:200, with lower ratios on indices and commodities. futures firms do not use a ratio at all - intraday margin is set per contract by the clearing broker.

divide the dollar risk by the stop distance. on eurusd, $1,000 of risk with a 40-pip stop is $25 per pip, or 2.5 standard lots. margin is checked afterwards and is rarely the binding constraint on a prop account.

the daily loss limit, in almost every case. on a $100,000 account with 1:100 leverage, margin would permit a position that risks more than 20% per trade - the rules end the account long before the platform would.
is a tight stop and a large position the same as a wide stop and a small one?

the dollar risk is identical and the probability of being stopped out by noise is not. tight stops on large size typically produce a long sequence of small losses that breaches the daily limit without any single trade being wrong.
no. the target is a percentage of the account, so larger size shortens the path only by raising the probability of a failure that costs the fee and several weeks.
at elitepropx, one third of the daily budget, with size reduced near the target. the flat fee is $220 for any firm and any account size, with retries on rule breaches covered and no profit split.
yes. a micro es contract at $5 per point breaks the coarse granularity of futures contracts into $50 steps, which makes it possible to follow a risk plan precisely rather than approximately.

a pass is not a promotion. it is a change of contract: a new agreement, a different drawdown, new payout conditions, and a set of administrative steps that run on their own clock. most traders prepare for the evaluation and improvise the funded month, which is why newly funded accounts are lost faster than evaluation accounts ever were. this guide covers what actually arrives, which rules get tighter, and how to trade the first thirty days.
a pass triggers a new agreement with its own drawdown, payout conditions and conduct clauses - reread it before the first funded trade.
the funded drawdown is usually tighter as a percentage than the evaluation's, so the correct first move is to halve the risk.
verification is administrative and can be completed in week one; leaving it until the payout request is the most common avoidable delay.
profit is not income until it is withdrawn, and on a trailing structure an unwithdrawn balance makes the account more fragile.
the first payout cycle matters more than the first payout amount: it establishes the route, the timing and the conditions for every cycle after it.

during an evaluation, the trader's relationship with the firm is simple: a fee has been paid and a target has to be met. on funding, that relationship becomes a commercial arrangement with ongoing conditions, a revenue split and a set of conduct clauses that apply to every trade.

the practical difference is that evaluation rules are designed to test a strategy, while funded rules are designed to protect the firm's capital. those two objectives produce different numbers. a firm can be generous about a target because a failed evaluation costs the trader a fee; it cannot be generous about the funded drawdown, because a funded breach costs the firm money.

that asymmetry explains almost every surprise in the first funded month. the drawdown is tighter, the daily limit may be calculated differently, the consistency condition applies to profit that is being withdrawn rather than to a target, and the conduct clauses - news, overnight holding, permitted instruments - are enforced rather than observed.

so the first action after a pass is not to trade. it is to read the funded agreement as a document, with a pen, and to write down five numbers: the funded maximum loss, the funded daily limit, the minimum profitable days, the profit threshold before withdrawal, and the consistency condition. those five numbers define the account that will actually be traded, and none of them can be inferred from the evaluation's rules.
if any of the five is unclear, ask support in writing before the first trade. a written answer is the only version of the terms that can be relied on later, and the cost of asking is a day.

the sequence after a pass is administrative and reasonably consistent across firms, though the timing varies. knowing the order prevents the most common mistake, which is treating a pending step as a completed one.

the step that most often goes wrong is the credentials. a funded account is frequently on a different platform server or a different data feed from the evaluation, and the difference changes the spread, the fill quality and the timestamp on every trade. a trader who assumes the environment is identical calibrates against the wrong numbers for the first week.

the second most common problem is verification timing. identity and address checks have nothing to do with the trading record, and they are frequently the reason a first payout takes longer than expected. submitting them on the day the funded login arrives removes the only part of the chain that cannot be fixed later.

the third is a version problem. firms revise agreements, and a trader who saved the evaluation terms may be holding a document that no longer governs the funded account. save the funded version in force on the day it was accepted, including any email confirming a specific clause. it is the only reliable reference if a payout question arises three months later.
four conditions typically change between evaluation and funding, and every one of them changes in the direction of less room.

the drawdown. usually tighter as a percentage of balance on the funded side, because the firm is now carrying real risk. the mechanism may also change - a structure that trailed during the evaluation may be static on funding, or the reverse. both directions exist, and the only way to know is to read the funded terms rather than assume continuity.

the daily limit. often similar in percentage but measured from a different reference point: balance rather than equity, or the day's opening balance rather than the previous close. a small change in the reference point is a large change in behaviour for a trader who holds positions through the session.

the consistency condition. almost always more prominent on the funded side, because it governs what can be withdrawn rather than what can be earned. a rule that was a formality during the evaluation becomes a hard constraint on daily profit once a payout depends on it.

the conduct clauses. news windows, overnight and weekend holding, permitted instruments and any prohibition on third-party trading are enforced on the funded account in a way they rarely are during an evaluation. a trader whose evaluation contained a small breach that went unnoticed should not assume the same tolerance applies now.
the funded budget is smaller and the reserve matters more, because there is no reset behind it.

there is a fifth change that is not a rule at all: the absence of a reset. an evaluation that is breached can be bought again. a funded allocation that is breached is usually gone, and with it the record that would have supported a scaling request. that asymmetry, more than any individual clause, is why the first funded month should be traded more conservatively than the evaluation was.
the first week has two jobs, and neither of them is making money.

the first is administrative: submit verification, confirm the payment method, save the agreement, and confirm the platform server time and the exact hour at which the trading day begins. each takes minutes and each is capable of delaying a payout by weeks if neglected.

the second is calibration on the funded account. trade at a quarter to a half of the evaluation's risk for the first five sessions and measure the same three things measured during the evaluation: planned risk, realised risk including spread and commission, and time in the trade. the funded environment may be a different server, a different feed or a different commission schedule, and those differences compound over a month.

week one is also the right time to establish the funded risk line in writing. it has the same four components as the evaluation's - risk per trade, trades per session, maximum daily loss, and the stop rule - but every number is smaller. a line carried over unchanged from the evaluation is a line written for a different account.
funding adds a parallel track of administration that runs alongside the trading plan.

two things should not happen in week one. the first is a size increase to "make the funded account count". the account counts from the first payout cycle, not from the first trade, and the fastest route to that cycle is a size that survives ordinary variance. the second is a strategy change. a plan that passed an evaluation has demonstrated one thing - that it can produce a positive expectation under a rulebook - and the funded month is not the place to test a different one.
week two is where the funded account is either established or lost, and the pattern is consistent enough to describe in advance.

the first pattern is the return of the evaluation's size. calibration goes well, the account is up slightly, and the trader concludes that the smaller size was unnecessary. risk returns to the old number on the first genuinely uncertain trade, which is exactly the trade where the account cannot afford it. the rule that prevents this is mechanical: the size increases only after a completed payout cycle, not after a good week.

the second pattern is the profitable day that raises the floor. on a trailing structure, a strong session moves the failure point up, and the following day's ordinary retracement is measured against a higher floor. the trader believes the account is healthy because it is in profit; the mechanism disagrees. the countermeasure is to recompute the distance to the floor at the start of every session and to treat the result as the account's real risk capacity.

the third pattern is boredom. a funded account with a small position and no target produces long stretches with nothing to do, and the trades taken to fill them have no setup behind them. during an evaluation, the target absorbed that energy. on funding, the payout threshold is distant and abstract, so the discipline has to come from the session cap: a fixed number of trades and a fixed number of sessions, decided before the week begins.

the fourth pattern is the early withdrawal request. a trader reaches a modest profit and requests a payout before the minimum-day count or the consistency condition is satisfied, is refused, and concludes that the firm is withholding. in almost every case the conditions were published and unmet. checking the three conditions before requesting - day count, threshold, consistency - prevents the entire episode.

none of these patterns requires a different strategy to fix. they require the funded rules to be treated as a new specification rather than as a continuation, and the funded risk line to be smaller than the evaluation's rather than equal to it.
the funded risk line is not a scaled copy of the evaluation's. it is derived again from three inputs: the funded drawdown, the funded daily limit, and the payout conditions.

start with the drawdown. divide the distance to the funded floor by the number of consecutive losses the plan should survive, and treat the answer as a ceiling rather than a target. on a fully funded account the design case is usually stricter than on an evaluation - ten to twelve consecutive losses rather than eight - because there is no reset and because the first payout cycle is worth protecting.

then check the daily limit. multiply the per-trade risk by the number of losses a session should absorb and compare. if the product exceeds the daily limit, reduce the trade count first; the per-trade risk is already at its survivability floor.

then apply the payout constraint, which has no equivalent during an evaluation. if the consistency condition caps a single day's share of total profit, the plan needs a daily profit cap as well as a daily loss limit. a trader aiming for a payout threshold and a consistency ratio simultaneously is solving two equations, and the daily profit cap is the variable that satisfies both.

finally, fix the withdrawal cadence in advance. deciding to withdraw "when it looks good" produces either an accumulation that makes the account fragile or a series of premature requests that fail the threshold. a fixed schedule - the same day each month, at the smallest permitted size for the first cycle - converts an emotional decision into a calendar entry.
the daily drawdown guide covers the reference-point arithmetic in detail, and the consistency guide covers the ratio calculations for the common thresholds.
two conditions run on their own clocks after a pass, and both are satisfied by behaviour rather than by profit.

the minimum-day count is the simpler of the two. it requires a number of trading days with a qualifying result, and it is usually satisfied long before the profit threshold on a plan of any reasonable pace. the trap is the trader who reaches the threshold early and then trades to fill the count: those sessions are the ones taken without a setup, and they can give back a meaningful portion of the profit. trade the count at reduced size, accept flat days, and treat it as a calendar problem.

the consistency condition is the subtler one. expressed as a best-day share of total profit, it means the largest day sets the minimum total. under a share of around a third, total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day. a trader whose best day was a fifth of the threshold needs five times that day in total profit before the ratio permits a full withdrawal.

there are only two ways to satisfy the condition once a dominant day exists: earn more, or withdraw less. earning more takes time and risks the account; withdrawing less is immediate and costs only the delay. most traders choose the first when the second is correct - a partial withdrawal that satisfies the ratio and completes the cycle is worth more than a full withdrawal three months later, because it establishes the payment route and the timing.

the preventive measure is a daily profit cap set well below the threshold, applied from the first funded session. a cap converts the ratio from a problem discovered at the request into an arithmetic fact known in advance. the payout process guide walks through the sequence of conditions in order.
four situations present as a firm refusing to pay and are almost always something else.

a day-count shortfall. the threshold was reached, but the account had not traded the required number of qualifying days. nothing is wrong; the condition is simply unmet. it is the most common cause of a first refusal and the easiest to avoid by counting the days before requesting.

a consistency shortfall. the profit is real, but one day dominates it. the refusal is procedural rather than punitive, and the remedy is to keep trading to a total that satisfies the ratio, or to withdraw a smaller amount that does.

unfinished verification. documents pending, address mismatched, or a payment method in a name that does not match the account. this is administrative and entirely under the trader's control in week one.

a conduct-clause question. a trade that appears to breach the news, overnight or permitted-instrument rules, or an arrangement that the firm classifies as third-party trading. this is the only category where the outcome can be genuinely adverse, which is why the clause should be confirmed in writing before the arrangement begins rather than defended afterwards.

the pattern across all four is that the trading was fine and a condition was not. that is why the funded month should be planned around the conditions rather than around the profit: the profit is the part the trader already knows how to make.

the first payout cycle is the real milestone. it is worth more than a large balance, more than a second evaluation, and more than any single month's result, because it establishes that the whole chain works.

the cycle has six elements, and all of them should be completed before the size increases: the minimum-day count, the profit threshold, the consistency position, verification, the withdrawal request itself, and the receipt of funds. a trader who has completed all six knows the payment route, the processing time, the fees involved and the treatment of the payment. a trader who has completed five of six knows nothing about the sixth and will discover it at the least convenient moment.
six conditions, one payment. the cycle is the milestone, not the balance.

the size of the first withdrawal is a separate decision from the size of the profit. withdrawing the smallest permitted amount completes the cycle sooner and leaves more buffer in the account; withdrawing the maximum leaves less buffer and takes longer to qualify. for a first cycle, the smaller amount is usually the better trade, because the information is worth more than the difference.

after the cycle completes, two things become possible that were not possible before: a scaling request, where the firm's programme rewards completed payouts, and a considered decision about running a second allocation. both should wait until the cycle is complete rather than run in parallel with it.
there is a point on a funded account where the correct action is to stop, and it is worth defining it in advance because it is never obvious in the moment.

the first trigger is a drawdown that has consumed more than a set share of the funded limit - a half is a reasonable threshold. at that point the account can still be recovered, but not by trading the same size, and not within the same month. reducing size by half and extending the calendar is the only survivable response; continuing at the original size converts a recoverable drawdown into a closed account.

the second trigger is a breach of the plan's own rules, as distinct from the firm's. a stop widened, a size doubled, a trade taken without a setup: these are plan breaches, and a plan that has been breached once is statistically more likely to be breached again in the same week. the response is a mandatory pause of several sessions, not a resolution to be more careful.

the third trigger is a change in the funded terms. if the firm revises the drawdown, the payout conditions or the conduct clauses, the plan built on the old version may no longer be viable. re-deriving the risk line from the new terms is the minimum response; stopping until that is done is usually the correct one.

the fourth trigger is life. a funded account requires attention, and a trader who cannot give it for a fortnight - travel, illness, work - is better off flat than holding positions they cannot monitor. the account does not expire because it is not traded.

defining these four triggers before the first funded trade is the difference between a drawdown that is managed and one that is discovered. a trigger written in advance is a decision; a trigger recognised in the moment is a rationalisation.
the evaluation had a target, a deadline and a fee already paid. the funded account has none of those, and the absence changes behaviour in predictable ways.

without a target, there is no natural stopping point, so trades continue past the point where the plan would have stopped. without a deadline, the calendar stretches, and a drawdown that would have been decisive during an evaluation becomes something to trade through. without a fee at stake, the cost of a breach feels abstract until the allocation is gone - at which point the cost is the whole account rather than a resettable purchase.

the countermeasure is to invent the missing structure. a monthly target, expressed as a payout threshold rather than a profit goal. a fixed number of sessions per week. a daily profit cap as well as a daily loss limit. a review every friday with the same four numbers used during the evaluation. none of these is required by the firm, and all of them reproduce the conditions under which the evaluation was passed.

there is a second psychological shift worth naming. during an evaluation, the money is not real: the target is a number and a breach costs a fee. on funding, the profit is real and withdrawable, which makes the risk feel larger than it is and the reward feel smaller. traders respond by taking profits early and letting losses run - the exact inversion of the plan that passed. the written rule matters more here than anywhere else, because the feeling is strongest precisely when the trade is working.

a third shift is identity. a trader who has passed is now, in their own mind, a funded trader, and funded traders are expected to size up. that expectation is not in any agreement. the only thing a funded account rewards is a plan that survives its own rulebook, which is exactly what the evaluation rewarded.
thirty days is enough to complete a first cycle on most firms and long enough to establish whether the funded plan is sound. the checklist runs in order.

day 1. read the funded agreement. write down the five numbers: funded maximum loss, funded daily limit, minimum profitable days, profit threshold, consistency condition. submit verification and confirm the payment method.

day 2. confirm the platform server, the data feed and the exact time the trading day begins. compare the spread and commission with what the evaluation delivered. write the funded risk line with all four components.
days 3 to 7. calibrate at a quarter to a half of the evaluation's risk. two trades per session maximum. record planned risk, realised risk and time in the trade for every position.

days 8 to 20. move to the funded size if the calibration matched. keep the session cap. recompute the distance to the floor at the start of every session and the size every monday. set a daily profit cap below the consistency threshold.

days 21 to 30. check the three payout conditions - day count, threshold, consistency - and request the first withdrawal at the smallest permitted size if all three are satisfied. if they are not, extend rather than increase size.

two rules apply throughout. no size increase before a completed cycle, and no strategy change during the first month. the first protects the account; the second protects the only evidence the trader has that the strategy works.

if a passing service produced the pass, the post-pass work is the account holder's regardless. the firm's terms on third-party trading must be confirmed for the funded stage as well as the evaluation, and the funded login should be in the trader's own name with credentials under their control. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, and takes no profit split - the passing services guide explains what to check before paying anyone.
what is the first thing to do after passing a challenge?

read the funded agreement and write down five numbers: funded maximum loss, funded daily limit, minimum profitable days, profit threshold and consistency condition. then start verification. none of the five can be inferred from the evaluation's rules, and the funded drawdown is usually tighter.
how much should i risk on a newly funded account?

half or less of the evaluation's risk for the first five to ten sessions. the funded drawdown is frequently tighter, the server and feed may differ, and there is no reset behind a breach. increase size only after a completed payout cycle.
why is the funded drawdown tighter than the evaluation drawdown?

because the firm is now exposed to real payouts rather than to a fee. evaluation rules are designed to test a strategy; funded rules are designed to protect capital. the two objectives produce different numbers, and only the funded one governs the account that pays.

when three conditions are met: the minimum number of qualifying trading days, the profit threshold, and the consistency condition on the profit being withdrawn. check all three before requesting - a request that fails a condition is the most common reason a payout appears to be refused.
should i withdraw the maximum or the minimum on the first payout?

the smallest permitted amount, for the first cycle. completing the cycle establishes the payment route, the processing time and the fees, and leaves more buffer in the account. the information is worth more than the difference in amount.

almost always, and in the first week rather than at the first withdrawal request. verification is administrative, has nothing to do with the trading record, and is routinely the step that delays a first payment. name and address mismatches are the usual cause.

a cap on the share of total profit that can come from one day, commonly around a third. it means total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day before a full withdrawal. set a daily profit cap below the threshold from the first session so the ratio is satisfied when the threshold is reached.

yes, but only after a completed payout cycle rather than after a good week. scaling programmes generally reward completed withdrawals and consistent results, and increasing size before the first cycle means scaling a process that has not been tested end to end.

the allocation is typically closed and the fee is not refunded. that is the main structural difference from an evaluation, which can be bought again. treat the funded account as an allocation with no reset and size it accordingly.
why do traders lose a funded account in the first month?

four reasons: returning to the evaluation's size, a trailing floor raised by a strong session, trading without a setup because there is no target, and requesting a payout before the conditions are met. all four are planning failures rather than strategy failures.

the profit split is defined in the funded agreement, and profit only becomes income when it is withdrawn. unwithdrawn profit sits in the account, counts in the drawdown calculation, and on a trailing structure raises the floor. withdraw on the earliest permitted schedule after the first cycle.

the post-pass work belongs to the account holder regardless: verification, the payout conditions and the funded rules are theirs. confirm the third-party clause covers the funded stage as well as the evaluation, and keep the funded login in your own name.

apex is the best-known futures prop firm, and its difficulty comes from one mechanic: an intraday trailing threshold that follows unrealised profit upward. this guide covers what that means for sizing, why the 30% consistency rule blocks so many payouts, and how to pace an evaluation that punishes success.
the trailing threshold follows your peak unrealised equity, so a strong session reduces your remaining cushion rather than increasing it.
risk must fall as the target approaches - the opposite of the instinct to press a winning account.
a 30% best-day consistency rule applies at payout: a $6,000 day requires $20,000 of total profit.
account sizes extend to $300,000, which is larger than almost any competitor, and the same discipline scales.
apex trader funding runs futures evaluations with dollar-based targets and thresholds rather than percentages, and the account range extends higher than most of the industry.

two features define the assignment. the first is the trailing threshold: apex's failure level is not fixed at a distance below the starting balance - it follows your equity upward as you make money, which means the cushion between equity and failure shrinks as the evaluation progresses. the second is the payout-stage consistency rule, which is covered in detail below and in the consistency rule guide .

strategic context worth having before choosing an account size: apex's evaluation pricing is among the most aggressive in futures, and promotional discounts are frequent. cheap entries are good for testing a plan and bad for encouraging discipline - a trader who has spent $40 on an evaluation is more inclined to gamble than one who spent $400, and the rules do not care which it was.

most traders understand a maximum loss as a fixed line below the starting balance. a trailing threshold is different, and the difference is the single most common reason an apex evaluation ends unexpectedly.

on a trailing structure, the failure level rises with your peak equity. suppose a $100,000 account starts with a threshold at $96,000 - a $4,000 cushion. if the account reaches $103,000 in unrealised open profit, the threshold rises to roughly $99,000 and the cushion is still $4,000 in absolute terms, but the account now has to fall $4,000 from a higher peak to fail. that sounds neutral until you note what happens next: the cushion is measured from the peak, and a $3,000 retracement from $103,000 puts equity at $100,000 with the threshold at $99,000 - one bad trade from failure, despite being up on the day.

now add the most important detail. on an intraday trailing structure, the threshold follows unrealised profit. a position that is $5,000 in open profit and then gives back $4,000 has already lifted the floor, and the retracement leaves the account with $1,000 of realised profit and a threshold that has permanently moved. the trader did nothing wrong, took no loss, and is nonetheless far closer to failure than they were that morning.
an intraday trailing floor follows unrealised equity, so a retracement reduces the cushion even on a profitable day.

this is why apex evaluations are harder than their headline targets suggest, and why traders who arrive from static-drawdown forex firms find the structure unforgiving. the rules do not punish losing; they punish giving back , which is a different behaviour and requires a different plan.

on a fixed floor, the calculation of how much room remains is a subtraction from a constant. on a trailing floor, it is a subtraction from a moving number, and the correct response is to treat the peak - not the balance - as the reference point.

the table hides the danger, so it is worth spelling out. the absolute room to failure stays constant because the floor moves with the peak - but the room only stays constant if equity stays at the peak. every dollar of retracement from the peak is a dollar closer to failure, and retracements are normal. a trader at a $112,000 peak with $9,000 of realised profit who gives back $3,000 is at $109,000 with a floor at roughly $108,000 - one average losing position from a failed evaluation, on an account that has already passed its target.

the practical consequence is that on a trailing structure the last portion of an evaluation is the most dangerous part, not the safest. that is the opposite of a static account and the opposite of most traders' instincts.

size for the implied daily budget, not the headline target. because the threshold trails, the effective room for a day's adverse movement is smaller than it looks. treat the trailing distance as the day's practical risk budget and divide it into thirds.

scale risk down as progress increases - never up. full planned size to 40% of target, three quarters of planned size from 40% to 70%, half size from 70% to completion. this is counter-intuitive and it is the difference between passing and failing.

close open profit deliberately. on a trailing structure, unrealised profit is dangerous because it lifts the floor without banking anything. taking profit at planned levels converts a liability into a real gain and stops the floor from chasing a number that never materialised.

do not trade the same instrument continuously for hours. continuous exposure on a trailing account means continuous floor movement. shorter, planned sessions reduce the total number of ticks that can drag the threshold upward.

the one-line version: on a trailing account, an untouched pass is worth more than extra progress. a trader at 95% of target with the floor far below is in a better position than one at 130% of target with the floor directly beneath current equity.

apex applies a consistency rule when a payout is requested: no single day should account for more than 30% of total profit. the arithmetic is set out fully in the consistency rule guide , but the shape of it is simple. a $6,000 best day requires at least $20,000 of total profit; a $3,000 best day requires $10,000.
a dominant day can block a payout even on an account with a passed evaluation.

the interaction with the trailing threshold is what makes the combination difficult. a trader on a trailing account is tempted to bank one large day and finish, but a large day is exactly what the consistency rule penalises at payout. the two rules pull in opposite directions: the threshold punishes holding runners, and the consistency rule punishes taking them. the resolution is to cap daily profit at roughly a third of the eventual total - which on a $6,000 target means about $2,000 per session, spread across several sessions rather than concentrated in one.

a second interaction is less obvious. because the threshold trails unrealised profit, a large winning day also raises the floor substantially, so a trader with a $5,000 day on a $100,000 account finishes the session with less room than they started despite being significantly up. combining a large day with a raised floor is the worst of both: the consistency problem and the trailing problem in the same session.
a realistic pace for a $100,000 account with a $6,000 target is eight to fourteen trading days, structured as follows.

sessions 1-3: prove the plan works, do not chase the target. full planned size, one or two setups per session, and an explicit cap of about $1,200 of profit per session. expected outcome: 20-30% of target with the floor moved modestly.

sessions 4-7: the working middle. size reduced by a quarter from here. daily profit capped at $2,000, which is a third of the target and therefore satisfies the consistency rule by construction. target completion should reach 60-70% by the end of this phase.

sessions 8-14: protect the pass. half size, shorter sessions, and a hard rule that any session ending more than $2,000 up is closed rather than extended. the remaining 30% is collected in small increments, and the floor is recalculated every morning rather than assumed.

completion. the evaluation is finished when the target is reached and the minimum trading days are satisfied. at that point trading stops entirely - on a trailing structure, continuing to trade after reaching target is the single most expensive habit available.
holding a runner through a retracement. the floor has already moved; the retracement is measured from the peak, not from the entry. this is the defining apex failure.
increasing size as the target approaches. the instinct that ruins trailing evaluations, because progress simultaneously reduces the room available.
one dominant day. efficient for reaching the target and immediately expensive at payout under the 30% rule.
trading beyond the target. continuing after completion on a trailing account adds risk with no objective.
assuming the floor has not moved. traders who calculated their room once at the start of the evaluation and never recalculated it are consistently surprised.
treating a discounted evaluation as low-stakes. cheap entries encourage over-trading, and the failure mode is identical at any purchase price.
futures firms differ less on targets and splits than on how their failure thresholds behave, and that is the axis worth comparing on.

the most consequential comparison is between intraday trailing and end-of-day trailing structures. an end-of-day trailing floor updates only on profit closed at the end of a session, so intraday swings - including a large unrealised gain that later retraces - do not move it. on the same equity curve, an end-of-day trailing account finishes the session with more room than an intraday trailing one, purely because of when the floor is recalculated.

for a trader who intends to trade futures seriously, that difference is worth more than a few percentage points of profit split. where a firm offers both structures across different plans, the end-of-day version is generally the better assignment, and the price difference between the two plans is usually smaller than the cost of a failed attempt.
apex's range extends to $300,000, which is larger than almost any competitor, and the temptation is to buy the biggest evaluation available. three reasons argue against starting there.

costs do not scale, targets do. commission, spreads and slippage are dollars per contract, and on a trailing evaluation the threshold distance is fixed in dollars. a larger account does not proportionally reduce the cost drag; it increases the absolute value of a single mistake while offering the same rules.

the failure mode is behavioural, not financial. a trader who size-mismanages a $50,000 evaluation will size-mismanage a $300,000 one. the ruleset is identical, so the larger account tests nothing new - it simply costs more when the same behaviour recurs.

the funded phase is where size pays. a funded $150,000 account with a 90% split and a satisfied consistency rule produces real income; a failed $300,000 evaluation produces nothing. the efficient path is to prove the plan on a mid-size account, then scale on the firm's own terms once payouts are established.

traders who run several accounts in parallel face an additional constraint that apex is explicit about: correlated positions across accounts are treated as a single exposure. holding four long index positions across four accounts is one position from the firm's perspective, and it can breach a threshold on the aggregate rather than on any single account.
a $100,000 apex-style evaluation with a $6,000 target, an intraday trailing threshold and a 30% payout-stage consistency rule, traded at a plan that reduces size as progress increases.
session 1 - +$480. half the planned size while the plan is being tested against real conditions. the floor moves up modestly with the peak. nothing remarkable, which is the intention.

session 2 - +$1,240. full planned size. the session caps itself at $1,240 rather than pushing for more, because the daily cap is $2,000 and a session that overshoots it raises the consistency burden later.

session 3 - −$320. one loss at planned size, then closed. on a trailing account a losing day does not move the floor - the floor only ever rises - so this session costs money and no cushion. that asymmetry is why losing days are cheap on trailing structures and giving back a peak is expensive.

sessions 4-6 - +$2,730 combined. target completion reaches 74%, so risk per trade drops to half size from here. the daily cap of $2,000 means no single session is capable of breaching the consistency rule even if the target is reached on its own.

session 7 - +$360. a small session at reduced size, deliberately short. the floor is now close enough beneath current equity that the value of another dollar of profit is lower than the cost of a retracement.

sessions 8-10 - +$1,420 combined. the remaining 16% is collected in three small sessions at half size. the target is reached on session 10 with a best day of $1,240 - about 15% of total profit, comfortably inside the 30% rule.

after completion. trading stops. on a trailing account, continuing after the target is reached offers no benefit and a genuine risk: any retracement from the current peak moves the account closer to failure while the evaluation has already been won.

what the sequence shows: the largest day was 15% of total profit, the floor was never the binding constraint because size fell as progress rose, and the consistency rule was satisfied before the payout was ever requested. none of that required a single exceptional trade.
a trailing evaluation is the case where a structured service differs most from a trader working alone, for three reasons.

floor recalculation is mechanical and relentless. the failure level must be recomputed after every session and intrasession, because unrealised profit moves it. that is bookkeeping, not judgement, and it is the kind of work that gets skipped on a bad day - which is precisely when it matters.

size reduction contradicts conviction. reducing position size while an account is winning feels like abandoning a working approach. on a trailing structure it is the correct behaviour, and it is easier to execute when it is a written rule rather than a decision made in the moment.

the consistency rule is a scheduling problem. capping daily profit at a third of the eventual total requires a plan that has already decided how many sessions the target will take. that decision is cheap before the evaluation starts and expensive in the middle of one.

all three of those are properties of the ruleset rather than of a trader's skill, which is why apex evaluations pass reliably when they are paced and fail unpredictably when they are traded session by session on instinct. elitepropx trades them for a flat $220 with retries covered and no profit split, applying the same scaling discipline described in this guide.
when to stop for the day on a trailing account

the daily stop rule on a trailing structure is different from the one that applies on a static account, and the difference is easy to miss. on a static account, the day ends when the loss budget is spent. on a trailing account, it ends at whichever comes first: the loss budget, or a profit level that has lifted the floor close enough to current equity to make further trading imprudent.

that second condition is the one traders never plan for. it has no fixed number, because it depends on where the peak is relative to realised profit - but it can be expressed as a rule: if the buffer between current equity and the trailing threshold falls below the risk of a single planned trade, the session is over regardless of how profitable it has been. on a $100,000 account where a planned trade risks $600, a session ends the moment the remaining buffer to failure drops under $600, whether that day is up $400 or up $2,000.

expressed that way, the rule is mechanical and can be checked in seconds before each trade. traders who adopt it stop ending sessions with a raised floor and a thin cushion - which is the precise combination that turns a profitable evaluation into a failed one.

it follows your peak equity upward, including unrealised profit, and does not move back down. the absolute distance from peak to threshold stays roughly constant, which means any retracement from the peak moves you closer to failure even if the account is well up on the day.
a 30% best-day rule applies when a payout is requested: no single day may exceed 30% of total profit. a $6,000 best day requires at least $20,000 of total profit before the withdrawal is allowed.
typically eight to fourteen trading days with proper pacing on a $100,000 account. faster passes are possible on a favourable rulebook but usually create a consistency problem at payout instead.
yes, and this is the defining rule on a trailing account - full size to 40% of target, three quarters from 40-70%, half size beyond. progress makes a trailing account more fragile, not safer.
what happens if i give back profit after a strong day?

the failure threshold has already risen with the peak, so the retracement is measured from that peak. a $5,000 peak followed by a $3,000 retracement leaves $2,000 of realised profit and a much thinner buffer - which is why closing profit deliberately matters so much.

structurally yes, for the same headline difficulty. an intraday trailing floor is stricter than the static drawdowns used by most forex firms, and it is the reason traders who pass static-drawdown accounts comfortably can struggle here.

yes, for a flat $220 with retries covered and no profit split. the plan mirrors the sizing reductions described above, and the payout-stage consistency rule is planned for during the evaluation rather than repaired afterwards.

on some firms a trailing floor stops following once it reaches the starting balance, which materially reduces the risk in the later part of an evaluation. on firms where the floor keeps following regardless, plan for risk reduction as progress increases. confirm which applies on the plan you are buying rather than assuming either behaviour.

contract count is a sizing decision and should be derived from the trailing distance rather than from conviction. work out the dollar risk per contract on the instrument being traded, divide the practical daily budget into thirds, and let that number set the contract count. most apex failures involve too many contracts held for too long rather than too few opportunities.
what time of day is best for a trailing evaluation?

sessions are chosen around the permitted hours and the instrument's liquidity rather than around a fixed clock. what matters on a trailing structure is session length: shorter planned sessions produce fewer ticks of floor movement, and the earliest part of the session tends to carry the widest spreads and the most news risk. deliberate, bounded sessions are easier to manage than open-ended screen time.
a funded account is issued with its own conditions: minimum trading days before the first payout, a profit threshold, the consistency check and kyc. the payout process guide covers the sequence.

apex is unusual among futures firms in making it straightforward to hold several evaluations and several funded accounts at once, and that structural choice changes the strategy more than most traders expect. the question stops being "how do i pass one account" and becomes "how do i run three without turning them into one large position".

the temptation is obvious: three $50,000 accounts traded with the same setup is a $150,000 position with three times the risk and, crucially, three failure thresholds that trip together. correlated accounts do not diversify anything; they multiply the same decision. a trader who takes the same eurusd or es setup across five accounts has not built a portfolio, they have built leverage with extra paperwork.

sequencing is slower and it is the only version that survives a bad week. a trader with one funded account that is 4% up and a second evaluation three days old has two independent problems; a trader with five accounts opened the same monday has one problem that arrives five times, and the response - cutting all five at once - is the same as cutting one position at five times the size.

if several accounts are running, the sensible approach is to treat the whole book as one risk budget and divide it. a trader who risks 1.5% per trade per account with three accounts is risking 4.5% of the combined equity on a single idea, which is above the daily limit of any individual account. the per-account percentages look compliant while the aggregate does not.

a practical rule is to halve the per-account risk for each additional concurrently traded account: 1.5% on one, 0.75% on two, 0.5% on three. the combined exposure stays near 1.5% and each account's failure threshold remains proportionate to the plan. the cost is that each account progresses slowly; the benefit is that no single trade can end more than one account at a time.
the payout cycle, and why it drives the whole plan

apex payouts are not on demand in the way a bank withdrawal is. there is a minimum number of trading days before the first request, a profit threshold, a consistency requirement on the best day, and a processing schedule. those four constraints interact, and the interaction is what most traders fail to plan.

the consistency requirement is the one that surprises people, because it is measured against total profit at the moment of the request rather than across the evaluation. a trader who makes $3,000 on a single strong session and $1,200 across the following fortnight has a best day of roughly 71% of profit - the account is profitable, the evaluation was passed cleanly, and the withdrawal is refused until enough ordinary profit is added to bring that ratio under the threshold.
a payout can be blocked by distribution even when total profit is comfortably above the threshold.

the two constraints usually have different deadlines, and the efficient plan lands them on the same date. if the profit threshold is reached on day five but the minimum day count is twenty, the remaining fifteen sessions exist to add ordinary profit without adding a dominant day. that is not a waiting period to be endured; it is the window in which the consistency ratio gets repaired.

the arithmetic is worth doing on paper before the payout request rather than after. required total profit equals best day divided by the consistency percentage. with a $2,400 best day and a 30% rule, the account needs $8,000 of total profit before the request; if it is showing $5,000, another $3,000 spread across small sessions is the fix, and a second large day is the opposite of a fix.

trade smaller, not bigger. a payout request that is waiting on a day count is a period in which the only objective is not to lose what has already been earned, and the failure mode is a trader who uses the waiting period to "make the payout worth having". the payout is already worth having; the marginal profit from pressing is small compared with the risk of resetting the account to zero.

a useful discipline is to set a hard cap for the waiting period at half the normal daily budget. it feels like wasted time and it is the cheapest insurance available, because the account has already done the thing it was bought for.

multiple accounts make sense when each one is independently funded and independently traded, and when the combined risk stays inside a single account's daily budget. they make no sense as a way to increase exposure to the same idea, and they make no sense for a trader who has not yet traded one funded account through a full payout cycle.

the sequencing that works is unglamorous: pass one, trade it to a payout, then decide whether a second account adds anything. most traders discover that the second account adds administration rather than profit - the payout ceiling on a single account is usually well above what their strategy generates in a month, so the constraint is not the number of accounts but the size of the edge.

where a second account does add something, it is usually diversification across rulebooks rather than across positions: one account at a firm with a static drawdown and one at a firm with a trailing floor behave differently in a bad week, and having both spreads the risk of a single rulebook decision going wrong.

most ftmo advice is either obvious or useless - "be disciplined", "manage risk", "stick to your plan". this is the other kind: twenty-two specific behaviours, each with the arithmetic behind it, that separate accounts which reach verification from accounts which expire quietly three weeks in.
the 5% daily loss limit is measured on equity, floating positions included, which makes it the strictest number on the account.
most failed ftmo attempts are not stopped by the target being hard - they are stopped by a single session that broke the daily budget.
there is no time limit on the standard challenge, so speed is a choice, and almost always the wrong one.
a sixteen to twenty day pass at modest size beats a nine day pass that leaves no margin for verification.

advice about prop trading is cheap, and most of it is unfalsifiable. "trade with discipline" cannot be measured, cannot be checked against a result, and cannot be improved. a useful tip has three properties: it names a specific action, it can be verified from an account statement, and ignoring it has a predictable cost. everything in this article is written to meet that standard - if a tip cannot be checked against your own trade history, it does not belong in the list.

the second filter is structural. ftmo's challenge is a rules puzzle before it is a trading puzzle. a trader with a modest edge and perfect rule compliance funds an account; a trader with a better edge and one careless thursday does not. that imbalance is why so much of the advice here concerns arithmetic rather than entries, and why the single highest-value habit is recalculating your limits every morning instead of relying on memory.

third, the target is not the hard part. ten percent on phase one, at a risk level that keeps a normal losing sequence survivable, is reachable in a few weeks by most traders who can already trade. what ends attempts is the interaction between the target and the two loss limits: the closer you get, the more tempting it becomes to press, and pressing is what converts a 7% gain into a 5% daily loss on a tuesday afternoon. most of the tips below are defences against that specific moment.

finally, treat every tip as a hypothesis about your own trading, not a rule handed down. the list is drawn from patterns that repeat across attempts, but your statement is the only evidence that matters about you. adopt two or three, run them for a full attempt, and check whether the failure mode they address actually appears in your journal. a tip that solves a problem you do not have is just extra friction.
the cheapest tips are the ones applied before a fee is paid. five things are worth settling first, because each of them costs a full attempt if discovered later.

ftmo's headline structure - 10% phase one target, 5% phase two, 5% daily loss, 10% maximum loss, four minimum trading days per phase - has been stable for years, but the firm layers changes on top: different account sizes, swing versus normal, and periodic adjustments to payout terms. read the current rulebook page for your specific account type on the day you purchase and write the numbers into your plan. traders fail on rules they assumed rather than rules they read, and the assumption is usually a year out of date.
choose an account size you can lose without changing behaviour

account size does not change difficulty in percentage terms, so the only rational reason to buy larger is the payout ceiling - and the only irrational reason is the feeling of trading more. take the smallest size whose payout would still be meaningful to you, and resist the temptation to scale up until you have passed and been paid once. a trader who is afraid of the fee trades differently from one who is not, and the difference shows up as hesitation on valid setups.

mt4, mt5 and ctrader all calculate floating equity the same way, but order handling, hedging behaviour and the exact place the stop sits differ. a week of demo trading on the same platform and instrument set removes a category of error that has nothing to do with skill: fat fingers, wrong lot sizes, stops placed on the wrong side because the chart was inverted. these are embarrassing failures and they are entirely preventable.

ftmo permits forex, indices, commodities, crypto and stocks, but permission is not a strategy. pick one to three instruments whose session behaviour you know, and write the list down. a challenge is a poor time to discover that you cannot read gold on a friday afternoon. the narrower the instrument set, the more comparable your trades become, and comparability is what makes a weekly review possible at all.

a journal with five fields is enough: date, instrument, direction, risk in percent, result in r. add a sixth for the reason, in a single clause. the purpose is not record-keeping for its own sake; it is to answer one question at the end of each week - is my risk per trade stable, and are my losses smaller than my wins in r terms? an account statement shows the money; only a journal shows whether the process was repeatable.
sizing is where most of the passing is done, and it can be reduced to four numbers that fit on an index card.

the fourth number is the one traders rarely compute, and it reframes the whole challenge. at 1.65% risk per trade, a 10% target is roughly six full-risk wins. six. spread across sixteen trading days with a normal mix of wins, losses and scratches, that is an entirely ordinary month of trading - which is why the honest advice is that ftmo's target is small and the discipline required is large.
tip 1: risk one third of the daily budget, not one half

half the daily budget per trade means two consecutive losses end the day, and two consecutive losses are not an anomaly - they happen in any sample of twenty trades with a 45% win rate. a third means three losses are needed to end the day, which turns a bad session into a bad session rather than a blown limit. the cost is that reaching the target takes slightly longer, and time is the one resource the challenge does not meter.

the most common sizing error is not over-sizing; it is variable sizing. a trader risks 0.8% on the setup they like least and 3% on the one they like most, and the resulting equity curve is dominated by the trades they felt best about - which is usually a smaller sample than they think. constant risk makes the statement readable. readability is what allows you to tell skill from luck at the end of the attempt.

above 70% of the target, halve your risk. the mathematics is unglamorous: the remaining 3% of target is worth less to you than the 5% you could lose in a single session, and the expected value of pressing at that point is negative even with a genuine edge. traders who respect this rule pass more slowly and fail far less often. it is the single highest-yield tip in this article.
tip 4: translate risk to lots before you enter, not after

calculate the position size from the stop distance and the dollar risk, then place the order. doing it the other way - picking a familiar lot size and seeing where the stop lands - is how a 1.65% trade becomes a 3.4% trade with a stop that "felt right". on a $100,000 account, 1.65% is $1,650; if the stop is 22 pips, that is 0.75 lots on eurusd at $10 per pip, and the arithmetic should already be done before the chart is opened.

the daily limit is measured on equity, which means floating losses count against it in real time. that single detail changes the way a session has to be managed, and it is the rule most attempts die on.
a daily budget divided into three tranches, with the session closed at eighty percent of the limit rather than at the limit itself.
tip 5: stop at 80% of the daily limit, always

if the daily budget is $5,000, the working limit is $4,000. the remaining $1,000 is not unused capital; it is insurance against the float. a position that is open when the market gaps, or a spread that widens at the london close, can move equity several hundred dollars in seconds. traders who stop at 80% almost never breach a daily limit; traders who stop at 100% breach it eventually, because the limit is measured before they have a chance to close.
tip 6: count floating loss toward the budget the moment it exists
