the account is at its daily low when a position is at its worst, not when a trade is closed. if you have closed two losers and have a third position $900 in the red, your budget is $4,000 minus $900, not minus the two closed trades. doing this arithmetic in your head during a session is unreliable, so write the running budget next to the platform and update it whenever a position is opened or closed.

two losses in a session initiates a hard stop for the day, regardless of the remaining budget. this is a behavioural rule rather than an arithmetic one, and it exists because the third trade after two losses is the one most often taken for emotional reasons - recovering the day rather than exploiting an edge. the cost is occasionally missing a good setup; the benefit is never being in the position of defending a nearly-broken limit.
tip 8: close before high-impact news if you cannot watch it

ftmo permits trading the news, but floating exposure during a release is a different risk from a stop measured in pips. spreads widen, slippage is real, and a stop can fill well beyond its level. if you cannot sit through the release, be flat. if you can, reduce size to a fraction of normal and accept that the outcome is a coin flip on a wider distribution than your plan models.

the maximum loss is static: on a $100,000 account the failure level sits at $90,000 and never moves, whatever you earn along the way. that sounds generous next to a trailing drawdown, and it is - but it also creates a specific trap, because a static floor means a trader can lose the daily limit five days running and still be in the challenge, which encourages continuation after evidence has already arrived.
a static floor stays where it started, which is why ftmo attempts tend to fail through repeated daily breaches rather than one catastrophic day.
tip 9: track maximum loss from the starting balance, not the peak

because the floor is static, the number that matters is distance from $100,000, not distance from your highest equity. a trader at $106,000 who has a bad week still has $16,000 of room. a trader at $94,000 has $4,000. write the current distance on the same index card as the daily budget, and update it once per session - it is the only number that tells you whether the challenge is genuinely in trouble.
tip 10: treat three consecutive losing days as a structural problem

three consecutive days of losses is not a variance event to trade through; it is a signal that the market regime has changed or the process has drifted. stop for two sessions and review the journal before the next trade. the cost is two days out of an unlimited calendar; the alternative is discovering the problem at $93,000, when the remaining room forces a size that no longer resembles your plan.

averaging into a loser is the fastest route from a normal drawdown to a static-limit breach, because the second entry doubles exposure at exactly the moment the first is wrong. on a challenge with a static floor the temptation is stronger than on a trailing account - the floor does not move against you, so it feels as though there is room. there is room, and using it this way is how a 2% loss becomes a 7% one.

ftmo's standard challenge has no overall time limit, and the minimum is four trading days per phase. those two facts together define the strategic question: how fast should you go? the answer that maximises the probability of being funded is slower than most traders expect.

the patient row is not merely safer; it is faster in expected terms, because a failed attempt costs the fee and the whole elapsed period before restarting. an aggressive trader who passes on the second attempt in twelve days has spent more time and money than a patient trader who passed on the first in twenty.
tip 12: set a floor for days, not a ceiling

commit to a minimum of fourteen trading days in phase one before requesting evaluation of the target, even if you hit 10% on day eight. the purpose is not superstition: it forces a sample large enough that the result reflects process, and it prevents a lucky week from producing a trader who believes they have an edge they cannot repeat in verification.
tip 13: pass verification the same way you passed phase one

phase two has half the target and the same loss limits, which makes it feel like a formality. it is not - it is where the account is won or lost by traders who raise size because the target is lower. keep the same risk per trade and the same instrument set. verification at 1.65% risk needs roughly three full-risk wins, and there is no deadline at all.
tip 14: bank the target before you stop, then stop

when the target is reached, close everything and stop trading for the day. the remaining session has nothing to offer and a full daily budget to lose. this sounds trivial and it is the most common way a completed challenge turns into an incomplete one - the target was hit, the trader kept trading, and the day closed below the finish line.
the routine exists to spend a budget deliberately rather than discover it is gone.
structure beats motivation across a three-week attempt. two routines carry most of the weight.

before the first trade, write four numbers: current equity, distance to the static floor, today's daily budget in dollars, and today's maximum position size in lots. then check the economic calendar for high-impact releases during your session. that is five minutes and it eliminates the two most expensive categories of error - trading a stale risk figure and being surprised by a release. traders who skip this step are not undisciplined in general; they are simply relying on memory for numbers that change daily.

once a week, answer three questions from the journal. was risk per trade stable within 10%? were losses smaller in r terms than wins? did any trade violate a written rule, and if so which? a single violation is a coaching note; two of the same violation is a structural problem to fix before the next session. the review is what converts a challenge from a gamble into a measurement, and it takes less time than a single trade setup.

the challenge has no deadline, but traders impose one within the first week - usually a vague target like "pass by the end of the month" - and then trade as though it were a firm rule. nearly every psychological failure in prop trading traces back to that self-imposed clock.
tip 17: delete the deadline and replace it with a day count

instead of a finish date, track a running count of trading days completed and a running count of rule violations. the first number should grow slowly and steadily; the second should stay at zero. this reframes progress from "am i close to the target" to "is the process intact", which is the only question that predicts the outcome.
tip 18: pre-commit to a stop after a rule violation

if you break a written rule - oversized, revenge trade, holding through a release you said you would avoid - stop for the rest of the day and the next session. the penalty is decided in advance, when you are calm, precisely because the moment after a violation is when judgement is worst. a trader who enforces this ends most attempts with zero violations. a trader who forgives themselves once will forgive themselves again.

the fee is sunk at purchase; it is not recoverable by trading harder, and treating it as a debt to be repaid is how a $540 challenge turns into a $3,000 series of resets. the correct frame is that you have bought a three-week evaluation of your process, and the fee buys information either way. traders who think this way take the same trades in week three as in week one, which is exactly the behaviour that passes.
ftmo's rules permit news trading, and that permission is a trap for anyone who reads it as encouragement. two tips cover the ground.

london, new york and the asian session have different volatility profiles, and a strategy calibrated on one rarely transfers. choosing a single session reduces screen time, makes the journal comparable, and removes the temptation to force a trade at 22:00 because nothing happened earlier. the exception is a genuinely session-agnostic strategy, which most are not.
tip 21: treat the first friday of the month as a separate regime

non-farm payrolls produce spreads and slippage that a normal stop distance does not account for. either be flat, or trade at a third of normal size with a wider stop and a smaller position. the same applies to central bank decisions and cpi releases. none of these events is unpredictable - they are on a calendar you can read in thirty seconds, which makes exposure through them a choice rather than an accident.
across attempts that fail, the causes cluster tightly. recognising the pattern in your own behaviour is more useful than any entry technique.
the single oversized trade. one position at three or four times normal risk, usually taken after a good week, that consumes the whole daily budget.
the three-loss session. risk set at half the daily budget, two losses, then a third taken to recover the day.
the giving-back day. a profitable morning held into the afternoon until the position reverses through the entry and the stop.
the deadline sprint. size increases in the final week because an invented finish date is approaching.
the news gap. a stop that fills beyond its level during a release, converting a planned 1.5% loss into 4%.
the rule misread. a swing account traded overnight when the plan was normal, or a position held over a weekend that the account type does not permit.
the abandonment. a drawdown to $94,000 followed by two weeks of no trading, then a return with a size chosen to recover the loss in one trade.

six of the seven are budgeting failures rather than analysis failures, and all six are prevented by the same three habits: a written daily budget, a hard stop at 80% of it, and a constant risk per trade. that is an uncomfortable conclusion for anyone hoping the answer is a better indicator, and it is the conclusion the data supports.

when an attempt ends, the instinct is to review the last trade - the one that broke the limit - and look for what went wrong in the entry. that is almost never where the problem is. the last trade is the symptom; the cause is usually two sessions earlier, when the budget was spent to the last dollar, or a week earlier, when risk per trade drifted upward and nobody noticed.

a useful post-mortem asks four questions in order. how many sessions did the attempt last? on how many of them was risk per trade outside 10% of the plan? which session came closest to the daily limit, and what was different about it? and if the attempt had ended one day earlier, would it have passed? most failures answer the last question with yes, which is the most useful thing an attempt can teach.

write the answers down, date them, and keep them with the next attempt's plan. a trader who can describe why the last two attempts ended in the same way has a specific problem with a specific fix. a trader who says only that the market was difficult has bought information and thrown it away.

keep the post-mortems in one place and read them before the next purchase. three dated notes are worth more than any article about discipline, because they describe a specific trader's specific leak - and the leak is usually the same one in all three.

that is also the test for whether any of this advice is working. if the post-mortems keep naming the same leak, nothing has been fixed and no amount of extra reading will fix it; if they start naming a different one, the process is moving and the remaining work is smaller than it looks.

there is a practical version of this test that costs nothing: read the last post-mortem before placing the first trade of a new attempt. it is a two-minute habit that closes the loop between information and behaviour, which is the loop most traders leave open. a note that is written and never re-read is a diary, not a process.

everything above can be executed alone by a trader with a routine and a journal. where a service adds something specific is in the discipline rather than the analysis: recalculating the daily budget each morning, enforcing the 80% stop, and resisting the deadline sprint in week three - sustained across two phases without drift.

one third of the 5% daily loss budget, which is about 1.65% per trade on a $100,000 account. that allows three losses in a session before the day ends and keeps a normal losing sequence survivable.
is the 5% daily loss measured on balance or equity?
equity, including floating positions. a trade that is open and losing counts against the daily limit in real time, which is why the working stop should be 80% of the budget rather than 100%.

most evaluation accounts are not lost mid-trade. they are lost in the fifty hours when the market is closed and the position is still open - a gap that opens beyond the stop, a swap charge that lands three times, or a firm rule that treats a weekend hold as a prohibited exposure. this guide covers the mechanics behind each of those outcomes, the rule variations worth checking in your firm's terms, and the sizing maths that makes a weekend hold survivable when the rules do permit it.
a stop loss is an instruction, not a guarantee: over a weekend gap it fills at whatever price exists when the market reopens, which can be far beyond the level on the ticket.
firms handle weekend holding in three ways - permitted with gap risk, prohibited on evaluation accounts, and permitted only flat by a stated cut-off. the third is the most commonly breached.
swap and financing charges accrue on held positions, and on wednesday many instruments book triple swap. that is a direct cost against a fixed drawdown budget.
on a trailing-drawdown account a weekend gap is doubly dangerous: it can breach the floor and simultaneously erase the cushion that allowed the position to exist.
the sizing rule that makes a hold survivable is to price the gap as if it were the stop - typically a multiple of the planned risk, not the planned risk itself.

during the trading week, a stop loss behaves approximately as advertised. price moves continuously, liquidity is present in normal size, and a level a few pips or ticks away is usually reachable within a fraction of the planned risk. the whole architecture of risk management - position sizing, daily budgets, trailing floors - assumes that the stop is the worst case.

the weekend removes that assumption. the market closes on friday evening, reopens on sunday or monday depending on the instrument, and the price at the reopen is whatever the accumulated news of the interval produces. nobody was there to fill the orders in between. a stop placed at a sensible distance does not fill at that distance; it fills at the first available price, which is a fact rather than a rule of any firm.

this is the difference between volatility and gap risk. volatility is price movement inside a session, and stops work in it. gap risk is price discontinuity across a closed market, and stops do not work in it. an evaluation account can survive a volatile week at disciplined sizing; it can be ended by a single event over a weekend that never appeared in the trader's risk model.

two properties make it worse on an evaluation than on a personal account. first, the account has a hard failure threshold rather than a margin call, so there is no buffer between a large gap and a closed account. second, most evaluation plans are calibrated to the daily loss limit, which is measured on intraday movement - a budget that is irrelevant to a fifty-hour price jump.

the mechanism is simple and worth walking through in numbers, because the intuition most traders carry is wrong in a specific way. they assume a losing weekend position costs the amount at risk on the ticket. it costs whatever the reopen gives them.

the table is not a worst-case fantasy. currency pairs have opened tens of pips away from friday's close after a weekend of central-bank commentary, and index instruments have opened hundreds of points away after a geopolitical event. in each case the stop that looked like 1% was filled at a multiple of it, and the daily loss limit was irrelevant because the loss did not happen inside a session.

there is a second-order effect that catches traders who survive the fill. many firms measure the daily loss limit against the previous day's closing balance or equity, which means the monday reopen loss is attributed to monday. a trader who gaps through half the drawdown at the open has a second, independent budget to spend later that day - and a natural instinct, after a loss of that size, to try to recover it.

that instinct is the actual killer in most weekend stories. the gap is a finite, calculable event; the recovery attempt afterwards is where the rest of the account goes. any plan that permits a weekend hold should state in advance that the monday session after a gap is closed, with no new positions taken until the following day.
measurement matters: a floating loss counts against an equity-based limit before the position is ever closed.
firms do not share a single policy. there are three positions, and they exist in roughly equal numbers across the industry.

permitted with gap risk borne by the trader. the firm allows positions to be held across the weekend and states that the account is subject to gap risk, including the possibility that the failure threshold is exceeded at the reopen. this is the most honest position: the risk is disclosed, and the trader is free to accept it. it is also the position that most often produces a failed account, because disclosure is not the same as protection.

prohibited on evaluation accounts. the firm requires all positions to be flat before the weekly close, usually by a stated cut-off in server time. holding through that cut-off is a rule breach regardless of whether the position was profitable. this is common among firms that regard overnight and weekend exposure as an unacceptable risk on an account they have not yet funded.

permitted with conditions. the firm allows holdings but restricts them: a reduced effective leverage over the weekend, a cap on the number of open positions, an exclusion of specific instruments, or a requirement to reduce size below a threshold. this is the position most likely to be breached accidentally, because the conditions live in the terms rather than on the evaluation page.

the practical advice is uncomfortable but simple: read the clause for the specific instrument you intend to hold. firms sometimes permit weekend holding on major currency pairs and prohibit it on indices, or allow it on the funded account while prohibiting it on the evaluation. the unit of the rule is the instrument and the stage, not the account.

where the rule is a cut-off time, convert it before friday afternoon. firms state cut-offs in server time, which frequently does not match the trader's local clock or the platform's displayed time. a trader who assumes the cut-off is midnight local and discovers it is 22:00 server time has already breached.
a held position carries a cost independent of price movement, and beginners routinely forget it because it never appears on the trade ticket.

on forex and cfd accounts the position is financed: the platform applies a swap charge, which can be positive or negative depending on the interest-rate differential between the two currencies. on most instruments the charge is small per night and material across weeks. on a fixed daily budget, it is a slow leak rather than an event - but on a trailing account it is worse, because it reduces equity and therefore the cushion without producing a visible loss on the chart.

the detail that catches people is the triple charge. most brokers and platforms book three days of financing on the weekday that accounts for the weekend settlement, which for many instruments is wednesday. a trader who holds one position over a weekend pays the weekend financing, but a trader who positions on wednesday specifically to hold through friday pays it up front, and the amount is triple the nightly figure rather than a single night.

futures accounts do not pay swap; they carry contracts with expiry and exchange margin rules instead. the equivalent weekend consideration is the contract's expiry and any roll, plus the fact that holding a futures position into a weekend exposes it to the same gap without any financing cost as an offsetting signal. traders coming from forex often read the absence of swap as an absence of cost, which is not the same thing.

the planning implication is to price the hold as a total: expected gap exposure plus financing over the number of nights, compared against the remaining drawdown budget. on a position held for two weeks, financing alone can consume a meaningful fraction of the daily limit without a single adverse price move.
the reopen is a distinct market event rather than a continuation of friday's session, and it behaves like one.

liquidity at the open is thin relative to the middle of the day. spreads are wide, and the first prints can be far from the level at which the market eventually trades an hour later. for a trader holding a losing position, that thinness means the fill can be worse than the gap itself suggests - the market opens at one price, the stop fills a moment later at another.

stops placed inside the gap are not magic. a stop ten points below friday's close on an instrument that opens a hundred points lower fills near the open, not ten points below the close. this is the single fact that traders find hardest to accept, and it is the reason firms with tight drawdowns prohibit weekend holds outright: the risk is not linear in the stop distance.
a gap does not respect the floor: it moves equity past it, and on a trailing account the cushion was already thinner than it looked.

there is a subtler effect on a trailing account. the failure threshold is computed from peak equity, and peak equity includes unrealised profit. a position held over a weekend can be in profit on friday, pushing the floor upward, and then gap through the floor on monday without ever being closed. the trader's mental model - "i was up, so i had room" - is inverted: being up is what removed the room.

for a trader who does hold, the useful discipline is to decide the monday action before friday's close. if the position is stopped out at a loss, the day is closed with no new risk. if it gaps in favour, the position is reduced rather than held, because the same gap that helped can reverse on the next news item. neither decision should be made while looking at a monday screen.
if the rules permit a weekend hold, the sizing calculation changes. the planned stop is no longer the risk; the plausible gap is.

a workable method is to price the gap at a multiple of the stop and require that the total still fits inside the remaining drawdown. if a trader's normal position risks 0.5% with a stop, and the instrument has historically gapped three stop distances over a weekend, the true risk of that position is 1.5% rather than 0.5%. the position should be reduced by the same factor - to roughly a third of normal size - if the account is to keep the same exposure.

that arithmetic produces positions that feel too small to matter, which is precisely why traders ignore it. it is also why the accounts that survive weekend events are the ones holding trivial size at the close rather than the ones with a strong view.
sizing to thirds is the same logic applied to a hold: the loss you can survive is the one you planned for, not the one you hoped for.

two further refinements are worth making. first, cluster instruments rather than counting positions: two correlated pairs held over a weekend are one exposure, and a trader holding three of them has not diversified, has tripled a single bet. second, account for the financing over the expected hold duration before deciding the size, because a position that is fine for one night may not be for five.

the final piece is a hard cap. set a rule that no weekend exposure may exceed a fixed percentage of the remaining drawdown - a third is a reasonable ceiling - and treat it as non-negotiable regardless of conviction. conviction is exactly the variable that fails to predict gaps.
some approaches are structurally compatible with holding, and others are not. the distinction is not about timeframe but about how the edge is produced.

strategies that depend on precise entries and exits - scalping, mean reversion with tight stops, anything where the stop distance is a meaningful part of the thesis - are incompatible with gap risk. the gap destroys the relationship between the risk taken and the loss realised, and the plan's statistics stop describing the plan.

strategies that depend on a broad directional view over weeks, with wide stops and small size relative to the account, are compatible in principle. a position risking a quarter of a per cent with a stop three times wider than the gap history is not meaningfully exposed to a weekend event, and the financing is a rounding error against the expected move.

there is a middle category that looks compatible and is not: positions with a wide stop but a large notional value. these are the trades that produce the horror stories, because the stop is far away, the trader feels safe, and the gap is large enough to matter anyway. the test is not the stop distance in price terms but the loss in account percentage if the worst historical gap is applied.

for an evaluation account specifically, the asymmetry argues for flat fridays regardless of compatibility. a hold can produce a modest additional opportunity or a large unplanned loss, and on an account whose purpose is to reach a threshold, the variance is not compensated by the extra hours of exposure. the profitable weekend hold is a real thing; it is a poorly priced thing on an evaluation.
most traders read a guide like this on a friday afternoon with a position open. the decisions available are limited, and the order they are worth considering is not the intuitive one.

check the rule first. before deciding whether to hold, establish whether the firm permits it for that instrument on your account stage. if it is a breach, the position must be closed regardless of profit or loss. a rule breach voids the evaluation whether or not the trade would have worked, and a trader who holds hoping the position offsets the breach has misunderstood the transaction.

check the cut-off in server time. if the firm requires flat positions by a stated time, convert it to your clock and to the platform clock, and close with a margin. the last fifteen minutes before a cut-off are the worst possible time to be executing, because spreads widen as liquidity thins.

then decide on the position, not on the p l. a losing position is not more worth holding because closing it realises a loss; that is the disposition effect wearing a risk-management costume. the question is whether the position would be opened today at this size given the weekend ahead. if the answer is no, the position should not exist.

reduce rather than close where the thesis is intact. cutting to a third of the size keeps a view while bringing the gap exposure inside the drawdown budget. that is the compromise for a trader who genuinely believes the position has weeks to run and whose firm permits the hold.

record the decision and the reason. the journal entry that matters is written on friday, not on monday. a trader who wrote "held 0.2% exposure over the weekend, gap risk priced at three stops, no new positions on monday" has a defensible process even if the gap goes against them.
weekend holding rarely operates in isolation. four other rules commonly interact with it, and each changes the calculation.

news windows. a weekend can contain scheduled events in markets that trade outside the trader's normal hours, and the firm's news rule may still apply at the reopen. being flat avoids the question entirely.

maximum position caps. firms that cap the number of open positions often count a weekend hold as occupying a slot, which reduces the capacity available on monday. on a small cap that is a real cost, not a technicality.

consistency rules. a gap in favour produces a large single day, which is exactly the pattern a best-day consistency rule penalises at payout. a weekend win can therefore create a payout problem that a weekend loss would not have created.

drawdown measurement timing. where the firm measures the daily limit at a specific server-time reset, a gap loss can be split across two days depending on when the reopen falls relative to the reset. that changes which budget absorbs the loss, and it is worth knowing before rather than after.
none of these makes a weekend hold impossible. they do mean that the decision is a compound one, and that "the rules allow it" is a necessary condition rather than a sufficient one.
six questions, answered before the close, cover the decision completely.
does my firm permit a weekend hold on this instrument, at this account stage, under its current terms?
if there is a cut-off, what is it in server time, and am i reliably flat before it?
what is the worst historical gap on this instrument, expressed as a percentage of my remaining drawdown?
does the financing over the expected hold fit inside my daily budget, including the triple charge day?
are my open positions correlated, and what is the combined exposure rather than the per-position risk?
what is my monday action if the position gaps against me, written down now rather than decided later?

a trader who can answer all six in under a minute is operating a process. a trader who cannot is holding a position they do not fully understand, which is the condition in which weekend risk does its damage.

numbers make the trade-off concrete. take a $100,000 evaluation with a 10% maximum loss, a 5% daily limit, and a trader who is $2,000 in profit on friday afternoon with one position open. the position risks 0.5% - $500 - and the stop is 40 pips away.

option one: close before the bell. the trader banks the profit, ends the week with $2,000 of buffer, and starts monday with a full daily budget and no exposure. nothing about the weekend can affect the account. the cost is the possibility that the position would have continued in their favour, which is a real cost and a small one relative to the remaining drawdown.

option two: hold at full size. the nominal risk is $500. but the instrument has gapped up to 120 pips over a weekend twice in the last three years, which is three times the stop distance. the plausible loss is therefore $1,500, and the plausible adverse tail is larger. on a 5% daily limit of $5,000 that is survivable; on the maximum loss it consumes 15% of the entire remaining drawdown in a single fill.

option three: hold at a third of size. the nominal risk falls to $167 and the gap-adjusted exposure to roughly $500. the trader keeps a view, the account keeps its buffer, and the worst plausible outcome is an amount the plan can absorb without changing the week. this is the only version of the hold that respects both the thesis and the threshold.

the example is unremarkable, which is the point. there is no exotic instrument and no extreme assumption - just a normal winning position, a normal weekend, and a gap multiple that has occurred recently enough to be in the data. almost every weekend disaster looks like this at the moment of decision rather than like an obvious gamble.

one detail in that example deserves emphasis. the trader was in profit. on a trailing-drawdown account, that profit had already lifted the failure floor, so the cushion was smaller than the balance implied. holding a winner over a weekend is therefore riskier than holding a loser, which inverts the instinct that keeps traders in profitable positions.
traders often lump overnight and weekend exposure together, and firms usually treat them as separate rules. the distinction matters because the mitigations are different.

an overnight hold is a gap of a few hours inside a continuous market. for most instruments the reopened price is close to the previous close, the funding cost is one night, and the adverse move is usually a fraction of the daily range. overnight risk is real but bounded, and it is the reason many plans allow a position to be held from the new york afternoon into the asian session.

a weekend hold is a gap of one to two days in which the market is closed to everyone. the information that accumulates is not filtered by trading, so the first price after the reopen can be a step change rather than a continuation. funding can be charged at triple rate, scheduled events may occur in unrelated markets, and the firm's cut-off rules - which often apply only to the weekend - come into play.

the practical consequence is that a plan can reasonably permit overnight holds and prohibit weekend ones. many do exactly that, and it is a coherent position rather than an inconsistency. if your firm's rules make that distinction, respect it in the plan rather than treating the weekend as an extended night.

there is a second, mechanical difference worth knowing. overnight gap risk on a trailing account is usually absorbed because the floor moves on unrealised profit and the position is rarely held through a large adverse step. weekend gap risk arrives when the trader cannot respond: no ability to reduce size, no ability to close early, no ability to adjust the stop as the market approaches it. that asymmetry - the inability to act - is what turns a manageable exposure into a rule breach.

finally, consider the sequencing across a month rather than a single friday. a trader who holds every weekend takes that risk forty or fifty times a year. at even a modest probability of a large gap per hold, the annual probability of at least one damaging event approaches certainty. the individual decision looks trivial; the habit does not.
can i hold positions over the weekend on a prop firm evaluation?

only if the firm's terms permit it for that instrument and account stage. policies range from permitted with gap risk borne by the trader, to prohibited on evaluation accounts, to permitted with conditions such as reduced leverage or position caps. read the clause for your specific instrument rather than the general faq.
does a stop loss protect me over a weekend gap?

no. a stop is an instruction to trade at the market when a level is reached, and over a closed market the level is skipped. the order fills at the first available price after the reopen, which can be well beyond the stop distance.

the risk is a discontinuity: a price jump that makes the realised loss a multiple of the planned one. on an account with a hard failure threshold, a single gap can consume the remaining drawdown, which is why sizing for a hold should price the gap rather than the stop.

most platforms book three days of financing on the weekday that settles the weekend, which is wednesday for many instruments. a position held from wednesday pays the weekend financing up front, on top of the nightly charge.

no, futures do not pay swap; they carry contracts with expiry and exchange margin rules. the weekend risk is the same gap without a financing charge, which traders sometimes mistake for a lack of cost.
can holding a winner over the weekend cause a consistency problem?

yes. a favourable gap produces a single large day, and a best-day consistency rule penalises exactly that pattern at payout. a weekend win can therefore leave an account at target but unable to withdraw until the ratio normalises.

size from the plausible gap, not the stop. if the instrument has gapped three stop distances historically, true exposure is three times the planned risk, so the position should be cut to roughly a third. a ceiling of one third of remaining drawdown for total weekend exposure is a reasonable hard cap.

on firms that prohibit holding, the account is typically void regardless of the position's outcome. there is no partial credit for a profitable breach. the only defence is to convert the cut-off to your own clock and close with time to spare.

not with a fresh position in the first minutes. spreads are wide, prints can be far from the eventual price, and a trader who has just taken a gap loss is the least objective participant in that session. treat the reopen as a measurement and the rest of the day as closed.

it depends on when the firm resets the day. if the reopen falls after the reset, the gap loss lands in the new day's budget; if before, it lands in the previous one. either way the maximum loss rule applies, and that is the one that closes accounts.
is holding over the weekend ever a good trade on an evaluation?

rarely. the extra opportunity is modest and the variance is large, and an evaluation's purpose is to reach a threshold rather than to maximise expected value. the traders who hold successfully are usually running very small size against a wide stop, which is not the trade most holders are actually taking.

the terms of service or the trading rules document, searched for words like "weekend", "overnight", "market close" and "holding". where the evaluation page and the terms disagree, the terms are enforced. a written answer from support is worth keeping.

the rulebook summary is written before the evaluation starts. it lists the firm's target, daily loss limit, maximum loss, drawdown type, minimum trading days, consistency requirement and any instrument or news restrictions. if a firm's rule is ambiguous - and many are - the ambiguity is resolved conservatively, in the direction that protects the account.

the risk plan converts those rules into numbers: maximum risk per trade as a percentage of the daily loss limit, maximum number of trades per session, and the conditions under which trading stops for the day. the plan is deliberately unsophisticated. its purpose is to survive the sequences that end evaluations, not to maximise return.

the rule is simpler than any of that: the firm's rules always beat the market view. an opportunity that looks exceptional is skipped if taking it would put the account within reach of the daily limit. evaluations are not passed by finding the best trade of the month; they are passed by never letting a bad sequence matter.
pacing is arithmetic before it is judgement, which is why the same plan transfers across account sizes.

abstract descriptions of risk discipline are easy to write and hard to apply. a concrete example is more useful, so here is how a standard two-phase forex evaluation - 10% target on phase one, 5% on phase two, 5% daily loss limit, 10% maximum loss - is typically paced when elitepropx trades it.

balance $100,000. profit target phase one: $10,000. daily loss limit: $5,000. maximum loss: $10,000. minimum trading days: four. no time limit, which is the single most helpful rule in the rulebook, because it means a flat week costs time rather than the account.

the plan sets maximum risk per trade at $1,600 - roughly a third of the daily limit. that number is chosen so that three consecutive losses, which happen regularly to any strategy with a normal win rate, still leave the account intact and the day unfinished by only a fraction of its budget.

the first sessions are about creating separation between equity and the $90,000 failure level. sessions are short: one or two high-quality setups per day, no chasing, no averaging into losers. a realistic week-one outcome is $2,000 to $3,500 of profit, or a small loss with the daily budget barely touched. both are acceptable. the purpose of week one is not progress toward the target; it is arriving at week two with a cushion and no rule breach.

with a cushion in place, the same risk per trade can produce a larger share of the target, because a losing sequence no longer threatens the maximum loss level. sessions lengthen slightly and the target is approached in increments. traders who want to know the arithmetic can check it directly: at $1,600 risk per trade and a 1.8:1 average reward-to-risk, roughly nine winning trades at $2,880 each reach the $10,000 target - a quantity of trades that fits comfortably inside two to three weeks of disciplined execution.

the second phase usually has a smaller target and the same daily limit, which sounds easier and is not. complacency is the failure mode here: traders who sprinted phase one with loose sizing discover that a 5% target still has a 10% maximum loss attached, and one oversized attempt can erase both phases of work. the second phase is traded more conservatively than the first, with maximum risk per trade reduced and the profit taken in smaller pieces.

each session is logged with four numbers: closing equity, distance from the failure floor, percentage of target completed, and trading days used against the firm's minimum. a client reading the log can see immediately whether the evaluation is ahead or behind, and whether the risk budget was respected. there is no interpretation layer between the numbers and the client, which is deliberate - a summary can hide a week, a log cannot.

the point of the example: passing is a pacing problem with a fixed risk budget, not a forecasting contest. almost every failed evaluation breaches the daily limit or the trailing floor in a single session, and almost every one of those breaches was avoidable by sizing for the downside instead of the target.

three situations justify doing the evaluation yourself. first, your firm prohibits third-party trading and enforces the policy - in that case any passing service puts the funded account at risk, and the correct answer is to trade it yourself or choose a different firm. second, you are deliberately using the evaluation as practice to build evaluation-specific discipline, which many traders do as a form of training. third, your strategy is already producing consistent results within your firm's constraints; if the constraint set is not the bottleneck, removing it saves nothing.
for everyone else - traders who can trade but keep breaching one rule - the arithmetic usually favours paying once for execution rather than paying repeatedly for attempts.

nothing there requires a purchase. some readers use it to pass their own evaluation without us, which is a perfectly good outcome.

the typical relationship is short and transactional. a trader arranges an evaluation, it is passed in around two weeks, the funded credentials are handed over, and that is the last we hear from them unless they come back for a second account - which many do, because a firm's scaling plan makes multiple evaluations worthwhile.

a minority of clients want to talk through the funded phase: how to keep the consistency rule satisfied, when to request a payout, how to handle the first withdrawal thresholds. that advice is part of the handover and is not billed separately. it is also not trading advice - we will discuss rules and mechanics, not which way the market is going.
turning work away is the clearest signal of what a business actually believes. four categories are routinely declined.

firms that explicitly prohibit third-party trading and enforce it. if a firm's terms state that the account must be traded personally by the holder, the risk of a voided funded account falls on the client, not on us, and that is a bad trade for the client regardless of how attractive the account size is. those enquiries are redirected to firms with clearer terms, or to passing the evaluation themselves.

evaluation models where the outcome is genuinely random. some promotional evaluation structures use tight limits and no time limit, which is workable; others use short windows, tight limits and aggressive trailing floors, which compresses the pass into luck. when the rules leave no room for normal variance, the honest answer is that nobody can pass it reliably, including a service that claims to.

requests to keep trading the funded account. clients occasionally ask whether the same arrangement can continue after funding, sometimes offering a profit share that looks generous. the answer is always no. running funded accounts for a cut turns a fixed-fee execution business into a profit-sharing arrangement with payout-timing conflicts, and it takes the account out of the hands of the person whose name is on it.

impatient timelines that conflict with the rules. "can this be passed by friday?" is a fair question and sometimes the answer is yes. when the firm requires a minimum number of trading days, or when a target that large cannot be reached inside the daily loss budget without gambling, the timeline is refused rather than attempted. a rushed evaluation fails and consumes a retry that a correctly paced attempt would not have needed.
say what the fee is. one price, stated before the work starts, with the firm's own fee clearly distinguished from ours.
say what is not included. retries, kyc, the funded phase and any compliance consequences of a firm's terms are explained up front rather than discovered later.
report the boring weeks. a flat week is reported as a flat week. an operations culture that only communicates winning sessions is a culture that hides the information clients need to judge risk.
refuse the wrong jobs. if a firm prohibits third-party trading and enforces it, or if an evaluation's rules make the outcome a coin flip, the assignment is declined.
never touch the funded account. the handover is the end of our involvement in trading. no managed funded accounts, no performance fees, no exceptions.

two risks belong to the client and should be stated plainly. the first is firm policy: some prop firms prohibit third-party trading, and enforcement can happen after funding rather than during the evaluation, so an account can be voided later even if the evaluation itself was clean. terms change frequently and nobody can promise what a firm will enforce in six months. the second is the funded phase: an account that is passed and then traded without a plan will be lost, and no service can prevent that.
everything else - the rulebook reading, the sizing, the pacing, the retries - is what we are paid $220 to get right.

no. elitepropx does not hold client funds, does not run a proprietary trading desk, and does not offer accounts of its own. it trades evaluations issued by third-party prop firms and hands the funded account to the account holder.

the trader who registered for the evaluation. registration, kyc and payouts are all in their name. elitepropx has no ownership claim, no profit split and no ability to withdraw funds from the account.

retries are included when an attempt breaches a rule, which is the practical form of protection for a rules-based service. refund terms for a specific engagement are confirmed in writing before payment, and the firm's own challenge fee is always outside our control.

no, and any service that offers a guarantee is misrepresenting how evaluations work. firm rule changes, platform outages and market gaps can all end an attempt. what can be controlled is sizing, pacing and adherence to the published rules, which is where the completion rate comes from.

ask for the certificate. firms issue confirmation documents when an evaluation is passed, and they include the account size, the firm's name and often a reference number. the passed challenges page shows exactly what to look for.

most of what decides a pass happens before the first order and after the last one, so it is worth describing the process in the order it actually happens rather than presenting the outcome as though it were the method.

every firm publishes terms pages, and most of them contradict themselves somewhere between the marketing page and the schedule of charges. the first task on an assignment is to reconcile those pages into one sheet: what the daily limit is measured on, whether the maximum loss trails or stays static, whether the target is balance or equity based, what the minimum trading days are, and what happens at payout. where the published terms are genuinely ambiguous, the firm is asked directly and the answer is kept in writing.

this stage is unglamorous and it is where most of the value sits. a trader who misreads one line - for instance treating a trailing maximum loss as static - is not making an analysis error, they are solving a different puzzle than the one they bought.

the rulebook becomes an index card: daily loss budget in dollars, distance to the failure level, target expressed in r multiples of the per-trade risk, and any consistency constraint that applies at payout rather than during the evaluation. those four numbers decide position size, session length and pacing. they are recalculated every morning of the assignment, because three of the four change as equity moves.

the evaluation itself is deliberately boring. a fixed instrument set, a fixed session, constant risk per trade, and a hard stop at eighty percent of the daily budget. progress is measured in trading days completed and rule violations incurred, not in distance to target - because distance to target is the number that produces the behaviour which fails accounts.

where a firm permits leverage that would allow a target to be reached in a single session, the correct response is to ignore it. the target is not the constraint; the constraint is surviving a normal losing sequence while reaching it, and that arithmetic does not care how much margin the firm offers.

on a pass, the firm issues the funded account in the client's name. the handover includes the certificate or dashboard evidence, the rulebook as it stood on the day of the pass, and the payout schedule. what it does not include is ongoing discretionary trading on the funded account: the account is the client's, and whether it is traded by them or by another service is a separate decision with its own terms.

two numbers appear on this site: challenges passed and pass rate. both are self-reported and both should be read with that caveat. the pass count is the number of evaluations completed to target or to a funded certificate, and it excludes attempts that were abandoned by the client. the pass rate is calculated against evaluations started in the same period, not against enquiries, which is the more generous denominator and the more misleading one.

what is not claimed is equally important. there is no claim of a proprietary edge, no claim that a pass is guaranteed, and no claim that past results predict the next attempt. prop firm evaluations are a rules puzzle with a variance component; a service that has solved the rules puzzle still loses to variance sometimes, and the retry clause exists for exactly that reason.

firm rulebooks change without notice, and this site carries a lot of numbers that can go stale. where a figure is found to be wrong - a loss limit, a target, a fee, a payout term - it is corrected on the page and the review date in the header is updated. where a firm has changed its terms in a way that invalidates an article's central argument, the article is rewritten rather than patched, because a page whose conclusion no longer follows from its evidence is worse than no page at all.

complaints are handled the same way. a client who believes a fee was misquoted, a timeline misrepresented or a rule misread is asked for the correspondence and the date. where the complaint is correct, the fee is refunded and the page that caused it is fixed. where it is not, the reasoning is written out in full - a service that cannot explain its own pricing to an unhappy client has a pricing problem, not a communication problem.
why the site carries long articles rather than a sales page

a single-page service site has to compress everything into persuasion, which is why so many of them are unreadable. the articles here exist for a different reason: the questions clients ask before buying - how a trailing drawdown actually updates, why a consistency rule blocks a payout after a clean pass, what happens when a firm forbids third-party trading - have long answers, and a client who has read the long answer tends to make a better decision than one who has read a bullet list.

that also sets the editorial standard. pages are dated and reviewed, firm numbers are attributed to the rulebook rather than to memory, and where a rule varies between account types the variation is described instead of averaged away. none of that makes the content immune to being wrong; it makes being wrong visible, which is the more useful property.

a trailing drawdown is the only risk rule that can close an account which has never been in loss. the floor follows peak equity upward, so a winning position raises the level at which the account fails - and a normal retracement from a good session is enough to breach it. this guide sets out the arithmetic: how the floor moves, how to recompute position size from the remaining room, and which exit rules make a trailing structure survivable.
a trailing floor follows peak equity, so unrealised profit tightens the account before it is banked.
the same headline drawdown is a different account under intraday trailing, end-of-day trailing and static mechanisms.
position size must be recomputed from the remaining room , not from the starting balance, every week.
winners need an exit rule, because a retracement from a peak is measured against the new floor.
if the floor locks at a defined level once a threshold of profit is reached, the account stops getting tighter - check whether that clause exists.

every other risk rule in a prop firm rulebook is about losing money. a trailing drawdown is about making it. the floor rises with equity, so profit is not merely unprotected until it is withdrawn - it actively reduces the room available for the rest of the account's life.

that inverts the intuition most traders carry. in an ordinary account, being up on the day is unambiguously good: it creates a cushion. on an intraday trailing account, being up on the day moves the failure point closer to the current price, and a normal retracement from the peak can breach the account while the balance is still above where it started.

the traders this punishes most are not the reckless ones. it punishes traders who hold winners, which is the behaviour most trading education recommends. a trader who buys a position, watches it run, and holds through a pullback is doing exactly what a trend-following plan prescribes - and on an intraday trailing structure, the pullback is measured from a floor that the run has already raised behind them.

there are only two defences. one is technical: know precisely how the floor moves, and recompute size from the room that remains rather than from the account's nominal size. the other is behavioural: give winners an exit rule that banks profit or advances a protective stop, so that a retracement cannot erase more than a planned amount of the peak. this guide is mostly about the first, because the second only works once the first is understood.
one profit path, three failure points. the mechanism decides which trades are survivable.
firms describe drawdown with a single figure and implement it in one of three ways. the figure is what comparisons quote; the mechanism is what governs the account.

the fourth row is the one that causes the most confusion. a mechanism that samples once daily but samples the highest equity of the session behaves like intraday trailing for anyone who holds a winner, because the peak is recorded even if it is not banked. the distinction between "end of day" and "end of day on closing price" is the difference between a forgiving account and a punishing one.

two further clauses complete the specification. the first is the measurement basis: balance only, or balance including open positions. an equity-based floor counts unrealised losses continuously, so a position can close the account before it is closed by the trader. the second is the direction of the trailing: most structures trail upward only, but a few reset the floor when the account is funded or when a withdrawal is made, which changes the arithmetic entirely.

every one of these details is in the terms, and every one of them is more important than the headline number. a comparison of two firms on the size of the drawdown alone compares two different products and calls it a price.
the arithmetic is simple enough to do on paper and is worth writing out once so that it becomes automatic.

let the starting balance be b and the stated maximum drawdown be d . on a static account the floor is b − d and stays there forever. on a trailing account the floor is p − d , where p is the highest equity the account has reached.

two consequences follow immediately. the room available - the distance from the current equity to the floor - is e − (p − d) , which equals d − (p − e) . that is the whole rule in one expression: remaining room equals the stated drawdown minus the current drawdown from the peak .

read that expression in the two directions it applies. when the account is at a new peak, p = e and the room is the full d . when the account has given back part of a peak, the room is d minus that give-back. profit does not add room on a trailing account; it only restores room that a prior retracement consumed.

the practical version of the same equation is a table a trader can keep next to the platform: the peak the account has reached, the floor that peak implies, the current equity, and the resulting room in money. four columns, updated at the end of each session, which is enough to make every sizing decision correct.
on a trailing account the budget is measured from the peak, not from the starting balance.

one further detail matters on instruments with a daily settlement: whether the peak is taken from equity during the session or from the settlement price. a contract that settles at a different level from its intraday high produces a peak the trader can see and a floor the firm calculates from a slightly different number. where the terms are ambiguous, the conservative assumption - that the peak is the highest equity of the session - is the one to plan against.
a representative sequence makes the mechanism concrete. the figures are illustrative; the arithmetic is what transfers.

the account is breached having never closed below its starting balance minus 600. its balance on the final day is 9,400 - above the starting balance by nothing, and above the static floor that a non-trailing account would have had. the trader who believed the room was a fixed 1,000 spent the first half of the sequence with a false picture: after day two the real room was 600, and after day three it was 100.

this is why the peak column must be recorded rather than assumed. most traders track their balance, and on a trailing account the balance is the second most important number on the screen. the distance from the peak to the floor is the one that governs size.

there is a second lesson in the sequence. the loss on day two was 400, which was inside the plan's per-trade risk, and day three's 500 was also inside it. nothing in the plan was violated in dollar terms; the account was closed by the interaction of two ordinary losses with a floor that had risen in between. that interaction is invisible on a balance chart and obvious on a peak-versus-floor table.
the floor moves; the target does not. size must follow the floor.
the single habit that prevents most trailing-drawdown breaches is to size from the remaining room rather than from the account's stated drawdown.

the two numbers diverge as soon as the account has given back any part of a peak, and they diverge most dangerously after a strong session followed by a weak one - which is exactly the sequence a trader is least likely to analyse, because the account is "still up".

the recomputation is a morning task, and it takes under a minute. find the peak equity the account has reached, subtract the drawdown to get the floor, find the current equity, and the difference is the room. write it down. then derive the per-trade risk from that number: room divided by the streak the plan must survive, with a quarter held in reserve.

a concrete illustration of why this matters. an account with a 10,000 drawdown that has reached a peak 3,000 above its start and given back 1,500 has 8,500 of room, not 10,000 - a 15% reduction in the size the plan can carry. trade the original size and every subsequent loss is 15% larger than the budget allowed, which shortens the survivable streak by the same proportion.

two refinements. first, apply the recomputation to the session budget as well: the daily limit multiplies out against a smaller room, so the number of losses a session can absorb also falls. second, treat the reserve as a fraction of the room rather than of the original drawdown, because on a trailing account the reserve is what carries the plan through a streak that the floor has already tightened around.
position size is a function of three numbers on a trailing account, and only one of them is stable.

the first is the room, which changes daily. the second is the tick or pip value of the instrument, which does not. the third is the stop distance, which is a property of the strategy and the timeframe rather than of the account.

the calculation therefore repeats every week, and sometimes more often after a strong session: room divided by streak tolerance gives the maximum loss per trade; that figure divided by the tick value of the stop gives the contract count, rounded down. on a forex account the same calculation uses the pip value and the lot size.

three practical consequences for trailing accounts. first, the derived size shrinks after a strong run that retraces, which is counter-intuitive but correct - the account has less room than it had before the run, because the floor has moved and the profit has not been banked. second, the derived size grows only when the account reaches a new peak, which means the correct time to increase is boring and infrequent. third, a size computed once and carried for the life of the account will be too large in the final third, which is where most trailing breaches occur.

rounding always goes down. on a contract-based account the difference of one contract can be a large fraction of the budget, and on a leveraged forex account the difference between rounding to 0.4 and 0.5 lots is 25% of the risk the account can carry.
a trailing floor changes the optimal management of a winning position, and the change is not the one most traders expect.

on a static-drawdown account, holding a winner is cheap: the floor is fixed, so a retracement costs profit but not room. on a trailing account, the same retracement costs both, because the floor has already followed the peak. the correct behaviour is therefore to convert unrealised profit into either banked profit or a raised stop, and to do it at defined points rather than by feel.

three rules cover most situations. move the protective stop to breakeven once the position has travelled a stated distance - not before, because a stop too close converts winners into scratches. bank a defined portion of the position when it reaches a second stated distance, which locks in some of the peak and therefore leaves the floor a little further behind. and close the remainder by a fixed time or at a fixed level rather than holding indefinitely, because the longer a winning position stays open on an intraday trailing account, the more of the account's room it has already consumed.

there is a specific case worth naming: the position that is up strongly and then reverses into a loss. on a static account this is merely the trade not working. on a trailing account it is worse, because the floor has risen and the reversal is measured from a peak that no longer exists. the trader experiences it as a losing trade; the account experiences it as a loss plus a raised failure point. this is the single most common description of a trailing-drawdown breach, and the exit rules above are the only reliable defence.
the session budget shrinks as the floor rises, even when the daily limit itself has not changed.
the daily limit and the trailing floor interact, and the interaction is what makes the final days of an evaluation fragile.

the daily limit is usually a fixed percentage of the balance or of the starting balance, while the floor is not fixed. so the daily limit is a constant and the room is a variable, and the ratio between them changes as the floor moves. a session budget that was a fifth of the room in week one can be a third of the room in week four, which means the same session carries a much higher breach probability than it did earlier.

the correct response is to recompute the session budget as a proportion of the room each morning and to reduce the number of trades the session may take when the proportion is high. a simple rule works: if the daily limit is more than a quarter of the remaining room, cut the session cap to a third of its normal value. on a trailing account, the last stretch of an evaluation is not the time for the normal session.

the second interaction is with the day boundary. the daily limit resets on the firm's server day, but the trailing floor does not reset at all. so a trader who has a bad day and then trades the overnight session is starting from a floor that includes the previous day's losses, against a daily budget that has just been replenished. the two clocks are different, and the correct planning assumption is that the room is what it is regardless of which day it is.

where the terms permit holding overnight, the gap risk has to be priced as a multiple of the normal stop - the weekend holding guide covers that arithmetic. on a trailing account the cost of a gap is higher than on a static one, because the gap consumes room that cannot be replaced by subsequent profit.

many trailing structures include a clause that stops the floor moving once a defined level of profit has been reached. whether that clause exists changes the account's entire risk profile, and it is frequently buried in a footnote.

the typical form is a threshold expressed as an amount of profit or a percentage of the target: once the account has gained that much, the floor locks at a defined level - often the starting balance, sometimes the starting balance plus a fixed amount. above that point the account behaves like a static one, and holding winners becomes cheap again.

the practical consequence is a change in strategy at a specific point in the evaluation. below the lock threshold, the plan should be defensive: small size, tight exit rules, and profit banked promptly, because every new peak raises the floor. above the threshold, the same plan can hold winners with the ordinary tolerance, because the floor no longer follows.

establishing whether the clause exists, and where the threshold sits, is therefore one of the first things to read in the terms. it also changes the answer to a common question: whether to push for a large day or a steady sequence. below the lock threshold, the steady sequence is strictly better, because a large day raises the floor and a steady sequence does not.

where the clause does not exist, the account stays trailing for its entire life on the evaluation and, usually, for the first part of the funded stage. that is not a reason to avoid the firm; it is a reason to build a plan whose profit-taking is faster than it would otherwise be.
the funded stage frequently inherits a trailing mechanism, and the conditions around it change in three ways.

the first is that withdrawals interact with the floor. if a withdrawal reduces the balance but the peak is not adjusted, the room shrinks by the amount of the withdrawal until the account reaches a new peak - which means withdrawing can make an account more fragile than the profit did. some firms reset the peak on withdrawal and some do not; the difference is material, and it belongs in the first reading of the funded terms.

the second is that the funded drawdown is often tighter as a percentage while the trailing mechanism remains. a tighter trailing floor is the harshest combination available, because the floor moves quickly and the room is small. the correct first fortnight on such an account is at half the evaluation's risk or less.

the third is that unwithdrawn profit is genuinely dangerous rather than merely suboptimal. on a static account, leaving profit in the account is a choice about cash flow. on a trailing account, leaving profit in raises the floor behind the trader, so a large unwithdrawn balance is a larger target with less room underneath it.
on a funded trailing account, a large day raises the floor and constrains the payout at the same time.

the plan that follows is unglamorous: halve the risk, cap daily profit so the consistency condition is satisfied at the threshold, recompute the room every morning, and withdraw on the earliest permitted schedule at a size that leaves the floor comfortably behind. the payout process guide covers the withdrawal sequence, and the profit target guide covers the daily cap arithmetic.
seven items, checked once at the start and then daily. together they cover every trailing-drawdown failure mode.

one: identify the mechanism precisely. intraday trailing, end-of-day trailing on closing balance, or end-of-day on peak equity of the session. write the answer down, and where the terms are ambiguous, assume the harshest reading.

two: find the measurement basis. balance or balance including open positions. on an equity basis, an open position consumes room continuously, so the plan's protective orders become part of the drawdown budget rather than a separate safety net.

three: locate the lock-in clause, if any. threshold level and locked floor. note the point in the evaluation at which losses stop following the peak, because the plan's aggressiveness should change there.
four: record peak equity daily. four columns - peak, floor, current equity, room in money. this table is the only reliable input to position sizing on a trailing account.
five: recompute size weekly and after any strong session. room divided by the streak tolerance, divided by the tick or pip value of the stop, rounded down.
six: write the exit rules for winners. a stop to breakeven at a stated distance, a partial bank at a second distance, and a time or level limit on the remainder.
seven: cut the session cap when the room is small. if the daily limit exceeds a quarter of the remaining room, reduce the session's trade count rather than trying to trade the normal plan carefully.

the list is short because the mechanism is simple. what makes trailing drawdown hard is not complexity but direction: every instinct a trader has about a profitable position tells them it is safe, and on a trailing structure that instinct is precisely wrong. the topstep guide works through a rulebook with two simultaneous loss rules, and the rulebook comparison covers how trailing and static mechanisms differ in practice.
three results of the room equation contradict the intuition of traders arriving from static-drawdown accounts, and each is worth stating plainly.

profit does not create room; it only restores room a retracement consumed. a trader who is up 2,000 from the start has the same room as on day one if the account is at a new peak, and less than on day one if it is not. there is no point at which a trailing account becomes safer because of profit - only points at which it becomes less fragile than it was an hour earlier.

the best session of the evaluation can be the most dangerous. a large winning day sets a new peak and raises the floor immediately, so the following session starts with less room than the one before it. consistency rules at the payout stage point the same way, which is why a daily profit cap belongs in every trailing-account plan.

a loss is larger than it looks after a good week. a 500 loss that was a fifth of the room in week one can be a third of the room in week three, because the floor followed the profit. the dollar amount is identical and the consequence is not, which is exactly why the room has to be recorded rather than remembered.

none of these is a hidden trap - the mechanism is published. they are traps in the sense that every instinct about what makes an account safe is inverted, and instincts govern behaviour while a position is open.

a maximum loss limit whose floor rises as the account reaches new peaks. the failure point is not fixed at the starting balance; it follows the highest equity reached, so profit reduces the room available to the account rather than adding to it.
how can i breach an account that is in profit?

because the floor moved up behind the peak. if the account reached a peak of 10,500 with a 1,000 drawdown limit, the floor is 9,500 - so a normal retracement from a winning position can breach it while the balance is still above where it started.

remaining room equals the stated drawdown minus the give-back from the peak. if the floor trails peak equity, find the highest equity reached, subtract the drawdown to get the floor, and take the difference between that and the current equity.
should i size from the drawdown or from the remaining room?

from the remaining room, always. the two are equal only at a new peak. after any retracement the room is smaller than the headline drawdown, and trading the original size means every subsequent loss is a larger fraction of the budget than the plan assumed.

intraday trailing follows peak unrealised equity continuously, so open profit raises the floor immediately. end-of-day trailing resets to the closing balance, so intraday spikes are forgiven but completed gains still raise the floor. a mechanism that samples peak equity once a day behaves like intraday trailing in practice.
do i need different exit rules on a trailing account?

yes. holding winners is expensive because the floor has already followed them. move the stop to breakeven at a stated distance, bank a portion at a second distance, and close the remainder by a fixed time or level rather than holding indefinitely.

a clause that stops the floor moving once a defined profit threshold is reached, after which the account behaves like a static-drawdown account. find the threshold in the terms, because it changes whether pushing for a large day is a good idea - below the threshold, a steady sequence is strictly better.

check the funded terms, because it varies. if a withdrawal reduces the balance without adjusting the peak, the room shrinks by the withdrawal amount until a new peak is set - which means withdrawing can temporarily make the account more fragile, not less.
how does the daily limit interact with a trailing floor?

the daily limit is fixed while the room is variable, so the session budget becomes a larger share of the room as the floor rises. when the daily limit exceeds a quarter of the remaining room, cut the session's trade count - the last stretch of an evaluation is not the time for the normal session.
should i trade a trailing account differently from a static one?

yes, in three ways: bank profit sooner, size from the remaining room rather than the headline drawdown, and avoid holding winners through retracements. the strategy can be identical; the profit-management rules cannot be.
why do most trailing-drawdown breaches happen in the final third?

because the floor has risen behind accumulated profit, so the room is much smaller than it was at the start, while the position size is often still the one derived in week one. recomputing the size from the current room every week removes most of that risk.

more forgiving in the sense that profit cannot reduce room, but it usually comes with a smaller starting buffer as a percentage, and the account cannot grow its room at all. for a plan that holds winners, static is easier; for a plan that banks profit quickly, the difference is smaller than the headline suggests.

"easier" is a question with an arithmetic answer, and the answer changes with the trader. two evaluations with the same headline target can be 40% different in difficulty depending on how the failure floor behaves, how the daily limit is measured, and what a funded payout requires. this comparison sets out the dimensions that decide difficulty, the sizing method that compares two rulebooks against one strategy, and the profiles each structure suits.
difficulty is a function of effective room and the number of simultaneous limits, not of the headline target.
a smaller target on a tighter drawdown is often harder than a larger target on a static floor.
daily limits and consistency rules shorten the survivable streak even when the maximum loss looks generous.
the right comparison sizes one strategy against both rulebooks and compares the resulting streaks and calendars.
both firms revise terms; read the current evaluation and funded documents before paying either.

two traders ask the same question for opposite reasons. one wants the account that is hardest to fail on the way to the target. the other wants the account that produces a payout soonest once the target is met. those are different accounts, and a comparison that does not separate them produces an answer that is right for nobody.

for the first trader, difficulty is a function of effective room - the amount the account can lose before it closes, once the floor mechanism has been accounted for - and of how many limits apply at once. a 10% maximum loss on a static floor and a 10% maximum loss on an intraday trailing floor give the same headline number and materially different room.

for the second trader, difficulty is a function of the payout conditions: the minimum profitable days, the profit threshold, the consistency ratio and the payment interval. a pass that cannot be withdrawn is not a pass. those conditions are set independently of the evaluation rules and are usually published in a separate document.

there is a third dimension that both traders need and neither usually computes: the calendar. two rulebooks with identical limits can imply very different completion times, because a daily limit caps the trade count and a time limit caps the calendar from the other direction. the calculator page sets out the formulas for converting a target into a calendar.
difficulty is only comparable once both rulebooks are matched against one strategy.

both firms sit in the percentage-based forex and cfd category: targets and losses expressed as percentages of the balance, position sizes in fractional lots, and a rulebook built around a maximum loss, a daily loss limit and, often, a consistency condition.
that shared architecture reduces the comparison to a set of specific clauses. where the two firms differ is in how those clauses are configured rather than in which clauses exist.

two generalisations hold in this category and matter more than any firm-specific detail. first, percentage targets are scale-free, so the same plan transfers across account sizes - which means the smallest account whose rules can be satisfied is usually the correct purchase, and a larger account is a bigger fee for the same arithmetic. second, a time limit converts the target into a required pace, and the required pace has to be checked against the daily limit before the fee is paid; if the required weekly return does not fit inside the rules at a survivable size, the evaluation is not passable as configured.
