the ftmo playbook covers the same percentage-rulebook mechanics in procedural form, and the rules matrix places the structures side by side across firms.
the single most consequential clause in either rulebook is what happens to the failure floor as the account makes money.

a static floor is fixed at the starting balance and never moves, so profit cannot reduce the room available. an end-of-day trailing floor resets at the daily close, so completed gains raise the floor while intraday spikes are forgiven. an intraday trailing floor follows peak equity continuously, so a winning position raises the failure point immediately and a retracement can breach an account that has never been below its starting balance.

percentage rulebooks in the forex category predominantly use static or end-of-day structures rather than intraday trailing ones - the trailing mechanism is more common on the futures side. that is a genuine advantage for a plan that holds winners, and it means the floor clause is often a smaller differentiator between two forex firms than between two futures firms. where one of the two does use a trailing mechanism, however, the difference swamps everything else in the comparison.
static, end-of-day trailing and intraday trailing: three different accounts behind one headline percentage.

two secondary clauses complete the picture. the first is the measurement basis: balance only, or balance including open positions. an equity-based limit counts unrealised losses continuously, so a position can breach the account before it is closed. the second is whether the floor is affected by withdrawals on the funded account - a withdrawal that reduces the balance without adjusting the peak temporarily shrinks the room, which matters for a trader planning a first payout.
the daily drawdown guide covers the reference-point arithmetic in detail, and the trailing drawdown guide covers the room formula if either firm uses a trailing structure.
the daily limit is the constraint that ends the most attempts in this category, because it fires on ordinary variance rather than on a catastrophic error.

the arithmetic is a single division: the daily limit in money divided by the risk per trade in money gives the number of losing trades a session can absorb. a limit that absorbs two is a session decided by the first two trades of the day. a limit that absorbs six allows a bad start and still leaves the session functional. the design target is four to six.

what matters beyond the percentage is the reference point. a limit measured on equity includes open positions, so an intraday drawdown consumes budget that a balance-based limit would ignore. a limit measured from the day's opening balance behaves differently from one measured from the previous close, particularly for a trader who holds positions overnight. and a limit expressed as a percentage of the starting balance behaves differently again once the account is up or down.

the second measurement that matters is the day boundary. forex sessions span the firm's server day rather than the trader's local day, and the boundary often falls in the middle of a trading session for traders in some time zones. a position opened late in the trader's evening can belong to the next server day, which means the loss lands against a budget that had not started when the trade was planned. two evening positions that feel like one day's risk can be counted against two days' limits.
the daily limit is a session budget, and its reference point decides what counts against it.

the practical implication for the comparison is that two firms with the same daily percentage can present materially different constraints. where one measures on equity and the other on balance, the equity-based limit is the tighter rule for any trader who holds positions through drawdowns. where the two firms' day boundaries fall at different hours, one may align with the trader's session and the other may not - and a misaligned boundary can cost a session's worth of capacity every day.
the leverage guide covers why a leverage cap is usually not the binding constraint on an account like this, and the weekend holding guide covers the gap arithmetic for positions held across a close.
targets decide the calendar, and the calendar decides how much variance the plan must survive. that makes the target a difficulty factor even though it is not a risk factor.

the useful ratio is the target divided by the maximum loss. a target that is a small fraction of the loss limit is reachable at a survivable size with a short calendar; a target that approaches the loss limit requires either a higher trade count or a lower risk per trade, and either of those lengthens the attempt and increases the number of sessions exposed to a losing streak.

staging changes the arithmetic in two directions. a staged evaluation splits one large target into smaller ones, which lowers the size needed per stage and reduces the cost of an early failure relative to a single-phase account. against that, the total sequence is longer, and a breach in the final stage wastes the earlier stages as well as the fee. the staged evaluation guide covers that trade-off and the pacing problem it creates.

time limits are the part of the target specification that traders most often ignore and most often fail against. a stated limit converts the target into a required weekly return, and that number has to be checked against the daily limit: if the required pace implies a risk per trade larger than the daily limit can absorb across a normal losing sequence, the evaluation is not passable at a survivable size. doing that check before the fee takes five minutes and occasionally saves a purchase.

minimum trading days run the other way - they are satisfied by activity, not profit, and are rarely the binding constraint on a conservative plan. the trap is a trader who reaches the target early and then trades to fill a count, giving back part of the profit in sessions that had nothing to gain. if the count is longer than the plan, slow the plan so that both finish together.
a consistency rule is where a percentage rulebook gets harder than it looks, and the two firms may apply it at different stages of the account's life.

three variants exist. applied during the evaluation, a consistency condition caps the share of the target that may come from one day, so a trader who reaches the target in a single strong session has not passed. applied at the payout stage, it caps the share of withdrawn profit attributable to one day, which constrains the first withdrawal rather than the pass. applied at every withdrawal, it becomes a permanent constraint on daily profit and therefore on position size.

the arithmetic is the same in every variant: if the best day may be no more than a stated share of the total, total profit must reach the largest day divided by that share. under a one-third rule, $3,000 requires $9,000 of total profit; under a one-fifth rule, the same day requires $15,000. the difference between the variants is where the constraint lands, and a rule applied during the evaluation is materially harder than one applied only at payout.
the same ratio is a mild condition at payout and a hard constraint during the evaluation.

the mitigation is structural rather than psychological: set a daily profit cap below the permitted share from the first session, and the ratio is satisfied automatically by the time the target or threshold is reached. on a plan with a daily average well below the cap, the cost of the cap is negligible; the alternative - discovering the ratio at the payout request - costs a month.

where one firm applies the rule during the evaluation and the other does not, that is a genuine difficulty difference and should be weighted accordingly. the consistency guide covers each variant and the arithmetic for the common ratios, including how to fix a check that has already failed.
the funded stage is a different product with the same brand on it, and the differences decide whether a pass becomes income.

three things change. the funded drawdown is usually tighter as a percentage, because the firm is now exposed to real payouts rather than to a fee. profit becomes income only when it is withdrawn, which means an unwithdrawn balance is a larger target under the same rules. and the payout sequence adds conditions that run on their own clock.

the common structure has four gates: a minimum number of profitable days, a profit threshold, a consistency check on the profit being withdrawn, and identity verification - followed by a payment interval. each can fail independently of the trading record, and three of the four are administrative.

comparing the two firms on this dimension means asking four questions of each. what is the funded drawdown as a percentage of balance, and is it measured on balance or equity? what is the profit threshold before a first withdrawal, and is the whole balance above it withdrawable? is the consistency rule applied at the first payout only or at every payout? and what is the interval between a successful request and the funds arriving?

the interval is the most under-weighted of the four. a firm with a generous split and a ninety-day payment cycle pays a trader less in the first year than a firm with a smaller split paying within a week, and the difference is a cash-flow fact rather than a marketing claim. the payout process guide covers the sequence and the common delays, and the post-pass guide covers what to do in the first funded month.
a comparison of two rulebooks is only meaningful when both are sized against the same strategy. the method takes about twenty minutes and replaces every ranking table.
step one: write down the strategy's fixed parameters - stop distance in pips, trades per session, sessions per week, measured win rate and reward-to-risk ratio. these do not change between firms.

step two: for each firm, derive risk per trade twice. from the maximum loss: loss percentage divided by the number of consecutive losses the plan should survive. from the daily limit: daily percentage divided by the losses a session should absorb. take the smaller.

step three: convert each to a calendar. expectation per trade equals win rate times average win minus loss rate times average loss. divide the target by that figure for the trade count, then by trades per week.
step four: record three numbers for each firm - risk per trade as a percentage, survivable streak, and calendar in weeks. those three are the comparison.

the method also exposes the case where neither fits. if both rulebooks produce a survivable streak below eight at the account size in question, the plan is too aggressive for that size, and the correct change is a smaller account or a smaller position - not a different firm. if one firm's calendar exceeds its own time limit at a survivable size, that evaluation is not passable as configured and should not be bought.
the comparison resolves differently by profile, and the profiles are more useful than a ranking.

a trader with a high win rate and small targets. a consistency rule applied during the evaluation is the main obstacle, because tight profit-taking rarely produces a dominant day - but the rule can still bite if the target is reached in one session. whichever firm applies the rule only at payout is the easier account for this profile.

a trader with a low win rate and a wide stop. the daily limit is the binding constraint, because each trade consumes a larger share of the session budget. whichever firm measures the daily limit on balance rather than equity, and whichever has the later day boundary relative to the trader's session, is easier for this profile.

a trader with a slow, low-frequency plan. the calendar and any time limit dominate. whichever firm allows the longer calendar at a survivable size is easier, and recurring platform and data costs matter more than the fee.
a trader who holds winners for days. the floor mechanism dominates. a static structure suits this profile; a trailing one does not, and no other clause compensates for it.

a trader who expects to fail the first attempt. the reset structure and the total cost to funding dominate. a firm with a cheap reset and a monthly fee structure is easier for this profile in the only sense that matters: it leaves capital for the second attempt. running the same strategy on a smaller account is often the better version of that decision, since percentage rules are scale-free.

a trader using a passing service. the decisive clause is whether third-party trading is permitted, separately for the evaluation and the funded account. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid the arrangement. the passing services guide covers what to require from any provider, and the scam guide covers the failure modes on both sides of that market.
cost is a difficulty factor in the practical sense: a cheaper route to a funded account leaves more capital for a second attempt if the first fails.

the total is the evaluation fee, plus platform and data subscriptions for the duration of the calendar derived above, plus reset charges for any failed attempt, plus any activation fee on funding. because subscriptions accrue monthly, a plan with a long calendar pays more for the same fee - which means the firm with the longer calendar needs a real price advantage to be the cheaper option overall.

running that number is straightforward once the calendar is known. twelve weeks at a monthly data and platform cost is three times the same subscriptions over four weeks, and on many accounts that difference is larger than the fee itself. the beginners guide covers the selection criteria that matter when there is no track record to compare against, including the recurring-cost trap.

reset structure belongs in the same calculation. a one-off fee with a paid reset makes each attempt a deliberate purchase; a subscription with unlimited retries lowers the marginal cost of failure and, in doing so, the cost of not fixing the plan first. for a trader whose breach rate is high the subscription is cheaper; for a trader whose plan is sound, the one-off is.
ten checks, run against each firm's current documentation. together they replace every comparison, including this one.
one: the maximum loss percentage, and whether the floor is static or trailing, measured on balance or equity.
two: the daily limit percentage, its reference point, and the exact server hours of the trading day.
three: the target per stage, and whether a time limit applies.
five: the consistency rule - ratio, and whether it applies during the evaluation, at the first payout, or at every withdrawal.
eight: the payout threshold, the profit split, the payment interval and the verification requirements.

nine: the conduct clauses - news windows, overnight and weekend holding, permitted instruments, and any prohibition on automated or third-party trading, stated separately for the evaluation and the funded stage.
ten: total cost to funding, including data and platform over the calendar the plan actually needs.

keep both sets of answers side by side and check them against the sizing method above. where a clause cannot be resolved from the published terms, ask support one specific question in writing and keep the reply - a clause that cannot be checked before purchase is a clause that cannot be relied on afterwards. the 2026 comparison covers the wider market including futures-side structures, and the ftmo playbook walks the same percentage mechanics in procedural order.
most of the analysis above collapses into three questions that can be answered from the two sets of terms in under half an hour. where the answers disagree, the sizing method breaks the tie.

one: is the floor static or trailing, and on what basis is it measured? this is the first question because it changes the room available for the rest of the account's life. a static floor means the sizing calculation performed on day one remains valid; a trailing floor means it must be rerun weekly, and a plan that holds winners is more fragile than the same plan on a static structure.

two: which limit binds first, the maximum loss or the daily limit? divide each by its own tolerance - the streak the plan must survive, and the losses a session should absorb - and see which produces the smaller risk per trade. that figure is the plan's size, and the limit that produced it is the constraint the plan will live with. a daily limit that binds is easier to trade around than a maximum loss that binds, because it resets.

three: what must be true before a payout is made? minimum profitable days, profit threshold, consistency condition, verification and payment interval. a pass that cannot be withdrawn is not a pass, and this is the question most often deferred until after the funded login arrives.

where the three answers point to different firms, the tie-break is the survivable streak from the sizing calculation - the higher number is the safer account for the strategy in hand. where they point to the same firm twice, the remaining question is cost, and the calendar from the same calculation converts a monthly subscription into a total figure.

one caveat that applies to every answer here: these terms change. a comparison can only teach the method, which is why this page contains the arithmetic rather than a table of current percentages. ten minutes with the two firms' current documents and the four formulas above produces a better answer than any published comparison, including this one.

there is no general answer. size the same strategy against both rulebooks - risk per trade from the maximum loss, then from the daily limit - and compare the survivable streak and the calendar. the firm that produces the higher streak for that plan is the easier account for that trader.

only within the same rulebook. a small target on a tight trailing drawdown with an equity-based daily limit can be harder than a larger target on a static floor. the ratio of target to maximum loss matters more than the target alone.

if it applies during the evaluation, reaching the target in one strong day does not count. expressed as a best-day share, a one-third rule means total profit must reach three times the largest day. applied only at payout, the same ratio is a milder constraint on the first withdrawal.
what risk per trade should i use on a percentage account?

divide the maximum loss percentage by the streak tolerance - eight to ten for a plan with a win rate in the forties - and the daily limit by the losses a session should absorb. take the smaller, keep a quarter of the drawdown in reserve, and round position size down.
how do i compare the two firms in twenty minutes?

six inputs from each set of terms: maximum loss and mechanism, daily limit and reference point, target and time limit, minimum days, consistency rule, and funded payout conditions. then run the sizing method and compare survivable streak and calendar.
does the evaluation's drawdown carry over to the funded account?

no - the funded account has its own, usually tighter, drawdown and its own payout conditions. read the funded document before paying the evaluation fee, because it determines whether the plan that passed can be traded afterwards.

more often than most traders expect, which is why any comparison quoting specific percentages is accurate only until the next revision. read the current evaluation and funded documents on the day you pay, and save the version you agreed to.

only after comparing total cost to funding. the fee plus platform and data subscriptions over the calendar the plan needs, plus reset charges, is the number that matters. a long calendar can make a cheap fee expensive.

that is a valid result. options are a smaller account with the same percentage rules, a different rulebook model, or a revised plan. changing firms does not fix a plan whose stop distance and trade frequency do not fit the rules.

only where the terms permit third-party trading, which must be confirmed separately for the evaluation and the funded account. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid it.

read the funded terms for the profit threshold, the consistency condition, the payment interval and any first-payout restriction. the interval matters more than the split: a larger percentage paid in ninety days is worth less in the first year than a smaller one paid within a week.

five calculations decide whether a prop firm evaluation is passable and how long it will take: position size from the drawdown, position size from the daily limit, required trade count from the target, remaining room on a trailing account, and the payout ratio from a consistency rule. this page sets out each formula, the inputs it needs, worked examples, and the order in which to apply them.
position size is the smaller of two derivations: one from the maximum loss, one from the daily limit.
the target never sets the size; it sets the calendar, through expected value per trade.
on a trailing account, remaining room equals the drawdown minus the give-back from the peak - not the headline number.
a consistency rule converts into a daily profit cap, which is the only way to satisfy it automatically.
every formula here is arithmetic on numbers your firm publishes; none of it requires a spreadsheet.

most evaluation failures are not caused by bad arithmetic. they are caused by doing the arithmetic in the wrong order - sizing from the target, then discovering the daily limit was the real constraint, then adjusting in the middle of an attempt.

the correct order runs from the constraint inward. the maximum loss fixes the size. the daily limit may reduce it further. the target plays no part in the size at all; it determines how many trades the plan needs, and therefore how long the attempt takes. the trailing mechanism determines whether the size is still valid next week. the consistency rule determines how much profit can be taken in a single day once the target is met.

applied in that order, the numbers are consistent by construction: the size fits the room, the session budget fits the day, and the calendar is a consequence rather than a hope. applied in any other order, the plan contains a contradiction that shows up under pressure, usually in the final third of an attempt when the contradiction is most expensive.

five calculations follow, each with one input list and one output. they can be done on paper in about ten minutes and should be redone weekly, because two of the inputs - the remaining room and, on a trailing account, the size itself - change as the account progresses.
one drawdown, three lines: per trade, per session, and a reserve that is never spent.
six numbers, all of them published by the firm or measurable on the platform. collect them before calculating anything; a plan built on estimated inputs is a plan with an unknown error term.

two of those inputs are frequently guessed and should not be. the stop distance is a property of the strategy and the timeframe; if it changes with the account size, the strategy is not being traded as designed. the expectation per trade is the output of a sample of the trader's own trades, including costs - and it is the single input most often replaced by optimism.

where an input is unknown - for example, the exact reference point of a daily limit, or whether a floor samples equity or balance - use the harsher reading. the only cost of an over-conservative assumption is a slower calendar; the cost of an over-optimistic one is a breached account.
inputs: maximum loss, streak tolerance, instrument value, stop distance. output: the maximum position size in lots or contracts.

the formula has two steps. first, the money risked per trade: maximum loss divided by the number of consecutive losses the plan should survive. eight to ten is a reasonable design case for a discretionary plan with a win rate in the forties, because runs of that length recur within a few hundred trades. second, the size: money per trade divided by the stop distance multiplied by the value per unit of distance.

worked example. a 10% maximum loss on a $100,000 account is $10,000. at a streak tolerance of ten, risk per trade is $1,000. if the instrument is worth $10 per tick and the strategy's stop is 40 ticks, the cost of the stop at one contract is $400, so the maximum size is $1,000 ÷ $400 = 2.5 contracts, rounded down to two. rounding up to three would put risk per trade at $1,200 - 20% above the plan.

for a forex account the same formula uses pip value and lot size: money per trade divided by the stop in pips, divided by the value of one pip per lot. the result is lots, rounded down to the platform's minimum increment.

three refinements worth building into the calculation. deduct the expected cost per round turn - spread plus commission - from the money per trade before dividing, because on a small account the cost can be a fifth of the risk. keep a quarter of the maximum loss in reserve, which means using 75% of the derived size rather than 100%. and cap the result at the firm's lot or contract limit, which is a ceiling the formula can exceed on a large account or a tight stop.
size comes from the loss limit. the target only decides how long the account has to survive.
inputs: daily limit, the money risk per trade from calculation one. output: the maximum number of losing trades a session can absorb.
the formula is the daily limit divided by the money risk per trade. the result is the session's capacity for losses, and it is the number that decides whether the plan is executable as designed.

worked example. a 5% daily limit on a $100,000 account is $5,000. at $1,000 risked per trade, a session absorbs five consecutive losses. that is workable: the plan can take a bad start and keep trading. at $2,500 per trade it absorbs two, which means the third loss closes the platform and the session was decided by the first two trades of the day.

the useful rule of thumb is a design target of four to six losses of capacity. below four, the daily limit is doing the job the maximum loss should be doing, and the plan will spend a significant number of sessions on the sideline. above six, risk per trade is so small relative to the day that the calendar stretches and recurring platform and data costs start to dominate the economics.

the second half of the calculation is the trade cap. it should be set below the capacity for losses, because not every bad session is composed of clean stop-outs: a trade can lose more than planned through slippage, and an early stop-out followed by re-entry is still two positions. a cap of roughly two-thirds of the calculated capacity is a reasonable convention.

two inputs change the answer and are easy to miss. if the daily limit is measured on equity rather than balance, open positions consume the budget continuously, so the effective capacity is lower than the division suggests. and if the firm's day boundary falls in the middle of the trading session, the capacity has to be divided across two server days rather than treated as one budget.
inputs: target, money risk per trade, reward-to-risk ratio, win rate, trades per week. output: the number of trades and the calendar.

expected value per trade is the win rate multiplied by the average win, minus the loss rate multiplied by the average loss. with risk per trade fixed, the average loss is known and the average win follows from the ratio. divide the target by the expectation per trade to get the trade count; divide by trades per week to get the calendar in weeks.

worked example. risk per trade $1,000, ratio 1:2, so average win $2,000 and average loss $1,000. at a 45% win rate, expectation is 0.45 × 2,000 − 0.55 × 1,000 = $350 per trade. on a $100,000 account with an 8% target, that is $8,000 ÷ $350 = 23 trades at expectation. at two trades per session and five sessions a week, the calendar is about two and a half weeks.

the same calculation run at a different size illustrates the point of the whole page. doubling the risk per trade doubles the expectation in dollars but also halves the streak tolerance, so the trade count falls to twelve and the breach probability rises by more than the calendar improves. the faster plan is not merely riskier; it is riskier in exchange for a smaller benefit than it appears.

three legitimate ways to shorten the calendar, in order of preference: raise the reward-to-risk ratio by improving exits, raise the win rate by becoming more selective, or add sessions within the daily limit. each changes the plan's quality. increasing size changes only the distribution around it.

where the calendar produced by this calculation exceeds the firm's deadline, the conclusion is arithmetic rather than motivational: the plan cannot pass that evaluation at a survivable size. the correct responses are a smaller account with the same percentages, a different rulebook, or a slower target - not more risk.
inputs: peak equity reached, current equity, maximum loss. output: the room available now, in money.
remaining room equals the maximum loss minus the amount the account has given back from its peak. expressed in levels: floor equals peak minus maximum loss; room equals current equity minus floor.

worked example. start $100,000, maximum loss $10,000, so the floor starts at $90,000 and the room is $10,000. the account reaches a peak of $104,000, which lifts the floor to $94,000. equity then falls to $101,000. the room is $101,000 − $94,000 = $7,000, not the $10,000 the terms advertise and not the $11,000 of profit above the starting balance. the account is up $1,000 and its room has fallen by 30%.

the same calculation feeds the size derivation. with $7,000 of room and a streak tolerance of ten, risk per trade is $700, not $1,000 - a 30% reduction in size, which is exactly the adjustment most traders skip. that omission is the single most common cause of a breach in the final third of a trailing-drawdown evaluation.

two variants change the formula. on a static account the peak is irrelevant and the room is always the maximum loss. on an end-of-day trailing account the peak is the highest closing balance rather than the highest intraday equity, which is a meaningfully more forgiving number. establish which applies before relying on the result - the trailing drawdown guide covers the variants and the lock-in clauses that stop the floor moving.
three mechanisms, one headline number. only the room figure governs size.
inputs: the consistency ratio, the payout threshold. output: the maximum profit to take in one day.

if the best day may be no more than a stated share of total profit, then the cap on a single day is that share multiplied by the profit at the point of withdrawal. a ratio of one-third with a $6,000 threshold allows a best day of $2,000; a ratio of one-fifth allows $1,200.

the reverse calculation is the one that matters mid-attempt: given the largest day already recorded, what total profit is required before a full withdrawal is permitted? the answer is the largest day divided by the ratio. a $1,500 best day under a one-third rule requires $4,500 of total profit. under a one-fifth rule it requires $7,500 - the same trading record, a materially longer road to a payout.

worked example. a plan with an 8% target on $100,000 produces $8,000 of profit. under a one-third rule, a single day of up to $2,666 is permitted inside that record; under a one-fifth rule, $1,600. a trader whose average winning day is $400 is comfortably inside both. a trader whose best day is $3,000 has already broken the one-third rule inside an otherwise successful evaluation, and the consequence lands at the payout request rather than at the pass.

the practical output of this calculation is a daily profit cap: set it below the permitted share, and the ratio is satisfied automatically by the time the threshold is reached. the consistency guide covers the common ratio variants and how each is applied at payout.
all five calculations applied to one account, in order. the figures are illustrative; the sequence is the part to copy.
the account. $100,000, two-phase evaluation, 8% target per phase, 10% maximum loss measured from the starting balance, 5% daily limit, consistency rule of one-third applied at payout.

step one, size. $10,000 maximum loss ÷ 10 = $1,000 per trade. reserve-adjusted to 75%, $750. on an instrument worth $10 per tick with a 30-tick stop, the cost per contract is $300, so the maximum size is two contracts ($600 risked, comfortably inside $750). three contracts would be $900, above the reserve line.

step two, session budget. $5,000 daily limit ÷ $600 actual risk = eight losses of capacity. with a trade cap of five, the session is well inside the limit, and a normal losing run cannot close the day.

step three, calendar. at a 1:2 ratio, an average win is $1,200 and an average loss $600. at a 45% win rate the expectation is 0.45 × 1,200 − 0.55 × 600 = $210 per trade. the $8,000 target therefore needs 38 trades at expectation: at three trades a session across five sessions a week, about twelve sessions - two and a half weeks - for phase one, and the same again for phase two.

step four, trailing check. there is no trailing floor on this account, so the room is a constant $10,000 and the size derived in step one holds for the whole attempt. if the floor trailed, this step would have to be rerun every monday and after any strong session.

step five, consistency. a one-third rule against an $8,000 profit permits a best day of $2,666. a daily profit cap of $1,500 keeps the ratio intact with margin, and at an average winning day of $1,200 it costs very little pace.

the gates. at 25% of target, compare realised with planned cost per trade. at 50%, compare the calendar against the trade count. at 75%, confirm the daily limit has not been touched more than once. at 90%, halve the size, hold the profit cap, and accept the extra sessions.

nothing in that sequence required a spreadsheet, and every number came from the firm's terms or from the trader's own records. that is the point of writing the formulas down: it converts a rulebook into a plan, and a plan is the only thing that can be followed under pressure. the profit target guide covers the levers this arithmetic exposes, and the recovery guide covers what to do when a plan produced by it still fails.
four unit errors account for most of the gap between a calculated plan and a plan that behaves as calculated.

rounding up. position size must always round down, because rounding up increases risk above the derivation. on a contract-based account the nearest whole contract may be a large jump; on a forex account the difference between 0.4 and 0.5 lots is 25% of the risk budget.

mixing tick and point values. a contract specification quotes a value per tick and the platform may quote points. where a point is a multiple of a tick, using the wrong one changes the size by that multiple. the safe method is to express the stop in the same unit the value is quoted in, and to verify the result against the platform's own profit calculator for a single contract.

percentage against balance or equity. a daily limit described as a percentage of equity changes as open positions move; one described against balance does not. for the session budget calculation, use the harsher interpretation - equity - because that is what the firm's server is most likely measuring continuously.

currency of the account. a target expressed in dollars on an account denominated in another currency, or a profit denominated in the instrument's currency, needs converting at the rate the firm applies - which may be the platform's current rate rather than the rate on the day of the trade. where the account currency differs from the instrument's, apply a small haircut to the derived size rather than assuming the conversion is neutral.

the remedy for all four is a verification step. before the first real trade of an evaluation, open a single minimum-size position and check that the platform's own risk figure matches the calculation. one trade's worth of verification removes a class of error that would otherwise compound across the attempt.
every input has a home in the firm's documentation, and knowing where to look turns a fifteen-minute read into a three-minute one.

the rules matrix collects these fields across firms, and the 2026 comparison covers the wider market. both are useful for shortlisting; neither replaces the firm's current terms, which are the only document that governs the account.

where a number cannot be found, the fastest route is a support ticket asking one specific question. firms revise terms, and a written answer is both an input to the calculation and evidence of the version in force when the account was bought.

two of the five calculations change over time even when the terms do not. on a trailing account the room shrinks with any give-back from a peak, and the size derived from it must follow. and expectation per trade is only knowable from records, which accumulate.

a weekly review covers four numbers and takes about ten minutes: trades taken, expectation per trade, worst drawdown so far, distance to target. a monthly review reruns calculations one, two and four from the current state of the account, and answers one question - is the plan still passable at the size it is currently being traded?

if the answer is no, the correction is size down and calendar up. that feels like failure in the moment and is, in fact, the arithmetic working as intended: the whole purpose of the calculations is to discover the problem on paper rather than in a breached account. a plan that is reviewed weekly rarely fails on the day nobody was looking.
the five calculations cover the stretch between choosing an account and reaching a funded payout.

where the evaluation is being traded on the trader's behalf, the same five calculations form the specification. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid third-party trading. the passing services guide covers what to require from any provider, and the faq answers the questions that come up most often.
two errors account for most of the gap between a plan that works on paper and one that behaves as calculated, and both are visible in the formulas rather than in the trading.

mistake one: computing size from the target. it is the single most common error in evaluation preparation, and it appears whenever a trader divides the target by the number of trades they intend to take. the output looks like a risk plan and is actually a schedule with the risk left unspecified. the correct derivation never mentions the target: size comes from the floor and the session budget, and the target is used afterwards to check whether the resulting calendar fits.

mistake two: treating the derived size as permanent. on a static account it is permanent, which is why the error goes unnoticed for years. on a trailing account it is valid only until the floor moves, which can happen within a session. the correction is a weekly recomputation and, after any strong session, an immediate one. the formula is the same in both cases; only the input has changed.

there is a third error worth naming because it is an error of omission rather than arithmetic: failing to convert the terms into a specification. a trader who has read the drawdown clause but never written down the resulting contract count has the information and not the plan. the five calculations exist to force that conversion, and the output should sit on one page next to the platform - four numbers and a calendar, updated weekly.
what is the formula for position size on a prop firm account?

maximum loss divided by the number of consecutive losses the plan must survive gives the money risked per trade. divide that by the stop distance multiplied by the value per unit of distance to get lots or contracts. then check it against the daily limit and round down.
should i size from the profit target or the drawdown?

from the drawdown and the daily limit - never from the target. the target determines how many trades the plan needs and therefore the calendar. sizing from the target is how a plan that is passable on paper becomes one that breaches in practice.

eight to ten for a discretionary plan with a win rate in the forties, because runs of that length recur within a few hundred trades. a higher tolerance means a smaller size and a longer calendar, which is the correct trade-off after a failure.

expectation per trade equals win rate times average win minus loss rate times average loss. divide the target by that figure for the trade count, then divide by trades per week. a conservative plan usually lands between twenty and forty trades.
how do i calculate remaining room on a trailing account?

remaining room equals the maximum loss minus the give-back from the peak. in levels: floor is peak minus maximum loss, and room is current equity minus floor. it is smaller than the advertised drawdown whenever the account is not at a new peak.
why did my position size need to shrink after a profitable week?

because on a trailing account the floor rose behind the profit. if the account peaked and then gave part of it back, the room is smaller than it was before the run, even though the balance is higher. recompute the size from the current room.
how do i convert a consistency rule into a daily cap?

multiply the ratio by the payout threshold. a one-third rule with a $6,000 threshold permits a best day of $2,000, so cap daily profit below that. set the cap from day one and the ratio is satisfied automatically when the threshold is reached.

about two-thirds of the number of losses the daily limit can absorb. if the limit permits eight losses at the plan's risk, cap the session at five trades. the margin covers slippage, re-entries and the fact that not every loss is a clean stop-out.

because rounding up raises risk above the derivation. one extra contract on a large index future can double the risk of a position, and 0.5 rather than 0.4 lots is 25% more risk than the plan specified. always round down; if the result is zero, use a smaller contract size.
what if the required calendar is longer than the firm's deadline?

then the evaluation is not passable at a survivable size, and that is an arithmetic conclusion rather than a motivational one. options: a smaller account with the same percentage rules, a different rulebook model, or a longer target - not more risk per trade.

weekly, using four numbers: trades taken, expectation per trade, worst drawdown and distance to target. on a trailing account, rerun the room and size calculations after any strong session as well, because the floor may have moved.

no. all five calculations are two or three divisions, and the output is four numbers that fit on a card: risk per trade, trade cap, daily profit cap and the calendar. the value is in doing them in the right order rather than in automating them.
where do i find each input in my firm's terms?

maximum loss, daily limit, target and minimum days come from the evaluation terms; the consistency rule and payout threshold usually live in the funded terms. where a number is missing or ambiguous, ask support in writing and keep the reply - it is an input and a record.

goat funded trader belongs to the contract-based end of the market, where targets and losses are quoted in dollars and a position is a whole number of contracts. that single fact changes the arithmetic of passing: size is quantised, the stop is measured in ticks, and a drawdown that trails a peak can end an account that was never losing. this guide covers the mechanics, the sizing, the failure patterns, and what to confirm in the current terms before paying.
futures rules are dollar-based and quantised: contract count is derived from the tick cost of the stop, then rounded down.
a trailing floor turns open profit into a rising failure point, so winners need an exit rule as well as losers.
the daily limit is the constraint most attempts touch first - derive risk from it, not only from the maximum loss.
micro contracts let a strategy keep its stop distance on a small account; full-size contracts usually wait until after funding.
funded conditions, not evaluation rules, decide whether a pass becomes a payout - read them before the fee.

futures evaluations are shortlisted for reasons that have little to do with the marketing and a lot to do with the instrument. a trader who already reads an index future does not want a currency-pair rulebook with percentage targets and fractional lots; they want a dollar target, a dollar stop and a contract count. that is the product category this firm sits in.

the second reason is speed. contract-based evaluations typically complete faster than staged forex evaluations, because the target is smaller in absolute terms and the calendar is shorter. that suits a trader with a defined setup and limited patience for administration, and it is a legitimate advantage as long as the size is derived rather than chosen.

the third reason is transparency of risk. a dollar loss limit is easier to reason about than a percentage one, because it converts directly into contracts and ticks. a trader can compute the survivable position size in a minute, and can see the remaining room on the platform without translating percentages in their head during a losing session.

the cost of those advantages is precision. a percentage-based account forgives imprecise sizing because position size is continuous; a contract-based account does not, because rounding up by one contract can double the dollar risk on a large index future. the rest of this guide is essentially about that precision - where it comes from, how it is maintained across a month, and what breaks it.

the evaluation is a paid assessment with a dollar profit target, a dollar maximum loss, a dollar daily limit, a contract cap and a minimum number of trading days, followed by a funded allocation with a profit split and withdrawal conditions.

two ratios inside that table determine whether the evaluation is a reasonable purchase for a given plan. the first is the target divided by the maximum loss: if the target is a large fraction of the loss limit, a survivable risk per trade needs many trades to finish, and the calendar becomes the constraint. the second is the daily limit divided by the maximum loss: a small fraction forces low risk and a long calendar, a large fraction makes one bad session expensive.

both ratios should be computed before the fee, along with the resulting calendar and the monthly cost of platform and data subscriptions over that calendar. an evaluation that is affordable at signup and expensive over four months is a different purchase from the one advertised, and the difference only appears in the arithmetic.
dollar rules and percentage rules produce different plans from the same strategy.

one structural note that applies to every firm in this category: the evaluation document and the funded document are separate. the evaluation terms describe what must be achieved; the funded terms describe what the achievement is worth. a trader who reads only the first is buying a qualification without checking what it qualifies them for, which is the single most common way a pass produces no income.
the maximum loss is the number everyone compares and the mechanism almost nobody reads, and the mechanism is what decides whether a plan survives.

three variants exist. a static floor is fixed at the starting balance and never moves, so profit cannot reduce the available room. an end-of-day trailing floor resets at settlement, so completed gains are locked in and intraday spikes are forgiven. an intraday trailing floor follows peak unrealised equity continuously, which raises the failure point behind a winning position and can close an account that is above its starting balance.

the intraday variant punishes a specific and very common behaviour: holding a winner through an afternoon retracement. the trade was never at a loss, the trader felt safe because it was in profit, and the account closed anyway. that is not a risk-management failure in the ordinary sense; it is a mechanism the plan did not account for, and it is why the phrase "i was up on the day" appears so often in accounts of a breach.
the same profit path touches three different floors. the mechanism costs more than the number.

two clauses belong in the same reading. the first is the measurement basis: balance only, or balance including open positions. an equity-based limit counts unrealised losses continuously, which means a position can breach the account before it is closed. the second is the sampling moment: continuous, at the close, or at the firm's server close. a mechanism described as end-of-day that samples the session's highest unrealised equity is intraday trailing with a delay, and the difference will be discovered at the worst possible time.

for planning, convert the mechanism into the one number that matters: the current distance from balance to floor, in dollars. on a static structure that number never changes; on a trailing structure it changes daily and must be recomputed. a plan that uses the starting distance for the whole attempt is a plan that becomes oversized as soon as the account is in profit on a trailing account.
the daily limit is a session budget, and the arithmetic is more useful than the number.

divide the daily limit by the risk per trade to get the number of losing trades a session can absorb. if the answer is two, the session is decided by the first two trades of the day, and a normal losing run closes the platform. if the answer is six, the session can absorb a bad start and still trade the plan. the design target is usually four to six losses per session.

then check the opposite direction. if the per-trade risk is so small relative to the daily limit that the account needs forty sessions to reach the target, the calendar cost - platform, data, attention - starts to dominate the economics. the fix in that case is a tighter stop or a better reward-to-risk ratio, not a larger position at the same stop.

there is a time-zone trap on every futures daily limit. the trading day is defined by the firm's server, and futures trade nearly around the clock. a position opened in the trader's evening can belong to the next server day, which means the loss lands against a budget that had not started when the trade was planned. two evening positions that feel like one day's risk can therefore be counted against two days' limits.
a session budget, spent by trades rather than by time.

two rules complete the arithmetic. write the daily loss in dollars and keep it visible during the session, because the moment of maximum loss is the worst time to calculate. and cap the number of trades independently of the dollar limit, because the dollar limit is enforced by the firm and the trade cap is enforced by the trader - and only one of those survives a bad mood.
this is the calculation that decides the attempt, and it fits in three lines.

maximum dollar loss per trade. take the distance to the floor and divide by the number of consecutive losses the plan must survive - eight to ten for a discretionary plan with a win rate in the forties, since runs of that length recur within a few hundred trades.

contract count. divide that dollar figure by the tick value multiplied by the stop distance in ticks. round down. if the result is zero, the strategy's stop does not fit the account at that contract size; the fix is a micro contract or a larger account, never a wider stop.

session check. multiply the per-trade loss by the planned number of trades and compare with the daily limit. if the total exceeds the limit, cut the trade count, not the size - the size is already at the survivability floor.

four consequences follow. one contract is not a proxy for small risk, because a wide stop on a single contract can exceed a tight stop on three. micro contracts are the correct instrument for a small account, since they preserve the stop distance while reducing the dollar risk by an order of magnitude. the contract cap in the rules is a ceiling, not a target, and the derived number is usually far below it. and scaling into a position can breach a cap that the initial entry satisfied, which is a rules breach rather than a sizing error.
three lines, one budget: per trade, per session, and a reserve that is never spent.

keep a quarter of the drawdown in reserve, and recompute the contract count every monday from the floor as it then stands. on a trailing structure the floor moves up with profit, so a size that fitted in week one may not fit in week three. recomputing is a minute of arithmetic that prevents the most common late-evaluation breach.

expected value per trade, in dollars, is the product of the win rate and the average win minus the product of the loss rate and the average loss. divide the target by it to get the number of trades required at expectation, then divide by planned trades per week for the calendar.

run honestly, that calculation usually produces twenty to forty sessions for a conservative plan. the number is the plan's own pace, and it is almost always slower than the marketing implies. the gap between the two is where traders get into trouble: they expect two weeks, discover the arithmetic implies six, and close the gap by increasing size. size does not change expectation per trade; it changes the distribution around it, which is the same thing as changing the survival probability.

there are three legitimate ways to shorten the calendar: improve the reward-to-risk ratio, raise the win rate by becoming more selective, or add sessions within the daily limit. all three improve the plan. increasing size improves only the speed with which a bad sequence reaches the floor.

minimum trading days are usually satisfied long before the target at this pace, so they are not the binding constraint. the trap runs the other way: reaching the target early and then trading to fill the count can give back a meaningful share of the profit. if the count is longer than the plan, slow the plan from the start so that both finish together.

a calendar rule worth adopting: fix the number of sessions per week, and put a review in the diary for the same day every week. the review compares four numbers - trades taken, expectation per trade, worst drawdown, distance to target - and decides whether to continue, extend or stop. without a scheduled review, the decision gets made by mood on the day of the largest loss.
funded conditions decide whether a pass produces income, and they are usually stricter than the evaluation's in ways that are easy to overlook.

the common structure is a minimum number of profitable days, a profit threshold before the first withdrawal, a consistency expectation, and identity verification. each is a separate gate, and each can fail independently of the trading record.

consistency is the one that catches traders who finished the evaluation with a strong final push. expressed as a best-day share of total profit, a limit of around a third means total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day before a full withdrawal. a trader whose largest day is a fifth of the threshold needs five times that day in total profit - usually more than the evaluation required.

the mitigation is structural: set a daily profit cap well below the consistency threshold from the first day, rather than discovering the ratio at the payout request. a trader who reaches the target in one dominant session has passed the evaluation and created a payout constraint at the same time, and the constraint is the part that costs money.

minimum profitable days are satisfied by activity rather than profit, so the correct approach is a reduced size and an acceptance of flat sessions. a trader who tries to make the count productive usually makes it expensive. the consistency guide covers the arithmetic for the common thresholds, and the payout process guide covers the full sequence from pass to payment.

confirm two things before the fee: whether the consistency condition applies once at the first payout or at every withdrawal, and whether it is measured on the evaluation or only on the funded account. applied every time, it becomes a permanent constraint on daily profit and therefore on position size. applied once, it is a hurdle that can be cleared and then forgotten.
failures in this category cluster into five patterns, and each one has a signature visible before the fee is paid.

the daily limit on an ordinary day. risk per trade was set from the maximum loss and never checked against the daily limit, so three consecutive losses close the session. signature: per-trade risk above a fifth of the daily limit.
the trailing floor from a winning position. a profitable position was held through a retracement on an intraday trailing account. signature: an exit plan for losers and none for winners.

rounding up. the contract calculation produced a fraction and the trader took the next whole contract, doubling risk on a large tick value. signature: a size one contract above the survivable maximum.
oversizing after a drawdown. behind on the calendar, the trader increases size to catch up. this is the most reliably fatal pattern because it occurs when the account has the least room.

losing the funded allocation in the first fortnight. the evaluation's size is carried into a tighter funded drawdown, and the first normal losing sequence ends it. signature: no reduction in size at funding.

all five share a cause: a rule understood in principle and never converted into a number. the remedy is a written plan with the contract count, the stop in ticks, the dollar risk, the session cap and the weekly recomputation - checked against the firm's current terms rather than against a comparable firm's.
the funded allocation is a different product, and three things change at once.

the drawdown usually tightens as a percentage, because the firm is now exposed to payouts rather than to a fee. the profit becomes real only when withdrawn, which means an unwithdrawn balance is not a high score - it is a larger target under the same rules, and on a trailing structure it also raises the floor behind the trader. and the payout sequence adds administrative steps that run on their own clock.

the first fortnight on the funded account should be run at half the evaluation's risk. complete verification in week one. satisfy the minimum-day count with planned, small sessions. cap daily profit so the consistency ratio is intact by the time the threshold is reached. then withdraw at the smallest permitted size on the earliest permitted schedule, because a completed cycle establishes the payment route and timing, which are otherwise guesses.

only after that cycle should size return toward the evaluation plan, and only then does a scaling request make sense. scaling programmes are judged on completed withdrawals rather than on a strong month, so a trader who increases size before the first payout is scaling an unverified process - the most common reason someone who has passed twice still has no payout history.

one further check belongs here rather than in the marketing: whether the funded account carries the same conduct clauses as the evaluation, or stricter ones. overnight holding, news windows and permitted instruments can differ between the two documents, and the funded version is the one that governs the money.
three models dominate the futures side of the market, and the choice between them is a choice about which constraint is tolerable.

the single-phase contract evaluation is the fastest route to a funded allocation and the least forgiving of a slow start, because one target and one loss limit cover the whole attempt. it suits a trader with a measured, repeatable setup and a short calendar.

the staged contract evaluation splits the target in two, which reduces the size of each step and increases the cost of a late breach. it suits a trader who has failed a single-phase attempt in the final stretch, since the arithmetic per stage is smaller.

the percentage-based forex evaluation is a different product with a different sizing model: fractional lots, percentage targets, and a plan that is scale-free. a trader with a currency edge is usually better served there, and the fundednext versus topstep comparison sets the two rulebooks side by side.

the futures firm guide covers the seven criteria that separate contract-based firms, the mff guide works through a comparable structure, and the topstep guide covers a combine with two simultaneous loss rules. the rules matrix lists the structures across firms for a side-by-side read.
six checks, each answerable from the firm's documentation in under an hour, replace every review including this one.

one: the drawdown mechanism and its sampling. static, end-of-day trailing or intraday trailing; balance or equity; continuous or sampled. convert the answer into the current distance to the floor in dollars.

two: the daily limit and the server day boundary. the dollar amount, the reference point, and the exact hour the trading day starts and ends in server time - then how that interacts with the hours actually traded.

three: the funded-stage conditions. funded drawdown, minimum profitable days, profit threshold, consistency rule and whether it applies at every payout, verification requirements, and the payment interval.

four: the conduct clauses. news windows, overnight and weekend holding, instrument restrictions, contract caps, and any prohibition on automated or third-party trading. where a definition is broad, ask for a specific written example.
five: whether assistance is permitted, on both stages. the evaluation and funded documents answer separately, and the funded answer is the one with money attached.

six: total cost to funding. fee, platform, data, any activation charge, and the cost of a reset - divided by the realistic number of weeks the plan needs, remembering that a data subscription is a monthly cost rather than a per-attempt one.

keep the answers, including the version of the terms in force on the day of purchase. terms change, and a trader holding the version they agreed to is in a materially better position than one relying on memory.
four weeks is roughly twenty sessions, which is a realistic horizon for a plan at survivable size.

week one: calibrate at half size. two trades per session, half the eventual contract count, and three measurements per trade: planned risk, realised risk including slippage and commission, and time in the trade. the purpose is to establish whether the stop distance the plan assumes is the stop distance the market delivers at the hours being traded. most plans are wrong about this, and week one is the cheapest place to find out.

week two: full size, fixed cap. if the calibration matched, move to the full contract count and keep the two-trade cap for a week before relaxing it to the planned maximum. if it did not match, shorten the stop distance rather than increasing the size - slippage is a property of the instrument and the session, not of the account.

week three: protect the buffer. ahead of pace, reduce the contract count by a quarter and keep the target in view. behind pace, keep the size and move the calendar. the daily limit is never increased to catch up, and the contract count is never rounded up.

week four: decide deliberately. review the four numbers and choose: continue, extend, or stop. a plan with a negative expectation should stop, because another fortnight of the same process produces the same result at a higher cost in data and platform fees.

two habits hold the month together. recompute the contract count from the current floor every monday, and never open a position in the final hour of the firm's trading day, where the day-boundary and trailing-floor traps live. if the evaluation is being traded on the trader's behalf, add a third: written confirmation that third-party trading is permitted on both the evaluation and the funded account. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid it - the passing services guide explains what to check.

divide the distance to the drawdown floor by the number of consecutive losses the plan must survive, then divide by the tick value of the stop distance and round down. check against the daily limit and the contract cap. if the result is zero, use a micro contract or a larger account.

read the current terms rather than any guide. establish whether the floor is static, end-of-day trailing or intraday trailing, whether it is measured on balance or equity, and when it is sampled. then convert it into the current distance to the floor in dollars, which is the number position size must be built from.

because it fires on routine variance. if risk per trade is a large fraction of the daily limit, two or three consecutive losses close the session, and runs of that length occur regularly at a win rate in the forties. derive risk from both limits and use the smaller figure.

usually yes. a micro carries a fraction of the tick value, which lets the strategy keep its stop distance while risking a fraction of the dollars. many experienced futures traders run micros during evaluation and full-size contracts only after the first payout cycle completes.

twenty to forty sessions for a conservative plan, derived by dividing the target by expected value per trade and then by planned trades per week. if that calendar is longer than the trader is willing to fund, the fix is a better reward-to-risk ratio or a more selective entry, not a larger position.

most futures firms permit it with conditions: reduced size across the settlement window, restrictions around certain releases, and a daily limit that resets on server time. where holding is allowed, price the gap as a multiple of the stop - the weekend holding guide covers the arithmetic.
