how do i avoid breaching a trailing floor from a winning position?

give winners an exit rule. on an intraday trailing structure, a position in profit has already raised the floor, so the plan needs a defined point at which profit is banked or the stop moves. write the rule before the trade, because in the moment the position feels safe precisely because it is up.

usually a cap on the share of total profit from one day, often around a third, meaning total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day before a full withdrawal. cap daily profit from the first session so the ratio is satisfied automatically when the threshold is reached.

usually not before the first payout cycle completes. parallel accounts multiply fees, data costs and daily limits but not attention, and combining allocations before a completed withdrawal means scaling a process that has not been tested end to end.

a failed evaluation is the most informative thing most traders ever buy. which limit broke tells you which part of the plan was wrong; your own records tell you whether the strategy had an edge at all. this guide is the sequence to work through before paying another fee - diagnosis, records audit, the reset decision, and the specific changes that make a second attempt a different attempt.
diagnose first. a maximum-loss breach, a daily-limit breach and a rule breach have three different causes and three different fixes.
a reset that changes nothing is the same attempt at a higher price; change one measurable number or do not pay.
records decide whether the strategy had an edge. without them, a second fee buys another sample of the same distribution.
recovery sizing - increasing risk after a drawdown - is the single most reliable way to convert a recoverable account into a closed one.
sometimes the correct answer is a different account size, or no evaluation at all until the plan is measured.
the hour after an account closes is the worst time to make a decision about the next one, and the best time to collect evidence. two rules make that possible.

the first rule is no new account, no reset, no deposit for at least twenty-four hours. every platform makes the next purchase easy and the decision feels urgent, which is precisely why it should be delayed. a reset bought in the first hour is usually bought with the same plan that just failed and with the same size, which is a purchase of the same outcome.

the second rule is to capture the record immediately. export the trade history, screenshot the equity curve, note the dates, and write down in one paragraph what happened in the trader's own words while it is still fresh. that paragraph is worth more than a reconstructed account of the failure written a week later, because it captures the reasoning rather than the summary. it is also the only part of the record that will show whether the breach was a plan failure or a plan that was abandoned.

then stop. not trade a different account, not move to a demonstration account to recover confidence - stop, for a day. the decision about a second attempt is materially better with twenty-four hours of distance and a written record than it is in the moment.
most breaches are visible in the session that preceded them, which is why the record matters.
three limits can close an account, and each failure carries a different diagnosis. getting this wrong is expensive, because each has a different fix and only one of them was caused by the market.

a maximum-loss breach. the account reached its failure floor. this is a sizing failure: the risk per trade permitted a losing sequence the account could not absorb. diagnostic questions: how many consecutive losses occurred before the breach, and would the design case have survived them? if the streak was shorter than the design case, the risk per trade was too high. if the streak was longer than the design case, the survival assumption was wrong for the instrument or the timeframe.

a daily-limit breach. the account closed on a single day's loss. this is a session-design failure: either the risk per trade was too large relative to the daily limit, or the trade count was, or both. diagnostic questions: how many losing trades did the session take, and what did the plan say the cap was? in most cases the answer is that the cap existed on paper and the session drifted past it.

a drawdown breach on a trailing account, from a winning position. this presents as a maximum-loss breach but has a different cause: the floor rose behind a profitable position and a retracement closed the account. diagnostic question: what was the plan's exit rule for winners? if the answer is "none", the mechanism was not accounted for, and the fix is an exit rule rather than a smaller size.

a fourth, less common variant: the target was reached and the account was then breached before the firm processed the pass. this is not a trading failure at all; it is a failure to stop. the fix is procedural - once the target is met, the account is closed to new trades.

naming the breach correctly is most of the recovery, because it eliminates the two most common wrong conclusions: that the strategy does not work, and that the trader lacks discipline. neither is established by a breach alone.

a rule breach is different in kind from a limit breach, because it is a reading failure rather than a trading failure - and it is the category that can void a payout rather than merely close an account.

the usual candidates are news restrictions, holding positions through a restricted window, exceeding a lot or contract cap, trading an instrument outside the permitted list, or an arrangement the firm classifies as third-party trading. each of these can be present in a plan that is working perfectly, which is what makes them dangerous: the account is healthy, the target is close, and the breach is administrative.

the recovery for this category is not a change in size or strategy. it is a rewrite of the plan's constraints as explicit no-go conditions: no position opened within a stated window around listed releases; no position held across a stated period; no size above the derived maximum, checked before entry rather than after; and, where anyone else trades the account, written confirmation from the firm that the arrangement is permitted on both the evaluation and the funded account.

where the clause was unclear rather than ignored, the correct response is a support ticket with the exact question and a saved reply. firms interpret their own terms, and an interpretation received in writing before an attempt is worth more than any number of forum posts about what the terms mean. the scam guide covers the cases where a firm's terms are vague by design rather than by accident.
the records decide everything that follows, and most failed attempts have enough of them to be conclusive. the audit takes an hour and answers four questions.

how many trades were taken? compare the number against the plan. a trader who planned two trades a session and took six has a discipline problem, and the size was not the cause of the breach - the trade count was. a trader who planned two and took two has a plan problem.

what was the average win and the average loss in money? if the average loss is larger than the plan's stop distance implies, the plan was not being executed as written - stops were widened, or slippage was underestimated. if the average win is smaller than planned, profits were being taken early, which changes the reward-to-risk ratio and therefore the expectation.

what was the realised cost per trade? spread, commission and slippage, measured rather than assumed. on a plan with a small expectation per trade, a cost that is a fifth of the planned risk can turn a positive expectation into a flat one, and on a leveraged account the cost is paid on every round turn.

what was the largest loss and the longest streak? the largest loss should equal the plan's risk per trade. if it does not, the plan's central assumption was violated. the longest streak is the number the drawdown should have been sized against, and comparing it to the design case tells you whether the sizing was wrong or the estimate was.
the audit replaces the question "was i unlucky?" with numbers that can be checked.

the audit answers a second, harder question: whether the strategy had a positive expectation over the attempt. this is the question traders avoid, because the answer determines whether another fee is a purchase or a donation.

the calculation is simple. multiply the win rate by the average win, subtract the loss rate multiplied by the average loss, and compare the result to the cost per trade. if the result before costs is positive and the costs are smaller, the strategy had an edge and the breach was a sizing or execution failure. if the result before costs is negative, the strategy did not have an edge over that sample and no amount of discipline would have saved the account.

sample size matters, and it cuts in a specific direction. a few dozen trades cannot establish an edge, so a positive result over that sample is not proof either. what the sample can do is set a limit: if a plan with a claimed 50% win rate and 1:2 ratio lost money over forty trades, the realised distribution is different from the claimed one, and the difference is the finding.

between the two conclusions lies the most common outcome: an edge too small to survive the realised execution cost. that is not a strategy to abandon, it is a strategy to trade more selectively and with a tighter relative cost - fewer, better trades rather than more. the profit target guide covers the levers that change expectation per trade without changing risk per trade.
the reset decision is not "should i try again". it is "what, specifically, will be different, and is that difference measurable".

three conditions justify paying again. there is a named cause of failure: a limit, a rule, or a measured expectation gap, rather than a feeling. there is a specific change that addresses it, expressed as a number: risk per trade, trade cap, session count, instrument, or selectivity criterion. and the change is testable at small size before the fee is paid, ideally on a demonstration account with the same feed and order types.

if all three are present, a reset is a second experiment with a controlled change, and it is worth paying for. if any is missing, the reset is a repeat, and the expected outcome is the same with a different story about why.

two further considerations belong in the decision. the first is the retry structure itself: a one-off fee with paid resets makes each attempt a deliberate purchase, while a subscription with unlimited retries lowers the marginal cost of a failed attempt and, in doing so, lowers the cost of not fixing the plan. the second is the calendar. time spent on a failed attempt is time not spent trading a funded account, and at some point the sequence of attempts becomes more expensive than a longer, slower attempt that is actually passable.

there is also a version of the decision that is not a reset at all: moving to a smaller account. a smaller account with the same percentage rules has the same percentage arithmetic and a lower fee, which makes it the correct place to establish a working plan. many traders fail twice on an account that is too large for the stop distances their strategy needs, when the same strategy on a smaller account would have passed.
five changes address almost every diagnosis from the audit, and each is expressed as a number rather than an intention.

risk per trade, re-derived from both limits. divide the maximum loss by the streak tolerance and the daily limit by the losses a session should absorb. use the smaller result, then halve it for the second attempt. the halving is not superstition: the first attempt produced evidence that the survival assumption was optimistic.
a hard trade cap per session. written down, counted during the session, and treated as binding when the session is going badly rather than when it is going well.
a daily profit cap. this protects the payout-stage consistency condition and prevents a good session from being given back. set it at two to three times the average winning day.

an exit rule for winners. on a trailing-drawdown account, a profitable position that is held too long closes accounts. the rule should state the point at which profit is banked or the stop is advanced, and it should be written before the position is opened.

the rulebook as no-go conditions. news windows, holding restrictions, size ceilings and third-party clauses rewritten as conditions in the plan rather than as facts in a document the trader read once.
five numbers, written down, replace the resolution to be more careful.
the second attempt should be sized more conservatively than the first, and the conservatism should come from the derivation rather than from an arbitrary haircut.

start with the streak the account must now survive. the first attempt produced evidence: if it breached on a seven-loss run, the design case of eight was too thin and should become twelve. higher streak tolerance means lower risk per trade, which is the correct direction of travel after a failure.

then increase the reserve. in the first attempt a quarter of the drawdown was held back; in the second, hold back a third. on a trailing structure the reserve is arithmetic rather than psychological, because the floor moves and the reserve is what allows the plan to continue after a sequence the design case did not anticipate.

then extend the calendar deliberately and price it. a slower plan costs more in platform and data subscriptions, so the calendar has a dollar figure. comparing that figure against the fee of another failed attempt makes the choice concrete: a longer, slower, survivable attempt is usually cheaper than two fast attempts, even before the funded-account time that the fast attempts consumed.

finally, test the new size at demonstration scale before the fee. the purpose is not to prove the strategy - that takes hundreds of trades - but to confirm that the new risk per trade permits the stop distances the instruments require and that the trade cap is achievable in a normal session. those two checks take a week and eliminate the most common cause of a second breach.
timing is a real variable, not a matter of morale. two signals say start now; two say wait.

start now when the diagnosis is complete, the change is measurable, and the new numbers have been tested at demonstration size. under those conditions a delay adds nothing; the plan is different and the evidence is in hand.

start now also when the failure was procedural - a rule clause or a day-boundary error - because those are fixed by reading, not by trading. there is no reason to wait for a discipline that was never the problem.

wait when the failure was emotional rather than mechanical: a stop widened, a size doubled, a trade taken to recover. that behaviour has a half-life, and starting again immediately increases the chance of repeating it under the same conditions. a fortnight of trading the plan at small size on a demonstration account is the cheapest way to re-establish the habit.

wait when the audit showed a negative expectation. paying again before the strategy is fixed buys another sample of the same distribution. the correct sequence is to fix the plan, measure it over a proper sample, and only then buy an evaluation - which is the same argument that applies to a first attempt, applied with the benefit of evidence.
not every failure is the trader's. four situations point at the firm, and each has a recognisable signature.

terms changed mid-attempt. a drawdown mechanism, a daily limit or a target altered while an account was live, with no notice. if the change was applied to the existing account, the attempt was conducted under terms the trader did not agree to - and a firm that does this once will do it again.

the day boundary was reported differently than it behaves. a trader who planned around a stated server boundary and was breached against a different one has a legitimate complaint, and the evidence is the support reply and the trade timestamps.

a payout clause was undocumented. conditions applied at withdrawal that do not appear in the terms - a consistency rule in a separate faq page, or a minimum-day requirement disclosed only at the request - indicate a firm whose revenue comes from payouts not being made.

execution was materially different from the stated feed. persistent slippage far beyond what the instrument and session justify, or a platform whose protective orders do not sit on the server. this is a platform-and-routing problem, and no sizing discipline compensates for it.

the action in all four cases is a written complaint with evidence and, where the terms were misrepresented, a chargeback where the payment method permits it. the more useful action is not to fund the same firm again. the scam guide covers the patterns, and a firm's support responsiveness before a purchase - measured by asking one specific clause question in writing - is a better predictor than any review, including this one.

for a trader whose audit shows a sizing problem rather than a strategy problem, a passing service is a legitimate option: it converts an uncertain attempt into a fixed cost. the economics are straightforward, and they should be compared against expected cost rather than against the fee alone.

expected cost of attempting alone is the fee divided by the probability of passing, plus the calendar cost. a trader with a one-in-three pass rate on a comparable plan faces an expected cost three times the sticker price, before the platform and data subscriptions consumed by the failed attempts. against that, a fixed price per evaluation is a cheap conversion - provided the service is legitimate and the firm's terms permit the arrangement.

four checks before paying anyone. the price should be flat and independent of account size and stage, so it can be compared. retries should be covered, because a fixed price with retry fees is a per-attempt price with extra steps. the funded account should be in the trader's name with credentials under their control, and the service should take no share of payouts - a service that shares in payouts has an incentive to keep trading after the pass. and the firm's terms must permit third-party trading on both the evaluation and the funded account, confirmed in writing before payment.

elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid the arrangement. the passing services guide sets out the full checklist, including the questions to ask before paying anyone else.
there is a point at which the correct decision is to stop buying evaluations, and it is worth defining in advance because it is never obvious in the moment.

the first trigger is arithmetic: if the cumulative fees and subscriptions spent on attempts exceed the value of the funded allocation's expected first-year payout, the sequence is not an investment. this calculation requires an honest view of the pass probability, which the records now provide.

the second is diagnostic: if two consecutive attempts failed for the same named reason after a specific change was made to address it, the change did not work. a third attempt with the same plan buys the same result. the alternative is a different account size, a different rulebook, or a different route to funded capital.

the third is behavioural: if the pattern includes any instance of increasing size after a loss, the plan is not being executed and the problem is not the account. funded capital amplifies behaviour rather than correcting it, so the funded account would be lost the same way, with more at stake.

what a trader does after stopping is a separate decision, and there are legitimate options that do not involve a fee: a demonstration account with real measurement, a small personal account with the same rules imposed voluntarily, or an instant funding route that removes the evaluation stage if the trader's edge is real and only the calendar is the problem. stopping attempts is not stopping trading.

between the diagnosis and the next fee there is a reconstruction period, and four weeks is enough to complete it properly. the purpose is not to prove the strategy over a meaningful sample - that takes hundreds of trades - but to confirm that the five changed numbers are executable.

week one: rewrite the plan. produce a one-page document containing the risk per trade, the trade cap, the session count, the daily profit cap, the exit rule for winners, and the rulebook's no-go conditions. every entry is a number or a condition, not an intention. a plan that still contains the phrase "be more careful" has not been rewritten.

week two: run it at demonstration size. trade the plan on a demonstration account with the same feed and order types as the firm's platform. the two things being measured are whether the derived risk per trade permits the stop distances the instruments require, and whether the trade cap is achievable in an ordinary session. both are structural questions, and both are answered in a week.

week three: run it at real size, small. a small live account imposes the same psychological conditions as an evaluation at a fraction of the cost, and it reveals the behaviours that a demonstration account hides - hesitation on entries, premature profit-taking, and the temptation to hold a loser because the day is not yet over.

week four: review and decide. compare the records against the plan. if the realised cost per trade and the win rate are consistent with the audit's estimates and the rules were followed, the plan is ready and the fee is a purchase rather than a lottery ticket. if behaviour drifted, the correction is another fortnight at small size - cheaper than discovering the same drift on a fresh evaluation.
i just failed a challenge. what should i do first?

nothing impulsive for twenty-four hours. export the trade history, screenshot the equity curve, and write one paragraph on what happened while it is fresh. then diagnose which limit broke - maximum loss, daily limit, or a rule clause - because each has a different fix.
how do i know whether the strategy or the sizing was the problem?

from the records. calculate the win rate, average win and average loss, then compare expectation per trade against the realised cost. a positive expectation with an orderly execution record points to sizing; a negative expectation points to the plan, and no amount of discipline would have saved the account.

only if there is a named cause, a specific measurable change that addresses it, and evidence that the change works at small size. otherwise a reset is the same attempt at a higher price, and the expected outcome is the same with a different explanation.

until the diagnosis stops changing. a second attempt with a controlled change is a legitimate experiment; a third attempt that failed for the same reason as the second is a purchase of the same result. compare cumulative fees against the expected value of the funded allocation before deciding.
what risk per trade should i use on the next attempt?

lower than the first, derived rather than guessed. increase the streak tolerance the account must survive based on what actually happened, keep a third of the drawdown as a reserve rather than a quarter, and halve the previous risk per trade if the breach was a maximum-loss event.

possible but rarely decisive. a losing streak longer than the design case is bad luck; a breach caused by it means the design case was too optimistic, which is a planning error. the distinction matters because only one of them is fixed by trying again unchanged.

often yes. percentage rules are scale-free, so the same plan has the same arithmetic on a smaller account with a lower fee, and it leaves room to establish working numbers. many traders fail twice on an account that is too large for the stop distances their strategy needs.

that is a legitimate complaint, and the evidence is the terms version you agreed to plus the trade timestamps. raise it in writing, and consider a chargeback where the payment method permits it. the more useful decision is not to fund the same firm again.

no wait is needed for a procedural failure - a rule clause or a day-boundary error is fixed by reading. for an emotional failure such as a widened stop or recovery sizing, wait a fortnight and trade the plan at small size first, because that behaviour has a half-life.

it can, if the failure was sizing rather than strategy. compare the flat fee against the expected cost of attempting alone - fee divided by pass probability, plus subscription costs over the calendar. elitepropx charges $220 flat per evaluation, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid third-party trading.

when cumulative fees and subscriptions exceed the expected value of the funded allocation, when two consecutive attempts failed for the same reason after a targeted change, or when the pattern includes recovery sizing. stopping attempts is not stopping trading - demonstration measurement and instant funding are both legitimate next steps.
can i still pass after a breach on the same account?

no. a breached evaluation is closed, and the account cannot be recovered by trading on it. the only decision available is whether to buy another attempt, for this firm or a different one, with a plan that has changed in a measurable way.

"safer" is not a marketing word on an evaluation - it has a definition. an account is safer when the probability of breaching a limit before reaching the target is lower, given a fixed strategy and a fixed risk per trade. this comparison works through the mechanics that determine that probability: how the failure floor behaves, how many loss limits apply at once, how profit targets and minimum days interact, and what the funded stage does to all three.
safety is measurable: for a fixed strategy, the account with the higher survivable streak and looser daily constraint is safer.
a trailing floor and a static floor are different products, even when the headline drawdown percentage is identical.
two loss rules at once (a daily limit plus a maximum loss) reduce the survivable streak, because the shorter one binds first.
payout conditions decide whether a pass becomes income, and they are set independently of evaluation rules.
read the current terms for both firms; targets and drawdown mechanics are revised more often than any comparison can track.

traders ask which of two firms is safer and usually mean which one they are less likely to fail. that is a reasonable question with an arithmetic answer: given a fixed strategy, a fixed win rate and a fixed reward-to-risk ratio, the safer account is the one where a given losing streak is less likely to close the account before the target is reached.

two mechanisms decide that. the first is how much room the account has, which is a function of the drawdown percentage and the way the floor behaves - a trailing floor gives less effective room than a static one at the same headline number. the second is how many limits apply simultaneously, because each additional limit shortens the streak the account can survive.

against those stand the factors that make an account more passable but not safer: a smaller target, a longer calendar, fewer minimum days. those affect how likely a trader is to finish, not how likely a trader is to blow up on the way. a comparison that ranks firms on the target size alone has answered the wrong question.

the rest of this page separates the two. it compares the mechanics that determine breach probability, then the conditions that determine whether a pass produces money, and only then the calendar and the fee. every specific number - drawdown percentage, target, minimum days, payout split - has to be read from the firms' current terms, because all of them are revised regularly and a comparison that quotes them is accurate only until the next revision.
comparisons are only meaningful once the two rulebooks are laid out structurally.

both firms sit in the contract-based futures category: targets and losses are quoted in dollars, positions are whole contracts, and the evaluator trades index or commodity futures rather than currency pairs. that shared architecture means the differences between them are almost entirely in the details rather than in the category.

read as a specification rather than a scoreboard, the table produces a short list of questions for each firm. the answers are in the terms, and where a term is ambiguous the fastest resolution is a written question to support - the reply is both the answer and a record of the version in force when the account was bought.

one generalisation holds across the category and is worth stating: futures evaluations tend to carry two loss rules rather than one, because the daily limit is standard in contract-based accounts. that single structural feature is the most common cause of failure in the category, and it interacts with everything else in this comparison.
the failure floor is the single most consequential clause in either rulebook, and it is the one most often reduced to a single number in a comparison table.

a static floor is fixed at the starting balance. profit cannot reduce room, so the available cushion is the same in week four as it was in week one. an end-of-day trailing floor resets at settlement: gains banked in a completed session are locked in and the floor rises with them, but intraday spikes that reverse are forgiven. an intraday trailing floor follows peak unrealised equity continuously, so a winning position raises the failure point immediately and an ordinary retracement can close an account that has never been below its starting balance.

the practical difference between the trailing variants and a static floor is not a percentage; it is a change in which trades are survivable. a strategy that holds winners through pullbacks is viable on a static structure and structurally fragile on an intraday trailing one. a strategy that banks profit quickly and rarely gives back a session's gains is affected far less by the difference.
the same profit path touches three different floors. the mechanism, not the percentage, decides survival.

two secondary clauses complete the comparison and are frequently missed. the measurement basis decides whether open positions consume room continuously (equity) or only when realised (balance). and the lock-in clause, where it exists, converts the account from trailing to static once a defined profit threshold is reached - which changes not just the room but the optimal behaviour at a specific point in the attempt.

the trailing drawdown guide sets out the full arithmetic, including the room formula and the exit rules that make a trailing structure survivable. any comparison of trailing firms should be read alongside it, because the differences between them are differences in those clauses rather than in the headline drawdown.
the number of simultaneous loss limits is the most underrated factor in breach probability, and it is where the practical difference between rulebooks shows up fastest.

a single maximum-loss rule defines one failure condition: the account's distance to its floor. a second rule - a daily loss limit - defines a shorter, independent failure condition that resets each day. both must be satisfied simultaneously, and the account fails when either is breached.

the effect on the survivable streak is geometric rather than linear. if risk per trade is a fifth of the daily limit, the session can absorb five losses; if it is half, two. a plan sized from the maximum loss alone can therefore be perfectly safe against the account floor and simultaneously one bad morning away from a daily breach. the correct size derivation uses the smaller of two answers: maximum loss divided by streak tolerance, and daily limit divided by losses per session.

there is a second-order effect worth naming. a daily limit makes the calendar longer, because sessions end early after a bad start - a plan that expected five sessions a week may average four. on an evaluation with a fixed deadline, that hidden reduction in trade count matters as much as the risk cap.
the daily limit is a session budget, and on a futures rulebook it is usually the constraint that fires first.

where one firm applies a daily limit and the other does not, the comparison is not close in safety terms: the account without the daily rule has the larger survivable streak at the same headline drawdown. that is a real advantage for a trader with a slow, low-frequency plan, and close to irrelevant for a trader whose plan takes two or three positions per session and would rarely approach a daily limit anyway.
targets and minimum trading days affect how long an attempt takes rather than how likely it is to breach, but they interact with the loss rules in a way that changes both.

a smaller target shortens the calendar, which reduces the number of sessions exposed to variance and lowers the probability of a losing streak long enough to breach. a larger target does the reverse. since both firms quote a dollar target on a fixed account size, the comparison is direct once the current numbers are read - but the target ratio to the maximum loss matters more than the target itself. a target that is a large fraction of the loss limit compresses the number of trades available to reach it at survivable size.

the profit target guide covers the ratio arithmetic and the three levers - ratio, selectivity, sessions - that shorten a calendar without raising risk. applying those levers is the way to make a large target survivable; raising size is not.

minimum trading days are usually satisfied long before the target at a conservative pace, so they rarely bind. the exception runs in the same direction as the daily-limit issue: a trader who reaches the target early and then has to trade for several more sessions to satisfy a count is trading with nothing to gain, and those sessions can give back a meaningful share of the profit. where one firm requires a longer minimum count, that is a genuine, if second-order, safety difference.

one structural question worth asking each firm: whether the target must be reached without breaching any daily rule at any point, or whether a breach on day two is simply a closed account. in practice it is the latter, but the phrasing sometimes clarifies whether a breach closes the account or only that day's trading - a distinction with obvious consequences for the daily limit calculation.

the useful comparison is not which firm is safer in the abstract but which is safer for one specific strategy. the method is to size the same plan against each rulebook and compare the resulting survivable streaks.

take a strategy with a fixed stop distance measured in ticks and a fixed risk tolerance. size derivation runs twice for each firm: once from that firm's maximum loss and streak tolerance, and once from that firm's daily limit and session capacity. the smaller result is the size the plan can carry there. then convert each size back into a streak tolerance: how many consecutive losses can that account absorb at its own derived size?

the firm with the higher number is safer for that strategy . the comparison is not transferable, because a strategy with a wider stop or a higher trade frequency will size differently against the same two rulebooks.

run for both firms, the output is two numbers rather than a preference: a survivable streak and a calendar. those two decide which rulebook suits the strategy, and they are the only comparison that accounts for the trader's own plan rather than the marketing on the site.

where both accounts come out with a survivable streak below eight, the honest conclusion is that neither rulebook fits the strategy at that account size, and the correct change is a smaller account, a smaller contract, or a different plan - not a different firm.

the evaluation rules decide whether an account is passed; the payout conditions decide whether the pass is worth anything. they are set separately, and on both firms they usually live in a different document from the evaluation terms.

the common payout structure has four gates: a minimum number of profitable trading days, a profit threshold before the first withdrawal, a consistency condition on the profit being withdrawn, and identity verification. each is independent, and each has a failure mode unrelated to trading skill.

the consistency condition is the one that catches traders who passed with a strong final push. expressed as a best-day share of total profit, a one-third rule means total profit must reach roughly three times the largest day before a full withdrawal. a trader whose largest day is a fifth of the threshold needs five times that day in total profit - usually more than the evaluation required.
a dominant day is a payout constraint, not an achievement.

comparing the two firms on this dimension means asking four specific questions of each. is the consistency rule applied once at the first payout or at every withdrawal? is it measured on the evaluation record or only on the funded account? is profit above the threshold withdrawable in full, or is a portion retained as buffer? and what is the interval between request and payment? a generous split paid in ninety days is worth less than a smaller split paid in five.

the payout process guide covers the sequence step by step, and the consistency guide covers the ratio arithmetic for the common variants. both are worth reading before the fee rather than after the funded login.
cost is not a safety dimension, but it is the one that decides how many attempts a trader can afford - which changes the practical outcome of a comparison considerably.

the total cost of reaching a funded account is the fee, plus platform and market-data subscriptions for as long as the attempt lasts, plus any reset or retry charges, plus any activation fee on funding. a monthly data subscription is a cost per month, not per attempt, so a plan with a long calendar pays more for the same fee.

that produces a specific arithmetic: the firm with the longer calendar needs a larger price advantage to be the cheaper option overall. running the calendar calculation from the sizing section for each firm gives the number of weeks, and the subscriptions multiply out from there. the calculator page sets out the formulas, including the calendar conversion.

reset structure belongs here too. a one-off fee with a paid reset makes each attempt a deliberate purchase; a subscription with unlimited retries lowers the marginal cost of a failed attempt and, by doing so, the cost of not fixing the plan first. for a trader whose breach rate is high, the subscription is cheaper; for a trader whose plan is sound, the one-off is.
the comparison resolves differently for different plans, and the honest version of the answer is a set of profiles rather than a ranking.

a trader who holds winners. a static or end-of-day structure is materially safer than an intraday trailing one, because the retracement that closes a trailing account costs a static account only the profit. this is the largest single difference available in the category, and it is decided by the floor clause rather than by the target or the fee.

a trader with a low-frequency, wide-stop plan. the daily limit is the constraint, because each trade risks more of the session budget. the safer rulebook here is the one with the most generous daily limit relative to the maximum loss, and the one whose day boundary aligns with the hours actually traded.

a trader who trades a defined session. the day boundary matters less, and the target-to-loss ratio matters more: a smaller target relative to the loss limit means fewer trades at survivable size, therefore fewer days exposed to variance.

a trader who expects a long calendar. recurring costs dominate, so the cheaper firm on a per-month basis is safer in the sense that matters - it leaves money for a second attempt if the first fails. a slower plan also benefits from any lock-in clause, because it spends more time past the threshold where the floor stops moving.

a trader using a passing service. the comparison shifts to the compliance clauses. whether third-party trading is permitted, on the evaluation and on the funded account, is the only question that matters; a firm whose terms forbid the arrangement is unavailable regardless of how good its drawdown mechanism is. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid it - the passing services guide sets out what to check with any provider.
eight checks, applied to each firm, convert every comparison - including this one - into a decision that is specific to the trader's own plan.
one: floor mechanism and sampling. static, end-of-day trailing or intraday trailing; balance or equity; continuous or sampled. then convert to the current distance to the floor in dollars.
two: lock-in clause. whether the floor stops trailing at a threshold, and where that threshold sits.
three: daily limit and day boundary. the dollar amount, the reference point, and the exact hour the trading day starts and ends in server time.
four: target and minimum days. per stage or cumulative, and whether the two finish together on a conservative pace.
five: contract cap. per position and per account, and whether scaling into a position can breach it.
six: funded-stage conditions. funded drawdown, payout threshold, consistency rule and whether it applies at every payout, verification requirements and payment interval.
seven: conduct clauses. news windows, overnight and weekend holding, permitted instruments, and any prohibition on automated or third-party trading.
eight: total cost to funding. fee, platform, data, activation and reset, divided by the calendar the plan actually needs.

keep the answers for both firms side by side. where a firm's answer is unresolvable from the published terms, treat that as a finding in itself: a clause that cannot be checked before purchase is a clause that cannot be relied on afterwards.
a worked comparison makes the method concrete. the figures below are illustrative placeholders; the sequence is the transferable part.
the strategy. one index future, a 30-tick stop worth $300 at one contract, a 45% win rate, a 1:2 reward-to-risk ratio, two setups per session, five sessions a week.

firm a, trailing structure. maximum loss $2,000 with an intraday trailing floor. streak tolerance of ten gives $200 per trade; the stop costs $300 per contract, so the derived size is zero contracts. the strategy does not fit that account at all - a finding that would have been invisible in any comparison table.

firm b, larger drawdown, static floor. maximum loss $3,000, static. streak tolerance of ten gives $300 per trade, which is exactly one contract before costs. adjusting for commission and slippage, the plan fits at one contract with a thin margin, and the survivable streak is ten losses.

the daily limit check. if firm b's daily limit is a fifth of its maximum loss, the session absorbs three losses at $300 - a workable cap of two trades per session. if the daily limit is a tenth, only one loss fits, and the session cap must fall to one trade, which doubles the calendar.

the calendar. at $300 risk and a 1:2 ratio, average win $600, expectation per trade 0.45 × 600 − 0.55 × 300 = $105. a $3,000 target needs 29 trades at expectation; at two trades a session that is fifteen sessions, three weeks.

the conclusion. firm b is the safer rulebook for this strategy, and the reason is not the target or the fee. it is that the trailing floor on firm a made the effective room too small to place the strategy's stop at a survivable size. that is the kind of answer the comparison should produce, and it is available in ten minutes with the firms' current terms in hand.

where an attempt is being run on the trader's behalf, the same arithmetic forms the brief: the contract count, the stop in ticks, the session cap and the calendar are the specification, and they should be derived from the chosen firm's actual clauses rather than from a review. the futures firm guide covers the seven criteria that survive marketing, and the topstep guide works through the two-loss-rule structure in detail.

after the mechanisms have been compared, it is worth noting how much of the two rulebooks is identical - because most of the difficulty difference comes from a small number of clauses rather than from the overall design.

both accounts quote a dollar target and a dollar maximum loss on a fixed account size. both restrict the trader to contracts rather than fractional positions, which means the sizing calculation is the same arithmetic in both cases. both require a minimum number of trading days that a conservative plan satisfies long before the target. and both place the payout conditions in a separate document from the evaluation rules, which means reading the funded terms is mandatory rather than optional with either.

that shared structure is why the comparison reduces to four clauses: the floor mechanism, the presence or absence of a daily loss rule, the lock-in threshold if one exists, and the consistency condition at payout. everything else - the platform, the data feed, the contract list, the minimum days - is either identical or second-order.

there is a practical benefit to that reduction. a trader evaluating three or four futures firms does not need to study four rulebooks; they need to extract those four clauses from each and run the sizing calculation against them. the rules matrix collects exactly those fields, and the futures firm guide sets out the criteria in the order that matters.

one final convergence worth stating: on both accounts, the traders who pass are rarely the ones with the best strategy. they are the ones whose risk per trade was derived from the rules rather than chosen from preference, and who recomputed it when the room changed. that behaviour is transferable between rulebooks; a strategy tuned to one is not.

there is no general answer, because safety depends on the strategy being sized. size the same plan against both rulebooks - maximum loss and daily limit for each - and compare the resulting survivable streak. the rulebook that produces the higher streak for that strategy is the safer one.

two things: how much room the account has once the floor mechanism is accounted for, and how many loss limits apply at once. a static floor gives more effective room than a trailing one at the same percentage, and a second loss rule shortens the survivable streak to the tighter constraint.

for a strategy that holds winners, yes - a retracement from a peak closes a trailing account and only costs a static one the profit. for a strategy that banks profit promptly, the difference is much smaller.

once the floor stops trailing, the account behaves like a static one, so holding winners becomes cheap again. if one firm has a lock-in and the other does not, the second half of an attempt is materially different between them.

read it from the current terms for both, because targets are revised regularly. what matters more than the size is the ratio of the target to the maximum loss: a target that is a large fraction of the loss limit needs more trades at survivable size and therefore a longer calendar.

indirectly. a cheaper account leaves more capital for a second attempt, and a plan with a long calendar pays more in recurring subscriptions. compare total cost to funding - fee plus platform, data, activation and reset - rather than the signup price.

they determine whether a pass becomes income. ask each firm four questions: whether the consistency rule applies at every payout or only the first, whether it is measured on the evaluation record, whether profit above the threshold is fully withdrawable, and how long payment takes.

the daily loss limit ends more evaluations than any other rule, and it is the one traders most often monitor incorrectly. this page covers how it is measured, when it resets, how a floating loss counts against it, and the sizing that keeps it out of reach.
most firms measure the daily limit on equity, including floating positions, so an open losing trade counts before it is closed.
the reset is usually at midnight server time, not at the session close - the gap matters for anyone trading late.
the daily limit is a session rule, not an account rule: breaching it ends the day, not the account, unless the terms say otherwise.
sizing at one third of the daily budget and stopping at eighty percent of it makes a breach practically unreachable.

a daily loss limit is a percentage of the account that may be lost in a single trading day. on a $100,000 account with a 5% limit, the number is $5,000. that much is agreed by everyone. what differs between firms - and what decides how the rule behaves in practice - is the point at which the figure is measured.

three measurement points are in common use. on closed balance, only realised losses count, so a position that is down $3,000 intraday and recovers to break-even never touches the limit. on equity including floating, the worst moment of the day counts, so the same position is $3,000 into the budget while it is open. on the day's starting equity, some firms measure from the balance at the open rather than the current balance, which means a profitable morning raises the day's floor rather than creating a cushion.

the second row is the most common and the one that catches traders. a position that is $2,000 in the red at 10:15 has already consumed $2,000 of the day's budget, whatever it does afterwards. if it recovers and closes at a profit, the budget is restored - but the trader who added a second position at the moment of maximum drawdown may have breached the limit before the recovery.
the same day, two rules: measured on equity, the limit is reached at the low point rather than at the close.

because a floating loss is economically real. a trader who is $4,500 down with a position open has $4,500 less equity than at the open, and the firm's exposure to a further adverse move is the same as if the loss had been banked. measuring on closed balance would allow a trader to run an unlimited floating loss and hope, which is precisely the behaviour a daily limit exists to prevent.

it is stated in the terms, usually in the drawdown or loss section, in one sentence. where the wording is ambiguous - "maximum daily loss of 5%" with no measurement point - ask the firm in writing and keep the reply. this is a question worth a support ticket, because the answer changes position sizing rather than merely the odds.
the reset point decides whether a late-session trade belongs to today's budget or tomorrow's, and it is stated fewer times than you would expect. four conventions exist.

the most common. the budget refreshes at 00:00 in the firm's server timezone, which is often gmt or gmt+3. a trader in new york finishing a session at 17:00 local has several hours of the same daily budget left; a trader in sydney starting at 08:00 local may be in a new budget before the london open.

usually 17:00 new york, aligning with the forex rollover. under this convention the budget refreshes in the middle of the new york afternoon, which means an asian-session trader and a us-session trader are drawing on the same budget at different times of their own days.

rare, and usually found on futures accounts where the trading day is defined by the exchange session. a trader holding a position across the session boundary needs to know whether the loss belongs to the closing day or the opening one.

the least common and the most confusing. the budget is measured over a moving window rather than a session, which means a loss at 09:00 prevents an identical loss at 08:55 the following morning. traders who assume a midnight reset on such an account eventually breach without understanding why.

the useful habit is to write the reset time next to the daily budget on the index card and to treat the last hour before it as belonging to the next day. a trade opened twenty minutes before a reset with the intent of correcting the day's losses is the single most expensive form of impatience in prop trading, because it commits tomorrow's budget to a decision made today.
the equity measurement creates a specific trap that has nothing to do with being wrong about direction.

a position moves into profit by $3,000 and the trader mentally banks it. the position then retraces and closes at break-even. on a closed-balance rule, the day's result is zero. on an equity rule, the run-up was never banked, and the retracement of $3,000 was a $3,000 move against the day's budget even though nothing was lost.

this is why the daily limit and a trailing maximum loss feel similar in practice: both charge for movement that was never realised. on an equity-measured daily limit, the relevant figure is the distance from the day's high-water equity, not from the day's opening balance.

three positions each risking 1% of the daily budget can all be in floating loss at once, which consumes 3% of the day's allowance before any of them is closed. if the plan allowed five such trades, the fifth would breach the limit while every individual trade was sized correctly. the number to track is the aggregate open loss, not the per-trade risk.

around a major release, spreads widen and equity moves against every open position simultaneously. a trader with three positions open through a release can see several hundred dollars of paper loss appear in seconds, charged to the day's budget even if the underlying prices never move. this is the strongest argument for being flat through releases on an equity-measured account.

three rules cover the trap. keep one position open at a time whenever the aggregate floating loss would otherwise be unmonitored. reduce size so that three full-risk losses fit inside sixty percent of the daily budget, leaving room for the float. and close positions before releases rather than sizing for them.
the consequence of a breach is stated in the terms and varies more than traders assume.

the most common arrangement: reaching the daily limit stops trading for that day and the account survives, with a fresh budget at the reset. this is the version that makes the daily rule a session constraint rather than an account constraint, and it is why a single breach does not have to be terminal.

some futures firms treat a daily breach as a failure of the evaluation outright. where that is the case, the rule is effectively a second maximum-loss rule with a twenty-four-hour window, and the sizing discipline has to be correspondingly tighter.

a middle position: a first breach produces a warning, a second ends the account. useful to know, because a firm that warns gives a trader a chance to correct sizing at a cost of nothing but the warning.

stop for the day regardless of what the terms permit, write down the session, and identify the moment the budget was committed - usually the second or third position rather than the first. then reduce per-trade risk by a third for the remainder of the evaluation. a breach is a sizing event, not a market event, and the correction belongs in the size.
sizing is what makes a daily limit a formality rather than a threat.
the daily limit should be a number a trader has to work hard to reach. two decisions make that true.

sizing each trade at a third of the daily budget means three consecutive full-risk losses are required to end the day. with a realistic win rate, three consecutive losses occur often enough that a trader will see them, and rarely enough that they will not see them weekly. sizing at half the budget means two losses end the day; sizing at a quarter means four, which is better still for the limit and slower for the target.

stop the session once eighty percent of the daily budget is spent. the remaining fifth is not unused capital; it is the float that a widening spread or a fast market can consume on a position that is already open. traders who stop at one hundred percent eventually breach, because the limit is measured before the last position is closed.

at 1.65% per trade with an 80% stop, a trader stops after two losses and part of a third. reaching the limit requires ignoring the stop rule, which is a discipline failure rather than a sizing failure and is therefore visible in a journal before it is visible in an account.
the daily budget is one of four numbers on the index card, and it is the one that changes least during a session - which is exactly why traders neglect it.

the budget in dollars, the maximum risk per position, and the current aggregate floating loss (zero at the open). then update the third whenever a position is opened, closed or extended. on an equity-measured account, this running figure is the real distance to the day's limit, and it is the number that should be watched rather than the day's profit and loss.

three positions each risking 1.5% are a 4.5% exposure, not three separate decisions. traders who size each trade correctly while holding four correlated positions at once have followed the rule per trade and breached it in aggregate, which is the most common misreading of the daily limit on multi-position accounts.

once a week, count the sessions in which the budget was more than half spent. if that number is above two, the per-trade risk is too high relative to the plan, and the correction is size rather than selectivity. the budget should be a bound that is approached occasionally and crossed never.

forex firms usually pair a daily limit measured on equity with a static maximum loss, which makes the daily rule the strictly binding constraint. futures firms often express the daily limit in dollars and pair it with a trailing maximum loss, so the two rules are both live and the smaller distance governs. firms offering swing accounts keep the same daily limit but permit overnight exposure, which raises the probability of a gap consuming the budget at the open.

in every case the plan is the same: find the measurement point, find the reset time, size at a third of the budget, and stop at eighty percent of it. those four steps are the difference between a rule that is managed and a rule that ends attempts.
numbers make the measurement point concrete. a $100,000 account, a 5% daily limit - $5,000 - and a trader using 1.6% per trade, or $1,600 per position.

the first position loses $1,600 and the second loses $1,600. closed balance is down $3,200, leaving $1,800 of the budget. the trader has followed the plan: two losses, both at plan size, and the session is still live.

the third position moves against the trader by $1,900 at its worst point. on an equity-measured account the day's drawdown is now $5,100 - a breach, at 11:15, while the position is still open. the position then recovers and closes at a $200 loss, leaving the day at $3,400 in the red, comfortably inside the limit on closed balance.

two things follow from this. first, the breach occurred at the moment of maximum floating loss, not at the close, and no subsequent recovery undoes it. second, the rule that was breached was not the per-trade risk - each position was correctly sized - but the aggregate: the third position's floating loss was counted on top of two realised losses.

after two realised losses, the remaining budget was $1,800. a third position risking $1,600 has $200 of headroom, which is not enough to absorb normal adverse movement. the correct decision at that point was either no third trade or a reduced one at half size - and the rule that produces that decision is the eighty percent stop, which would have ended the session at $4,000 of drawdown rather than continuing into the marginal zone.

had the firm measured closed balance, the day would have finished at $3,400 in the red with no breach. that is the entire practical difference between the two measurement conventions, and it is why a trader moving between firms should not carry a sizing plan from one to the other without re-reading the loss section.
the daily limit resets; the failure floor may not. the two clocks have to be tracked separately.

the two loss rules are usually read separately and they interact all the time. the daily limit governs a session; the maximum loss governs the account. where the maximum loss trails, the daily limit becomes the first line of defence and the trailing floor the second, and the gap between them shrinks as profit accumulates.

on a $100,000 account with a 5% daily limit and a 10% maximum loss, the account can absorb two full daily breaches before failing, if the firm treats a daily breach as survivable. where the maximum loss trails from peak equity, a $4,000 profit reduces the distance to the floor from $10,000 to $6,000, which is barely one daily budget. from that point, a single bad session is a failure, and the sizing that was safe at the start of the evaluation is no longer safe.

plan against whichever is closer, and recompute it each morning. early in an evaluation on a static-drawdown account, the daily limit binds. near the target on a trailing account, the floor binds, and the daily budget should be reduced to a fraction of its original figure rather than held constant.

because the daily limit is the more vivid rule - it ends the session visibly - while the trailing floor moves invisibly as equity rises. a trader who checks the daily budget each morning but not the distance to the floor is monitoring the rule that will end their day and ignoring the rule that will end their account.
breaches are not random. these eight causes cover almost every case, and each has a fix that costs nothing but a written rule.
the recovery trade. two losses followed by a doubled position to get back to flat. the fix is a hard stop after two losses, regardless of the budget remaining.
the uncounted float. three positions sized correctly in isolation, all losing at once. the fix is tracking aggregate floating loss rather than per-trade risk.
the news position. a stop that fills beyond its level during a release, converting a planned loss into an outsized one. the fix is flat through releases or a third of normal size.
the late-session entry. a trade opened twenty minutes before the reset, committing tomorrow's budget to today's frustration. the fix is a hard cut-off time.
the widening stop. moving a stop to avoid a loss, which converts a sized risk into an unsized one. the fix is reducing size instead.
the correlated book. three long dollar positions treated as three decisions. the fix is a two-position cap and treating correlated pairs as one.
the annualised mistake. sizing from the monthly or annual target instead of the day's budget. the fix is writing the daily figure in dollars on the card.
the profitable-morning story. assumption that a good morning creates a cushion, on a firm that measures from the day's opening balance. the fix is asking which convention applies.

every one of them is a decision made before the session rather than during it. that is not a coincidence: the daily limit is breached in the four minutes after a loss, when judgement is worst, so the rules that protect it have to be written when judgement is best.
the daily limit is also the best single question to ask a passing service, because the answer reveals whether the process is rule-driven or outcome-driven.

"what is your per-trade risk against my firm's daily limit, and do you stop at the limit or before it?" a process answer gives a fraction - a third of the budget, stopped at eighty percent. a marketing answer gives a percentage of the account or a statement about how often evaluations pass.

two providers on the same firm with the same target can produce different outcomes purely on the fraction. one uses half the daily budget per trade, which means two losses end the day and the evaluation lasts as long as the losing streaks allow. the other uses a third and stops at eighty percent, which means a bad week costs a few sessions rather than the account.

six lines, written before the first trade and kept next to the platform. together they make the daily limit a bound that is approached rarely and crossed almost never.

the protocol works because it removes the decision from the moment. a trader who has to decide whether a third position is acceptable while two are losing will make a worse decision than one who wrote the answer yesterday.

the last column is identical at every size, which is the point: percentage rules scale exactly, so an account four times larger is not easier, it is the same challenge with larger numbers. the trader who can maintain the protocol on a $25,000 account will maintain it on a $200,000 account, and the trader who cannot will fail at both sizes.

first, stop the session on the loss side at the point the protocol names, not at the point the budget allows. the gap between those two moments is where accounts fail. second, record the day's result in a journal with the highest floating loss reached, because on an equity-measured account the second figure explains breaches that the first figure does not show.

written down, the daily drawdown stops being a rule to fear and becomes a number that is monitored. that transformation - from threat to figure - is what separates traders who finish evaluations from those who repeat them.

the daily limit is measured on equity at most firms, which means an open losing position consumes the budget before it is closed. the reset is usually at midnight server time, so a late trade belongs to tomorrow's budget in effect if not in name. a reachable limit is a badly sized plan, and sizing at a third of the budget with a stop at eighty percent puts it out of reach in ordinary conditions. the maximum loss interacts with the daily rule near the end of an evaluation, when equity has moved and the room for a normal losing sequence has shrunk. and on an account traded by someone else, the fraction of the daily budget used per trade is the single most revealing question to ask before paying.

two actions, both ten minutes. look up your firm's loss section and write down the measurement convention and the reset time, then recompute your per-trade size from the daily budget rather than from your account balance. if the resulting figure feels small, that is the point - the daily limit is meant to be a bound you rarely approach, not a target you spend.

where the evaluation is being traded for you, send those two numbers to the provider and ask whether they match the plan being used. providers who cannot answer in figures are describing an intention rather than a process, and this is one of the cheapest ways to tell the difference before money changes hands. at elitepropx the answer is one third of the daily budget, stopped at eighty percent, for a flat $220 on any firm and any account size, with retries on rule breaches covered, and the daily budget recalculated every morning against the current distance to the failure level rather than against the opening balance.

that last clause is the one most traders skip. on a trailing account, the number that decides position size changes every day the account makes money, and a budget computed once at the start of an evaluation is stale within a week. recomputing it takes ninety seconds and is the difference between a plan that tracks the account and a plan that describes a version of it that no longer exists. do it before the first trade, not after the first loss, and the daily limit becomes a number you watch rather than a rule you fear - and the evaluations that finish are the ones where the numbers were the boring part and the trading was the easy part and the arithmetic was finished before the open, written on a card, and checked twice each morning before the first trade and again at the session's end.

usually equity, including floating positions, which means an open losing trade counts against the limit before it is closed. a minority of firms measure closed balance only - the wording is in the loss section of the terms.

most often at midnight server time, sometimes at the broker's daily close, and occasionally on a rolling twenty-four-hour window. the reset convention is worth writing next to the budget on your card.

it depends on the firm. many end the day only and the account continues with a fresh budget; some futures firms treat it as a failure of the evaluation. the terms state which, and the difference is worth knowing before the first trade.

on an equity-measured account, the drawdown is charged while it exists. if the position recovers and closes flat, the budget is restored, but a breach occurring at the low point stands - the account cannot un-breach.

can the daily limit be repaired if it is nearly spent?

no - the remedy is to stop. the next session starts with a fresh budget, and the account is unaffected unless the firm treats a breach as failure. trying to recover a nearly-spent budget is the behaviour that turns a bad day into a failed evaluation.

firms differ far less than their marketing suggests. almost every evaluation is one of four rulebook families, and once a plan is written for a family, the numbers change between firms but the method does not. that is what makes a flat fee possible. this page sets out how the service adapts to each family, what the terms check covers before any payment, how the handover works, and what the funded stage asks of the account holder afterwards. one flat $220 for any firm and any account size, retries covered while the evaluation runs, no profit split.
evaluations cluster into four families: static drawdown, trailing drawdown, staged targets and instant funding. the family decides the plan; the firm decides the numbers.
a trailing floor requires size to fall as progress accumulates; a static floor does not. that single difference changes the whole risk plan.
the terms check happens before payment and covers the evaluation and the funded account separately.
a pass typically runs one to five weeks depending on the family, the target and the minimum day count.
the service covers the evaluation only. the funded account keeps its own thresholds and belongs to the client.

firms market themselves as unique, and the flourishes are real - different platform, different fee curve, different customer service. the failure mechanics are not unique. nearly every evaluation sold today belongs to one of four families, and identifying the family is the first step in any plan.

static drawdown. the failure floor is fixed, usually as a percentage of the starting balance. profit does not move it, so the account becomes safer as it succeeds. this is the most forgiving structure and the one that permits constant position size from first session to last.

trailing drawdown. the floor rises with equity and never falls. where it trails on closed profit, the risk is that progress reduces the cushion. where it trails on unrealised profit, a winner that retraces has already consumed room. this is the strictest family and the one that punishes otherwise good trading.

staged targets. two or more phases, each with its own target and minimum day count. the mechanic is not the drawdown but the calendar: the evaluation has to be completed across checkpoints, and each phase is an opportunity to breach a conduct rule.

instant funding. no evaluation; the account is funded immediately, and the conditions that would have been an evaluation are attached to the payout instead. the trade-off is usually a smaller initial balance, a longer path to a first withdrawal, or a fee structure that recovers the cost across more accounts.
one curve, three floors. identifying the family takes a minute and decides the entire risk plan.

two clarifications save a lot of confusion. first, families combine: a staged evaluation with a trailing floor is common, and then both the calendar and the cushion have to be managed. second, the basis of a percentage rule matters as much as the percentage, because a limit measured from the current balance behaves differently from one measured from the starting balance once the account moves. both questions belong in the first two minutes of reading any terms page.

the plan is written from the family rather than from the firm, and four numbers carry across every family: risk per trade, the daily stop, the daily profit cap and the weekly pause. what changes between families is the size ladder and the pace.

on a static drawdown evaluation , the ladder is flat. risk per trade is set at a third of the daily limit and stays there. the pace is the target divided by the sessions available, and if that consumes more than a fifth of the daily budget, the schedule is extended rather than the size increased. there is no reason to reduce size near the target, because progress does not make the account fragile.

on a trailing evaluation , the ladder steps down. full size to roughly 40% of the target, three quarters from 40% to 70%, and half beyond 70%. the reason is ratio arithmetic: as completion rises, the gain at risk grows while the buffer shrinks, so the trade that produced the first 70% is not the trade to take at 70%. on a floor that trails unrealised profit, there is a fifth rule: winners are cut at a target rather than ridden, because an excursion that retraces has already moved the floor.

on a staged evaluation , the pace is planned backwards from the day counts rather than forwards from the target. the risk per trade stays at a third of the daily limit throughout, and the numbers are recomputed at the handover against the new balance. the critical discipline is refusing to increase size at a phase boundary: finishing phase one proves the plan works at that size, not that the size was too small.

on an instant funding account , there is no evaluation to pass, so the work is the payout plan. the threshold, the minimum qualifying days and the consistency condition are the constraints from day one, and the daily profit cap is set at a fraction of the threshold so that the payout gate is satisfied by construction rather than repaired later.
one budget across four families. what changes is the ladder, not the arithmetic.

the consistency condition deserves a note because it appears in a different place depending on the family. on an evaluated account it usually binds at the payout, which means the daily profit cap is a planning decision taken weeks before it matters. on an instant funding account it binds from the first payout request, which means the cap is a day-one decision. either way, required total profit equals the largest day divided by the permitted share, and capping the day at a fraction of the target satisfies it before it is ever tested.
two asset classes dominate the industry, and they differ in ways that change the plan beyond the rulebook family.

futures accounts are denominated in contracts with a fixed tick value, so position sizing is discrete and the dollar risk of one contract is knowable to the cent. that is a genuine advantage for a rules-based plan: the daily limit expressed in dollars translates directly into a contract count. the complication is that futures firms enforce conduct rules harder - session windows, news restrictions, contract caps and, at some firms, a cap on how many contracts may be held at any moment. those rules fail accounts quietly because they are often stated in the terms rather than on the evaluation page.

forex accounts are denominated in lots, so sizing is continuous and dollar risk depends on the pair, the lot size and the stop distance. that flexibility makes it easier to fit a risk number to a daily limit, and harder to know what the risk actually is without doing the arithmetic. forex firms tend to be more explicit about percentage limits than futures firms are about conduct, which inverts the failure profile: forex accounts fail on limits, futures accounts fail on rules.

the practical consequence for a service pass is that the plan is the same shape in both cases but the risk of a conduct breach is concentrated differently. on futures, the first thing read is the conduct schedule. on forex, the first thing read is which balance each percentage limit is measured from. the micro futures sizing guide covers the contract arithmetic, and the leverage guide covers the forex equivalent.

before any payment, the terms for the specific firm and program are read and the answer is confirmed in writing. the check is free, it happens before anything is bought, and it produces one of three answers: permitted, prohibited, or silent - and silent is treated as prohibited unless the firm confirms otherwise in writing.

five steps, in order, and each one is documented so that nothing depends on memory.
one - terms check. firm, program and size are read against the current terms, and the answer is confirmed in writing, including the conduct schedule the plan has to respect.

two - purchase. the client buys the evaluation directly from the firm, in their own name, with their own payment method. the evaluation fee is never routed through the service, which keeps ownership unambiguous and puts the client's identity where the firm expects it.
three - handover of access. the scope of access is agreed in writing before it is granted and limited to the evaluation account. nothing else is requested, and the funded account is never accessed.
four - trading. the evaluation is traded to the target within the family-appropriate plan, with progress reported at agreed checkpoints and a failure reported the day it happens.

five - pass and return. the evaluation completes, the firm's own confirmation is shared with the client, access is returned or removed, and the funded account passes to the client with a written summary of its conditions.
five stages, one refusal check, and a handover that returns control rather than retaining it.

two points in that sequence are worth emphasising because they are the industry's usual failure points. step one: a provider that accepts any firm without reading the terms has not checked whether the pass can be paid for. step five: credentials should be returned or removed at handover, and the password changed afterwards regardless - a completed job does not require continuing access to a funded account.
clients ask for a date, and the honest answer depends on the family and the day count rather than on effort.

two habits keep a timeline honest. first, the day count is planned backwards so the profit target and the minimum sessions complete on the same date; a trader who reaches the target early still waits. second, restricted news windows are subtracted from the calendar in advance, because a week with several scheduled releases has a materially shorter usable window than a quiet one.

what a timeline should never do is imply speed. a provider promising a three-day pass on a staged evaluation has not read the day counts, and one promising a fixed date regardless of the firm has not read the rulebook at all. the honest version is a range with the constraint named, which is what the table above provides.
