the case against the service is straightforward and worth stating: a disciplined trader who passes first time is better off self-trading. at a firm fee of roughly $500, one attempt on your own costs about $500 and the service costs about $720 - so the service is $220 worse, and the client also gives up the experience of trading the evaluation. from the second attempt the arithmetic reverses, because the service absorbs retries while self-trading is billed each time. break-even is a single failure.
fee times expected attempts. one failure is the break-even point against the flat fee.

three costs the fee does not remove: the firm's evaluation fee, the firm's reset charge where one applies, and the calendar. minimum day counts apply to a service pass exactly as they apply to anyone else, which is why no honest provider can compress a staged evaluation indefinitely. what the fee does buy is the removal of the reset multiplication and of the attention cost - the weeks a trader would have spent on a failed attempt, which for most people is worth more than the fee difference.
for the payout side of the arithmetic, the profit calculator models what an account produces once its conditions are met, and the 2026 service review applies the same tests to other providers.

the pass produces a funded account and transfers responsibility. the service covers the evaluation; the funded account is governed by the firm's payout conditions, which are usually stricter than the evaluation was.

three conditions carry over and three are new. carried over: the loss limits in some form, the conduct schedule, and the permitted trading hours. new: a profit threshold before any withdrawal, a minimum number of qualifying days, and a consistency condition capping the largest day as a share of total profit.

the consistency condition is the one that catches clients who assume the hard part is done. required total equals the largest day divided by the permitted share, so a single large session can multiply the requirement several times over. the remedy is the same as during the evaluation: cap daily profit at a fraction of the threshold and the gate is satisfied before it is tested.

four steps in the first week, in order. change the password regardless of how access was provided. confirm the account is in your name with your payment details and verification complete. read the funded terms yourself rather than relying on a summary. and write the funded plan before the first trade: risk per trade, daily stop, daily profit cap, minimum qualifying days.

the payout process guide covers the withdrawal sequence and the delays that block first requests, and the failure recovery guide covers what to do if the funded account is lost. the short version of both: complete verification early, request the first payout on the earliest permitted date rather than at the largest available amount, and treat that payment as a test of the process rather than as income.
four refusals define the service as much as the fee does, and each exists because the alternative moves risk to the client without saying so.

we will not hold the funded account. the account is in the client's name and access is returned or removed at handover. continuing to trade someone else's funded account is a managed account in disguise and is prohibited by most firms.

two practices are worth mentioning because they are the shortcuts this industry usually takes. we do not purchase evaluations on the client's behalf - the purchase is made in the client's name with the client's payment method, because ownership is what keeps a funded account valid. and we do not request identity documents, because verification is the account holder's step and cannot be delegated.

the clearest way to see why the family matters is to run one identical sequence of trades against three structures. the plan is deliberately ordinary: 1% risk per trade, a session stop at 3% of the account, a daily profit cap of 2%, and no size increase at any point.

the trade record over ten sessions: plus 1.6%, plus 2.0%, minus 1.0%, flat, plus 1.8%, minus 1.0%, minus 1.0%, plus 2.0%, plus 1.2%, plus 0.8%. total: plus 6.4%. the largest day is plus 2.0%, which is a little over 30% of the total.

on a static drawdown account , the sequence is unremarkable. the failure floor does not move, so the cushion at the end is the starting cushion plus the profit. the only gate left is the consistency ratio, and a 2.0% best day against 6.4% of total profit sits just outside a 30% limit - close enough that a cap of 1.5% would have settled it in advance. the plan was sound; one setting was a little loose.

on a trailing account following closed profit , the picture changes once. profit raises the floor, so the cushion at the end is smaller relative to the balance than at the start. the evaluation survives because the sequence is profitable and the losses are shallow, but the room available at the end is thinner than on the static account, and the size ladder should have stepped down after the fourth session.

on a trailing account following unrealised profit , the same trades are riskier than they look. assume the 2.0% days touched 2.8% and 2.6% before closing at 2.0%. those peaks moved the floor, so the cushion is smaller than the closed profit implies. nothing in the record shows a loss, and yet the account ends the sequence with less room than either of the other two structures.

two lessons fall out of the table. the consistency ratio is identical on all three accounts, because it is computed from realised profit and the rulebook does not change that. and only the failure floor diverges, which is the dimension that closes accounts. a trader who assumes the strictest structure is stricter everywhere is half right: it is stricter in exactly one place, and that place decides survival.

the pacing consequence is worth stating plainly. on the static account the sequence above could have been spread over fourteen sessions at no cost other than calendar. on the intraday trailing account, the same spread would have saved the room that the peaks consumed, because smaller size on the strong sessions would have moved the floor less. same trades, same profit, different outcomes - decided entirely by which family the rulebook belongs to.
seven steps, and each takes minutes. they apply whether the evaluation is traded by a service or by its owner, and they decide whether a pass is worth having.
identify the family. static, trailing, staged or instant - and if trailing, which equity the floor follows.
establish which balance each limit is measured from. starting balance and current equity behave differently the moment the account moves.
convert the target to a percentage and check it against the daily limit rather than against the account size.
read the conduct schedule. news windows, size caps, session hours and holding policies are the rules that fail accounts quietly.
read the funded terms, not just the evaluation. the threshold, the qualifying days and the consistency share are part of the product.
confirm the ownership rules. the account must be in your name, verified by you, with your payment method on it.
write the plan before the first trade. risk per trade, daily stop, daily profit cap, weekly pause - four numbers that survive every firm on the market.

the seventh step is the one that makes the other six worth doing. a rulebook is only as good as the plan applied to it, and a service pass is no different: the deliverable is a completed evaluation, and the account that follows it needs its own plan. the flat-fee model explained covers the pricing side, the complete passing guide covers the plan, and the rules matrix lets you check a firm's mechanics against the rest of the market before buying.

three numbers decide whether an evaluation is worth passing: how many trades the target needs, what the profit is worth after the firm's split and the consistency rule, and how much has to be earned before the evaluation fee and subscriptions are covered. this page works through all three with the formulas written out, plus worked examples at the account sizes most traders buy. for the risk-side calculations - position size, session budgets and trailing room - use the risk and target calculator .
the target is a schedule, not income: what matters is the profit after the split, after the consistency cap, and after costs.
an evaluation fee is a break-even threshold, and it is usually smaller than traders assume once the first payout lands.
the consistency rule, not the split, most often reduces a first withdrawal - plan the daily cap before you trade.
staged evaluations multiply the number of target cycles but keep the same arithmetic per stage.
every input here comes from the firm's current terms; if you use a passing service, the fee comparison changes shape entirely.

most evaluation arithmetic is about risk: how much can be lost, how large a position fits, how many sessions a plan can survive. that is the necessary half, and it is covered by the risk calculator . this page covers the other half, which decides whether passing is actually worth the effort.

four questions, in the order that matters. how many trades does the target require at the plan's measured expectation, and therefore how long will the attempt take? what is the profit worth after the firm's profit split? how much of it can actually be withdrawn on the first request once the consistency rule is applied? and how much profit must be earned before the evaluation fee, platform subscription and data costs are covered?

those four answers change decisions that traders usually make on feel. they decide whether a $25,000 account is worth the same attention as a $100,000 one (it often is, because the fee is lower and the arithmetic is identical). they decide whether a split of 80% with a one-third consistency rule pays more on the first withdrawal than a split of 90% with a one-fifth rule (it frequently does). and they decide whether a passing service at a flat fee is a bargain or a luxury - a comparison that is impossible to make without the payout arithmetic.

one warning belongs at the front rather than the end. profit splits, consistency ratios, payout thresholds and payment intervals are revised regularly, and a page that quotes them is accurate only until the next revision. the formulas below are the durable part; the inputs have to be read from the firm's own terms on the day the account is bought.
everything before the withdrawal is a condition. the payout is the number that matters.
six numbers, all published or measurable. two of them come from the firm and four from the trader's own records, which is why an evaluation bought before the records exist produces surprises.

two of these are commonly replaced with guesses, and both replacements are expensive. expected value per trade is a measurement, not an intention: it should come from at least a month of recorded trades including spread, commission and slippage, not from a backtest or a memory of a good week. total cost to funding is not the signup fee: it is the fee plus every month of platform and market-data subscription the calendar requires, plus any activation charge on the funded account.

where a value cannot be found in the terms, the fastest route is a written question to support. firms interpret their own documents, and a reply saved before purchase is worth more than any comparison page - including this one, and including the 2026 comparison and the rules matrix , both of which are structured to make the extraction faster.
formula: trades to target = profit target ÷ expected value per trade.

expected value per trade is the win rate multiplied by the average win, minus the loss rate multiplied by the average loss, with all four figures in money and all of them net of costs. the output is the number of trades required at expectation - not the number that will be taken, because variance decides that, but the pace the plan implies.

divide by the planned trades per week to get the calendar. two trades a session across five sessions a week is ten trades weekly; 29 trades at expectation is therefore about three weeks. that number is the honest completion time, and it is the input to the break-even calculation later on.

two adjustments make the result realistic rather than optimistic. first, sessions lost to the daily limit reduce the effective trade count: a plan that averages four sessions a week rather than five takes 25% longer. second, the plan's own selectivity means some sessions produce no qualifying setup at all. both adjustments push the calendar out, which is the direction of safety.
target and loss limit define the same journey. the target sets the number of steps.

where the calculation produces a trade count that implies a calendar longer than the trader is willing to fund, the levers are the same three as ever: improve the reward-to-risk ratio, raise the win rate by becoming more selective, or add sessions within the daily limit. raising position size changes none of the four inputs to this formula; it changes the loss side of the plan, which is the subject of the risk calculator.

the split applies to what is withdrawn, not to the balance, and the distinction matters because profit left in the account is not income. on a trailing-drawdown account it is worse than that: unwithdrawn profit raises the failure floor behind the trader, making the account more fragile while paying nothing.

a worked illustration of why the split is rarely the deciding factor. two firms: one offers 90% with a one-fifth consistency rule, the other 80% with a one-third rule. a trader whose best day is $1,500 and whose profit at the threshold is $6,000 can withdraw the full $6,000 under the one-third rule - 80% of which is $4,800. under the one-fifth rule, the same best day limits the withdrawable amount to $7,500 of total profit, so a $6,000 record cannot be withdrawn in full; the trader can take $4,500, keeping a fifth as the permitted day, and 90% of that is $4,050. the nominally better split pays less on the first cycle.

that comparison is the single most useful output of this page, and it is invisible in any table that lists splits without the consistency rule attached. the consistency guide covers the ratio variants and how each converts into a withdrawal limit.

three further clauses change the net figure and belong in the same calculation. whether the split rises after a number of payouts or after a threshold of profit. whether the firm retains a buffer inside the account that must be maintained before withdrawal. and whether the payment method carries a fee - bank transfer, card or crypto routes differ, and on a small first payout the difference is material.
formula: withdrawable profit = largest day ÷ consistency ratio (and no more than the recorded profit).

if the best day may not exceed a stated share of the profit being withdrawn, then the withdrawable amount is limited by the largest day divided by that share. a $1,500 best day under a one-third rule permits $4,500; under a one-fifth rule, $7,500. recorded profit above the permitted amount simply waits until more trading brings the ratio back into line.

this is the calculation that most often determines the size of a first payout, and it is decided long before the withdrawal request - by whether the trader capped daily profit during the funded month. a plan with a daily profit cap set below the ratio satisfies the condition automatically; a plan without one discovers it at the request, when the options are to keep trading or to withdraw less.
the largest day sets the floor on the total that can be withdrawn. cap it early.

the reverse calculation is the one to run before the funded month begins: given the consistency ratio and the payout threshold, what daily profit cap satisfies the ratio at the point the threshold is reached? the answer is the ratio multiplied by the threshold. a one-third rule against a $6,000 threshold allows $2,000 in a single day, so a cap of $1,500 leaves margin and costs very little pace on a plan whose average winning day is a fraction of that.
formula: break-even profit = total cost to funding ÷ split percentage.

the break-even figure is the profit that must be withdrawn before the exercise has paid for itself. it is usually smaller than traders expect, and the reason is that the fee is a one-off while the payout recurs.

a worked illustration. fee $500, platform and data $100 a month over a three-month calendar, activation $150 on funding: total cost to funding is $950. at an 80% split, the break-even is $1,188 of withdrawn profit. on a $100,000 account with an $8,000 evaluation target, the first payout clears it several times over - provided the consistency rule permits a full withdrawal, which is precisely why calculation three has to be run first.

the same arithmetic run on a small account produces a less comfortable answer. a $25,000 account with a $200 fee, $100 a month in subscriptions, no activation and a three-month calendar has a total cost of $500; at 80% the break-even is $625 of withdrawn profit. on a plan whose funded profit is a fraction of a percent per day, that is a realistic first target rather than a formality.

two costs are frequently omitted and both belong in the total. subscriptions continue during a failed attempt, so the expected cost of success is the total divided by the probability of passing, not the total for a single attempt - which is where a flat-fee passing service changes the arithmetic entirely. and the calendar itself is a cost: every month spent in an evaluation is a month not producing funded profit, and on a monthly-fee structure it is also a direct charge.
all four calculations in sequence, with placeholder inputs. the numbers are illustrative; the order and the formula use is the transferable part.

terms assumed for the example. two phases, 8% target each, $100,000 account, 10% maximum loss, 5% daily limit, 80% split on the funded account, one-third consistency rule, $6,000 payout threshold, one-off $500 fee, $100 a month in platform and data, $150 activation on funding.

step one, trades to target. at $600 risk per trade, a 1:2 ratio gives an average win of $1,200 and an average loss of $600. at a 45% win rate, expectation is 0.45 × 1,200 − 0.55 × 600 = $210 per trade. the $8,000 target needs 39 trades at expectation; at ten trades a week that is four weeks per phase, eight weeks for both.
step two, cost to funding. $500 fee + $800 of subscriptions over eight weeks + $150 activation = $1,450. at 80%, the break-even is $1,812 of withdrawn profit.

step three, consistency cap. a one-third rule against the $6,000 threshold permits a $2,000 best day. a daily cap of $1,500 satisfies the ratio with margin. if the funded month produces $6,000 with a $1,500 best day, the ratio is 25% - inside the limit.

step four, net first payout. $6,000 withdrawn × 80% = $4,800, against a break-even of $1,812. the first cycle covers the cost of the evaluation roughly two and a half times, which is the number that makes the whole exercise worth doing - and it took four calculations to see it.

two sensitivities are worth running on the same inputs. if the calendar stretches to twelve weeks because sessions are lost to daily limits, subscriptions rise by $400 and the break-even moves to $2,062 - still comfortably covered, which is the reassuring direction. if the consistency rule were one-fifth rather than one-third, the permitted best day would fall to $1,200 and the withdrawable amount to $6,000 only once the ratio allowed it; the first payout would be smaller and the break-even further away.
the same formulas on a smaller account, which is where most first attempts happen and where the arithmetic is least forgiving.

terms assumed. single phase, 8% target, $25,000 account, 10% maximum loss, 5% daily limit, 85% split, one-quarter consistency rule, $1,500 threshold, $150 fee, $80 a month in subscriptions, no activation.

trades to target. a $150 risk per trade at a 1:2 ratio gives an expectation of about $52 per trade at a 45% win rate, so a $2,000 target needs 38 trades - the same count as the large account, because percentage targets are scale-free. the calendar is identical; only the dollars differ.

cost to funding. $150 + $320 over four weeks + $0 = $470. at 85%, break-even is $553 of withdrawn profit - about a quarter of the account's target, which is a more demanding ratio than the $100,000 example.

consistency. a one-quarter rule against a $1,500 threshold permits a $375 best day. that is a tighter daily cap than most plans naturally produce, which means the cap is not decorative: it changes position size, because a $375 profit cap on a plan risking $150 per trade implies a limit on how far a winner can run.

the conclusion. the $25,000 account has identical percentage arithmetic and a slightly worse cost-to-payout ratio, which is the honest case for buying the smaller account first: it costs less to fail, and the plan that passes it passes the larger one unchanged. the beginners guide covers the selection criteria for a first account, and the passed challenges page shows what completed attempts look like in practice.
the comparison between buying a funded account and passing an evaluation is the one place where this arithmetic changes a decision outright.

an evaluation route costs the fee plus the subscriptions over the calendar, and it can fail. an instant funding route costs more up front and produces a funded account immediately, with its own drawdown and payout conditions. the comparison is expected cost against time, and both are quantifiable.

take an evaluation with a $500 fee and a four-month calendar at $100 a month, giving $900 at cost, and assume a one-in-two pass rate on a fair attempt. expected cost to funding is $900 ÷ 0.5 = $1,800, spread over an average of two attempts. now price an instant account at $2,500 with a similar funded drawdown. the instant route is more expensive on expected cost and cheaper in calendar time: it starts producing payout-eligible profit on day one rather than in month five.

whether that trade is worth making depends on the trader's own pass probability and on how much the calendar is worth to them. a trader who has failed two evaluations for the same reason is paying $1,800 to learn nothing new; a trader with a measured plan that fits the rules is paying $2,500 to skip a sequence they were likely to complete. the instant funding guide covers the conditions those accounts still carry, which are not identical to an evaluation's funded stage.

most traders choose an account by finding the largest one they can afford to fail. the arithmetic on this page suggests a different rule: choose the smallest account whose break-even is a small fraction of its first payout, because the payout ratio - not the balance - is what makes an evaluation worth repeating.

run the two worked examples side by side and the point is visible. on the $100,000 account the break-even was $1,812 against a first payout of $4,800, a ratio of roughly one to two and a half. on the $25,000 account it was $553 against a first payout of about $1,275, a ratio of one to two and a quarter. the larger account is marginally better on cost recovery and materially worse on cost of failure, because a failed attempt costs the same in calendar time and a larger fee.

the same calculation run on a very small account usually inverts. where the fee is a large fraction of the balance, the break-even stretches across the whole first payout and sometimes beyond it, so the account has to be passed twice to pay for itself once. that is the point at which a trader should stop looking at the account sizes and start looking at the firm selection criteria again.

a practical rule follows. compute the break-even for each candidate account, then divide it by the expected first payout. if the result is above a third, the account is too expensive for the plan at that stage and a smaller one will recover its cost faster even though it pays less in dollars. once a first cycle has completed and the payment route is known, size can be increased with the whole chain tested.

two costs belong in that decision and are easy to leave out. subscriptions continue during a failed attempt, so the break-even figure should be computed for an expected cost of success rather than for a single attempt - the fee divided by the pass rate, essentially. and the calendar is the largest invisible cost: months spent in an evaluation are months not producing funded profit, and on any plan with a recurring monthly charge they are a direct addition to the number.

treating the target as income. the target is an evaluation condition. what can be withdrawn is the funded-stage profit, after the split and the consistency cap, and the two numbers are unrelated in size.

comparing splits without consistency rules. a 90% split with a one-fifth rule can pay less on a first withdrawal than an 80% split with a one-third rule, as the earlier example shows. the split is the multiplier; the consistency rule sets the multiplicand.

using the signup fee as the cost. subscriptions accrue monthly and activation can be charged on funding. the total cost to funding - divided by the pass probability - is the figure to compare against any alternative, including a flat-fee service.

ignoring the payment interval. a higher split paid quarterly can pay less in the first year than a smaller split paid monthly. on a first funding, the cadence matters more than the percentage, because the information gained from a completed cycle is worth more than the difference in rate.
a passing service converts a variable cost into a fixed one, and the comparison is made with this page's arithmetic rather than with the fee alone.

the calculation is straightforward. the expected cost of attempting alone is the total cost to funding divided by the probability of passing, plus the funded profit not earned during the attempts. against that, a flat fee per evaluation is a known number. a trader with a one-in-three pass rate on a $900 cost base has an expected cost of $2,700 before the platform months consumed by the failures; a flat fee below that is cheaper in expectation, and it removes the variance as well as the average.

four checks make the comparison valid. the price should be flat and independent of account size and stage, so it can be compared directly. retries should be covered, since a fixed price with retry charges is a per-attempt price with extra steps. the funded account should be in the trader's name with credentials under their control, and the service should take no share of payouts - a provider paid from payouts has an incentive to keep trading after the pass. and the firm's terms must permit third-party trading, separately for the evaluation and the funded account, confirmed in writing before payment.

elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid the arrangement. the passing services guide sets out the due diligence script, the service review works through how providers are compared, and the client feedback page collects what buyers report. all three are written to be read before payment rather than after. to start an attempt, the contact page is the entry point; the faq answers the questions that come up most often.

two of the six inputs change over time - expectation per trade, which accumulates evidence, and the calendar, which either shortens or extends. a monthly review of four numbers keeps the arithmetic honest in about ten minutes.

record trades taken, expectation per trade, worst drawdown so far, and distance to target. then rerun calculation one to see whether the calendar has moved, and calculation four to see whether the break-even is still within reach. if the expectation has fallen, the plan has drifted and the correct response is to trade less rather than more. if the calendar has extended, the cost to funding has risen and the break-even figure with it.

the value of the review is that it makes the decision monthly rather than continuously. a trader reviewing every session reacts to noise; a trader reviewing monthly reacts to the plan. on an evaluation with a fixed deadline, that difference is the whole discipline - and it is the same discipline the post-pass guide applies to the funded month, where the payout threshold replaces the target as the thing being measured.
four calculations cover the distance between buying an evaluation and being paid for passing it.
how do i calculate what a prop firm payout is worth?

multiply the profit being withdrawn by the profit split. before that, work out the withdrawable amount: the largest single day determines the maximum under the consistency rule, so permitted profit is the largest day divided by the ratio. then apply the split.
how many trades does it take to hit a profit target?

divide the target by expected value per trade, where expectation is win rate times average win minus loss rate times average loss, net of costs. divide that trade count by trades per week for the calendar. most conservative plans need twenty to forty trades.
how much profit do i need to cover the evaluation fee?

divide total cost to funding by the profit split. total cost is the fee plus platform and data subscriptions over the calendar plus any activation charge. on a $100,000 account with a $500 fee and a three-month calendar, break-even is typically around $1,200 of withdrawn profit.

only after applying the consistency rule. a 90% split with a one-fifth rule can pay less on a first withdrawal than an 80% split with a one-third rule, because the rule sets the maximum withdrawable amount and the split only multiplies it.

the largest amount that can be withdrawn when a best-day share applies: divide the largest trading day by the consistency ratio, and cap it at the recorded profit. a $1,500 best day under a one-third rule permits $4,500.

in dollars, yes, because targets and thresholds scale with the balance. in percentage terms the arithmetic is identical, which is why the plan that passes a $25,000 account passes a $100,000 one unchanged - the only difference is the fee and the dollars per cycle.
how long does an evaluation take to pay for itself?

usually the first payout cycle, if a full withdrawal is permitted. break-even is total cost to funding divided by the split; on most accounts that is a fraction of one threshold, provided the consistency rule does not restrict the first withdrawal.
why does the payment interval matter more than the split?

because it multiplies over a year. a larger split paid quarterly can pay less over twelve months than a smaller split paid monthly. on a first funding, completing a cycle matters more than the rate, because it establishes the route and the timing.
should i buy a bigger account for a bigger payout?

usually not for a first attempt. percentage rules are scale-free, so a smaller account costs less to fail and teaches the same arithmetic. buy size after a completed payout cycle, not before the first one.

divide the evaluation's total cost to funding by the pass probability to get expected cost, then compare with the instant account's price plus the calendar time each route consumes. the instant route is usually more expensive and quicker to produce payout-eligible profit.

it replaces expected cost with a fixed one. compare the flat fee against total cost to funding divided by the pass rate, plus the funded profit not earned during failed attempts. elitepropx charges $220 flat per evaluation, covers retries, and takes no profit split.

in the funded terms, which are usually a separate document from the evaluation rules. if either is missing or ambiguous, ask support in writing before paying the evaluation fee and keep the reply - it is both an input and a record.
what if my records are too thin to calculate expectation?

then the plan is not ready to be bought. a month of recorded trades at small size produces the win rate, average win, average loss and realised cost per trade that the formulas need. buying an evaluation to discover those numbers is the most expensive way to learn them.

these two firms are often compared as though the question were which one is cheaper or which one is easier. neither answer survives contact with the rulebooks. ftmo imposes a deadline and a strict set of loss rules; the5ers removes the deadline and, on its staged model, makes the failure floor static. that single difference changes the arithmetic of every trade, the pace a plan must hold, and the kind of trader who finishes. this comparison works the mechanics rather than the marketing.
a static drawdown measured from the starting balance is the most forgiving structure available, because progress cannot make the account more fragile.
a deadline is a constraint, and removing it removes the mechanism that forces a trader to compute a pace - so the pace has to be self-imposed or the evaluation drifts.
both firms apply a daily limit and a maximum limit. the question is which balance each is measured from, because that decides how the account behaves after a drawdown.
neither firm's evaluation is the hard part. the payout gate - minimum days, consistency, verification - is where a pass stops being an achievement and starts being an income.
cost per funded account is fee multiplied by expected attempts, not the fee on the pricing page.
terms change. confirm current figures on both firms' pages; this comparison describes structure, not a contract.

start with the structural differences, because they determine everything downstream. both firms are forex specialists. both run staged evaluations. both apply a daily loss limit and a maximum loss limit, and both require a minimum number of trading days. the differences are concentrated in four places.

the table looks mild. it is not. two of those rows - drawdown basis and time limit - interact in a way that makes the two firms suit genuinely different people, and a trader who ignores the interaction will choose the wrong one and then blame their own trading.

consider the interaction directly. on a static floor, a winning account's cushion does not shrink as profit accumulates, so a trader can keep size constant from the first session to the last. on a trailing floor, the cushion shrinks with progress, so size must fall. on a deadline, the trader must compute a required weekly profit to finish on time; without a deadline, no such computation is forced, so the trader must impose one. put those together and the two firms ask for opposite disciplines: ftmo asks for a pace and a shrinking size ladder, the5ers asks for a self-imposed pace and a constant size.
static, end-of-day and intraday structures. the5ers' staged model sits at the forgiving end; ftmo's limits are fixed percentages rather than a trailing peak.
drawdown is the only rule that can end an account in a single day, so it deserves to be read before the target. the relevant questions are not "how much" but "measured from what" and "does it move".

a static floor measured from the starting balance never moves. if the floor is a fixed percentage of the initial balance, then a $100,000 account with a 10% floor fails at $90,000 forever, whether the trader is at $100,000 or at $130,000. the cushion grows with profit: at $130,000 the trader has $40,000 of room. this is the most forgiving structure in the industry, and it is what makes the5ers' staged model attractive for a trader who expects to be profitable but uneven.

a relative floor measured from current equity moves with the balance. a 10% limit on a $100,000 account fails at $90,000; after profit to $120,000 it fails at $108,000. the cushion stays at 10% of equity, so it grows in dollars as the account grows but never as a share. this is stricter than a static floor after a winning run, and more forgiving after a losing run - which is the opposite of what most traders assume.

a trailing floor that follows peak equity is the strictest of the three, because it responds to unrealised profit on an intraday basis. profit raises the floor immediately, so a winner that retraces permanently reduces the cushion. this structure is common on futures accounts and rare on staged forex evaluations, but it is worth knowing because traders move between asset classes and carry assumptions with them.

the middle row is the one traders misjudge. a relative limit is described as "10% drawdown", which sounds identical to a static 10%, and it is - until the account moves. after a 30% gain the relative floor has climbed $27,000 while the static floor has not moved at all. on a winning account, that difference is the entire margin between a comfortable evaluation and a tight one.

so the first thing to establish about either firm is which basis applies, and whether the evaluation and the funded account use the same one. they often do not: it is common for an evaluation to apply a relative limit and a funded account to apply a static one, or the reverse. read both, and note that a stricter evaluation with a looser funded stage is a reasonable trade - the difficulty is front-loaded where it costs a fee rather than a payout.
progress against three floors. only the static structure gives the trader more room as the account grows.
a deadline is usually discussed as a source of pressure, which undersells it. it performs three separate functions, and only one of them is about pressure.

it sets a pace. if a target must be reached in a fixed number of weeks, a trader can divide and get the required weekly profit. that number is checkable: is it achievable at a risk per trade the daily limit can survive? with no deadline, this calculation is never forced, so traders drift. some go far too slowly and take a year to finish something that required two months. others trade as though there were a deadline without ever doing the arithmetic, which is the worst of both.

it legitimises stopping. reaching a target on a deadline account has a natural endpoint: the evaluation is complete. without one, reaching the target raises a question - should i keep going to build a buffer, or stop? that question has no correct answer, and traders answer it differently every day depending on mood. the result is an account that has already passed and keeps trading, which is the purest form of unnecessary risk available.

it bounds the exposure. every session is a chance to breach a rule. a deadline bounds the number of sessions, and therefore the number of chances. this is a genuine advantage of a deadline that is rarely stated, and it is the reason some traders pass faster firms more reliably despite the pressure.

removing the deadline removes all three. the5ers' staged model does not replace them with anything, which is a feature rather than an oversight - it simply returns the responsibility to the trader. the correct response is to impose all three yourself: pick a target date, work backwards to a weekly requirement, decide in advance what counts as finished, and stop.

the self-imposed deadline: choose a date, divide the target by the sessions available before it, and check the result against the daily limit. if the required pace consumes more than a fifth of the daily budget per session, the date is wrong - not the plan.

there is a second-order effect worth naming. without a deadline, a losing position has no external pressure to be closed, so it is held. on a static floor, holding is not neutral: the position consumes the buffer that the rules measure, and the buffer is the only thing between the trader and a reset. a deadline does not prevent this, but it does create a reason to resolve the position rather than defer it. on a no-deadline account the trader has to supply that reason, and supplying it is a skill that has to be practised.

both firms express targets as percentages of the account, which makes them directly comparable - unlike futures firms, where the dollar target has to be converted first. the comparison that matters is target percentage against daily limit, because that ratio decides how much variance a plan can absorb.

take a target of 8% and a daily limit of 5%, which is representative of the staged forex structure. over twenty trading sessions the required average is 0.4% per session, which is 8% of the daily budget. that is a comfortable plan: twenty losing sessions at a fifth of the daily limit would still leave the account alive, and the target is reached by ordinary trading rather than by a single exceptional week.

now take a target of 10% with the same daily limit and a deadline of ten sessions. the required average becomes 1% per session, a fifth of the daily budget, and the plan has five sessions of full-limit losses of tolerance before the maximum becomes the binding number. the target has not changed much; the tolerance has collapsed. that is what a deadline does to a plan, and it is why the same trader can pass one firm and fail the other without changing a single decision.
target as a percentage, pace as a fraction of the daily budget. the second number is the one that predicts survival.

the practical rule: a plan that requires more than a fifth of the daily budget per session is depending on the market rather than on execution. it can still pass, but it will pass in the fortnights when conditions cooperate, and those fortnights are not scheduled. a plan under a tenth is relying on the trader showing up, which is a bet worth making.
both firms gate withdrawals, and the gates are the part of the product that most comparisons omit. there are four, and each one has a failure mode.

minimum trading days. a payout requires a number of qualifying days, and a qualifying day usually requires a closed profit rather than merely activity. a trader who reaches the profit threshold in a week may still need two more weeks of small positive sessions, and a plan that does not land both conditions on the same date wastes calendar.

the consistency check. a cap on the largest day as a share of total profit. the arithmetic is a division: required total equals best day divided by the permitted share. a trader with a $3,000 best day under a 30% rule needs $10,000 of total profit before the withdrawal clears, and no amount of requesting changes that.

verification. identity and, in some cases, source-of-funds checks. complete them before the first request rather than at it, because a document request is the single most common cause of a delayed first payout.
processing schedule. payments run on a posted cadence, so the first request usually takes longer than later ones. treat the first withdrawal as a test of the process and size it accordingly.
four gates between a pass and a payment. only one of them is about trading.

the consistency gate is where the two firms' structures produce different advice. on a no-deadline account, a trader can afford to keep trading at small size until the ratio has headroom, because calendar is not the constraint. on a deadline account, the same trader has less calendar to spend, so the ratio has to be protected from the beginning - which means the daily profit cap is not optional, it is the mechanism that makes the deadline survivable.

a fee is a price per attempt. a funded account is the product. the number that compares firms is therefore fee multiplied by the number of attempts a trader of given discipline typically needs, plus reset charges along the way.

two firms can differ by 40% on the pricing page and reverse their ranking after two attempts. they can also reverse it after one, if the cheaper firm's structure produces a larger expected number of attempts. this is not a hypothetical: the whole point of a static floor is that it raises the pass rate, and a higher pass rate is worth a higher fee.
fee times attempts. the cheap evaluation stops being cheap the moment it needs a second purchase.

there is a third path that changes the shape of the curve rather than the height: a flat-fee passing service, which trades the evaluation once for a fixed price and covers resets while it runs. at a flat $220 for any firm and any account size, the expected cost is the fee plus the firm's own reset charge if one is needed - not fee times attempts. that does not make it automatically cheaper, because the trader gives up control of the evaluation and, more importantly, because many firms prohibit third-party trading. where a firm prohibits it, the service should decline the job rather than accept the risk on the client's behalf. the 2026 service review sets out what to verify, and the service comparison prices the alternatives.

for the do-it-yourself path, the comparison should include three costs the fee does not capture: the calendar, the attention, and the opportunity cost of a funded account that could have been earning during the attempts. a trader who needs three attempts and six weeks has spent more than three fees. the profit calculator handles the payout side of that question, and the firm comparison puts the fee in context against the rest of the field.
this is where a comparison becomes useful, because the honest answer is that each firm rewards a different temperament.

a deadline suits a trader who works best to a schedule. if you already trade a fixed session, keep a journal with dates, and find open-ended tasks difficult to finish, ftmo's structure supplies the pacing you would otherwise have to manufacture. the cost is a narrower tolerance for a slow start, and the mitigation is choosing a target date early enough that the required pace stays under a tenth of the daily budget.

no deadline suits a trader whose edge is uneven. if your profitable months are strong and your losing months are shallow, a static floor plus unlimited calendar is close to ideal: the good month does not make the account more fragile, and the shallow loss can be recovered without a clock. the risk is drift, and the mitigation is a written target date that you treat as binding even though the firm does not.

neither suits a trader without a written plan. this is arithmetic rather than judgement. both accounts have a fixed failure floor and a fixed target. a trader sizing by feel is running an uncontrolled process against a control system, and the control system wins on a long enough timeline. the fix is a page of numbers, not a different firm.

nor does either suit a trader who cannot trade the news windows. both firms restrict trading around scheduled releases, and both treat a breach as a breach regardless of outcome. if your available hours overlap the windows consistently, the evaluation is testing your schedule rather than your trading.

one further fit question that is rarely asked: which firm's rulebook does your existing strategy already satisfy? if your strategy holds positions for days, a no-deadline staged model with a static floor fits it and a weekend-holding restriction may not. if your strategy is intraday scalping with tight stops, the deadline matters less than the daily limit and the news windows. read the conduct rules of both before comparing fees, because the conduct rules decide whether your strategy is admissible at all.

the clearest way to see the difference is to run one plan against both structures with identical trades. the plan is deliberately ordinary: 1% risk per trade, a daily stop at 3%, a daily profit cap at 2.5%, four sessions a week, and a rule that size never increases.
the trade record over ten sessions: +1.8%, +2.4%, −1.0%, flat, +1.6%, −1.0%, −1.0%, +2.2%, +1.4%, +1.0%. total: +7.4%. the largest day is +2.4%, which is 32% of the total.

on a static floor the sequence is unremarkable. progress does not move the failure floor, so the cushion at the end is the starting cushion plus the profit. the only gate left is the consistency ratio: 32% against a 30% rule is a fail by a fraction, which is exactly the kind of near-miss that a daily cap at 2.2% would have prevented. the plan's structure was sound and its cap was one setting too loose.

on a relative floor the picture changes twice. early losses reduce the balance, so the 10% floor drops in dollars - the account loses room as it loses money, which is stricter than a static floor during a drawdown. later profits raise the floor, so the cushion at +7.4% is smaller in dollars than the static case. the plan survives both, but the margin is thinner in both directions, and a trader who had a 2% drawdown in week three would have had less room to recover than on a static account.

note what the table shows: the consistency ratio is identical on both accounts, because it is computed from realised profit and the rule does not change that. only the failure floor differs. traders routinely assume the stricter structure is stricter everywhere; it is stricter in exactly one dimension, and that dimension is the one that closes accounts.

the pacing lesson follows. on the static, no-deadline structure, the same seven-point-four percent could have been earned over fourteen sessions instead of ten with no cost other than calendar. on the deadline structure, those four extra sessions do not exist, so the plan has to earn the same amount faster - which means either more risk per trade or a better selection of setups. if neither is available, the deadline converts into a consistency problem, because the only way to compress time is to have a bigger day.
four questions, answered in order, produce a decision without reference to a review or a ranking.
does your strategy fit the conduct rules? holding period, instruments, news windows, weekend exposure. if the answer is no for one firm, the comparison is over, and no fee difference justifies it.

is your edge even or lumpy? even edges do well with a deadline, because the required pace is achievable by ordinary trading. lumpy edges do better without one, because the good month carries the evaluation.
do you finish open-ended tasks? be honest. a trader who drifts on open-ended work should buy the deadline, even at a higher pace requirement, because the alternative is an evaluation that never ends.

what is the cost per funded account? fee times expected attempts, including resets. compare that number, not the headline fee, and include the flat-fee alternative if the firm permits third-party trading.

the order matters. most traders start at question four because the fee is the only number on the page, and then discover at question one that their strategy was never admissible. reading the rulebook costs twenty minutes; failing an evaluation for a conduct breach costs a fee and a month.

there is no universal answer, and any comparison that offers one is describing its own preferences. what can be said with confidence is this: the static floor is strictly more forgiving than the relative floor at equal percentage, the deadline is strictly more helpful to a trader who needs pacing and strictly more harmful to a trader whose edge is lumpy, and the payout gates are identical in kind even when they differ in number.

the practical recommendation, for a trader who has not yet bought either, is to run the plan on a demo account under both sets of rules for four weeks. same trades, two rulebooks, and record which one your equity curve survives. that exercise costs nothing and answers the question more reliably than any review, because it tests your behaviour rather than the firm's marketing.

if the answer is that neither fits - because the fee is repeated, the pace is unreachable, or the calendar is short - the flat-fee route exists precisely for that case. at $220 for any firm and account size, with resets covered while the evaluation runs, it converts a repeated wager into a single fixed cost, and it is available only where the firm's terms allow third-party trading. the passed challenges page shows what completed evaluations look like, and the rules matrix lets you check any firm's mechanics against these two before committing.

whichever route you take, the same three rules travel with you: a written risk per trade, a daily stop at 80% of the limit, and a daily profit cap at about a third of the target. those three numbers survive every firm, every rulebook and every fee schedule, and they are the difference between an evaluation that measures your trading and one that measures your temperament.
comparisons fail in predictable ways, and each failure has a price.

comparing headline fees. the fee is per attempt, so the comparison is fee times expected attempts. a firm 40% cheaper that needs two attempts costs more than a firm that needs one, and the difference is larger than the fee gap.

reading the target and skipping the daily limit. the target sets the destination and the daily limit sets the route. a modest target with a tight daily limit is harder than a larger target with a generous one, because the second permits the losing days that a real plan contains.

assuming a percentage means a fixed dollar amount. "10% drawdown" describes a static floor, a relative floor, or a trailing peak, and the three behave differently the moment the account moves. the percentage is not the rule; the basis is.

ignoring the payout gates until after the pass. minimum days, consistency and verification are part of the product. a firm whose evaluation is easy and whose payout is gated at a 20% best-day share is harder to earn from than its evaluation suggests.

choosing the firm whose marketing matches your self-image. the trader who believes they are aggressive buys the tightest structure and discovers that aggression is a cost. the trader who believes they are patient buys the open-ended structure and discovers that patience needs a deadline. buy the rulebook your last twenty sessions would have survived, not the one that flatters you.

each of those mistakes is cheap to fix before payment and expensive to fix afterwards. a twenty-minute read of both rulebooks, a written plan, and one demo month under each structure is the entire preparation, and it costs nothing but attention.

for the mechanics of either firm specifically, the ftmo guide and the the5ers guide go deeper than a comparison can, and the ftmo versus apex comparison covers the cross-asset question. the faq answers the questions that recur, and the contact page is where a flat-fee evaluation starts if you would rather not run it yourself.

ftmo is harder on pace, because a deadline compresses the calendar and forces a required profit per session. the5ers is harder on self-discipline, because no deadline means nothing external enforces a pace or tells you when to stop. which is harder depends on which of those two constraints you handle worse.

on its staged model, the5ers uses a static floor measured from the starting balance, which is the most forgiving structure available - profit does not reduce the cushion. ftmo's percentage limits are applied to the account, so the cushion moves with the balance. read the current terms for both, because the basis can differ between the evaluation and the funded stage.

technically yes, practically no. the firm will not stop you, but an evaluation that runs for months has spent more in calendar and attention than it saved in pace, and the account remains exposed to a rule breach the entire time. impose your own target date and treat it as binding.

on a deadline structure, the phase length dictates the pace and a realistic pass uses most of the available sessions. on a no-deadline structure, fifteen to twenty-five sessions at a pace under a tenth of the daily budget is typical. faster passes on either are possible and usually create a consistency problem at payout.

a third of the daily limit at most, with the session closed at 80% of the budget. on a 5% daily limit that is roughly 1.7% per trade, which survives three consecutive losses and keeps the plan executable.

both gate payouts on consistency in some form, with the details varying by program and changing over time. the arithmetic is the same everywhere: required total profit equals the best day divided by the permitted share. cap the best day at a third of the target and the rule is satisfied by construction.

policies differ by firm and by program. where holding is permitted, size for the weekend gap rather than for the stop, because a gap can open beyond the stop and the loss becomes the gap. where it is restricted, be flat before the close.

no. correlated positions across accounts can be read as hedging, and split attention produces worse execution on both. sequential funding - pass one, trade it, then add another - is slower to start and faster to reach a first payout.

it depends on how many attempts each structure requires for a given trader. multiply each fee by the expected number of attempts, add reset charges, and compare. a cheaper fee on a stricter structure is bought more than once.

many prop firms prohibit third-party trading of an evaluation, and a funded account passed in breach of the terms can be voided at payout. the flat $220 arrangement is offered only where the firm's terms allow it, and declined where they do not. the service reviews explain how to check before paying.

increasing size after the pass. the evaluation rewards a controlled plan and the funded stage rewards the same plan, but the pressure that produced discipline disappears the moment the fee is earned. keep the risk per trade unchanged for the first three months.

read four things in this order: the drawdown basis, the target as a percentage, the daily limit, and the payout gates. then run your plan on a demo under those rules for four weeks. the demo month answers more than any review, because it tests your behaviour against the rulebook.

drawdown type matters more than target size. static beats end-of-day trailing, which beats intraday trailing.
futures firms are stricter at payout. consistency rules are common there and rare on forex evaluations.
instant funding is a different product - higher price, tighter early withdrawal rules, no evaluation.
headline percentages mislead. a 5% daily limit measured on equity is far stricter than the same number measured on closed balance.

most comparison tables are marketing with columns. they list account sizes and profit splits - the numbers firms advertise - and leave out the four rules that determine whether an evaluation is survivable. before looking at any table, including this one, decide what you are comparing.

drawdown structure. a static maximum loss never moves. an end-of-day trailing drawdown follows your closed profit higher, tightening the buffer at the end of each day. an intraday trailing threshold follows your unrealised equity, which means a normal pullback can end the account while the day is still net positive. identical headlines - "10% maximum drawdown" - describe three very different products.

daily loss measurement. firms publish a daily loss limit, but the basis varies: closed balance, equity including floating positions, or equity plus unrealised intraday peaks on trailing accounts. the stricter the measurement, the smaller the effective risk per trade, regardless of the number on the page.

consistency rules. some firms apply a consistency requirement during the evaluation, others only when you request a payout, and some not at all. a payout-stage rule is more manageable because you can add ordinary winning days before requesting a withdrawal. an evaluation-stage rule constrains pace from day one.

payout mechanics. minimum trading days, profit threshold, first-payout delay, split percentage and the withdrawal methods offered. a firm with a 90% split and a 30-day first payout is not better than one with 80% and a seven-day cycle for most traders.

the table below covers the forex firms most traders evaluate first. figures reflect published terms at the time of writing; firms revise structures regularly, so verify against the firm's own documentation before purchasing.

which forex firm is easiest to pass? on structure alone, firms with a single phase, a static maximum loss, no consistency rule and no time limit give the risk plan the most room. fxify, fundingpips, fx2 funding and the5ers-style structures fit that description more closely than firms with trailing floors or payout-stage consistency requirements.

which pays most reliably? payout reliability correlates with firm age, transparent terms and a public record of withdrawals - not with the advertised split. a firm offering 95% of profit but taking three weeks to process a withdrawal is a worse home for a funded account than one offering 80% on a weekly cycle.
futures evaluations behave differently from forex ones, and the differences are structural rather than cosmetic.

three patterns matter. first, futures firms almost universally use trailing thresholds, which makes them harder than forex evaluations with equivalent headline numbers. second, consistency rules are standard at payout - a 30% best-day rule is the common shape - which means an evaluation can be passed and the first payout request still refused. third, targets are dollar-denominated, so a $3,000 target on a $50,000 account is a 6% target, and that arithmetic is worth doing before comparing firms.

which futures firm is easiest to pass? whichever has the most forgiving trailing behaviour. a threshold that stops trailing once it reaches the starting balance, or trails only on closed profit, is materially easier than an intraday trailing floor on a small account. where a firm offers both an intraday and an end-of-day structure, the end-of-day version is the better assignment.
tables compress differences that matter, so here is what each firm's structure actually implies for someone trading it - or for a service trading it on your behalf.

the reference point of the industry: two phases, a 10% target on the first and 5% on the second, a 5% daily loss limit measured on equity including floating positions, and a 10% static maximum loss. no time limit, no consistency rule at evaluation, and an exceptionally well-documented rulebook. the static floor makes it the most workable large-scale forex structure available, and the fact that it is measured on equity is the detail that catches traders who assume closed-balance accounting. passing it is a test of pacing rather than of forecasting, which is exactly why it suits a structured approach.

offers both single-phase and two-phase structures, with the important caveat that some plans use a trailing drawdown rather than the static floor most traders assume. where a plan trails, the cushion shrinks as profit accumulates, and the plan must reduce risk toward the end of the evaluation. fundednext also applies consistency conditions at the payout stage on several plans, which means an evaluation can be passed cleanly and the first withdrawal request still refused if one day dominates total profit.

built around slower, lower-leverage progression rather than fast passes. targets are modest but so are drawdown allowances, and the firm's multi-stage structures reward patience: several of its evaluations expect the trader to grind a small return over a long period rather than hit a headline number. for a passing service this is a question of pacing, and the timeline is longer than the industry average for that reason. payout cycles are generally reliable, and the firm is well regarded for supporting traders who want to build slowly.

a broker-backed firm with single-phase and two-phase options, static drawdowns on standard plans, and no consistency rule at evaluation. the static floor plus the absence of a time limit makes it one of the more forgiving structures to pass, and the account ranges extend comfortably above where many competitors stop. where a plan mixes in trailing behaviour, the same caution applies as everywhere else: read which plan you are buying.

two-phase evaluation with 8% and 5% targets, static floors on standard plans, and a permitted instrument list that is narrower than some competitors. that restriction is the practical difference - fewer instruments per session means fewer legitimate opportunities, and evaluations tend to take a little longer even though the headline numbers look average. payouts are well documented and the firm has a solid record on withdrawals.

two-phase, 8% and 5%, static maximum loss, no consistency rule during the evaluation, and pricing that sits at the aggressive end of the market. structurally one of the friendlier evaluations for a rules-based approach, with the usual caveat that cheap challenge fees sometimes come with tighter payout-stage conditions - worth checking the current payout schedule rather than assuming last year's terms.

the most recognisable futures firm, with dollar-based targets, an intraday trailing threshold, and account sizes that extend to $300,000 - higher than almost any competitor. the trailing threshold is the defining feature: it follows unrealised equity, so the buffer shrinks on every tick in your favour, and the plan has to reduce size as the target approaches instead of accelerating. apex applies a consistency rule at payout, typically a 30% best-day expectation, which is the single most common reason a passed futures account cannot withdraw. discounted evaluation pricing and a large promotional cadence make it inexpensive to enter and easy to over-trade once inside.

futures combine with a trailing threshold, a fixed dollar target, a daily loss limit and a best-day consistency expectation. the combination of a daily limit and a trailing floor makes it stricter than a firm with only one of the two, and the consistency expectation shapes the evaluation itself rather than only the payout. apex and topstep are frequently compared directly; the useful distinction is that topstep's rules are more explicit about the failure conditions, which makes them easier to plan around once you have read them properly.

dollar-based futures evaluations with more flexibility on drawdown behaviour than most competitors, including end-of-day trailing options on some plans. end-of-day trailing is materially easier than intraday trailing, because the floor only moves on closed profit - a distinction worth a great deal in practice and invisible in a headline comparison. consistency is enforced at payout.

futures evaluations with a trailing threshold and a strong emphasis on payout-window mechanics. smaller account tiers are available, which makes it a reasonable first futures evaluation, and the trailing behaviour is the same trap as everywhere else: plan for a shrinking buffer rather than a fixed floor.

end-of-day trailing drawdown, dollar targets and a consistency requirement, with a smaller account range than the largest futures firms. the end-of-day trailing structure is the reason it appears on shortlists for traders who find intraday trailing impossible to manage.
two firms can look identical in a table and behave completely differently in an account.
most decisions come down to two firms with nearly identical headline numbers. five tie-breakers, in the order they usually matter.
which drawdown is static? if one firm's floor moves and the other's does not, the static one wins for almost every trader.
when is consistency enforced? at payout is easier than during the evaluation, and not at all is easier still.
what is the first-payout timeline? minimum trading days plus processing time. a fast cycle matters more than a marginally higher split percentage.
which firm's terms are clearer about third-party trading? clarity is protection. a firm that states its position explicitly is safer to work with than one that leaves it ambiguous.
which platform do you actually want to trade? mt5, ctrader, tradovate and ninjatrader behave differently, and the funded phase is where platform familiarity pays.

figures come from firms' published rulebooks and their own documentation pages, cross-checked against the terms shown at the point of purchase. where a firm operates multiple plan types, the table reflects the standard structure and the notes above flag where plans diverge - trailing versus static drawdowns, for example. firms change terms frequently, sometimes without a public announcement, so this page is a starting point rather than a substitute for the terms you agree to at checkout. corrections are welcome: if a number here contradicts your firm's current documentation, send it over and the page will be fixed.
instant funding skips the evaluation: you buy a funded account and trade it immediately, subject to early payout restrictions. it is not a shortcut so much as a different trade-off.

the mistake traders make with instant funding is treating the absence of an evaluation as the absence of constraints. instant accounts typically carry tighter early-stage rules: a higher profit threshold before the first withdrawal, a longer minimum period, or a restriction on how much of the account can be withdrawn in the early months. those restrictions exist precisely because the firm has skipped the screening step that an evaluation provides.
read the instant funding guide for the full breakdown of how the model works and when an evaluation is the better choice.
drawdown mechanism first, then the daily limit, then everything else.
across managed evaluations, four rules account for most outcomes. ranking them by how often they end an attempt produces a different order than ranking them by how prominently firms advertise them.
daily loss limit (measured on equity). the single most common cause of failure. firms measuring on equity including floating losses are far stricter than their headline number suggests.
trailing drawdown. the second most common cause, and the one most often misunderstood. traders habitually assume the floor is fixed and discover otherwise after a large winning day.
consistency at payout. not a cause of evaluation failure but a cause of refused payouts, which for a funded trader is the same outcome delayed.
minimum trading days. rarely fatal, frequently inconvenient: an evaluation finished in three sessions with a minimum of ten days is not finished at all.

sizing for the first two rules - and checking the third before requesting a withdrawal - removes most of the risk that a well-executed evaluation ends in disappointment. the consistency rule guide covers the arithmetic in detail.

the comparison above is about getting funded. staying funded is governed by a second set of terms that most comparison tables ignore entirely, and it is where a surprising share of otherwise well-executed plans fall apart.

the pattern is consistent across firms: evaluation rules punish risk, and funded rules punish concentration. a trader who passes by taking consistent, modest profits is in a good position; a trader who passes with one exceptional day has cleared the first test and walked into the second. that is the mechanism behind the most common surprise in this market - a passed account whose first payout request is refused for a consistency breach.
comparing split percentages instead of payout cycles. an 80% split on a weekly cycle delivers cash more often than 90% on a monthly one, and cash in hand compounds.

assuming percentages are measured the same way. a 5% daily limit on closed balance is roughly a third more forgiving than a 5% limit on equity including floating losses. the number is identical; the constraint is not.

ignoring instrument restrictions until the evaluation is live. a permitted list that excludes the instruments you actually trade does not just slow an evaluation - it changes the plan, sometimes mid-assignment.

treating a discount offer as a structural advantage. firms run heavy promotions precisely because discounted entries produce repeat purchases. the rules you agree to are worth more attention than the price you paid to agree to them.

elitepropx passes every firm in this comparison for a flat $220, including firms with trailing thresholds, consistency rules and minimum trading days. the firm's own challenge fee is separate and paid to the firm.

two honest qualifications belong here. first, firms whose terms prohibit third-party trading are flagged rather than quietly accepted - if your firm takes that position, using any passing service risks the funded account, and that risk is yours to weigh. second, the easiest firm to pass is not always the best firm to be funded with: a firm with a static drawdown and an 80% split on a fast payout cycle is usually a better home than one with a 95% split and a slow withdrawal process.

a practical sequencing rule that comes out of the tables above: pass the most forgiving structure first, even if it is smaller than the account you eventually want. a $50,000 evaluation at a firm with a static floor and no consistency rule builds the funded record, the payout history and the confidence that make a $200,000 trailing-threshold assignment at a stricter firm manageable. traders who start with the hardest structure available tend to spend their retries learning a lesson that a smaller account would have taught more cheaply.

there is also a third qualification that is easy to overlook: the best firm on this page for a trader who will manage their own funded account is not automatically the best firm to pass through a service. structures with intraday trailing thresholds are harder to pass reliably and slower to complete, which is a cost that only matters if you are paying for the pass. if you intend to trade the funded account yourself, the evaluation rules are transient and the funded rules are permanent - weight them accordingly.

one asymmetry is worth naming because it changes recommendations: passing a firm is a one-time event, but being funded with it is indefinite. a firm with an awkward evaluation and excellent payout reliability is a better long-term home than one with an easy evaluation and slow withdrawals - and no firm publishes a withdrawal-reliability column, which is why community reporting matters more than marketing on that specific point.

if you want a recommendation for your situation, send the market you trade and the account size you are targeting. the answer will come back with the sequencing rather than a single firm name, because most traders are better off passing a forgiving structure first and adding a stricter account afterwards.

firms with a single phase, a static maximum loss, no consistency rule and no overall time limit. those four properties, rather than account size or target percentage, determine how much room the risk plan has.
is a 10% target harder on a $200,000 account than a $50,000 one?

not in relative terms - a 10% target is 10% at any size. what changes is that absolute dollar slippage and per-trade costs are identical while the target scales, so costs consume a smaller share of the target on larger accounts. the rule structure, not the size, is what makes a large evaluation harder.

some do explicitly, and others enforce an equivalent constraint through the trailing threshold, which tightens as equity rises. on an intraday trailing account, the effective daily buffer shrinks through the day even without a separate daily rule.
what is the difference between a static and a trailing drawdown?

a static floor stays at a fixed level regardless of profit. a trailing floor follows equity upward, so a winning account has less room than a losing one. intraday trailing follows unrealised profit; end-of-day trailing updates only on closed profit.

most forex firms apply none during the evaluation, and several apply none at payout either. futures firms are the opposite: consistency expectations at payout are the norm. the rules matrix lists which firms enforce it and at which stage.
