comparison pages are usually ranked lists, and ranked lists hide the only thing that matters: the rules are not comparable across firms unless you convert them into the same units. a firm with a 6% target and a trailing drawdown is not easier than a firm with a 10% target and a static one, and a table that places them in order of fee tells you nothing about the difficulty of either.

the method below takes ten minutes per firm and produces a number that can be compared honestly: the number of consecutive full-risk losses it takes to fail, and the number of full-risk wins it takes to pass.

divide the daily loss limit by your per-trade risk. at 1.5% risk and a 5% daily limit, three losses end the day; at 2% risk, the same limit ends the day after two and a half. do the same for the maximum loss: 10% static at 1.5% risk is roughly six and a half full-risk losses from the starting balance. those two numbers - three and six - describe the account's tolerance far more usefully than the percentages do.

divide the target by the same per-trade risk. a 10% target at 1.5% risk is 6.7r; a 6% target at 1.5% risk is 4r. now the comparison has a shape: a firm requiring 6.7r of profit while tolerating 6.5 losses is a different proposition from one requiring 4r while tolerating 3.5. the ratio between the two figures is the closest thing to a difficulty score available without trading the account.

read the last column against the fourth. where wins needed are far above losses tolerated, the account demands a high win rate or a favourable distribution; where they are close, the account is symmetric and a normal sequence of wins and losses gets there. most traders assume the small-target firm is easier, and the arithmetic often says otherwise once the trailing mechanic is applied to the tolerance figure.

two firms can be identical on every evaluation number and completely different after funding. the variables to check are the profit threshold before a first withdrawal, any consistency requirement on the best day, the processing schedule, and whether the profit split changes at a particular level. a firm with a 30% best-day rule and a clean 40% best day will hold a withdrawal that an evaluation said was complete.

multiply the fee by the expected number of attempts at your realistic pass probability. at 50%, that is two attempts; at 30%, more than three. then add the elapsed time, which is the number traders forget: two attempts of three weeks each is six weeks, and six weeks is a meaningful share of a trading year for someone building a track record.

this is where a service's flat fee changes the comparison rather than the arithmetic. if a single fee covers retries at the same firm and size, the expected cost of a first-pass attempt is fixed at the price of the service, and the comparison between two firms becomes a comparison of difficulty rather than of fee. that is the right basis on which to choose.
three comparison errors account for most of the bad decisions in this market, and each is easy to avoid once named.

a $99 challenge with a 30% pass rate has an expected cost above a $540 challenge with a 60% pass rate, before counting the weeks. fees are the most visible number in the market and the least informative, which is precisely why they lead every advertisement.

a 6% target sounds easier than a 10% target until the drawdown is described properly. a trailing 6% maximum loss on a 6% target leaves almost no room once the account is 2% up, because the floor has followed the profit. comparing targets without comparing drawdown mechanics is comparing two different sports by their scorelines.

reviews describe payout experiences, and payout experiences depend on rules the reviewer may not have read. a firm with a consistency rule will generate one-star reviews from traders who passed cleanly and were then held, and the reviews are accurate about the experience while useless as a guide to difficulty. read the payout terms first, then the reviews, and the pattern usually becomes obvious.

if the evaluation is not going to be traded by you, the selection criteria shift slightly. the rulebook still decides difficulty, but two additional questions matter: whether the firm permits third-party trading, and whether the funded account is issued in the client's name with payouts paid directly.

on the first, there is no compromise worth making. firms that prohibit the arrangement and enforce the prohibition after funding are the single worst outcome available to a client, because the forfeit lands at the point of maximum value. on the second, a provider that wants to hold the funded login or receive the payouts is asking the client to accept counterparty risk in exchange for convenience, and that is a trade worth refusing.

a third question is worth asking too: what the provider does when a firm changes its rules mid-assignment. firms do revise terms, and a provider that has no answer has not thought about the case where its client's evaluation is invalidated by a rulebook update rather than by a trade.

the consistency rule caps how much of your total profit can come from one trading day. it is the reason a passed evaluation can still refuse a payout, and it is almost entirely a matter of arithmetic - which means it can be planned for.
a 30% consistency rule means your largest day must be no more than 30% of total profit - so total profit must reach at least 3.33× your best day.
most forex firms apply it at payout only; futures firms apply it at payout almost universally, and a few apply it during the evaluation too.
it is a distribution rule, not a performance rule: the fix is more ordinary winning days, not better trades.
planning for it during the evaluation costs days, not money - and it removes the most common first-payout refusal.

the consistency rule places a ceiling on the contribution of a single trading day to total profit. the most common formulation is 30%: no single day may account for more than 30% of the profit shown when a payout is requested. some firms use 40% or 50%, some measure it per day rather than per session, and a few express it as a maximum best-day profit in dollars rather than a percentage.

the purpose, from the firm's perspective, is straightforward. firms fund traders whose results look repeatable, and a single outsized day is the least repeatable way to reach a profit target. a trader who makes $9,000 in one session and $1,000 over the following month is a different risk to a firm than one who made $10,000 across six weeks, even though both hit a $10,000 target. the rule is a filter for distribution, and it is applied to the withdrawal rather than to the evaluation at most forex firms, though not all.

there is a second, less discussed consequence. because consistency is measured against total profit, the rule interacts with the funded account's profit threshold. if a firm requires 8% of profit before a payout and enforces 30% consistency, the best day must remain under 30% of whatever is accumulated - meaning the trader cannot simply reach the threshold quickly and withdraw.
the formula is simple: maximum permitted best day = total profit × consistency percentage . rearranged, the requirement is that total profit ≥ best day ÷ consistency percentage .

two things stand out from that table. first, the multiple is what matters: a 30% rule demands 3.33× your best day in total profit, and the required additional profit scales linearly with the size of the dominant day. second, a smaller best day is not merely better - it is dramatically better. halving the best day from $6,000 to $3,000 halves the total profit required from $20,000 to $10,000.
a single dominant day can fail a consistency check even when the profit target has been met.

a trader finishes a futures evaluation with a $6,000 best day and $9,500 of total profit, then requests the first payout after the minimum trading days. under a 30% rule, total profit needs to reach at least $20,000 for a $6,000 best day - so the request is refused even though the account is profitable and the evaluation was passed cleanly.

the remedy is not to trade bigger; it is to add ordinary days. another $10,500 of profit spread across normal sessions would satisfy the rule, and the important detail is that those additional days must stay small. a second $6,000 day would push the required total to $40,000 and make the problem worse rather than better.
three traders each make $10,000 total on a funded account with a 30% consistency rule.
trader a: one day of $7,000, five days of $600. best day is 70% of total. payout refused until total profit reaches $23,334.
trader b: one day of $3,000, ten days of $700. best day is 30% of total. payout permitted immediately - exactly at the threshold, with no margin.
trader c: best day of $2,000, remaining $8,000 spread across twelve sessions. best day is 20% of total. payout permitted with comfortable room.

all three have identical total profit and identical evaluation results. only the distribution differs, and only trader a is blocked. that asymmetry is the entire content of the consistency rule, and it is why planning the distribution during the evaluation is cheaper than repairing it afterwards.
there are three patterns in the market, and the difference between them matters more than the percentage itself.

two practical notes on reading a firm's rule. first, firms often describe consistency in the funded-account terms rather than in the evaluation terms, so a trader who only reads the evaluation page concludes the rule does not exist - until a payout request is refused. second, the percentage is not always expressed as a percentage: some firms state a maximum best-day profit in dollars, which is simpler to plan around but changes the arithmetic when the firm also scales account sizes.
an evaluation-stage consistency rule is the harder version, and it changes the plan from the first session.

the constraint is not that you must avoid big days - it is that your total profit must remain at least 3.33× your best day at the moment you reach the target (on a 30% rule). if the target is $10,000 and you have a $4,000 day, you cannot pass at $10,000; you must reach $13,334 before the ratio is satisfied. that is a 33% larger target than the firm advertised, arrived at by arithmetic rather than by choice.

cap any single day at a third of the profit target. on a $10,000 target, close the day once it is $3,300 up. this is the pre-emptive version of the rule and it keeps the required multiple satisfied automatically.
track the ratio, not just the balance. the number that matters is best-day ÷ total profit. keeping a running note of it costs nothing and turns an invisible threshold into a visible one.
prefer more sessions over larger ones. if the plan allows twenty sessions, spreading the target across them produces a ratio under 25% by construction, with no need to manage anything.

there is one counter-intuitive consequence worth stating: on a firm that enforces consistency during the evaluation, a slow, undramatic pass is not merely safer - it is the only way the advertised target is actually the target. a trader who reaches 10% with a 40% best day has not reached the target at all.
the payout-stage version is more forgiving because the problem can be repaired with time rather than avoided with discipline.

the mechanism is that consistency is measured on the profit shown when a withdrawal is requested. a trader with a dominant day has two options: wait and accumulate additional small days until the ratio is satisfied, or request a partial withdrawal calculated so the ratio holds at the amount requested. firms differ on whether partial withdrawals are permitted and how the ratio is measured in that case, so the specific answer belongs to the firm's terms rather than to a general rule.
consistency is one of several gates between a pass and a first withdrawal.

what makes the payout stage more workable is that the dominant day does not invalidate anything. the evaluation was passed, the account is funded, and the only constraint is on the timing and size of the withdrawal. that converts a failure into a delay - typically a few weeks of ordinary trading - which is a materially better position than being unable to pass at all.

it is also the reason our own plan caps individual days at a third of the target even on firms that apply consistency only at payout. the habit costs nothing during the evaluation on a static-drawdown structure, and it means the first withdrawal is available on request rather than after a repair period.
a consistency failure is a distribution problem, and distribution problems are solved with volume rather than with performance. there are four viable routes, in the order they usually make sense.

the direct fix. if total profit must rise so that the existing best day falls to 30% of it, the required increase is mechanical: required total = best day ÷ 0.30, and the gap is the difference between that figure and current profit. on a $6,000 best day with $9,500 banked, the gap is $10,500 - spread across sessions sized at a third of a day's budget, that is several weeks of boring execution rather than one large push.

the discipline required is to keep those additional days small. a trader who fixes a consistency problem with a second large day has simply raised the bar: the required total scales with the new best day, so a $9,000 day would demand $30,000 in total.

where the firm permits partial withdrawals and measures consistency against the amount withdrawn rather than the account's total profit, a smaller request can satisfy the ratio immediately. this is firm-specific and worth confirming in writing, because the two measurement bases produce different answers and the confusion between them is common.

whatever route is used, the fix only holds if the next session cannot recreate the problem. a cap of a third of the eventual total - enforced in the plan rather than in the moment - is what prevents a repaired ratio from being destroyed by one good morning.

if consistency applies during the evaluation and the target has been met but the ratio has not, the arithmetic can make the advertised target misleading. for a subsequent account, choosing a firm that applies consistency only at payout - or not at all - removes a constraint that costs days without adding anything to the funded account.

most forex and cfd evaluations apply no consistency rule during the evaluation, and several apply none at payout either. the rules matrix lists which firms enforce it and at which stage, and the 2026 comparison explains what each structure means in practice.

the trade-off is worth stating plainly. firms without a consistency rule are easier to pass and easier to withdraw from, and their profit splits or challenge pricing are sometimes slightly less generous to compensate. firms with a strict payout-stage rule often advertise attractive splits precisely because the rule reduces the amount that leaves the firm in the first months. when comparing two firms, a 90% split with a 30% consistency rule can pay out less, sooner, than an 80% split with none - and the difference is invisible in a headline table.

one further consideration applies to traders who intend to run several accounts. consistency rules compound across a portfolio, because each account has to satisfy its own ratio independently. three accounts at firms with payout-stage consistency rules require three separately distributed profit histories, whereas three accounts at firms without the rule can be traded on identical terms. for traders scaling deliberately, that is a meaningful operational difference rather than a marketing footnote.
the consistency rule caps the upside of a session while the loss limit caps the downside.
consistency and the daily loss limit pull in opposite directions
two rules govern the shape of every session on an account with a payout-stage consistency requirement, and they encourage opposite behaviour.

the daily loss limit says: the day's budget is scarce, so use it efficiently when a setup appears. the consistency rule says: daily profit is expensive, because a large day raises the ratio you must satisfy. a trader obeying only the first rule tends to take the biggest available opportunity each day, which produces exactly the concentrated distribution the second rule punishes.

the resolution is to treat the two as separate budgets with different ceilings. the loss budget is a floor on caution - it caps how much can be lost. the consistency rule is a ceiling on ambition - it caps how much should be won in one day. a session that is profitable beyond roughly a third of the eventual total is not a good session; it is a liability.

the fourth row is where the two rules reinforce rather than conflict. after a loss, the consistency rule gives no permission to increase risk: larger size after a loss raises the variance of the day, and a day that turns into a large winner creates the distribution problem the rule exists to prevent. the only correct response to a losing morning is a smaller position and, usually, a shorter session.

one consequence of that discipline is worth stating because it sounds wrong: on accounts with a 30% payout-stage rule, the optimal daily result is not the largest available profit but a repeatable one. traders who internalise this find the funded phase easier than the evaluation, because the funded account's constraints reward the same behaviour the pacing discipline already required. traders who do not usually discover the rule at the first payout request - which is the most expensive possible time to learn it.

myth 1: it only matters on futures accounts. futures firms enforce it most consistently at payout, but a number of forex and cfd firms apply equivalent conditions on funded accounts. the rule is not a futures feature; it is a payout feature, and it appears wherever a firm wants to encourage repeatable results.

myth 2: it can be solved by trading smaller everywhere. reducing every position lowers both the best day and total profit proportionally, which leaves the ratio unchanged. what changes the ratio is the distribution : more days, each of them moderate. size reduction helps only if it is applied to the largest days rather than uniformly.

myth 3: a big day is always bad. a large day is not a breach; it is a debt against future ordinary days. on a $10,000 target with a $4,000 best day, the account needs $13,334 in total - an extra $3,334 of ordinary trading. the day is affordable, just expensive, and the arithmetic is fully predictable at the moment it happens.

all four myths survive because they sound like discipline. capping daily profit sounds like timidity, and refusing to press a winning day feels like leaving money on the table - right up until the first payout request is refused and the repair costs three weeks of ordinary trading. the rule is not a judgement about how well you trade. it is a statement about how a firm reads a profit history, and it can be satisfied without trading any better than the target requires.

each of these myths leads to the same wrong remedy: adjusting effort rather than distribution. the rule does not reward trading harder, trading less, or trading on a second account. it rewards spreading the same profit across more sessions, which is a scheduling decision rather than a trading one.

myth 4: the rule can be worked around with a second account. consistency is measured per account, so trading a second account does not change the first account's ratio - and firms that detect correlated positions across accounts treat them as a single exposure, which can create a separate problem. the rule is satisfied by distribution within the account, not by spreading trades across accounts.
it caps how much of your total profit may come from a single trading day - commonly 30% - which means total profit must reach at least 3.33 times your best day before a payout is allowed.
which is worse: a consistency rule during the evaluation or at payout?

the evaluation-stage version is harder. a payout-stage rule delays a withdrawal that can be fixed by adding ordinary winning days; an evaluation-stage rule can mean the advertised profit target is not actually the target, because the ratio must also be satisfied.
how do i calculate whether i pass a 30% rule?

divide your best day by 0.30. on a $4,000 best day, total profit must reach $13,334. if your profit target is $10,000 and you have a $4,000 best day, you cannot finish at the target - you must exceed it by $3,334 or reduce the size of your largest day in future.

it depends on the firm. most measure a calendar trading day in the account's server timezone, which means a session that spans midnight is split across two days for consistency purposes. a few measure per session. where a trade runs overnight, the firm's definition matters and is worth checking before assuming either way.

yes. a single exceptional trade can produce a dominant day, and the ratio is measured on daily profit rather than on trade count. this is why capping daily profit - not just per-trade risk - is the practical defence.

no. the rule measures the concentration of profit, so losing days reduce total profit and make the ratio worse rather than better. this is why a drawdown during a repair period extends the wait rather than shortening it.

at payout stage, the withdrawal is refused until the distribution satisfies the rule - the account is not closed. where the rule applies during the evaluation, the evaluation cannot be completed until the ratio is met, which may require exceeding the stated profit target.

cap every session at roughly a third of the profit target, and if you have a strong day, close early rather than extending it. a trader who never has a day above a third of the target automatically satisfies a 30% rule at the moment the target is reached.

yes, and they are mostly forex and cfd evaluations. the rules matrix lists which firms enforce it and when, so a trader who finds the rule unmanageable can choose a firm where it does not apply rather than fighting it.

it plans for them. on firms that apply the rule at payout, sessions are capped at a third of the target so the first withdrawal is available on request; on firms that apply it during the evaluation, the pace is set by the ratio rather than by the target. either way it is arithmetic, not improvisation.

it depends on the gap. fixing a $6,000 best day from $9,500 of profit requires $10,500 more profit, which at a third of a day's budget on a $100,000 account is several weeks of ordinary trading. reducing the size of the dominant day in the first place is far cheaper than repairing it afterwards.
the 20%, 40% and 50% variants, and why the number is not the whole story

firms describe consistency in several ways, and two rules with the same percentage can behave very differently depending on what the denominator is and when it is measured. before planning around a threshold, identify which of the four common formulations applies.

the first row is the one most forex firms use, and it has a forgiving property: the requirement rises with the size of the dominant day, so the remedy is always available - add ordinary profit. the second row is harder, because a single large day during the evaluation can fail the account outright, and the trader has no opportunity to repair it. the fourth is the least understood and often the most disruptive, since an unusually large losing day can also distort an average-based measure.
why a 50% rule can be stricter than a 30% rule

it sounds impossible, and it happens regularly. a firm with a 50% threshold measured against a profit target, applied during the evaluation, is stricter than a firm with a 30% threshold measured against total profit at payout. in the first, one day at 50% of the target ends the attempt; in the second, a day at 60% of profit merely delays the withdrawal until more profit arrives.

the practical lesson is to read the sentence that follows the percentage, not the percentage itself. "no single day may account for more than 30% of total profit" and "no single day may exceed 30% of the profit target" differ by one word and are different sports.

most traders discover the rule at the payout request, which is the worst possible moment because the account is profitable and the instinct is to protect the gain by trading less - which is correct - while also wanting the payout to be worth having - which is the trap.

divide the best day by the threshold percentage. the result is the total profit the account must show. subtract current profit; the difference is the amount of ordinary profit still required. it is usually smaller than it feels: a $2,500 best day under a 30% rule needs $8,333 total, so an account at $6,000 needs another $2,333.
step two: size for an ordinary month, not a heroic week

the additional profit has to arrive without creating a new dominant day, which means the per-trade risk must fall. if normal risk is 1.5%, cutting to 0.75% doubles the number of sessions the work takes and halves the chance that any single session becomes the new best day. it also halves the chance of losing the gain that is already there, which matters more than speed at this point.

a request that is refused for distribution often triggers a second request the following week, and some firms count refusals or require a waiting period before another attempt. asking once, when the ratio is comfortably inside the threshold, is faster in practice than asking three times and being refused twice.
step four: if the ratio cannot be repaired, change the plan

there are accounts where the dominant day is simply too large relative to any achievable ordinary profit within the payout window. in that case the correct decision is to keep trading the account with tiny risk until the ratio normalises, or to accept that this account will pay out later than planned. neither option involves adding size to "get it over with", which is the move that turns a delayed payout into a failed account.

the cheapest fix is upstream. during the evaluation, cap any single session at roughly 20% of the total profit target. on a $10,000 target, that is $2,000 a day - not a small number, and achievable without concentrating the account's whole result into one tuesday.

a trader who respects that cap arrives at the payout stage with a distribution that already satisfies most plausible thresholds, and the remaining work is administrative. a trader who ignores it arrives at the payout stage with a profitable account and a blocked withdrawal, which is a strange thing to have paid for.

the cap also has a second benefit that has nothing to do with the rule: it forces a trader to leave the table while winning, which is the single behaviour most associated with accounts that survive their first month. the consistency rule, in that sense, is a firm imposing a discipline that profitable traders adopt voluntarily.

it also explains why firms with consistency rules tend to report lower failure rates among funded traders than firms without them, despite the extra hurdle. the rule does not just filter distributions; it filters for the temperament that produces them.

for a trader, that reframes the rule from an obstacle into a free diagnostic: an account that keeps tripping a consistency check is telling you that your profit depends on rare, large days. that is worth knowing regardless of which firm you trade with, because rare large days are exactly what a bad quarter removes.
it also makes the rule easier to explain to yourself when a payout is delayed: the firm is not questioning the profit, only its shape.

a profit target is a scheduling problem with a risk constraint attached, and most attempts fail because the two are solved separately. this guide treats them together: how to size a plan so that the target is reachable and the drawdown is survivable, how to de-risk as the target approaches rather than accelerate, and what the final ten percent of a target actually requires.
the target decides the calendar; the daily limit decides the risk per trade; the smaller constraint governs.
there are only three ways to finish faster - better ratio, higher selectivity, more sessions - and size is not one of them.
risk should go down as the target approaches, because the cost of a breach rises while the remaining target shrinks.
a daily profit cap is the tool that protects both the target and the consistency condition at the payout stage.
most targets are lost in the final ten percent, to a size increase rather than to a bad strategy.

traders read a profit target as an amount to be earned and plan for it the way they plan for a trade. it is more usefully read as a deadline with a distance: a certain percentage must be produced within a certain number of sessions, using a risk per trade that the firm's limits permit.

stated that way, the target becomes a scheduling problem with one hard constraint. the constraint is not the target; it is the drawdown and the daily limit, because those decide how much can be risked per session and therefore how many sessions the target needs. a plan that satisfies the target arithmetic and ignores the constraint arithmetic is a plan that finishes on paper and breaches in practice.

the two are solved together by working backwards. the drawdown fixes the maximum risk per trade that survives a losing streak. the daily limit fixes the maximum risk per session. the smaller of those two numbers is the plan's risk per trade. only then does the target come into play, because only then is the pace known: target divided by expected value per trade gives the number of trades, and trades divided by sessions per week gives the calendar.

everything else in this guide follows from that order. when a trader complains that a target is unreachable, the answer is almost never that more size is needed - it is that the plan's expectation per trade, its selectivity, or its session count is not sufficient for the calendar. those are the three levers, and they are the subject of the next section.

once risk per trade is fixed by the rules, there are exactly two things a trader can change about the pace: how often the plan trades, and how good each trade is. everything else - size, leverage, instrument - either changes the risk or changes the edge, and the second of those is not available on demand.

trade count. more sessions, or more trades per session within the daily limit, shortens the calendar proportionally. this is the cleanest lever because it does not change the risk per trade or the strategy. it does have a cost: more trades means more exposure to costs, more decisions, and a higher chance of a trade that does not match the plan. the practical limit is the point at which the marginal trade has a lower expected value than the earlier ones - usually when selectivity starts to slip.

expectation per trade. raising it means either a better reward-to-risk ratio or a higher win rate, and both come from selectivity rather than from effort. a plan that takes the best two setups per week instead of the best ten often has a higher expectation per trade, which offsets the lower count. this is why the two levers are not additive: increasing trade count without maintaining selectivity can reduce the total pace rather than increase it.

what is not a lever: position size. increasing size multiplies the outcome of the plan's existing distribution, which means it multiplies the drawdown in exactly the same proportion as the profit. on an account with a fixed failure floor, that is a change in survival probability rather than a change in speed. the trade-off is real and sometimes worth taking - but it should be taken deliberately, with the new breach probability written down, rather than as a response to being behind schedule.

a useful test for any proposed change: does it improve the plan, or does it only improve the timeline? a tighter stop, a better entry filter, or an extra session improves the plan. a larger position at the same stop does not.
the sizing calculation takes two passes, and the second one is the one traders skip.

pass one, from the drawdown. divide the distance to the failure floor by the number of consecutive losses the plan should survive. eight to ten is a reasonable design case for a discretionary plan with a win rate in the forties, because runs of that length recur within a few hundred trades. the result is the maximum acceptable loss per trade.

pass two, from the daily limit. divide the daily limit by the number of losses a session should absorb - four to six is a workable range. the result is usually smaller than the first, which is why the daily limit and not the drawdown is the binding constraint in practice.

the plan's risk per trade is the smaller figure. then, and only then, convert it into position size: for a forex account, lots from the pip value and the stop distance; for a futures account, contracts from the tick value and the stop in ticks. round down in both cases.
two derivations, one answer, and a reserve that is never spent.

two refinements make the result durable over a month. first, keep a quarter of the drawdown untouched as a reserve: on a trailing structure the floor moves, and a streak longer than the design case is precisely what the mechanism punishes. second, recompute both passes every week from the floor as it then stands, because on a trailing account the distance to the floor changes with profit - and the size that fitted in week one may not fit in week four.

the daily drawdown guide covers the reference-point arithmetic, including the difference between a limit measured on balance and one measured on equity, which changes the second pass materially for a trader who holds positions through drawdowns.

expected value per trade is the win rate multiplied by the average win, minus the loss rate multiplied by the average loss. with risk per trade fixed, that expression is a number, and the pace follows from it directly.

divide the target by expected value per trade to get the trade count. divide by trades per week to get the calendar. if the calendar is longer than the trader is willing to fund - remembering recurring platform and data costs - the answer is a better ratio, a more selective entry, or more sessions. it is never a larger size, because size does not appear in the expectation at all once risk per trade is fixed; it only sets the scale of the drawdown.

the equation also forbids a specific and common behaviour: raising the target's implied pace by trading instruments with larger tick or pip values at the same nominal position size. that changes risk per trade, not expectation, and it moves both the failure floor and the target by the same factor - leaving survival probability worse, not better, because the drawdown is now hit by a shorter losing streak.

finally, the equation is only as good as its inputs, and traders routinely use remembered numbers rather than measured ones. a month of records converts an assumed 45% win rate and 1:2 ratio into a measured figure, including the cost of spread, commission and slippage. that measurement is usually less flattering and considerably more useful, and it takes one month of trading at small size to obtain - a fraction of the cost of a failed attempt.
the counter-intuitive rule that saves the most accounts: risk per trade should fall as the target is approached, not rise.

the logic is asymmetric. early in an evaluation, distance to the target is large and the cost of a breach is a fee. late in an evaluation, distance to the target is small and the cost of a breach is every prior week of work plus the fee plus the calendar. the value of surviving the final week is therefore much higher than the value of surviving the first, even though the remaining target is smaller.

a workable schedule reduces risk per trade by a third at 75% of target and by half at 90%. the calendar stretches by a few sessions, and the probability of finishing rises out of proportion to the cost. the staged-evaluation guide makes the same point for multi-phase structures, where the final phase deserves the smallest size of the sequence.

two supporting rules complete the idea. set a daily profit cap and stop for the day when it is reached, rather than trading on because the session has gone well. and once the target is reached, stop entirely: an evaluation that has met its target and continues trading is exposed to a breach with nothing left to gain.
late in an evaluation the same dollar loss costs far more than it did in week one.
since pace is ultimately about trades and expectation, the choice of when to trade does more work than most position-sizing debates.

liquidity concentrates at session opens and closes, which is where spreads are tightest and fills most reliable. for a plan that needs a predictable cost per trade, trading one or two defined windows is better than trading a continuous session, because the cost measurement becomes meaningful rather than an average of very different conditions.

selectivity is the second half. a plan that requires a specific setup to appear will sometimes produce no trades in a session, and that is a completed session rather than a missed one. the alternative - trading because the platform is open - generates a second population of trades with a lower expectation that drags down the measured edge and consumes the daily limit.

instrument choice should follow stop distance rather than excitement. an instrument whose typical stop distance in ticks or pips is small relative to its spread has a structurally poor ratio for a small account, however readable its chart may be. this is the practical argument for trading the micro version of a contract: the ratio of stop to cost is identical, but the dollar risk fits the account's budget, which allows a more conservative size without abandoning the strategy.

one more selection rule that improves both levers at once: exclude the highest-variance windows a plan has not explicitly been built for. news releases, thin overnight periods and the first minutes after a cash open are where the plan's assumptions about fills and costs are least reliable, and the cost of avoiding them is a smaller trade count rather than a worse distribution.
a daily loss limit is provided by the firm. a daily profit cap is provided by the trader, and it serves two purposes that a loss limit cannot.

the first is consistency. payout conditions commonly cap a single day's share of total profit, so a trader whose best day dominates has created a problem that must be solved before a withdrawal. a daily profit cap set well below the eventual threshold means the ratio is satisfied automatically by the time the threshold is reached, rather than being discovered at the request.

the second is preservation of the target itself. late in an evaluation, a strong session followed by an attempt to compound it is the classic route to losing both. closing the platform at the cap converts a good day into a banked day, which is the only kind the target recognises.

the obvious objection is that capping profit caps the pace. in practice the effect is small: setting the cap at two to three times the average winning day keeps almost all of the plan's distribution while removing the tail that causes payout problems. a trader who would have produced 4% in a single session and closes at 1.5% has lost 2.5% of pace and removed a consistency breach, a drawdown risk and a decision they were likely to make badly.

there is an interaction worth noting with trailing drawdown. a large single day raises the failure floor on a trailing structure, which means the day's profit has made the account more fragile as well as more profitable. the daily cap limits that effect simultaneously with the consistency effect, which is a second reason it belongs in every plan that trades a trailing account.

losing streaks are not deviations from the plan; they are the plan's normal distribution arriving. a win rate in the forties produces five-loss runs several times within a few hundred trades, and an evaluation contains a few hundred trades at most.

the correct response is procedural, and it should be written before the streak happens. three losses in a session: reduce size by a quarter for the remainder of the session and keep the trade cap. three losing sessions in a row: keep the size but reduce the session count for the week, and review the records rather than the market. a drawdown of half the permitted amount: reduce size by half and extend the calendar, because at that point the account can still be finished but not by the original plan.

what is never correct is size beyond the derivation. recovery sizing is the most reliably fatal behaviour on a fixed-floor account, because it converts a normal variance sequence into a breach. the trader experiences it as determination; the account experiences it as a shorter distance to the floor.

two structural protections help more than resolve. the trade cap limits the number of decisions available to make badly in a single session. the weekly recalculation forces a pause where the size is derived from the current floor rather than inherited from the mood of the week. both are mechanical, which is the point.

scaling into a profitable position is one of the few techniques that genuinely raises expectation per trade, and it is also the fastest way to breach a daily limit or a contract cap. three conditions make it legitimate rather than impulsive.

the first is that the addition has its own protective order at a distance the plan specifies. adding without a stop on the new exposure is not scaling; it is an unbounded position with a bounded one behind it. on a futures account, the addition also has to respect the contract cap, which is checked at the moment of the trade and which a scaled position can breach even when the entry did not.

the second is that the total risk must remain inside the session budget. this is where the daily limit is most often lost: two entries, each sized within the per-trade risk, together exceed the number of losses the session was designed to absorb. the rule is that the added exposure counts against the daily budget at full value, not at the incremental value.

the third is that the addition should reduce the number of remaining opportunities, not increase it. a trader who scales in and then opens a new position has changed the strategy's risk profile mid-session. the position, not the idea, is the unit of risk.

where those three conditions cannot be satisfied within the rules - which is often on a small account with a tight daily limit - the honest conclusion is that scaling is not available to this plan, and the trade should be managed as a single entry. that is a limitation of the account, not of the trader.
the last stretch of a target is where most attempts are lost, and the mechanism is nearly always the same: a size increase to finish quickly.

the arithmetic explains why it is tempting. at 90% of target, the remaining distance is small in dollars, so a trade at double the usual size appears to finish the job in a day. what the trader is doing, though, is buying a coin flip on the whole evaluation - and the loss side of that coin is no longer a fraction of a drawdown but the entire attempt plus the calendar invested in it.

the correct treatment of the final ten percent has three parts. halve the size. cap daily profit so that no single session creates a consistency problem at the payout stage, which is the second cost of a fast finish. and accept the extra sessions, because the calendar spent finishing slowly is much smaller than the calendar lost to a restart.

there is also a specific trap on trailing-drawdown accounts at this stage. by 90% of target the floor has risen substantially behind the trader, so the remaining room is much smaller than it was at the start, even though the account looks comfortable. a size computed in week one is oversized now. recomputing from the current floor is not optional in the final stretch; it is the whole of risk management at that point.
a staged evaluation multiplies the arithmetic by the number of stages, and the multiplication is not neutral.

each stage has its own target and its own drawdown, and the funded account on completion has a third set of conditions. the cost of a breach in the final stage is the whole sequence plus the fee, which means the last stage should be traded at the lowest risk of the three. a common and expensive error is to treat the phases as repetitions of the same task at the same size.

there is a structural advantage worth using. percentage-based stages are scale-free, so the risk line written for stage one transfers to stage two unchanged in relative terms. only two numbers change: the size, because the account may be different, and the reserve, which should grow in the final stage because there is no reset behind it.

the records from stage one are the most valuable input to stage two, and they are usually ignored. measured expectation per trade, realised cost per trade and true win rate tell the trader whether stage two should be run faster or slower - and those numbers cannot be estimated from a chart. if the stage-one records show a thinner expectation than assumed, stage two should be slower and smaller, not braver.

one planning note on minimum trading days in staged structures: they are usually satisfied well before each target, so they rarely bind. where they are long relative to the plan, slow the plan from the stage's first session so the target and the count finish together, rather than reaching the target early and then trading to fill a count.
an example makes the arithmetic concrete. the figures below are generic because a plan has to be built on the trader's own numbers; what matters is the order of the operations.

inputs. a maximum loss of 10% of the balance, a daily limit of 5%, a profit target of 8%, and a funded consistency condition of roughly a third on the best day. assume a plan with a measured win rate of 45% at a 1:2 reward-to-risk ratio.

sizing. from the drawdown: 10% divided by ten consecutive losses is 1% per trade. from the daily limit: 5% divided by five losses per session is also 1%. the plan's risk per trade is therefore 1%, which is on the ceiling - so the reserve rule cuts it to 0.75%, leaving room for a streak longer than the design case.

pace. at 0.75% risk and a 1:2 ratio, the average win is 1.5%, the average loss 0.75%, and the expectation per trade is 0.45 × 1.5 − 0.55 × 0.75 = 0.26% per trade. an 8% target therefore needs about thirty trades at expectation. at two trades per session, that is fifteen sessions; at one, thirty. the calendar is fifteen to thirty sessions, and that is the honest number.

gates. at 25% of target, check realised versus planned cost per trade. at 50%, check the calendar against the trade count. at 75%, cut risk by a third and check that the daily limit has not been touched more than once. at 90%, halve risk, apply a daily profit cap of about 1.5% and accept the extra sessions.

consistency. with the cap at 1.5% per day and a best day no larger than that, a total profit of around 4.5% satisfies a one-third best-day share. the 8% target therefore clears the consistency condition comfortably, which is the point of setting the cap early rather than at the payout request.
the daily cap is set once and satisfies two conditions at the same time.

if the resulting calendar is unacceptable, the levers are the three from earlier: a better ratio, more selectivity, or more sessions. any of them improves the plan. raising risk per trade does not, and the arithmetic above shows exactly why - it would move the loss limit closer without moving the expectation.

where the evaluation is being traded on the trader's behalf, the same arithmetic is what a service is paid to execute. elitepropx charges a flat $220 per evaluation at any stage and size, covers retries, takes no profit split, and declines firms whose terms forbid third-party trading. the passing services guide explains what to check before paying anyone, and the failure recovery guide covers what to do when an attempt does not work.
what is the fastest way to hit a profit target?

increase trades or sessions within the daily limit, or improve expectation per trade through selectivity and a better reward-to-risk ratio. increasing position size raises the drawdown in the same proportion as the profit, so it changes survival probability rather than speed.
how much should i risk per trade to reach the target?

derive it from the rules rather than the target. divide the maximum loss by the number of consecutive losses the plan must survive, divide the daily limit by the losses a session should absorb, and use the smaller result. then keep a quarter of the drawdown in reserve.
should i increase size as i get closer to the target?

no - the opposite. reduce risk by a third at 75% of target and by half at 90%, because the cost of a breach rises as the target approaches while the remaining target shrinks. the extra sessions are far cheaper than a restart.
what is a daily profit cap and why do i need one?

a self-imposed limit on how much profit to take in one session. it protects the payout-stage consistency condition by preventing a dominant day, and it prevents a good session from being given back. setting it at two to three times the average winning day costs little pace and removes a tail risk.

enough that the worst session the plan permits cannot breach the daily limit. if risk per trade is a fifth of the daily limit, five losses would exhaust it, so cap the session at three or four. a trade cap also limits how many decisions can be made badly in one session.
how do i recover from a losing streak during an evaluation?

procedurally, not emotionally. three losses in a session: cut size by a quarter and keep the cap. three losing sessions: reduce the session count and review the records. half the drawdown consumed: halve the size and extend the calendar. never increase size to recover.

often yes, provided selectivity holds. more sessions shorten the calendar without changing risk per trade. the limit is the point where the marginal trade no longer matches the plan, which shows up as a falling measured expectation - the reason records matter more than intentions.

only if the addition has its own protective order, counts against the session budget at full value, and respects any contract or lot cap. on small accounts with tight daily limits, the honest answer is usually that scaling is not available and the trade should be managed as a single entry.

the final stage carries the cost of the whole sequence, so it should be traded at the lowest risk of the stages. percentage stages are scale-free, so the relative risk line transfers; only the size and the reserve change. use stage-one records to decide whether stage two should be slower.

a size increase to finish quickly, usually on a trailing-drawdown account where the floor has risen behind the profit and the remaining room is much smaller than it was at the start. recompute the size from the current floor and halve it for the last ten percent.

work backwards from the payout ratio. if the best day may be no more than a third of total profit, cap daily profit at roughly a third of the eventual threshold - then total profit will satisfy the ratio automatically when the threshold is reached, rather than at the withdrawal request.

these two firms appear in the same comparison tables and are almost never substitutes for each other. fundednext evaluates a percentage-based forex account that can be traded around the clock; topstep evaluates a dollar-based futures account tied to a single session. this guide compares the rulebooks line by line, then works backwards from the constraint that decides the outcome for most traders - the hours you can actually be at the screen.
the comparison is between rulebook models , not two versions of the same product: one measures targets and losses as a percentage of balance, the other as fixed dollar figures.
session availability decides the choice more often than the headline target. futures evaluations are effectively a new york and chicago session job; forex evaluations run around the clock.
a trailing dollar threshold punishes unrealised profit; a static percentage loss does not care what is open. the same equity curve therefore fails at different moments on each.
cost structure differs by shape, not just by size: one-off purchase versus recurring subscription. a slow pass is cheap on the first and expensive on the second.
whichever you pick, the $220 flat passing service quoted on this site is the same price for either firm.

fundednext is a forex and contract-for-difference firm. its instruments are currency pairs, metals and indices, priced in lots, quoted continuously from sunday evening to friday evening, and settled as a cash balance rather than through an exchange. topstep is a futures firm. its instruments are exchange-traded contracts - the micro and full versions of the equity index, energy and metals contracts - quoted in ticks, traded inside defined sessions, and subject to exchange margin and exchange hours.

that difference is not cosmetic. it changes the hours a trader must be available, the way a loss limit is expressed, the size of the smallest position that makes sense, and what happens if a position is held over a weekend. a comparison page that ranks the two firms on "profit target" alone is comparing a percentage to a dollar figure and calling the result a score.

so the useful question is not which firm is better. it is which rulebook fits the way you can trade. a trader with a day job and a laptop at 10pm has almost nothing to gain from a futures evaluation whose whole opportunity set lives between the new york open and 11:30am. a trader who is at a desk every morning and wants a cash-settled market with no swap charge and no overnight gap has reason to prefer futures regardless of how attractive a percentage target looks on paper.

there is also a structural difference in what the two firms are testing. a percentage rulebook is scale-free: the same 8% target and 10% maximum loss apply whether the balance is small or large, so a smaller account is neither easier nor harder in relative terms. a dollar rulebook is scale-dependent in a subtler way: the target and the loss limit both scale with account size, but commissions, slippage and the minimum tick value do not. on smaller futures accounts, fixed trading costs consume a larger share of the target, which makes the smallest tier marginally harder than the arithmetic suggests.

laid side by side, the two rulebooks differ in almost every row. the table below is the version worth memorising before you read any firm's marketing page, because it tells you which questions to ask.
the two evaluations differ in the unit of measurement before they differ in difficulty.
two rows in that table cause more damage than the rest when they are misread.

the first is the maximum loss row. a static percentage loss is measured from the starting balance and does not move. it means the account's failure point is a fixed distance away for the whole evaluation, so progress never makes the account more fragile. a trailing dollar threshold is measured from peak equity and moves upward as profit accumulates - including unrealised profit, on an intraday structure. progress shrinks the cushion, so risk per trade has to fall as the target approaches. these are opposite behaviours, and a plan written for one will be wrong on the other.

the second is the cost shape. a one-off purchase means a slow pass costs the same as a fast one. a recurring subscription means the calendar is a cost centre: every week spent not passing is a week paid for. that changes the correct pace for each model. on a one-off fee, patience is free; on a subscription, patience is a line item, which pushes traders towards taking the marginal setup they would otherwise skip.

most comparisons start with the profit target because it is the number on the sales page. it is the wrong place to start. the first question is where your trading hours fall, because a rulebook you cannot trade to is not a rulebook - it is a subscription you are paying for.
session availability routes most traders to one model before any other consideration is relevant.

futures liquidity is concentrated. the equity index contracts are at their most liquid and most orderly during the cash session, and activity thins considerably outside it. a trader operating at 9pm london time is trading the evening of a market that already had its day, with wider spreads, thinner books and a greater chance that a stop is filled somewhere other than where it was placed. none of that is fatal on a large account; on an evaluation with a fixed dollar threshold it is exactly the kind of cost that ends attempts.

forex is the opposite arrangement. the market transfers its liquidity from one centre to the next across the day, so there is a real, tradeable session at almost every hour. a trader who can only operate between 7pm and 10pm has a legitimate liquid window in the new york afternoon and the start of the asian session. the same trader attempting a futures evaluation is working with an instrument that has largely stopped moving in the way the plan assumes.

that asymmetry has a second consequence worth stating plainly: futures evaluations reward a fixed routine. the same two or three instruments, the same session, the same number of trades. forex evaluations reward a flexible one, because the session a trader can attend may shift through the week. if your schedule changes week to week, a percentage-based 24-hour market is the easier environment to build a repeatable process in.

there is one more practical point about session windows and daily limits. on a futures evaluation the daily limit resets with the session, which means the reset is a clean, predictable event you can plan around: the day's budget is restored at a known hour. on a forex evaluation the "day" is defined by the firm, often at a server-time rollover that does not correspond to anything meaningful in your own life. traders who lose track of the reset try to reason about a budget that has already changed, and the mistake is expensive because it usually happens on a day that is already going badly.
both models are arithmetic. the difference is which number is held constant, and that determines how a plan has to be written.

on a percentage model, the target and the loss limit are both fractions of the starting balance, so risk per trade can be expressed as a fraction too - one per cent per trade, three losses to a third of the daily budget, and so on. the advantage is that the same plan works at every account size. a trader who has tested a 0.5% risk model on a small evaluation can carry it unchanged to a larger one, and the only variable that changes is the value of the payout.

on a dollar model, the limits are quoted in dollars and the position is quoted in contracts, so risk per trade is computed in ticks: contracts multiplied by ticks at risk multiplied by tick value. that converts a percentage intention into a whole number of contracts, rounding down by necessity. on small accounts this rounding matters. if a 0.5% risk budget buys 1.4 micro contracts, the honest position is one contract, and the plan's real risk is closer to 0.35% than to 0.5%. the evaluation is not harder for that - it is slower, because the target is unchanged while the risk per trade has been rounded down.
the same profit path against a static floor and a trailing floor: the trailing account ends the sequence with less room, not more.

the trailing floor is where the arithmetic turns against an inexperienced trader. take a futures account that starts with a threshold a fixed distance below the opening balance. if equity reaches a new peak, the threshold rises with it. a $2,000 unrealised gain on one contract moves the floor before the position is closed. if the trade is then closed at +$700 after a retracement, the floor stays where the peak pushed it: the trader banked a third of the profit and surrendered the entire cushion. do that three times in a week and an account that looks flat on a statement is close to failure.

a static percentage loss has no equivalent mechanism. an open profit cannot tighten the failure point, so a trader is free to let a winner run without making the account more fragile. the trade-off is that the static floor is close from the beginning and never moves away - the protection that a trailing floor gives early in an evaluation is exactly the protection that a static floor never gives.

put together, the two models fail in different ways. a percentage account with a static floor is lost by an accumulation of losses that each looked small. a dollar account with a trailing floor is lost by a large winner that was given back, taking the cushion with it. a plan that names the dominant failure mode and prices the risk against it is worth more than a plan that optimises the target.
comparing the sticker price of the two firms is nearly useless without the time dimension. one charges per attempt; the other charges per period. those are different bets.

a one-off fee is a fixed cost per attempt. it makes a failed attempt cheap to repeat and a slow pass cost nothing extra, which is the arrangement that favours a patient trader. the risk it creates is the opposite of financial: because a retry is only the price of another attempt, the incentive to keep trying with an unchanged plan is strong. traders on one-off fee models fail repeatedly at the same rule, because nothing about the cost forces a review.

a subscription is a per-period cost, so the effective price of a pass rises with the number of weeks it takes. two consequences follow. the first is that a fast, disciplined trader pays considerably less than a slow one for the identical account - which is fair, but it means the cheapest tier is not necessarily the cheapest outcome. the second is behavioural: a recurring charge creates pressure to trade, and pressure to trade is the most common source of the low-quality setups that spend a daily budget for nothing.

whichever shape a firm uses, the real cost of an evaluation is the fee multiplied by the expected number of attempts, plus the cost of the time spent. a trader who fails three times on a subscription has spent three months of fees and three months of attention. a trader who fails three times on a one-off fee has spent three fees and, usually, less time - because there is no monthly meter running.
