the funding pips evaluation is best understood as a set of constraints that interact, not as a headline profit target with some footnotes. the target decides how much you have to make. the loss floor decides how much room you have to make it. the daily stop, if there is one, decides how quickly a bad session ends. the minimum-day rule decides how long the attempt takes even when the target is reached early. change any one of those and the same trading strategy produces a different outcome.

for funding pips, the published structure is a two-phase evaluation with a static loss floor. the loss floor is static, measured from the initial balance, the daily stop is yes, percentage based, and the consistency condition is usually none on the evaluation. billing is one-off per attempt, payouts follow profit split on a fixed cycle, and the supported platforms are mt4, mt5, ctrader. those are the rows that matter. marketing pages tend to foreground the profit target and the profit split because both are easy to compare; neither tells you whether a given trade is survivable.

a static loss floor is the simplest rule in the funding pips rulebook and the one traders most often misapply. the floor is anchored to the starting balance and does not move. on a $100,000 account with a 10% limit, the failure point stays at $90,000 from the first trade to the last, whatever the account does in between.

take an illustrative $100,000 account with a 10% static limit and a 5% daily stop. the maximum loss is $10,000 and the daily stop is $5,000. a trade that loses $2,000 leaves $8,000 of total room and $3,000 of daily room. a second loss of $2,000 the same day leaves $6,000 total and $1,000 daily. the total floor never moved, but the daily stop is now the binding constraint - and it resets at the firm's defined session boundary, which is usually midnight server time rather than your local midnight.
the daily stop and the total floor are two separate failure points.

the practical consequence is that the daily stop, not the total floor, decides most losing days. a trader who risks 1% per trade can absorb ten losses inside the total limit but only five inside a 5% daily stop, and only if all five happen on the same day. that is why the daily limit should be treated as the real risk budget and the total floor as the backstop. planning against the total floor alone produces a plan that dies on a normal bad day.

there is a second-order effect that matters on forex and cfd accounts. the loss is measured on equity, which includes floating profit and loss, spread and commission. on a forex account, swap and commission are deducted from equity, so a position held overnight can reduce the cushion without a price move. a risk plan that ignores costs will drift into the floor more slowly than expected, then all at once.

the fix is unglamorous: keep a running high-water mark, compute the remaining room before every trade, and express the stop as a percentage of the room rather than a percentage of the balance. if the remaining room is $6,000 and the rule is to risk 20% of the room, the maximum loss on the next trade is $1,200 - a number that changes as the account moves. a fixed dollar risk is easier to follow, but it is only safe while the room is at least five times that risk.

position sizing is where a rulebook becomes a trade. the percentage risk you choose means nothing until it is converted into lots, a stop distance and a lot or contract count. on a forex and cfd account the conversion has three inputs: the dollar risk, the distance between entry and stop in pips and lot value, and the value of one lot per unit of that distance. get any one wrong and the trade risks a different amount than intended.

the table is deliberately conservative. one percent per trade is the upper end of what a challenge rulebook supports, not a target. with a 10% total loss allowance, ten consecutive 1% losses use the entire budget; with a 5% daily stop, five losses in a day do the same. at 0.5% the account can absorb twenty consecutive losses, which is outside the range most strategies produce but inside the range a bad month can produce.

the stop distance is the input traders fudge most often. a stop placed at a round number because it "feels" safe is not a risk calculation. the stop belongs where the trade idea is invalidated, and the position size is whatever makes that stop equal the chosen dollar risk. if the invalidation point is far away, the position gets smaller; if it is close, the position gets larger. the dollar risk stays constant, which is the only way the loss column of a journal stays comparable across setups.
fixed dollar risk, variable position size: the stop location sets the size, not the other way round.

on forex, the arithmetic depends on the pair, the account currency and the lot size. a standard lot of eurusd is $10 per pip; a mini lot is $1; a micro lot is $0.10. a $500 risk budget with a 25-pip stop therefore allows two standard lots, or 20 mini lots, or 200 micro lots - the same exposure expressed three ways. on a pair quoted in another currency the pip value changes, and on metals or indices the contract specification does the same. the number that matters is the one in the platform's contract specification window, not a remembered rule of thumb.

two adjustments are specific to evaluation accounts. first, size against the remaining room rather than the starting balance once the account is in profit, particularly on a trailing threshold. second, size for the daily stop when a setup is taken late in the session: a trade that would be acceptable at 9am can breach the daily limit at 4pm because earlier losses have already consumed part of the budget. the correct size is the smaller of the two constraints, always.

a practical routine: before entry, write down the dollar risk, the stop price, the resulting size, and the remaining daily room. after entry, do not move the stop further away. after exit, record the realised risk as a percentage of the account and of the remaining room. ten trades of that record will tell you more about your sizing than any calculator, because it exposes the difference between the risk you intended and the risk you actually took.

a profit target is a distance, and the only useful question is how many trades it takes to cover that distance at a given risk-reward. on an illustrative $100,000 funding pips account with an 8% target, the account needs $8,000 of net profit. at a 1:2 risk-reward and 0.5% risk per trade, a winning trade makes $1,000 and a losing trade loses $500. a 50% win rate over 20 trades produces ten winners and ten losers: $10,000 gained, $5,000 lost, $5,000 net. that is short of the target. the same win rate over 32 trades produces $8,000 net, which is the target.

session-by-session plans look precise and are usually abandoned by day three. a more durable structure has four blocks: calibration, accumulation, protection and completion. each block has one objective, one size, and one reason to stop. because the blocks are defined by what the account is doing rather than by the calendar, the plan survives a bad week without needing to be rewritten.

the block sizes are deliberately not equal. calibration is small because its purpose is information, not profit. accumulation is the largest because the cushion is at its widest and the target is far away. protection reduces size as the floor closes in, and completion reduces it again because the remaining distance is small enough that a single loss would erase more than the gain available.
risk per trade falls across the four blocks; the target does not justify increasing it.

the exit rules matter as much as the entry rules. each block ends for a stated reason - two losses in a session, three in a row, 60% of the daily stop, the first breach - and when the reason appears, the block ends. the plan does not require the trader to judge whether the market will turn; it requires recognising a number that was written down when the account was calm.

two operating rules hold the blocks together. first, the daily check: before the first trade, state the remaining room, the daily stop and the risk unit for the current block. second, the weekly review: count the breaches, the average realised risk and the average r. if realised risk consistently exceeds planned risk, the blocks are fine and the execution is not; if realised risk matches planned risk and the expectancy is still negative, the strategy needs work before another fee is spent.

one more instruction belongs in the plan: what to do when the account reaches 70% of the loss allowance. the answer is stop trading for the day and review the last ten trades in writing. the rulebook will not stop the account there. the plan has to, and the moment to decide is now rather than at the floor.

failed attempts are not evenly distributed across causes. in practice a small number of behaviours accounts for most breaches, and they tend to arrive in the same order: the first mistake creates the condition for the second. understanding the sequence is more useful than memorising a list, because the sequence is what a trader can interrupt.

the first row causes the most failures because it is invisible. nothing about a fixed 1% risk unit feels wrong; it is taught as best practice in personal accounts. on a rulebook where the loss floor moves with equity, that same unit becomes more aggressive with every winner, which is the opposite of what the plan intended. the fix is a single line in the plan: risk is a percentage of the remaining room, recalculated daily.

the second row is the emotional one. moving a stop is a decision to accept a larger loss than the plan allowed, made at the worst moment for judgement. it is also the mistake most easily prevented, because a server-side stop does not ask permission. if the stop cannot be moved without deliberate action, the discipline gap narrows to whether that action is taken, which is a far easier question than whether the loss should be accepted.

the last row deserves a note of its own. traders who do the hard part well often fail in the final third because the finish line changes the perceived value of a small gain. a 0.5% gain that puts the account $400 from the target feels inadequate, so the size goes up. the rule that fixes this is deliberately unglamorous: the size near the target is smaller than the size at the start, and the last trades are taken at the plan's minimum size regardless of how close the target appears.

no rulebook is best for every trader, and the useful comparison is between structures rather than brands. funding pips fits a trader whose constraints match a static loss floor, a daily stop (percentage based) and one-off per attempt billing. a trader with a different constraint - a swing strategy, a session that does not overlap the market, a budget that cannot absorb a retry - will get a better expected outcome from a different structure, even if the other firm is less famous.

a consistency rule limits how much of the total profit can come from a single day. the usual form is a percentage: no single trading day may account for more than 30-50% of total profit at the time of payout. funding pips applies this condition as follows: usually none on the evaluation. the rule does not stop you passing the evaluation; it can stop you being paid, which is a more expensive failure because the fee and the time are already spent.

the arithmetic is simple and brutal. if the rule caps a single day at 40% of total profit, a $4,000 profit day requires at least $6,000 of profit on other days before the payout is valid. a trader who reaches the target with one $5,000 day and $3,000 spread across a month has an 62.5% concentration and fails the test. the same total profit earned as eight $1,000 days passes easily. the target is identical; the distribution is not.
same total profit, different distribution: consistency is a test of shape, not size.

that changes the correct plan. if a consistency condition applies, the target should be built from a repeatable daily edge rather than from one outsized trade. position size should be capped so that a single good day cannot exceed the concentration limit, even if the setup justifies more. in practice this means sizing for the rule, not for the opportunity: a 1:4 winner on a normal day is fine, but the same winner at triple size can make the account unpayable.

there is a second-order trap: the rule is usually assessed at payout, not at the moment of the trade. a trader can pass with a concentrated distribution and only discover the problem when requesting the first withdrawal. the time to check is before the first trade, by reading the funded terms and writing down the maximum single-day profit that keeps the account compliant at the expected total. if the expected total is $8,000 and the cap is 40%, no single day should exceed $3,200.

some firms apply consistency only to the evaluation, some only to the funded account, and some to both. the distinction matters because a rule that applies only at payout can be managed after the pass, while a rule that applies to the evaluation can fail the attempt outright. confirm which version applies to the plan you are buying, and if the answer is ambiguous, ask support in writing and keep the reply. ambiguity is resolved in the firm's favour in a dispute, so the only useful protection is documentation before purchase.

a prop evaluation has a visible price and an invisible total. the visible price is the fee on the checkout page. the total includes the expected number of attempts, the platform or data costs that continue between attempts, the cost of the time spent, and - if the attempt fails - the value of the information it produced. only the first is easy to compare, which is why it dominates the marketing.

stack those lines for two scenarios. a trader who passes first time at a $150 fee pays $150 plus one month of platform costs. a trader who takes four attempts pays $600 plus four months of platform costs plus the time - and if the entry fee is a subscription, the four attempts also carry the weeks spent in each. the second scenario is common, and it is the one the flat-fee model is priced against rather than the first.
the flat fee is priced against the realistic number of attempts, not the best case.

the comparison with a flat service is a comparison of two different bets. self-trading risks the fee repeatedly and keeps the skill; the service pays once and skips the execution work. neither dominates. a trader with a tested method and a record of passing should self-trade; a trader whose failures share one structural cause should either fix the cause or buy the outcome, not pay for the same lesson a third time.

whatever the route, the number to compare is the cost per funded account, not the cost per attempt. divide the total spent - fees, data, and any service fee - by the number of funded accounts actually produced. that figure is usually several times the checkout price, and it is the only one that is comparable across different routes.

the appeal of a passing service is straightforward: pay once, receive the outcome, avoid the execution work. the risks are less obvious, and all of them live in the firm's terms rather than in the service's marketing. a service can be honest and still be an unsuitable purchase for a particular account, because the rulebooks differ and the terms constrain what a third party may do.

the practical test is documentation. before paying anything, ask for the clause that permits the arrangement on the exact plan, and keep the reply with the dated terms page. a provider that answers with a guarantee rather than a clause has answered a different question. guarantees cannot be enforced across a rulebook the provider does not control; written confirmations can be relied on in a dispute.

there is also a compliance dimension after the pass. the funded account carries the same conduct rules as a self-traded one: no hedging across accounts, no prohibited news trading, no identity mismatch on the payout method. a pass obtained legitimately can still produce a withheld payout if the funded account is run outside those rules, which is why the handover matters as much as the work.

priced against the alternative, the flat fee is a bet on the number of attempts a rulebook would otherwise consume. if the honest expectation is one attempt, the fee is expensive. if it is three, the fee is cheaper than the fees plus the platform months. the useful discipline is to estimate that number from your own record before comparing prices, not after reading a sales page.

rules change between cohorts, plan names rotate, and the page a comparison article quoted may no longer be the page the firm publishes. none of that is a reason to avoid a firm; it is a reason to verify the exact plan before paying. the check below is deliberately mechanical, because a mechanical check is one that gets done.

save the pages. a dated copy of the terms as published on the day of purchase is the only document that settles an argument about which version applied. screenshots are sufficient; a pdf export is better because it preserves the date and the url. this takes two minutes and is the single most useful habit in this market.

ask one question in writing that the pages do not answer. for funding pips a good candidate is whether the loss floor is calculated on equity including open positions or on closed balance. the reply is specific, comparable between firms and impossible to spin. if support cannot answer a mechanics question, that is information about the operational depth of the firm before the fee rather than after it.

finally, check the plan name against the rulebook you planned for. multi-plan firms publish several products under one brand, and the search result for the brand will mix them. two pages from the same firm can describe different drawdown mechanics and both be accurate, because they describe different plans.

the pass email is the midpoint, not the finish. between the pass and the first payout there is a verification step, a contract, a funded login and a compliance period. each has its own failure mode, and none of them is about trading skill. the first week after a funding pips pass is mostly administrative, and treating it that way prevents the most avoidable loss of the whole process.

the frame matters because most prop-firm advice is written as if the only problem were finding a profitable strategy. it is not. an evaluation adds three constraints that a personal account does not have: a loss floor that ends the account, a calendar that may impose minimum days, and a payout condition that can reduce a profit after the pass. a method that ignores those constraints can be profitable in a demo and still fail the evaluation.

the rest of this guide works through those constraints in the order they bind: the loss floor first, because it decides position size; the target second, because it decides how many trades the plan needs; the calendar third, because it decides whether the plan is feasible; and the payout conditions last, because they decide whether a pass is worth anything. each section ends with a rule that can be written down and checked.

the weekend rule is easy to ignore during a winning week and impossible to ignore after a gap. prop firm treats weekend holding as follows: plan-specific, so confirm the funded terms as well as the evaluation terms. the rule usually interacts with two others: the daily stop, which may be calculated on the friday close, and the loss floor, which may be adjusted for the gap at the sunday open.

the risk arithmetic is straightforward. a position held over the weekend carries gap risk that cannot be stopped. on a $100,000 account with a 1% position and a 50-pip stop, a 150-pip weekend gap turns a $1,000 planned loss into $3,000. if the daily stop is 5%, that is 60% of the day's budget consumed by a single open position, before any decision is made. on a trailing threshold, the same gap can breach the floor outright.
a stop limits the loss only when the market trades through it; a gap does not.

where the rulebook allows weekend holding, the decision should still be deliberate. three questions: is the position small enough that a two-times-stop gap is survivable, is there a scheduled event over the weekend that could move the market, and does the strategy's edge depend on holding through the close? if the answer to the third question is no, closing is the cheaper choice. the foregone overnight move is a cost; the gap is a risk.

where the rulebook restricts weekend holding, the practical rule is a flat-by time well before the close. not at the close, when spreads widen and liquidity thins, but thirty to sixty minutes earlier, when the exit is still clean. the same applies to friday's daily stop: a position closed at the bell is a position that cannot gap, and a rulebook that resets the daily stop at the session close will not carry the loss into monday.

for swing strategies, the constraint may be the reason to choose a different firm rather than a different trade. a strategy that needs multi-day holds is incompatible with a rulebook that requires flat weekends, and no amount of position sizing fixes a structural mismatch. check the rule before buying the evaluation, not after the first friday.

the prop firm position on news trading is: plan-specific, and often restricted around major releases. read that as a constraint on the calendar, not as a suggestion. if the rule prohibits opening or holding positions in a window around a release, the correct behaviour is to be flat before the window and to stay flat until it closes. a stop is not a substitute for being flat, because the gap can be larger than the stop.

before paying for a prop firm evaluation, confirm every item below against the firm's own pages. the list is deliberately mechanical: each item is a question with a yes/no answer, not a judgement about the firm's quality. a firm can be legitimate and still be a poor fit for a particular trader, and the checklist is designed to expose fit rather than reputation.
the plan name is the one whose rulebook i have read, not a similar plan from the same brand.
the loss floor is defined on balance or equity, and i know which.
the daily stop, if any, resets at a stated time in a stated timezone.
the minimum trading days are compatible with the number of sessions my strategy needs.
the consistency rule, if any, applies to the evaluation, the funded account or both.
the first payout is eligible after a stated period, with a stated minimum.
news trading, weekend holding, hedging, copy trading, eas and account sharing are each explicitly allowed or prohibited.
the retry and refund policy is written down, not implied.
the total cost across my expected number of attempts is affordable without affecting my risk capital.
if i use a service, the terms permit third-party trading on this exact plan.
i have saved dated copies of the terms pages i relied on.

twelve items, ten minutes, and most of the expensive surprises in this market disappear. the items that most often fail are the consistency rule, the weekend restriction and the retry policy, in that order. each is buried in a terms page rather than a sales page, which is exactly why the checklist exists.

the last item is the one traders skip. a dated copy of the terms is not paranoia; it is the only way to resolve a dispute about what the rulebook said on the day of purchase. firms revise pages, and a revision is not a breach if the new terms were published before the trade. the copy establishes which version applied.

a trading journal is usually described as a tool for improving win rate. on an evaluation, its more valuable job is cost control: it identifies which losses were planned and which were caused by a rule breach, and it separates the two. a trader who knows that 70% of losses came from three breaches does not need a new strategy; they need three rules. a trader who knows that every loss was planned and the expectancy is still negative does need a new strategy.

the minimum viable journal is seven columns and takes ninety seconds per trade. the elaborate version with screenshots and sentiment scores is usually abandoned by day four. start with the seven, keep them for twenty sessions, and only add fields that answer a question you actually have. a journal that is too detailed to maintain produces no data at all.

review the journal weekly, not daily. daily review encourages reacting to noise; weekly review shows the distribution. count the breaches, the average planned risk, the average realised risk, the win rate and the average r. if realised risk is consistently higher than planned risk, the problem is execution. if realised risk matches planned risk and the expectancy is negative, the problem is the strategy. the two problems have different fixes, and the journal is what tells them apart.

keep the journal across attempts. a failed evaluation is only a total loss if it produces no information. the second attempt should start with the first attempt's distribution in hand: which setups worked, which sessions produced the losses, which rule was broken most often. that is the difference between paying for a retry and paying for a lesson.

lot size is the bridge between a percentage risk and a price stop. the formula is always the same: dollar risk divided by the value of the stop distance per lot. the inputs change with the pair, the account currency and the contract specification, which is why a remembered rule of thumb is unreliable. the consequence is a position size. once the stop distance and the instrument value are known, the calculation is exact, and an exact number is far easier to follow than an intention.

forex sizing starts with pip value. a standard lot of a usd-quoted pair is $10 per pip; a mini lot is $1; a micro lot is $0.10. the formula is: lots = dollar risk ÷ (stop distance in pips × pip value per lot). on a $100,000 evaluation risking 0.5% ($500) with a 25-pip stop, that is $500 ÷ (25 × $10) = 2.0 standard lots, or 20 mini lots, or 200 micro lots.

the table assumes a usd-quoted pair with a $10 pip value per standard lot. on pairs quoted in another currency, or on crosses, the pip value has to be converted into the account currency first. on gold the contract is usually 100 ounces and the tick value differs from a currency pair entirely, which is why a lot size copied from eurusd is not a size at all on xauusd.

the other input is the account currency. a euro-denominated account trading a dollar-quoted pair has a pip value in dollars that must be converted at the prevailing rate, and the conversion changes the risk slightly as the rate moves. for most evaluation sizes the difference is small, but it should be computed rather than assumed.
the stop distance sets the size; the risk budget stays constant.

a practical check: after entering the position, look at the platform's own profit-and-loss display for a one-pip move and compare it with the intended risk. if the numbers disagree, the lot size is wrong. this takes ten seconds and catches the most common sizing error before it becomes a loss.

a profit target is a distance, and the only useful question is how many trades it takes to cover that distance at a given risk-reward. on an illustrative $100,000 prop firm account with an 8% target, the account needs $8,000 of net profit. at a 1:2 risk-reward and 0.5% risk per trade, a winning trade makes $1,000 and a losing trade loses $500. a 50% win rate over 20 trades produces ten winners and ten losers: $10,000 gained, $5,000 lost, $5,000 net. that is short of the target. the same win rate over 32 trades produces $8,000 net, which is the target.

a passing service trades an evaluation on your behalf for a flat fee and returns a funded account in your name. the arrangement is only legitimate where the firm's terms permit third-party trading, and the fee is only fair where the retry policy is written down. the consequence is a contractual one. the firm's terms decide whether the arrangement is permitted, and the fee structure decides whether it is worth doing at all.

the process is deliberately narrow. you choose the firm and the account size; the service reads that firm's terms for the exact plan; if third-party trading is permitted, it trades the evaluation to the target inside the rulebook; if the account breaches, it retries under the same flat fee; when the target is reached, the funded account is issued in your name. the service does not hold the funded account and takes no share of its profit.

the parts that are not included matter as much as the parts that are. the firm's own evaluation fee and any reset charge are separate. the service cannot change the firm's rules, speed up a minimum-day requirement, or guarantee a payout that the funded terms make conditional. it removes execution risk, not counterparty or rule risk.

the market contains three kinds of provider: services that trade within the terms, services that ignore the terms, and services that take the fee and never trade. the first is a legitimate product; the second transfers a rules risk to the client; the third is fraud. the difference is visible before payment if you ask the right questions.

a guarantee is the least useful promise, because it is the hardest to enforce. a written terms check, a refund policy and a named contact are worth more than any claim about pass rates. if the provider cannot tell you which clause permits the arrangement, the arrangement is probably not permitted.

price is also a signal. a fee that is far below the market either buys a much smaller service or is not a service at all. a fee that is a percentage of the funded account aligns incentives but also gives the provider a claim on the account. the flat fee model is simple to audit: one payment, retries covered, no ongoing claim.

the clause that decides whether a service can operate is usually called "third-party trading", "account sharing" or "account management". some firms prohibit it on the evaluation, some on the funded account, and some on both. a service that does not ask which plan you bought cannot know which clause applies, because the same firm can publish different terms for different products.

where the terms permit the arrangement, the practical requirements are usually identity, login control and conduct. the account must remain in your name, the identity verification must be yours, and the trading must follow the same conduct rules as self-trading: no hedging across accounts, no prohibited news trading, no exploiting pricing errors. a service that treats the evaluation as a technical challenge rather than a compliance one is a risk to the account.

where the terms are silent, the safe reading is that the arrangement is not authorised. silence is not permission, and a firm that later decides the arrangement breached its terms can withhold a payout even after a pass. the only protection is a written confirmation before payment, kept with the dated terms page.

the flat $220 fee on this site is the same for any firm and account size, which makes the terms check the only variable. if the firm prohibits the arrangement, the job is declined before payment, and the fee is not collected. that is the correct order of operations: terms first, payment second.

trading the evaluation yourself is cheaper in cash if you pass first time. it is also the route that produces the skill, the journal and the evidence base for a second account. a service is not a substitute for those things; it is a way to buy the outcome when the execution, not the strategy, is the bottleneck.

the decision is therefore about what you are optimising. if the goal is to become a funded trader who can pass repeatedly, self-trading is the better investment even if it costs more in fees. if the goal is a funded account for a specific firm within a specific window, and the strategy is already sound, the service is the cheaper way to remove the execution variable.

a sensible sequence for many traders is self-trade the first evaluation, keep the journal, and use the service only for a firm whose rulebook has repeatedly defeated an otherwise working method. that sequence pays for the lesson once and buys the outcome once, instead of paying for the same lesson repeatedly.

a trailing threshold is the single rule most responsible for failed aquafunded attempts, and it is routinely described as a "drawdown" as if it were the same thing as a static loss limit. it is not. a static limit is anchored to the starting balance. a trailing threshold is anchored to the highest equity the account has reached, and on an intraday trail it is recalculated as open profit grows.

take an illustrative $100,000 account with a $6,000 trailing threshold. the account starts with $6,000 of room. a trade moves to $3,000 of open profit; the floor moves up to $97,000 and the room is still $6,000. the trade retraces and closes at break-even. the floor does not move back down. the account now has $3,000 of room, not $6,000, because the high-water mark was recorded. two break-even trades after a winner can leave an account with almost no cushion even though the balance never fell below its starting value.
the trailing floor follows the high-water mark; the static floor does not.

the practical consequence is that risk per trade has to fall as the target approaches. early in the attempt, with the full threshold ahead, a 1% risk per trade is comfortably inside the room. late in the attempt, after a run of profit, the same 1% risk can be larger than the remaining cushion because the cushion is measured from the new high, not from the original balance. traders who size every trade against the starting balance are therefore taking progressively more risk in relative terms without changing a single parameter.

the fix is unglamorous: keep a running high-water mark, compute the remaining room before every trade, and express the stop as a percentage of the room rather than a percentage of the balance. if the remaining room is $3,000 and the rule is to risk 20% of the room, the maximum loss on the next trade is $600 - a number that changes as the account moves. a fixed dollar risk is easier to follow, but it is only safe while the room is at least five times that risk.

there is a test that separates a trader who understands a tradify rulebook from one who has only read the sales page: ask what happens to the failure point after a winning trade. on a static floor the answer is "nothing". on a trailing threshold the answer is "it moves up, and it does not move back down". everything else in the risk plan follows from that answer.

sizing is not a judgement call; it is arithmetic with one fixed input and two measured ones. the fixed input is the dollar risk, which comes from the plan. the measured inputs are the stop distance, which comes from the chart, and the value of one point per contract, which comes from the instrument's specification. change either measured input and the size changes, even if the dollar risk does not.

on futures the numbers are exact. one micro e-mini s&p contract is $1.25 per tick and $5 per point; one micro nasdaq contract is $0.50 per tick and $2 per point. a 20-point stop on a micro s&p is $100, so a $250 risk budget supports two contracts with $50 left for commission. that residual is the part traders forget: on small accounts, commission can be a fifth of the risk budget, which means the effective stop has to be tighter or the size smaller.

a profit target is a distance, and the only useful question is how many trades it takes to cover that distance at a given risk-reward. on an illustrative $100,000 tradify account with an 8% target, the account needs $8,000 of net profit. at a 1:2 risk-reward and 0.5% risk per trade, a winning trade makes $1,000 and a losing trade loses $500. a 50% win rate over 20 trades produces ten winners and ten losers: $10,000 gained, $5,000 lost, $5,000 net. that is short of the target. the same win rate over 32 trades produces $8,000 net, which is the target.

finally, subtract costs before comparing any of this to a backtest. spread, commission, swap and slippage are charged whether the trade wins or loses. on a futures account, per-contract commission on a 20-trade month can equal a meaningful fraction of a small target. a backtest that ignores costs overstates expectancy, and an overestimated expectancy produces a plan that is too fast for the target and too large for the drawdown.

a plan is not a prediction. it is a set of rules that decides what you do on each of the twenty sessions an evaluation typically takes, including the sessions where nothing happens. the plan below is built around a 0.5% risk unit, a 1:2 minimum risk-reward and a hard stop at two losses per session. it assumes a futures account and a rulebook with a trailing loss floor. adjust the numbers to your own account, but keep the structure.

payouts from a prop firm are income, not capital gains from a brokerage account, in most jurisdictions. the firm pays a profit share for trading its capital; the trader receives a fee for a service, often with no employment relationship and no tax withheld. that classification drives the record-keeping: the relevant documents are the payout statements, the contracts and the fees paid, not a brokerage 1099 or equivalent.

the exact treatment depends on residence, the firm's jurisdiction and whether the trader operates as an individual or a company. this page cannot give tax advice and does not try to. what it can do is list the records that any adviser will ask for: every payout statement with the gross profit, the split, the fee deductions and the net received; every evaluation fee paid, including failed attempts; every platform or data subscription; and the dates of each.

the asymmetry that catches traders is that failed evaluation fees are usually deductible business expenses while the payouts are taxable income, but only if the activity is treated as a business rather than a hobby. that classification is jurisdiction-specific and depends on intent, organisation and repetition. a trader with one small payout and no records is in a different position from one running multiple accounts with a documented process.

keep the records in the currency you were paid and note the exchange rate on the payment date. a payout in dollars converted to another currency produces a gain or loss on the conversion that is separate from the trading result. ignoring it produces a reconciliation problem at year end that is much harder to fix than to prevent.

the practical rule is to treat the first payout as the moment the activity becomes a business for record-keeping purposes, and to keep everything from the first evaluation fee onward. the records are cheap to keep and expensive to reconstruct. a folder with dated pdfs of every fee, contract and payout is sufficient for most advisers to do the rest.

for funded engineer, the published structure is a two-phase evaluation with a static floor. the loss floor is static, the daily stop is yes, and the consistency condition is yes. billing is one-off per attempt, payouts follow profit split on a fixed schedule, and the supported platforms are mt4, mt5. those are the rows that matter. marketing pages tend to foreground the profit target and the profit split because both are easy to compare; neither tells you whether a given trade is survivable.

a static loss floor is the simplest rule in the funded engineer rulebook and the one traders most often misapply. the floor is anchored to the starting balance and does not move. on a $100,000 account with a 10% limit, the failure point stays at $90,000 from the first trade to the last, whatever the account does in between.

a profit target is a distance, and the only useful question is how many trades it takes to cover that distance at a given risk-reward. on an illustrative $100,000 funded engineer account with an 8% target, the account needs $8,000 of net profit. at a 1:2 risk-reward and 0.5% risk per trade, a winning trade makes $1,000 and a losing trade loses $500. a 50% win rate over 20 trades produces ten winners and ten losers: $10,000 gained, $5,000 lost, $5,000 net. that is short of the target. the same win rate over 32 trades produces $8,000 net, which is the target.

an evaluation is a performance with a deadline, and deadlines change behaviour. in an open-ended account, a losing week is a data point. in an evaluation with a target and a calendar, the same week feels like a countdown pressure, which produces the two behaviours that end most attempts: increasing size to catch up and taking setups that would not pass the checklist. neither is a character flaw; both are predictable responses to a finite runway.

the first defence is to make the deadline irrelevant to the decision. the target is a distance; the calendar is a separate constraint. if the strategy needs sixteen sessions and the rulebook allows sixty, there is no deadline in any meaningful sense. the trader who feels rushed is usually comparing their pace to someone else's screenshot, not to their own plan. writing the expected number of sessions next to the target, before the first trade, removes most of that pressure.

the second defence is a pre-mortem. before the attempt, write down the three most likely ways it fails, and the rule that prevents each. "i will increase size after two losses" is prevented by a fixed risk unit. "i will trade a news release to make back a loss" is prevented by a session checklist. "i will hold a loser overnight" is prevented by a hard flat-by time. the pre-mortem turns a vague intention to be disciplined into a specific rule that can be checked.

the third defence is a hard stop that is not negotiable in the moment. the rulebook's daily stop is a backstop, not a plan. the plan should stop earlier: two losses in a session, or a 1.5% drawdown on the day. once the stop is hit, the platform is closed for the day. the decision to stop is made once, when calm, rather than repeatedly, when not.

finally, separate the outcome from the execution. a losing trade taken according to plan is a good trade; a winning trade taken outside the plan is a bad one, because it teaches the wrong lesson. the journal should record the execution grade separately from the profit and loss. over twenty sessions, the execution grade is the variable the trader controls, and it is the one that predicts the next attempt better than any single result.

ask one question in writing that the pages do not answer. for funded engineer a good candidate is whether the loss floor is calculated on equity including open positions or on closed balance. the reply is specific, comparable between firms and impossible to spin. if support cannot answer a mechanics question, that is information about the operational depth of the firm before the fee rather than after it.

a profit target is a distance, and the only useful question is how many trades it takes to cover that distance at a given risk-reward. on an illustrative $100,000 ftmo account with an 8% target, the account needs $8,000 of net profit. at a 1:2 risk-reward and 0.5% risk per trade, a winning trade makes $1,000 and a losing trade loses $500. a 50% win rate over 20 trades produces ten winners and ten losers: $10,000 gained, $5,000 lost, $5,000 net. that is short of the target. the same win rate over 32 trades produces $8,000 net, which is the target.

there is a test that separates a trader who understands a ftmo rulebook from one who has only read the sales page: ask what happens to the failure point after a winning trade. on a static floor the answer is "nothing". on a trailing threshold the answer is "it moves up, and it does not move back down". everything else in the risk plan follows from that answer.

the platform is part of the risk system. it decides whether stops are server-side, how orders behave in fast markets and whether the trader can act when the connection is poor. the consequence is mechanical: an order that exists only on the chart is not a stop, and a setting that resets after an update is not a plan.
step 1: open the order ticket before you have a bias

open the ticket for the instrument and set the fields in the order the platform expects: instrument, size, stop, target. doing this before deciding direction prevents the common sequence in which the trade is sent and the protection is added afterwards, when the price has already moved. for prop firm mt4 mt5 ctrader platforms, the ticket is also the place to confirm the order type is the one the plan requires.

enter the stop as a price, not as a number of points or pips, unless the platform labels the field explicitly. a price is unambiguous; a distance depends on the platform's unit and on the direction of the trade. check the ticket preview, which shows the estimated loss at the stop, and compare it with the risk budget for the session.

after the order is accepted, open the order or position list and confirm the stop appears there. a line on the chart can be a client-side object that disappears when the terminal closes. if the list does not show the stop, the protection is not real; edit the position and attach it again.
step 4: test it on a demo with the same settings

place a small trade on a demo account, close the terminal, reopen it and confirm the stop is still present. this five-minute test catches the settings that reset after an update and the account types where the order is held differently. it is worth repeating after every platform update.
step 5: record the risk in the journal before the trade

write the planned dollar risk, the stop distance and the remaining room for the day. the journal entry is what makes the next review possible, and it forces the sizing decision to happen before the outcome is known. a trade without a recorded risk is a trade that cannot be evaluated afterwards.

after placing any protective order, verify it in three places: the order list, the position row and, where the platform offers it, the server-side order log. a stop that appears only as a line on the chart is a client-side object; it will not survive a disconnect. the order list is the authoritative view because it is populated from the server.

then test the behaviour on a demo account with the same broker settings. place a stop, disconnect the terminal, reconnect, and confirm the order is still there. this five-minute test is the difference between a stop and a hope. it is especially important after a platform update, because updates occasionally reset order defaults.

most traders arrive with one of four questions, and the guide they need depends on which one it is. if you are choosing a firm, start with the comparison and the rules matrix - they answer structural questions faster than any article can. if you have already bought an evaluation and failed it, the guides on drawdown mechanics and position sizing are where the answers are, because almost every failure comes from one of those two. if you have passed and cannot withdraw, the consistency rule and payout process articles cover the arithmetic that firms apply. and if you are deciding whether to use a passing service at all, the honest answer is in the sections below about when it is a bad idea.

three conventions are used consistently across the library. percentages are paired with currency wherever a limit is described, because a 5% daily loss limit means $1,250 on a $25,000 account and $10,000 on a $200,000 one, and only the second number makes clear how much room there actually is. trailing behaviour is always specified as intraday or end-of-day, never as just "trailing", because the two produce very different outcomes on the same equity curve. and timelines are given in trading days rather than calendar days, since firms count the days they count and weekends are not among them. if an article is missing one of those three details, it is a gap worth reporting.

everything here is written to be useful without a purchase. several readers use these guides to pass their own evaluation and never contact us, which is a perfectly good outcome - the material exists because understating evaluation mechanics is how traders lose money.

newest first. firm-specific guides cover the exact ruleset a trader is evaluating under, mechanics guides cover the rules that apply everywhere, and the payout section covers what happens after a pass. every entry lists its review date and approximate length, so it is clear before clicking whether an article is a quick explanation of one rule or a full walkthrough of a firm's entire evaluation structure. each article states the month it was reviewed, because firms change targets and drawdown behaviour more often than most traders expect.
the guides below are organised the same way: by rulebook model and by the decision they answer.
most of these guides are about one of two rulebook models, and the difference runs through all of them.
every article in this library eventually connects back to the same four constraints, and understanding them in advance makes the firm-specific guides much easier to apply.

the maximum loss permitted in a single day, usually around 5% on forex evaluations and enforced through a dollar threshold on futures ones. the detail that matters is the measurement basis: a limit calculated on equity including floating positions is considerably stricter than one calculated on closed balance, because an open trade that is temporarily deep in the red consumes budget even if it later recovers. traders comparing firms on headline percentages are comparing two different products.

static floors never move. end-of-day trailing floors follow your closed profit upward at the end of each session. intraday trailing floors follow your unrealised equity, which means a retracement can end an account while the day is still net positive. this is the single most consequential difference between firms, and it is invisible in most comparison tables - a firm advertising a "10% maximum drawdown" may be describing any of the three.

a cap on how much of your total profit may come from a single day, typically 30%. enforced at payout by most firms and during the evaluation by a few, it is the main reason an account that looks finished cannot withdraw. the arithmetic is unsentimental: a 30% rule means your largest day must be no more than a third of your total profit, so a $6,000 best day requires $20,000 overall.

usually four to ten days before an evaluation can be verified and, on funded accounts, before a first payout can be requested. this rule rarely ends an account, but it routinely delays one - and trying to reach the target quickly to finish sooner is what creates the consistency problem above.

if you read nothing else: size every trade against the daily loss limit rather than against the profit target, and read the drawdown type before the target percentage. those two habits prevent the majority of failed evaluations.
this site sells a service, so it is worth stating plainly when you should not buy it.

when your firm prohibits third-party trading and enforces it. the funded account can be voided after the fact, and that risk is yours. if your firm takes that position, either trade the evaluation yourself or move to a firm whose terms are clearer.

when the evaluation is not what is stopping you. if your failures come from market selection rather than from breaching limits, a passing service solves the wrong problem. the guides here are more useful to you than the service.
when you want to learn the constraint set. many traders pass their first evaluation deliberately as training, and a service removes that practice.

how to pass a prop firm challenge: the twelve-step version
everything in this library reduces to a sequence. followed in order, it removes most of the ways an evaluation ends early.

read the full rulebook before buying. target, daily loss limit, its measurement basis, maximum loss, drawdown type, minimum trading days, consistency rules, time limits, permitted instruments and news restrictions. most failures are traceable to a rule that was not read rather than a trade that went wrong.
convert every percentage into currency. a 5% daily limit on $200,000 is $10,000; on $25,000 it is $1,250. thinking in percentages hides how small the budget is on a small account.

identify the failure condition first. write down the exact equity level at which the account fails. on a static floor, that number never changes. on a trailing floor, it changes with every winning session and must be recalculated.

set risk per trade at no more than a third of the daily budget. three consecutive losses are a normal event, not a catastrophe, and sizing for that possibility is what keeps the account alive through ordinary variance.

set a hard daily stop in currency, not in feeling. when the day's realised loss reaches roughly 80% of the daily limit, trading stops. the last 20% exists to absorb slippage on a closing position, not to be spent on one more setup.

decide the pace before the first trade. calculate how many sessions the target requires at the planned daily profit. if the arithmetic says eighteen sessions and the firm has no time limit, the plan is eighteen sessions - not five sessions of over-sized attempts.

avoid the first hour if the rulebook is unclear. spreads are widest and news is most likely at the open. a plan that begins mid-session gives away less to execution costs and avoids the news windows firms restrict.

cap any single day at a third of the target. this is the consistency rule applied pre-emptively. even where a firm only enforces consistency at payout, building the habit during the evaluation makes the funded phase mechanical.

log every session with four numbers. closing equity, distance from the failure floor, percentage of target completed, and days used. a log is the only way to see a pattern - such as consistently losing on mondays - while it can still be corrected.

do not add size as the target approaches. the instinct to accelerate near the finish is the most expensive instinct in evaluation trading. reduce size instead: on a trailing structure it is required, and on a static structure it is still the lower-variance path to the same result.
check the minimum day count before declaring victory. reaching the target on day three of a ten-day requirement is not a completed evaluation.

read the funded rules before you request a payout. minimum days, profit threshold, consistency window and kyc are all separate conditions, and the first withdrawal usually fails for one of them rather than for performance.

steps five, six and ten do most of the work. almost every failed evaluation in our own records breached either the daily budget or the trailing floor in a single session - and almost all of those sessions were a plan failure rather than a market failure.
thirty terms that appear in rulebooks and forum threads, defined the way they are used rather than the way they are marketed.
challenge / evaluation: the assessment phase in which a trader attempts to reach a profit target without breaching a loss limit.
phase one / phase two: in a two-phase structure, the first assessment with the larger target and the verification phase with the smaller one.
verification: the second phase on firms that run two, generally with a reduced target and the same loss limits.
profit target: the return required to pass, expressed as a percentage on forex evaluations and as a dollar amount on futures ones.
daily loss limit: the maximum permitted loss in one trading day, resetting each morning.
maximum loss / overall drawdown: the total loss permitted before the account fails.
trailing drawdown: a failure level that follows equity upward, shrinking the buffer as profit accumulates.
end-of-day trailing: a trailing floor that updates only on profit closed at the end of a session.
intraday trailing: a trailing floor that follows unrealised equity, tightening on every favourable tick.
minimum trading days: the number of distinct days with qualifying activity required before verification or payout.
consistency rule: a cap on the share of total profit that may come from a single day, commonly 30%.
time limit: an overall window in which the evaluation must be completed, where the firm imposes one.
reset: restarting the same evaluation after a breach, sometimes free and sometimes charged by the firm.
breach: any rule violation that ends the evaluation, whether by loss limit, consistency failure or prohibited activity.
funded account: the live account issued by the firm after a passed evaluation.
profit split: the share of profit paid to the trader, typically 80-90% on funded accounts.
payout cycle: how often a firm processes withdrawals, from weekly to monthly.
profit threshold: the minimum profit required before a payout can be requested.
scaling plan: a structure that increases account size or split percentage as payout milestones are met.
instant funding: an account that starts funded with no evaluation, at a higher purchase price.
add-on / reset fee: a firm's charge for restarting or extending an evaluation.
account size: the nominal balance of the evaluation, which determines the dollar value of percentage-based limits.
drawdown (dd): the distance from peak equity to current equity, or the failure threshold itself depending on context.
passing service: a third-party operation that trades an evaluation on a trader's behalf for a fee.
one caution on abbreviations: firms share initials, and "max dd" means the failure threshold in one rulebook and the cushion above it in another. where a term matters, use the firm's own definition.
four of the five failure modes are sizing failures, which is why the risk budget is worth understanding first.

oversized position after a losing morning. the trader tries to recover the day in one trade and consumes the remaining daily budget. fix: fixed risk per trade at a third of the daily limit, and a stop when 80% of the day's budget is spent.

trailing floor after a strong session. a large winning day lifts the failure level, and the next normal pullback ends the account. fix: recalculate the failure level after every session, and reduce size as target completion rises.

consistency failure at payout. one dominant day makes up too large a share of total profit. fix: cap individual days at a third of the target during the evaluation and add ordinary winning days before requesting a withdrawal.

racing the minimum day count. the target is hit early and the trader keeps trading to "stay active" instead of stopping. fix: once the target is reached, trade minimum size on the remaining required days, or stop entirely where the firm permits.

ignoring news and instrument restrictions. a legitimate position is held through a restricted window or in a prohibited instrument. fix: write the restrictions into the plan as hard rules and treat ambiguous definitions as the stricter reading.
related reading: the ultimate guide covers each failure mode in depth, and the rules matrix shows which firms enforce which constraints and when.
a challenge fee is a small amount of money and a large amount of time. answering these questions first takes twenty minutes and prevents the most common purchases that were never going to work.

1. which market will i trade on the funded account? forex evaluations are percentage-based with static or end-of-day trailing drawdowns; futures evaluations are dollar-based with intraday trailing thresholds and payout-stage consistency rules. buying an evaluation in a market you do not intend to trade adds a variable you cannot control.

2. is the drawdown static or trailing? this is the single most consequential difference between firms and the one most often glossed over. if the answer is not immediately clear from the firm's documentation, that ambiguity is itself a warning.
3. is the daily limit measured on equity or on closed balance? the difference roughly doubles the required discipline at the same headline percentage.
4. is there a consistency rule, and when does it apply? at payout is more manageable than during the evaluation, and none at all is the easiest to plan around.
5. are there minimum trading days? and what counts as a qualifying day - a closed trade, an order fill, or a held position.
6. is there an overall time limit? a window compresses the required profit per session and removes the option of waiting out a bad week.
7. which instruments are permitted, and at what maximum size? instrument lists are usually published; lot and contract caps sometimes are not.
8. what are the news and weekend holding rules? and how strictly are they enforced relative to the published definition.
9. what are the payout conditions on the funded account? minimum days, profit threshold, consistency window, processing time and withdrawal methods.
10. what does a reset cost? free within a window, a reduced fee, or a full new challenge purchase - this changes the true cost of an evaluation substantially.

11. what does the firm's client agreement say about third-party trading? if it prohibits it and enforces the policy, the funded account can be voided after the fact. that risk is worth knowing before paying anyone.

12. if i fail twice on this rulebook, what will i change? if the answer is "try harder", the plan is not a plan. a useful answer names a specific change: a different firm, a smaller size, a lower profit target per session.

dividing the daily limit into thirds keeps a normal losing streak from ending the evaluation.

what a managed evaluation actually looks like, day by day

every evaluation follows the same rhythm, though the length changes with the firm. a two-phase forex challenge with no time limit is paced very differently from a futures evaluation with a thirty-day window, and the daily plan is written accordingly.

before a single trade is placed, the firm's rules are written into a one-page plan: the profit target in currency and percentage, the daily loss limit in currency, whether the maximum loss is static or trailing, whether the trailing stops at break-even or keeps following, the minimum number of trading days, any consistency requirement, and the restrictions on news trading, weekend holds, and instruments. this document is the only thing that decides whether the evaluation is passed. market opinion is secondary.

the opening phase is deliberately unremarkable. positions are sized so that a losing streak of three or four trades cannot approach the daily limit, and the target exposure is chosen from the firm's permitted instrument list rather than from a favourite pair or contract. the goal of the first days is not profit - it is distance between equity and the failure floor. a trader who is 1% up with the floor untouched has more room to work with than a trader who is 3% up with a trailing floor sitting just beneath the current price.

this is where most self-managed attempts die. once an account is halfway to target, the temptation is to accelerate, which means larger size, which means the daily limit is consumed by a single position. in a managed evaluation the daily risk budget is fixed at the start and does not expand because the account is winning. progress is reported as it happens, and if a day is flat, that is recorded as a flat day rather than an excuse to double up.

when the target is within reach, the priority flips from making money to not breaching anything. trading stops earlier in the session, size comes down, and the remaining ground is covered in small increments. where a firm requires a minimum number of trading days, those days are logged with legitimate activity - a requirement that catches out traders who sprint to target in three sessions and then discover the account is not eligible for funding until day ten. the final checkpoint is the consistency test: if one day is more than roughly a third of total profit, additional ordinary winning days are added until the distribution is acceptable.

when the firm verifies the pass, the account is funded and the credentials are handed over. from that moment the plan is yours to keep or throw away - and the funded phase has its own set of checkpoints before a payout clears.
