most services in this market charge a share of the funded account, typically somewhere between 10% and 30% of payouts, sometimes indefinitely. that model aligns incentives in theory - the service earns only if the trader earns - but in practice it changes what the service optimises for. a split model rewards large accounts and long retention; a flat fee rewards a clean pass and a client who comes back for a second account. the second incentive is easier to check: either the certificate exists or it does not.

there is a cost to the flat model, and it should be stated plainly. the service is paid whether or not the evaluation passes, so the only thing protecting quality is the retry clause and reputation. anyone comparing services should treat that as the key question: what happens on a failure, in writing, before money changes hands.
send the firm and the size. a short message naming the firm, the account size and the platform is enough to get a quote and a timeline. nothing else is needed to start.

confirm the firm's third-party policy. some firms prohibit third-party trading and enforce it after funding rather than during the evaluation. where a firm's position is clear and prohibitive, the honest answer is to pass it yourself or choose another firm.
rulebook translation. the firm's terms are reduced to four numbers that fit on an index card: daily loss budget, maximum loss distance, target in r terms and any consistency constraint at payout.
evaluation traded to target. pacing is deliberate rather than fast, typically two to three weeks, because a fast pass with no margin tends to fail the payout stage.
funded account issued in your name. the certificate or dashboard screenshot is the record. from that point the account, the payouts and the tax position are yours.

any firm with a published rulebook and an account size the client can afford is workable in principle. what is not workable is a firm whose terms are ambiguous on the two things that decide an evaluation: how the loss limit is measured and whether third-party trading is permitted. ambiguity in either direction turns a rules problem into a dispute, and a dispute is the one outcome that costs the client more than a failed attempt.

firms that explicitly prohibit third-party trading are refused, not worked around. the reason is not moral positioning; it is that enforcement after funding is the worst possible outcome for a client, since it forfeits the account at exactly the point where the work would have paid. a service that quietly accepts those terms is transferring its own risk to the person least able to absorb it.

everything else is negotiable, and most of it should be discussed before purchase rather than after. account size, platform, instrument set and even the timing of the attempt can all be adjusted to fit a client's circumstances - a trader who wants a small first account and a three-week window is a different assignment from one who wants the largest tier available this month. what cannot be adjusted is the rulebook, and that is precisely why it is the thing read first.

if you are undecided between two firms, send both names. the reply will usually be a recommendation with a reason attached, and the reason is the useful part: it tells you which of the two rulebooks is more forgiving at the account size you can afford, which is a question with an answer independent of anyone's opinion about the firms themselves.

"verified" is the most overused word in prop trading and the only one that can be checked independently. this page explains what a myfxbook-verified record does and does not prove about a passing service, and the four checks that separate a real track record from a screenshot.
a myfxbook account is a read-only record of closed and open trades, synced from a broker - not a picture that can be edited.
verification proves a trading history existed. it does not prove that the history came from a prop firm evaluation, or that it will repeat.
the four checks that matter are the sync method, the account age, the drawdown profile and the trade distribution.
any service claiming verification should be able to show the live link, not a pdf of a link.

myfxbook works by connecting to a broker or trading account with read-only access and importing the trade history. the resulting record is hosted on myfxbook's servers and updated as trades occur. because the service holds only read access, the account owner cannot edit history after the fact, and because the record lives on a third-party domain, it cannot be quietly adjusted when a bad month arrives.

that property - an external, read-only, time-stamped record - is the entire value. it is not that myfxbook is authoritative about skill; it is that it is authoritative about what trades were placed and when. most claims in this market fail on that much narrower test.

first, the screenshot. a cropped image of a platform with a balance and a profit figure is unverifiable by construction, and it takes about ninety seconds in an image editor. second, the demo account. a myfxbook page can be attached to a demo as easily as a live account, and the distinction is shown on the account page rather than in the marketing copy. third, the selective window. a verified account is real, but the link provided may cover only the profitable period, with an earlier link quietly retired.

all three are defeated by the same habit: follow the link, check the sync status, check the account type, and look at the full history rather than the headline percentage. none of that requires technical knowledge, and all of it takes about two minutes.

a prop firm evaluation is usually traded on a firm's own platform or a broker feed under the firm's account, and not every firm's accounts can be linked to myfxbook. where they can, the record will show the account's balance and equity curve, the trade list with timestamps, and the drawdown profile. where they cannot, verification has to come from the firm's own dashboard or certificate instead.

that is an important qualification and it is the reason this page does not present verification as a single standard. a certificate from the firm proves a pass on a date. a myfxbook record proves a trading history. neither proves the other, and a service that conflates them is either confused or hoping you are.
an honest reading of a verified record stops at four boundaries, and every one of them matters to a buyer.

a verified history is a sample. a sample of forty trades with a positive expectancy is evidence of a process; it is not a forecast. the stronger claim - that a service will pass the next evaluation - is not something a track record can support, which is why a retry clause matters more than a highlight reel.
it cannot prove the trades were placed on a funded account

unless the account is labelled by the firm, a verified record is a trading record. the step from a profitable trading account to a passed evaluation involves a rulebook: daily limits, maximum loss, consistency at payout. a trader can be profitable and still fail an evaluation by breaching a limit, and a track record does not show which rules were respected.

a verified account belongs to an account holder, and a service is an arrangement between people. the link proves the account exists and performed; it does not prove that the person operating it is the person who will trade your evaluation. that gap is closed by the certificate and by the funded account being issued in your name, not by the track record.

firms audit after the fact. a record can look clean and an account can still be closed for a position held over a weekend or a strategy the terms prohibit. the only defence is reading the firm's rules before the work starts, which is why the rulebook question comes before the evidence question in any sensible due diligence.
given a live link, four things are worth checking and each takes under a minute. they are ordered by how often they expose a misleading claim.

myfxbook shows whether an account is synced automatically or updated manually, and whether it is live or demo. a manual update means the owner chooses when the record advances. a demo label means the record describes a simulation, however profitable. both are legitimate for testing a strategy and neither is evidence of a prop firm pass.

look at the first trade date and the gaps. a record that starts three weeks before the screenshot and stops at the peak is a window, not a history. a record that runs through losing months is far more informative than one that does not, because the drawdown profile is what a firm's rules actually test.

find the worst peak-to-trough decline in the record and compare it with the daily and maximum loss limits of the firm being discussed. a record with a 14% drawdown cannot have been produced on an account with a 10% maximum loss without a reset, whatever the total return says.

sort the daily results. if 60% of the profit came from two sessions, the record describes a trader whose results depend on rare days - which is precisely what a consistency rule at payout is designed to catch. a record with a flatter distribution is more compatible with a funded account that has to survive months, not weeks.
verification comes in four flavours in this market, and they are not interchangeable. ranking them by how hard they are to fake is the quickest way to read a provider's claims.

the strongest package is a combination: a certificate that fixes the firm, size and date; a verified record showing the trading that produced it; and a payout receipt that closes the loop. any single item leaves a gap, and a provider who volunteers all three without being asked is doing something unusual in this market.

elitepropx charges one flat $220 for any prop firm and any account size, with retries on rule breaches at the same firm and size covered, no profit split, and the funded account issued in the client's own name. the fee structure is relevant to this page for one reason: a flat fee does not depend on how long an account is traded or how large it becomes, so there is no incentive to keep a client on an evaluation longer than the rules require.

evidence is provided before purchase rather than after. ask for the certificate from a comparable assignment - same firm, same account size - and a live verification link where the firm's platform allows one. if a firm's accounts cannot be linked to an external tracker, that is a property of the firm rather than a refusal, and the certificate plus the funded dashboard is the substitute.

what will not happen is a claim of a guaranteed pass. every evaluation contains variance, and the controls that produce a pass rate are budgeting controls rather than predictions. the retry clause exists because that is true.

the work does not scale with account size: the rulebook is read once, the plan is written once, and the daily discipline is identical whether the account is $25,000 or $200,000. what scales is the payout, and that belongs to the client. a percentage-based fee would make the service a partner in the upside while leaving the client with all of the downside, which is a worse arrangement for anyone who intends to keep the account.
can i see the live link, not a screenshot? a provider that cannot produce a clickable record is asking for trust instead of showing evidence.
which firm and which account size does it correspond to? a certificate is specific; a record is not, and the two need to match.
what happened to the attempts that failed? the answer describes the denominator, and the denominator is where claims are inflated.
does my firm permit this arrangement? ask both the provider and the firm, in writing, and keep the reply.
what is the retry policy if a rule is breached? the failure case is where a client has no leverage, so it should be settled before payment.

five questions, ten minutes, and the answers either hold together or they do not. that is a better use of an afternoon than comparing testimonials, because testimonials are written by people with a completed transaction and questions are answered by people who expect more.
an equity curve shows the shape of the risk, not just the result.

a verified record is usually presented as one number - total gain or percentage - and that number is the least informative thing on the page. five features carry almost all of the useful information, and each maps onto a rule that a firm will apply.

two records can show the same total return with completely different risk. one climbs steadily and gives back 2% at a time; the other gains 18% in a fortnight and then loses 12% before recovering. the first is compatible with a 10% maximum loss. the second cannot have been produced on such an account without a reset, and the difference is visible in the curve within ten seconds.

look for the worst peak-to-trough decline in percentage terms, and compare it with the firm's maximum loss once floating equity is counted. if the record's worst decline exceeds the limit, the account either was not subject to that limit or was reset after the fact.

frequency tells you which rulebook the record is compatible with. a record with forty trades a day describes a scalping approach, which suits a firm with intraday rules and no overnight holding. a record with one position held for a week describes a swing approach, which requires an account type that permits weekend exposure. a record that mixes both without explanation describes someone who has not settled on a process.
feature three: the win rate and the payoff ratio together

either number alone is meaningless. a 30% win rate is excellent with a 3:1 payoff and catastrophic with 0.5:1. reading them together tells you whether the approach survives a normal losing sequence, which is what a daily limit tests. a record with a 25% win rate and a 4:1 payoff will contain runs of six losses, and a trader using 2% risk on a 5% daily limit cannot survive a run of six losses inside a day.

if 80% of the profit came from one instrument, the record is a statement about that instrument rather than about a general process. that is not disqualifying - specialists exist - but it changes what a buyer should expect: the same approach may not transfer to a different market, and the evaluation must be traded on the instrument the record describes.

long flat periods - weeks with no trades or with results clustered around zero - are the most honest part of any record, because they show how the trader behaves when nothing is working. a record with no flat stretches either covers a short period or has been filtered to remove them, and the willingness to sit out is a better predictor of surviving a two-month evaluation than any win rate.
a verified record is evidence of a completed sequence, not only of a good month.
understanding the mechanics removes most of the mystique and most of the trust that providers ask for.
the account is connected. the trader supplies read-only investor access to myfxbook. no trading permissions are granted, which is why the record cannot be curated later.
history is imported. closed trades and balance movements are pulled from the broker or platform feed, and new trades are added as they occur.
the record is published under a permanent url. that url is what a buyer should be given. a pdf of a screenshot is not the same artefact, however professional it looks.
the account runs in public. the value of the exercise is that a bad month appears on the record as it happens, in the same place, with no opportunity to swap accounts quietly.

the practical consequence for a buyer is that the link must be live and must be the same link that was published earlier. a provider whose verification link changes each month has a verification problem, not a marketing one.

many prop firms run proprietary platforms and do not permit external account linking. in that case the honest substitute is the firm's own dashboard, a certificate with the firm's branding and account number, and payout receipts with dates. that is weaker evidence in one respect - it depends on the provider not doctoring an image - and stronger in another, because it ties the record to a specific firm, size and date, which an external tracker does not.
the loop closes at the withdrawal, which is the only step that proves the whole chain.
a pass is not money. the loop closes when a payout arrives, and that is the claim worth asking for first, because it is the hardest to fake and the most frequently omitted.

a useful payout record shows the date, the amount, the method and the account it relates to, with personal details redacted. requests, approvals and receipts are all part of it. one receipt is a data point; a series of them over several months is evidence that a firm's payout process actually works for that trader, which is the thing a new client is really buying into.

it is also worth asking about payouts that did not happen. every funded trader eventually has a request delayed, refused or reduced, and a provider who claims otherwise is describing a market that does not exist. the informative answer names a case, the rule that caused it, and what was done - which is usually nothing, because the rule was in the terms.

claims in this market come in four sizes, and each needs its own evidence. "i passed an evaluation" needs a certificate. "i passed evaluations on this firm at this size" needs several certificates with matching firm and size. "i get paid" needs payout receipts. "i can pass yours" needs the first three plus a written retry policy, because the only claim that matters to a buyer is the forward-looking one, and that can never be fully evidenced.

most buyers spend their first ten minutes on price and their next ten on testimonials, which are the two least informative things available. the order below uses the same ten minutes on the only questions that change an outcome.
read the firm's rulebook first. daily limit, maximum loss mechanic, target, minimum days, payout conditions. two minutes, and it determines whether the rest of the conversation is worth having.
ask whether the firm permits third-party trading. in writing, to the firm. if the answer is prohibition with enforcement after funding, stop.
ask the provider for a certificate from a comparable assignment. same firm, same account size, dated, with the account number visible.
follow any verification link rather than viewing a screenshot. check sync status, account type, age and worst drawdown against the firm's limit.
ask what happens on a breach. the retry terms, in writing, before money moves.
ask who the funded account belongs to. the account should be issued in your name, with payouts paid to you and no split.
ask about the failure case in the last twelve months. what went wrong, which rule, and what changed as a result.
only then discuss price. price is the last variable, not the first, because a cheap attempt on an unsuitable rulebook is the most expensive option available.

eight steps, ten minutes, and they produce a decision that can be explained to someone else. that is the practical test of due diligence: if the reasoning cannot be written in three sentences, it was not reasoning.
what to do when a claim turns out to be wrong

claims in this market are sometimes wrong without being fraudulent. rules change, accounts get closed after review, a certificate that was accurate in march is misleading in june. the informative thing is what a provider does when the gap is pointed out.

three responses are acceptable: a correction with the date, a removal of the claim, and an explanation of the rule that changed. one response is not: silence followed by a new claim. a buyer who has already paid is dependent on the first three, which is why asking about a past error is a reasonable question before paying rather than after.

the verification standards described here are not firm-specific, so they do not expire with a rulebook revision. the examples and thresholds are reviewed each quarter, and the page is dated in its header. where a claim in this article conflicts with a firm's published terms, the firm's terms win - the article explains how to read a rulebook, not what any particular rulebook says.

the service terms referenced here are the ones currently offered: one flat $220 for any prop firm and any account size, retries on rule breaches at the same firm and size covered, no profit split, funded account issued in the client's name. if those terms change, they change on the terms page first, and this page follows.
providers with no verification usually offer an argument instead. the arguments recur, and each has a short answer.
an external tracker does not disclose tax information or banking details; it shows trades. privacy about personal finances is legitimate and unrelated to whether a read-only link can be published.
a certificate with the account number redacted and the firm, size and date visible is enough to establish a pass. unwillingness to share even that is unwillingness to be checked.
it takes about twenty minutes, once, and then updates itself. the setup cost argument describes a provider who has never done it, which is the same as having nothing to verify.
results that cannot be inspected are claims, and claims are what the buyer is trying to avoid relying on. the phrase is a request for trust dressed as a statement of fact.
correct, and irrelevant. the claim being checked is not that the future is certain but that the past happened. that is a factual question with a checkable answer.
which is precisely why the buyers who insist otherwise get treated differently. the market's low standard is an opportunity for anyone willing to meet a higher one.

a hypothetical record will make the method concrete. a provider publishes a verified account showing a 34% gain over seven weeks, a 71% win rate, and a maximum drawdown of 11.4%. the marketing describes a $100,000 evaluation passed in nineteen days.

four checks, four problems. the drawdown of 11.4% exceeds a 10% maximum loss, so the account cannot have been that evaluation without a reset. the win rate of 71% combined with a small average win implies a payoff structure where a single loss costs several wins, which is incompatible with a 5% daily limit if two losses land in one day. the record's trade count - over nine hundred trades in seven weeks - is a scalping profile, which does not fit a nineteen-day pass on a firm with a four-day minimum unless the position sizing was tiny relative to the target. and the record shows no losing week at all, which across seven weeks is either remarkable or filtered.

none of those findings proves fraud. together they show that the record and the claim describe different things, and the correct response is to ask which is which rather than to accept the pair as a package.

the same claim, done properly, would show a drawdown comfortably inside the firm's limit, a trade frequency consistent with the evaluation length, at least one flat or negative week, and a distribution of daily results that would survive a consistency check at payout. it would be accompanied by a certificate naming the firm, the size and the date, and by a payout receipt if the service claims to have been paid.

that combination is unglamorous and it is the whole point: verification is not a marketing asset, it is a reconstruction of what happened. a buyer who can reconstruct the account from the evidence knows more than a buyer who has read a testimonial page twice.

a verified record is a fact about the past and a weak predictor of the future, and both halves of that sentence matter. treating it as worthless is as wrong as treating it as a guarantee: the provider who can show one has at least done the work of being checkable, and the buyer who insists on one has eliminated the easiest category of dishonesty in the market.

the rest of the decision - whether the rulebook suits the strategy, whether the fee structure aligns the incentives, whether the funded account lands in your name - sits outside the evidence and inside due diligence. verification tells you who you are talking to; the rulebook tells you what you are buying.

one further note on how to hold this standard without becoming impossible to please. a small provider may have three certificates and no public tracker, and three dated certificates from three different firms are stronger evidence than a single verified record of a personal account. the question to ask is not "do you have myfxbook" but "what can i check, and can i check it before i pay". the answers to that question separate providers far more reliably than any single tool.
that is the standard applied here: what can be checked is offered before it is requested, and what cannot be checked is described as such rather than dressed up.
everything above is checkable in an afternoon, and none of it requires trusting an article on the internet, including this one.

the record itself is hosted externally and synced read-only, so the history cannot be edited after the fact. what can be misrepresented is what the account is: a demo or a personal trading account can be presented as though it were a prop firm evaluation.

they prove different things. a certificate fixes the firm, account size and date of a pass. a verified record shows the trading that produced a result. the strongest claim uses both, plus a payout receipt.

the enquiries that go well are the ones where the trader has already thought about the shape of the engagement. four questions do most of that work.
1. do you want this evaluation passed, or do you want to learn to pass it yourself?

both are legitimate. the guides on this site cover the mechanics of passing in detail, and several readers use them to pass their own evaluation without paying anyone. if your goal is capability rather than an account, say so and the reply will point at the material that helps rather than a sales pitch.

if you have failed one or two evaluations, what ended them? a daily limit breach and a consistency failure call for different advice. knowing the failure mode is often the difference between recommending a firm with a static floor and one with a trailing threshold - and it occasionally reveals that the firm, not the execution, is the problem.
3. have you checked your firm's position on third-party trading?

this is the single most important pre-purchase check. some firms prohibit it outright, some restrict account sharing, and some are silent. if your firm's terms make the arrangement a breach, the honest advice is to pass the evaluation yourself or switch firms - and you will get that answer rather than a payment request.

you do not need a polished answer. but traders who arrive with a rough sense of how they intend to trade a funded account - risk per trade, maximum daily risk, when to withdraw - end up in a much better position than those who treat funding as the finish line. if the answer is "i have not thought about it", the handover material covers it, and it is worth knowing that going in.

firm compliance check: what we look for before accepting an assignment
every enquiry triggers the same document review before a fee is quoted. it takes about twenty minutes and it has stopped more bad assignments than any other part of the process.

some firms state plainly that the account must be traded by the holder. where that language exists and the firm enforces it, the assignment is declined and the client is told why. not every firm enforces what it writes - but the client should decide that risk with the facts in front of them, not after a funded account is voided.

a softer version of the same rule: the agreement may not ban third-party trading, but it may restrict credentials being shared or logins from multiple locations. those clauses are often unenforced in practice, and they sometimes create friction in the funded phase if a client later travels while the account shows a consistent access pattern from elsewhere.
3. what are the funded-stage rules, not just the evaluation rules?

consistency windows, first-payout delays and profit thresholds decide whether a passed account produces money. a firm with a comfortable evaluation and an aggressive payout-stage consistency rule is a worse assignment than the evaluation rules suggest, and it is worth knowing that before the client pays anything.

some promotional evaluations combine a short window, a tight trailing threshold and a large target. the result is an evaluation where the outcome depends on luck, and a service that takes the fee anyway is selling a lottery ticket with a process attached. those are declined, even when the account size looks attractive.

withdrawal methods, processing times, minimum withdrawal amounts and any restriction on taking profit in the first months. none of these affect passing, but all of them affect whether the funded account is useful to the person paying for it.

the outcome of that review is sent in the first reply: proceed, proceed with a caveat, or a recommendation against. roughly one enquiry in ten comes back with a caveat, and it is not always the one the client expected.
the first evaluation should match the plan, not the biggest advertised account.
the most common enquiry is not "can you pass my firm?" but "which firm should i buy?" - and the answer is driven by how much room the rules leave, not by the size of the account.

start with a static maximum loss. firms whose failure floor never moves give a risk plan its best chance, because profit does not shrink the buffer. on a $100,000 account with a 10% limit and a static floor, the failure level stays at $90,000 whether the balance is $100,000 or $115,000.

prefer no consistency rule during the evaluation. a payout-stage rule can be managed by adding ordinary winning days before a withdrawal. an evaluation-stage rule constrains pace from the first session and makes a fast target dangerous.

check for a time limit. no limit is better than thirty days, because a flat week costs time rather than the account. where a firm imposes a window, the plan has to be tighter and the required profit per session rises accordingly.

consider the payout cycle before the split percentage. an 80% split paid weekly delivers cash more often than 90% paid monthly, and for a trader withdrawing regularly the difference is larger than the headline suggests.

abstract process descriptions are hard to judge. here is what a real engagement looks like from first email to funded handover, using a typical case: a trader with two failed attempts behind them, evaluating a $100,000 two-phase forex account.
"i want to pass an ftmo $100k two-phase evaluation. i have failed twice, both times on the daily loss limit after a bad morning. what do you charge and how long does it take?"

three things in that message make the reply useful: the firm, the size, and the failure mode. the failure mode is the most valuable of the three - two daily limit breaches says the problem is sizing after a losing session rather than market selection, and it shapes the risk plan that will be used.

the response contains the flat $220 fee, a timeline in trading days rather than calendar days (sixteen to twenty), a note that ftmo measures its 5% daily limit on equity including floating positions, and confirmation that a reset is covered if an attempt fails on a rule breach. it also asks one compliance question: whether the trader has read ftmo's terms on third-party trading. a summary of what those terms say is included, along with the honest caveat that firms can change policy and that any enforcement decision is the firm's.

the trader reads the compliance note, decides the risk is acceptable to them, and pays. payment confirms the firm, size and structure in writing, including the point that the firm's challenge fee is separate and already paid to the firm.

two documents go out. the rulebook summary lists target, daily limit with its measurement basis, maximum loss and drawdown type, minimum trading days, instrument restrictions, news windows and the funded-stage payout conditions. the risk plan converts them into numbers: $1,600 maximum risk per trade, three positions maximum, a hard stop at $4,500 of realised daily loss, no trades inside a news window, and a target of $800-1,200 of profit per session rather than a large daily goal.

that last decision matters more than it looks. a trader aiming for $3,000 a day takes roughly three times the risk to reach it, and the daily limit ends the account long before the target arrives. a trader aiming for $1,000 a day reaches $10,000 in about two weeks with the failure floor never in play.

every session is logged with four numbers: closing equity, distance from the failure floor, percentage of target completed, and trading days used. week one finishes at $2,900 of the $10,000 target, with the account never closer than 8% to the failure floor and the largest single session at $1,150. nothing dramatic has happened, which is the point.

the evaluation reaches $10,400 by the ninth trading day. because ftmo requires four minimum trading days and applies no consistency rule at evaluation, verification proceeds immediately. phase two begins with risk per trade reduced by a quarter, since the target is $5,000 and over-sizing a smaller target is the most common way a clean phase one is wasted.

phase two completes on the sixteenth trading day. the firm verifies the pass and issues its certificate; the funded credentials are passed to the trader along with a funded-phase summary covering the minimum trading days before the first payout, the profit threshold, the firm's consistency position at payout, and the kyc documents that will be required.

the engagement closes at that point. the account is the trader's, no profit split applies, and questions about the funded phase are answered as part of the handover rather than as an ongoing service. traders who want a second account come back; the ones who do not are never contacted again.

what that sequence does not include: a dramatic single session, a large directional bet, or any claim about what the funded account will earn. the value is in pacing a fixed budget across a sufficient number of days and never letting one session decide the outcome.

every prop firm challenge, whatever the brand, is decided by four numbers and one behaviour. this guide sets out the numbers, explains how they interact, and describes the routine that gets an account funded - including what a flat-fee passing service does and does not change.
four numbers decide every evaluation: daily loss budget, distance to the failure level, target in r, and any payout constraint.
most attempts fail through a budgeting error in one session, not through a lack of analysis.
slower paths to target pass more often, because a failed attempt costs the fee and the elapsed weeks.
a flat $220 covers any prop firm and any account size - the rulebook, not the brand, decides the difficulty.

passing a prop firm challenge requires two things, and only one of them is trading skill. the first is a process that produces a modest positive return over a few weeks without a drawdown large enough to breach a limit. the second is compliance with a rulebook that was written by someone who expects most traders to fail it. traders over-invest in the first and under-invest in the second, which is why the market is full of capable traders with a drawer of failed evaluations.

the scale of the second problem is easy to see from the arithmetic. a target of 10% with a 5% daily loss limit and a 10% maximum loss is not a hard return to generate over an unlimited calendar - it is roughly seven full-risk wins at 1.5% risk. what makes it hard is that the same account can be ended by two careless sessions, and careless sessions are what a three-week deadline produces.

so the useful frame for an evaluation is not "can i make 10%" but "can i make 10% without ever losing 5% in a day or 10% in total, while keeping my per-trade risk constant". that is a budgeting question, and budgeting questions have answers that can be written down before the first trade. the rest of this guide is that answer, generalised across firms.

traders who fail almost never fail by being unable to reach the target. they fail by reaching it slowly and then giving it back, or by reaching it quickly and having no margin left for verification, or by reaching it and discovering a payout rule that the profit distribution does not satisfy. in all three cases the target was met; something else was not.

that is the single most valuable reframing available. it moves the work from the entry to the structure: how much is risked per trade, how many trades a session allows, how large a day is permitted to be, and how the account behaves near the finish. those are decisions a trader can make calmly on a sunday, rather than urgently on a wednesday afternoon.

what the firms are actually selecting for firms are not selecting for the highest return; they are selecting for traders whose results can be paid out without the account collapsing. that means they favour consistency over brilliance, and the rules reflect it: daily limits, consistency checks on the best day, minimum trading days, and payout thresholds that force a trader to keep the account alive after passing it. once that is understood, the rulebook stops looking arbitrary. a consistency rule is a filter for traders whose profit depends on rare large days. a minimum day count is a filter for traders who cannot sustain a routine. a trailing drawdown is a filter for traders who give back unrealised gains. none of those is an unreasonable thing to filter for in someone you are about to fund. the four numbers on one card whatever the firm, an evaluation reduces to four numbers. write them down, date them, and rewrite them each morning, because three of the four move as equity moves. number where it comes from what it controls daily loss budget firm's daily limit, in dollars maximum exposure in a session distance to failure level max loss mechanic, static or trailing size, once equity has moved target in r target ÷ per-trade risk trade count and pacing payout constraint consistency, day count, threshold what happens after a pass converting percentages into dollars and trades

on a $100,000 account with a 5% daily limit and 1.5% risk per trade, the daily budget is $5,000 and each trade risks $1,500. three losses end the day, four would breach, and the working stop is $4,000 - eighty percent of the limit, which leaves room for the float on the last position. the 10% target is $10,000, or roughly seven full-risk wins.

those five figures - $5,000, $1,500, three, $4,000, seven - are the entire plan for that account. everything else is execution. a trader who can recite them has a plan; a trader who knows the percentages has a brochure.

the payout constraint is the fourth number and it is the one that turns a pass into income. a firm requiring no single day to exceed 30% of total profit is asking for a distribution, not just a total. a trader with a $3,000 best day needs $10,000 of total profit before a withdrawal, which means the evaluation target and the payout requirement are different thresholds and the second is the binding one.
planning for that from the first session costs nothing. planning for it at the payout request costs weeks.

firm choice is a difficulty setting, and it is set before a single trade. two firms with the same target and the same headline drawdown can be materially different assignments once the measurement mechanics are applied, and the difference is usually invisible on a pricing page.

for a first attempt, the left-hand column is the correct column to pick, even at a higher fee. a forgiving rulebook bought twice is cheaper than a strict one bought three times, and the elapsed weeks are the real cost - a trader who spends nine weeks on two failed strict attempts has lost more than the fee difference by a wide margin.

brand reputation is mostly a proxy for payout reliability, which matters enormously and says almost nothing about difficulty. a firm can be excellent at paying and brutal at evaluating, or vice versa. treat the two questions separately: read the rulebook for difficulty, and read the payout record for reliability.

the practical test for reliability is whether the firm publishes clear payout terms and honours the ones it publishes. firms with vague payout language and a long list of conditions are telling you something about how a request will be handled when the money is due.
three numbers, written down once, replace every judgement made in the moment.
the plan is three decisions and one habit. the decisions are risk per trade, pace, and the session limit; the habit is recalculating the four numbers every morning.

half the daily budget means two losses end the day, and two consecutive losses are ordinary. a third means three losses are needed, which converts a bad session into a bad session rather than a failed account. the cost is that the target takes slightly longer; the benefit is that the account survives the variance it is certain to meet.

there is no prize for speed and no penalty for patience, because most firms either impose no overall deadline or set one long enough that a deliberate pace fits comfortably. a target reached in six days at aggressive size means the risk was high enough that a second attempt would have been likely; a target reached in eighteen days at 1.5% risk means the process was repeatable.

a session needs three closing conditions: a profit level at which you stop, a loss level at which you stop, and a time at which you stop regardless. the third is the one traders omit, and it is the one that prevents a drifting afternoon from spending the last of the daily budget on an entry nobody planned.

ninety seconds, four numbers, before the first trade. equity, distance to the failure level, today's budget in dollars, and today's maximum position size. the numbers change as the account moves, and the day they matter most is the day a trader feels most confident and therefore least likely to check.
failures cluster so tightly that seven patterns cover almost every case. six of them are budgeting failures, which is why the fix is arithmetic rather than analysis.
the oversized position. three or four times normal risk, usually after a good week, consuming the whole daily budget in one trade.
the third trade. two losses followed by a recovery trade, which breaches the daily limit rather than recovering the day.
the give-back. a profitable position held until it reverses through entry and stop, converting a good day into a bad one.
the deadline sprint. size increasing in the final week because an invented finish date is approaching.
the news gap. a stop filling beyond its level during a release, turning a planned loss into a large one.
the rule misread. positions held overnight or over a weekend on an account type that does not permit it.
the abandonment. a drawdown followed by a fortnight of inactivity, then a return with a size chosen to recover in one trade.

all seven share a signature: the trader knew the rule and did not apply it under pressure. that is why written numbers beat remembered ones, and why the eighty-percent stop exists - it is the only defence that works when judgement is compromised.

everything above can be done by a disciplined trader working alone, and many are. a service adds three specific things: the rulebook translation that identifies which constraint binds today, the daily recalculation and enforcement of the budget, and the discipline to cap a winning session and reduce size near the target - sustained for two or three weeks without drift.

ask four questions and insist on written answers. what happens when an evaluation fails? what do the retry terms actually cover? does the firm permit third-party trading, and is enforcement credible? what evidence exists beyond a testimonial? a provider that answers all four plainly is worth shortlisting; one that answers none has answered the most important question.

the third question is the one that decides whether a service is safe to use at all. where a firm prohibits third-party trading and enforces the prohibition after funding, the client carries the entire downside: the account can be closed at exactly the point where the work would have paid. any service that works around that has transferred its own risk to the person least able to absorb it.

passing is the second-hardest part of the process. the hardest is the first payout cycle, where the trailing floor or static limit applies from day one, the payout conditions are live, and there is no target to organise the trading around.

most funded accounts require a profit threshold, a minimum number of trading days, and a consistency ratio on the best day before the first withdrawal. they have different deadlines, and the efficient plan lands them on the same date rather than treating the day count as a formality to wait out.

the consistency condition is the one that blocks most first requests. required total profit equals best day divided by the threshold percentage, so a $2,400 best day under a 30% rule needs $8,000 of total profit. an account showing $5,500 needs $2,500 of ordinary profit, added without creating a new dominant day.

the instinct after funding is to make the first payout worth having. that instinct is the most common reason a funded account never pays. the first payout's purpose is to prove the pipe works; the size of it is a by-product of the account size, not of the risk taken in week one.
rulebook read twice - numbers, then exceptions - and dated.
four numbers written on a card: budget, distance, target in r, payout constraint.
risk per trade at one third of the daily budget, constant within 10%.
working stop at eighty percent of the daily limit, not one hundred.

ten lines, one page, and every one of them is a defence against a specific failure that recurs across firms and account sizes. traders who pass on the first attempt are rarely better analysts; they are the ones who did this arithmetic before the market asked them a question.

the rules of a prop firm evaluation look similar across markets and behave very differently in practice, and traders who move between them without adjusting tend to fail on mechanics rather than on analysis.

forex firms usually measure the maximum loss statically, impose a daily loss limit on equity, and apply no consistency rule during the evaluation. position sizing is continuous - lot sizes can be halved or doubled freely - which makes the risk arithmetic simple and precise. targets are typically 8% to 10% with a verification phase at half that, and there is often no overall time limit.

the forgiving part is the static drawdown: a good week cannot make the account more fragile, so a trader can hold size constant throughout. the unforgiving part is the daily limit measured on equity, because a floating loss counts in real time and leaves no room for a position to breathe through noise.

futures firms more often use dollar-denominated targets and trailing drawdowns, and consistency rules at payout are common rather than exceptional. position sizing is discrete - one contract is a large jump in risk relative to a small account - which makes precise risk budgeting harder than in forex.

the trailing floor is the defining feature, and it changes which strategies are viable: a plan that relies on holding a winner through a pullback is charged twice on a trailing account, once in the profit given back and once in the room that disappears. futures evaluations reward exit discipline and punish patience in a way forex challenges do not.

the budgeting method transfers completely: daily budget, per-trade risk at a third of it, a hard stop at eighty percent, and a written session limit. the instrument knowledge does not transfer, and neither does the exit style - a trader who scalps forex successfully will find the same approach viable on a futures account, while a trader who holds position trades will find it expensive on a trailing floor.

that is the practical reason a firm's rulebook matters more than its market. a trader with a swing style is better served by a static-drawdown forex evaluation than by an aggressively trailing futures one, even if they believe futures suit them better as a market.
an evaluation has two costs and traders usually count only one. the fee is visible and the elapsed time is not, yet the time is the scarcer resource for anyone building a track record.

at a realistic 50% pass probability, the expected number of attempts is two, so a $540 challenge has an expected fee cost of about $1,080 and an expected time cost of about six weeks. raising the probability to 70% by halving risk brings the expected fee to roughly $770 and the expected time to four weeks - a saving in both currencies from a change that feels like going slower.

this is also the arithmetic that makes a flat service fee interesting. where one fee covers retries at the same firm and size, the expected cost of reaching a funded account is fixed at the price of the service, and the comparison between firms becomes a comparison of difficulty and payout terms rather than of headline challenge prices.

the weeks matter for a second reason: firms change terms, and an attempt that stretches over two months may finish under a different rulebook than the one it started with. shorter, better-planned attempts are less exposed to that risk, which is another argument for the patient approach - it is slower per attempt but it fails less often, so it finishes sooner in expectation.

there is one further line worth adding to the budget: the cost of the funded account's first payout cycle, in time. most programs require a minimum number of trading days and a profit threshold before a withdrawal, so the real horizon from purchase to cash is typically six to ten weeks even after a clean pass. traders who plan for three are the ones who press, and pressing is what the plan exists to prevent.

written down as a calendar rather than a hope, the whole sequence becomes checkable: purchase date, expected pass date, earliest payout date. a trader who can see all three stops treating the middle one as a deadline and starts treating it as an estimate, which is what it is.

numbers generalise badly when they stay abstract, so here is one account taken from purchase to first withdrawal at every step. a $50,000 futures evaluation with a $2,500 maximum loss, a $1,100 daily loss limit, a $3,000 profit target and a minimum of five trading days.

daily budget $1,100. distance to failure $2,500. target in r at 0.75% risk - $375 per trade - is eight wins. payout constraint: a 30% best-day rule at withdrawal, which means the best day must stay under roughly $1,000 while profit accumulates. the card reads: 1100 / 2500 / 8 / 30%.

two things are immediately visible from those numbers and would not have been visible from the marketing page. first, the daily limit is only 44% of the maximum loss, so two bad days is all the account can absorb. second, the target is eight wins at a risk level that permits three losses a day, which is a patient profile rather than a fast one.
week one: three trades a day, flat by the close

four days, nine trades, five wins and four losses, roughly $1,050 net. the daily budget was never threatened because the worst day lost $375 twice - two trades at full risk, then stopped. the consistency ratio is already healthy because no day exceeded $525, well under the $1,000 ceiling that a 30% rule will imply once profit reaches $3,000.

a strong tuesday makes $1,150, which is the best outcome of the evaluation and the worst piece of news. if the account were at target, that day would be 38% of profit and the payout would be blocked. at $2,300 total profit it is 50% of profit, which means the next $1,000 of profit has to arrive without making another day of that size. the correct response is not to stop - the account is working - but to reduce size to 0.5% for the remainder so that a repeat session cannot dominate the distribution.
one dominant session changes the shape of the account even when the total is moving in the right direction.

the remaining $700 arrives over three sessions at reduced size. the account finishes at $3,080 with a best day of $1,150, which is 37% of profit - above a 30% threshold. the evaluation is complete and the payout is not yet available, and knowing that on day fifteen is the difference between a plan and a surprise.

two options exist. wait for the funded account and add ordinary profit until the ratio falls under 30% (another $750 at any pace), or, if the firm permits, continue on the evaluation to build a better distribution before requesting. the first is usually correct, because the funded account's profit counts toward the same ratio and the floor there is more forgiving than a fresh evaluation.

on the funded account, three sessions of small trades add $820, bringing total profit to $3,900 against a $1,150 best day - 29%, just inside the threshold. the minimum day count is already satisfied, so the request goes in on a tuesday with a flat book and verified payment details. processing takes three business days.
the lesson from the sequence is that the evaluation was never the binding constraint. the payout condition was, and it was visible on day zero to anyone who had written down the fourth number.
failure is normal and it is also information, but only if the cause is identified rather than felt. a useful post-mortem takes twenty minutes and answers four questions in order.
how many sessions did the attempt last? very short attempts indicate sizing; long attempts that end suddenly indicate a discipline break.
on how many sessions was risk outside 10% of the plan? any number above zero explains most of the variance in the outcome.
which session came closest to the daily limit, and what was different about it? the answer is usually time of day, a news event, or a trade taken after a loss.
if the attempt had ended one day earlier, would it have passed? most failures answer yes, which is the most useful sentence an attempt can produce.

then change exactly one thing before the next purchase. changing three things at once makes the second attempt unreadable, and a trader who cannot read their own attempts is buying lottery tickets with extra steps.

reset at the same size if the failure was a single identifiable discipline break and the rulebook suits the strategy. move down a size if the failure was caused by the pressure of the fee rather than by the rules - a cheaper account makes the same process easier to follow. change firm if the failure came from a mechanic the strategy cannot accommodate, such as a trailing floor against a strategy that needs to hold through pullbacks; in that case a second attempt on the same rulebook is a second purchase of the same problem.

in return terms it is modest - roughly seven full-risk wins at 1.5% risk for a 10% target. in rule terms it is hard, because two careless sessions can end the account regardless of the return. the difficulty is budgeting, not analysis.

sixteen to twenty-two trading days at 1.5% risk is the realistic range for a 10% target. faster passes are possible and usually mean the risk was high enough that a second attempt would have been needed.
one third of the daily loss budget. on a 5% daily limit that is about 1.65% per trade, which allows three losses in a session and keeps a normal losing sequence survivable.

why is a payout sometimes refused after a clean pass?

almost always the consistency ratio. the best day is measured against total profit at the moment of the request, so a profitable account can still be blocked until enough ordinary profit is added to bring the ratio inside the threshold.
continuing to trade after a strong session. the daily budget is smallest relative to the remaining target, and the trade taken to press an advantage is the one that gives it back.

ftmo's evaluation is a staged structure rather than a single target, and the two-phase shape is the reason a pass takes weeks rather than days. each phase has its own profit target, each has a minimum number of trading days, and both run against the same pair of loss rules: a maximum loss limit that governs the account and a maximum daily loss limit that governs the session.

the day count binds before the target does. a plan traded at a sensible risk per session usually reaches a phase target before it has completed the phase's minimum days. the efficient approach lands both conditions on the same date by deliberately pacing rather than by trading more size.

the daily limit sets risk per trade, not the target. risk is sized so that three consecutive losses remain survivable inside one session. that produces a slower pass than a trader imagines, and a materially higher completion rate than one built on maximum size.

the phase handover is a checkpoint, not a licence. clearing phase one proves the plan works at that size. it does not argue for a larger size in phase two, and traders who increase risk at the handover are the population that loses the evaluation from a winning position.

two phases, one plan. the plan does not change at the handover. what changes is the account's balance relative to its reset limits, and the correct response is to recompute the numbers rather than to trade them harder.
before any arithmetic, establish which balance each limit is measured from - it changes how much room exists after a drawdown.
the choice of challenge type matters more than the choice of account size, and both matter less than the rulebook behind them.

account size first. percentage rules are broadly constant across tiers, so a larger account buys a larger payout ceiling and a larger fee rather than an easier evaluation. fixed costs - commissions and spreads - are identical in dollars at every tier, which makes small accounts marginally harder to pass at identical discipline. the smallest tier that produces a meaningful payout is usually the right purchase, and the flat service fee does not change with size, so there is no reason for us to steer a client upward.

holding policy second. whether positions may be held overnight or across a weekend changes which strategies are admissible at all. a swing approach on a restricted account breaches without warning; an intraday approach on a permissive account leaves the weekend gap risk unaddressed. match the policy to the strategy before buying, because it is the one choice that can make an evaluation impossible for a given trader.

risk profile third. where a firm offers a stricter and a looser variant of the same evaluation, the looser one usually trades a lower target for a tighter daily limit or the reverse. the useful comparison is not the headline target but the ratio of target to daily limit, which is what decides how much ordinary variance a plan can absorb. a target that is twice the daily limit with a month of calendar available is easier than a target that is four times the daily limit with a fortnight.

one sequencing note that applies to every firm: buy the evaluation in your own name, with your own payment method, and complete identity verification yourself. ownership is what keeps a funded account valid at payout, and it is the first thing a firm checks when a withdrawal is reviewed.

before payment, we read the current terms for the specific challenge and confirm in writing whether the evaluation can be traded by a third party. that check is free, it happens before anything is bought, and it produces one of three answers.
permitted. the terms allow the evaluation to be traded externally, and the job proceeds at the flat fee.

prohibited. we decline and say so before payment. a funded account passed in breach of the terms can be voided at the payout, which is a worse outcome than a failed evaluation, because the client has paid the firm, paid the service and earned nothing.

silent. treated as prohibited unless the firm confirms otherwise in writing. a firm that has not addressed the question can address it at the payout, and the risk of that lands on the funded account rather than on the fee.

three details are checked alongside the main question. whether third-party trading is permitted on the evaluation and on the funded account separately, since some firms permit the first and prohibit the second. which conduct rules apply - news windows, maximum position size, prohibited strategies, holding restrictions - because they decide which session windows are usable and therefore how long the pass takes. and what ownership evidence the firm requires, which decides how the account has to be purchased and who completes verification.

where the terms are ambiguous, the honest move is to ask the firm directly and save the answer. a support response permitting third-party trading on the evaluation is worth having in writing, and it costs one message. where that message goes unanswered, the answer is no.

the evaluation is traded to the firm's rules, so the plan is written from the rulebook rather than from a view on the market. six numbers define it, and they are recomputed at the phase handover rather than carried over unchanged.
risk per trade: a third of the daily loss limit at most, so three consecutive losses leave the session survivable.
daily stop: stop opening positions once 80% of the daily budget is realised. the remaining fifth absorbs slippage on the closing trade.
daily profit cap: set at a fraction of the phase target that keeps the largest day small relative to total profit, which satisfies a consistency condition at the funded stage by construction.

phase pace: the phase target as a percentage of the account, divided by the sessions available in that phase, checked against the daily limit. if the required pace consumes more than a fifth of the daily budget, the phase is running too fast and the plan slows down.
day-count plan: the sessions needed to satisfy the minimum days, spread deliberately so that a small closed trade completes a qualifying day without adding meaningful risk.

weekly loss pause: a hard stop at two losing sessions in a week. on a staged evaluation the pause costs a few days of calendar and prevents the sequence that closes most accounts - three losses, a size increase, and a fourth.
one budget, three consumers. the untapped reserve is what makes a losing week recoverable.

the fifth number is the one clients question most, and it is the one that does the most work. a minimum day count is not a formality; it is a calendar requirement that runs in parallel with the target. a single closed trade that keeps a day green satisfies it. a trader who instead uses those days to press for profit is adding risk to a requirement that needed none, and on a staged evaluation that mistake has to be avoided twice.

at the handover, three numbers are recomputed: the maximum loss floor against the new balance, the daily limit against the new balance if it is expressed as a percentage, and the pace required for the second phase's target. nothing else changes, and the risk per trade stays where it was. that last point is worth restating because it is the most common self-inflicted failure on a staged evaluation.

a two-phase evaluation is not completed in a few days, and any provider promising that has not read the minimum day counts. the realistic window is three to five weeks, and the drivers are worth stating precisely so that the expectation is set correctly from the start.

phase one sets the pace and usually takes one to two weeks. at a risk per trade that keeps three losses survivable, a good week produces a modest percentage rather than a large one. two weeks is typical with four sessions a week, and the phase completes when both the target and the day count are satisfied.

the handover adds days, not hours. phase two starts against a reset balance with its own target and its own minimum days, so the calendar does not simply continue - it restarts in part. building that into the estimate is the difference between a plan and a hope.

conduct windows remove sessions. restricted releases can eliminate an hour of a session, and a week with several scheduled events has a meaningfully shorter usable calendar. the plan works around the windows rather than through them.

losing weeks are expected and budgeted. a plan that cannot absorb a two-loss week is not a plan, and the weekly pause means a bad week costs two sessions rather than five. that is calendar spent deliberately to protect the account.

reporting runs at agreed checkpoints, at minimum weekly, with immediate notice if an attempt fails. silence during an evaluation is indistinguishable from a failure, which is why the cadence is part of the product rather than a courtesy. where a phase completes, the client sees the firm's own confirmation rather than a summary from us.
the fee is $220 for any ftmo challenge and any account size. the scope is narrow and stated in full, because a vague scope is the most common source of dispute in this industry.

the comparison that matters is against doing it yourself, and the case against the service deserves stating as plainly as the case for it. at a firm fee of roughly $500, one attempt on your own costs about $500; a service costs about $720. if you pass first time, the service is $220 worse and you also gave up the experience of trading the evaluation. from the second attempt onward the arithmetic reverses sharply, because the service absorbs retries while your own attempts are billed each time.
break-even is one failure. past that, the flat fee is cheaper than the expected cost of self-trading.

three costs the fee does not remove are worth naming. the firm's evaluation fee is unaffected. the firm's reset charge, where one applies, remains the client's cost. and the calendar is not shortened: the minimum day counts apply to a service pass exactly as they apply to anyone else, which is why a two-phase evaluation cannot be compressed indefinitely by trading harder.

what the fee does buy is a removal of the reset multiplication and of the attention cost. a trader running two failed attempts has spent four to eight weeks that could have produced a funded account, and that calendar is usually worth more than the fee difference. for the arithmetic on the payout side, the profit calculator models what a funded account produces once its conditions are met.

the pass produces a funded account, and responsibility transfers with it. the service covers the evaluation; the funded account is governed by the firm's payout conditions, which are usually stricter than the evaluation was.

three conditions carry over and three are new. carried over: the daily and maximum loss limits in some form, the conduct rules, and the requirement to trade within permitted hours. new: a profit threshold before any withdrawal, a minimum number of qualifying days per payout cycle, and a consistency condition on how much of the total profit any single day may represent.

the consistency condition is the one that catches clients who assume the work is done. required total profit equals the largest day divided by the permitted share, so one large session can multiply the requirement. the remedy is identical to the evaluation plan: cap daily profit at a fraction of the threshold and the ratio is satisfied before it is tested.
the funded stage is a calendar with two mathematical gates. the service stops at handover; the plan continues.

four steps in the first week after handover, in order. change the account password regardless of how access was provided. confirm the account is in your name with your payment details and verification complete. read the funded terms yourself rather than relying on a summary. and write the funded plan - risk per trade, daily stop, daily profit cap, minimum days - before the first trade rather than after the first loss.

the payout process guide covers the withdrawal sequence, the verification steps and the delays that block first requests. the short version: complete verification early, request the first payout on the earliest permitted date rather than at the largest available amount, and treat that first payment as a test of the process rather than as income.
four refusals define the service as much as the fee does, and each exists because the alternative transfers risk to the client without saying so.

we will not trade a firm whose terms prohibit third-party trading. not quietly, not for a higher fee. a funded account passed in breach of the terms can be voided at payout, which converts a paid evaluation into the loss of both the firm's fee and the service fee.

we will not hold the funded account. the account is in your name and access is returned or removed at handover. continuing to trade someone else's funded account is a managed account in disguise and is prohibited by most firms.

we will not promise income. the deliverable is a completed evaluation. the funded account has to be traded by its owner under the firm's terms, and no service can promise a payout it does not control.

we will not take a profit share. a provider paid a percentage of earnings has a reason to keep trading an account after the job is done, which extends the exposure and can lose the account in pursuit of a larger fee.

two practices are worth stating because they are the industry's usual shortcuts. we do not buy evaluations on the client's behalf; the purchase is made in the client's name with the client's payment method, because ownership is what keeps a funded account valid. and we do not ask for identity documents, because verification is the account holder's step and cannot be delegated to anyone.

account size is the last decision and the one most often made backwards. clients choose the biggest account they can afford, on the assumption that a bigger account is a better account. under percentage rules that is only half true, and the other half costs money.

targets and loss limits scale with the balance, so difficulty per dollar is roughly constant across tiers. fixed costs do not scale: spreads, commissions and swaps are identical in dollars at every size, so they consume a larger share of a smaller target. that makes a small account marginally harder to pass at identical discipline - worth knowing before buying the cheapest tier in the belief that it is the easiest.

the benefit a larger tier genuinely buys is the payout ceiling. a payout cycle pays a percentage of the balance, so a bigger account pays a bigger amount for the same performance. that is real, and it is the only advantage.

the correct method is therefore a payout calculation rather than a budget calculation. decide the amount a payout cycle should produce, divide by the firm's payout split to get the profit the account must generate, then check whether that figure is reachable inside the daily limit at a pace that consumes under a fifth of it per session. if a small tier satisfies the calculation, buy the small tier: the extra fee for a larger account buys a bigger ceiling, not a bigger chance.

an illustration of the pace a compliant two-phase pass actually runs at, using a plan with risk at 1.5% per trade against a 5% daily loss limit, a session stop at 80% of the budget, and a weekly pause after two losing sessions.

phase one, week one. four sessions. two ordinary gains, one flat session, one small loss. progress around a third of the way to the phase target with no session anywhere near the daily limit. two qualifying days.

phase one, week two. three sessions complete the target, and the remaining sessions of the week satisfy the balance of the phase's minimum day count with single small closed trades. the phase is confirmed by the firm, and the second phase starts against a reset balance.

phase two, week three. the same plan, applied at the same risk per trade. four sessions, one of them a loss of half the planned risk because the setup invalidated early. progress roughly half the second target, with the day count tracking alongside the profit rather than behind it.

phase two, week four. three sessions complete the target, and the day count lands on the same date because the pace was planned backwards from the requirement. across the whole evaluation the largest day is a modest fraction of the total, so a payout consistency condition would clear comfortably if it were applied.

the features worth noticing are the absence of a dramatic week, the deliberate use of small closed trades to satisfy day counts, and the refusal to increase size at the phase handover. a pass built this way is slower than one built on a single large session, and it is considerably more likely to convert into a payout, because the consistency ratio is satisfied before it is ever tested.

the contrast is instructive. a trader who clears both phases quickly on the back of one dominant session has completed the evaluation and created a payout problem simultaneously. the consistency guide works that arithmetic through, and the daily drawdown guide covers the limit that decides risk per trade in the first place.
five steps, in order, and each one takes minutes. they are the difference between an evaluation that can be passed and one that cannot be, regardless of who trades it.

choose size by payout ceiling. decide what a payout cycle should produce, then work backwards to the smallest balance that satisfies it.
match the holding policy to your strategy. restricted holding makes some approaches impossible rather than merely harder.
have the funded plan written before the pass. risk per trade, daily stop, daily profit cap, minimum qualifying days. writing it after the pass is how funded accounts are lost in week one.
complete verification early. identity checks can be finished before the first trade, and doing so removes the most common cause of a delayed first payout.

four of the five take under an hour in total. the fifth - a plan for the funded account - is the one that decides whether the fee produces income or a screenshot. the service comparison sets out how the flat-fee model compares with the alternatives, and the passed challenges page shows what a completed evaluation looks like.

take profit trader runs dollar-based futures evaluations with a trailing threshold and a strong emphasis on payout-window mechanics. if the trailing floor keeps catching you, the problem is almost always sizing in the final third of the evaluation - and this guide is about fixing that.
the failure threshold trails peak equity, so the account gets more fragile as the target gets closer.
smaller entry tiers make this a reasonable first futures evaluation, but the fixed cost per contract is a larger drag on a small target.
payout conditions are the part worth reading twice: minimum days, profit threshold and processing windows all apply.
