evaluations here are futures-based, with targets and failure thresholds expressed in dollars rather than percentages. that has one direct consequence for planning: every rule must be converted into a percentage of account size before it can be compared with a forex evaluation or with a different tier at the same firm.
the account range makes this a sensible first futures evaluation for traders who do not want to start at a large tier. two arithmetic points follow.

small targets amplify fixed costs. commission and slippage are dollars per contract regardless of account size. on a smaller tier the target is smaller but the cost per round turn is identical, so the effective edge required is slightly higher. this does not make small accounts a bad choice - it makes the expectation of an identical pass rate unrealistic.

small targets also reduce the damage of a mistake. a single oversized position on a large tier costs proportionally the same and absolutely much more. for a trader new to trailing thresholds, learning the mechanic on a smaller account is the cheaper education.

a trailing threshold is a failure level that rises with your peak equity and never comes back down. on an intraday trailing structure it responds to unrealised profit, which is the detail that produces failures traders cannot explain by looking at their own p l.

work through a concrete sequence. an account opens with the failure level $4,000 below the starting balance. in the second session, an open position reaches $3,200 of unrealised profit; the threshold has now risen by $3,200. the position is then closed at $900 after a retracement. the trader has banked $900 and the floor has risen by $3,200, so the cushion has fallen by $2,300 - on a session that finished green.

nothing in that sequence was a mistake by any reasonable trading standard. the plan was followed, a profit was taken, and the account is worse positioned than it was at the start of the day. the only defence is structural: reduce risk as progress accumulates, and bank profit deliberately rather than holding for a larger number.
an intraday trailing floor follows unrealised equity, so a retracement reduces the cushion even after a winning session.

two questions decide how much room you actually have, and both should be answered from the terms rather than assumed. first, does the threshold follow unrealised equity or only closed profit? end-of-day trailing is a different and considerably easier structure. second, does it stop moving at any point - some firms stop the trail once the floor reaches the starting balance, which changes the arithmetic of the final third of an evaluation. where either answer is unclear, ask before buying; the difference between the two structures is larger than the difference between most firms' headline targets.
four numbers define a workable plan, and a fifth is a daily check rather than a parameter.
maximum risk per trade: a third of whatever the day's binding constraint is. on a trailing account that means a third of the smaller of the daily limit and the remaining buffer to the threshold.
daily stop: stop opening positions once 80% of the day's budget is spent, whether realised or floating.
daily profit cap: about a third of the total target, which keeps any payout-stage consistency rule satisfied by construction.
size ladder: full size to 40% of target, three quarters from 40% to 70%, half beyond 70%. this is the trailing account's equivalent of a stop loss, applied to the evaluation rather than to a trade.
daily floor check: before the first trade of each session, calculate current equity minus the threshold. if that number is smaller than the planned per-trade risk, reduce size or skip the session.

the fifth item is the one that separates plans that survive from plans that do not. it takes twenty seconds and it is the only mechanism that prevents trading into a buffer too thin to absorb a normal loss. traders who track it informally - rather than writing it into the plan as a rule - abandon it precisely in the session after a large winner, which is when it matters most.

the counter-intuitive part: on a trailing account, a losing day is cheap and a winning day is expensive. losing consumes the daily budget without moving the floor; winning raises the floor permanently. the correct response to a strong session is to reduce, not to press.
a realistic pace is eleven to sixteen trading days. the structure below assumes a mid-tier account, a dollar target, a trailing threshold and a payout-stage consistency requirement.

sessions 1-3 - establish the routine. half of planned size while the plan meets real conditions. one or two setups per session, each closed at a defined target rather than held, and a hard stop at the daily cap. expected outcome: 15-25% of target. the purpose of this phase is not progress; it is confirmation that the plan survives contact with an actual order book.

sessions 4-8 - the working middle. full planned size. daily profit is capped at roughly a third of the total target, which means no session can become a payout problem later. completion should reach 55-70% by the end of this phase, and the threshold should have risen by a similar amount in dollar terms - which is exactly why the size ladder begins here.

sessions 9-13 - reduce and finish. size falls to three quarters and then half as completion passes 70%. sessions shorten. the remaining ground is covered in small increments and any session that reaches the cap is closed rather than extended. this is the phase where trailing accounts are lost, because the buffer is thinnest and the temptation to press is greatest.

completion. trading stops when the target and the minimum day count are both satisfied. where the day count is the later of the two, the plan closes one small position per remaining day rather than maintaining normal exposure on an account that cannot improve its standing.

a pacing detail that catches traders out: the daily cap and the daily stop are not symmetrical in their consequences. breaching the cap costs a consistency ratio problem later; breaching the stop ends the account immediately. when a session is going well and the cap is near, the correct action is to close and stop - not to add one more position because the day is already green.
session 1 - +$420. half size. the threshold rises modestly with the peak. nothing notable; the routine is established.

session 2 - +$1,230. full size. a position reaches $1,850 unrealised before being closed at $1,230. on an intraday trailing structure the floor has moved by $1,850 and the buffer is $620 thinner than the banked profit implies - a concrete example of why closing early is the correct instinct on this structure.
session 3 - −$460. one loss at planned size, then closed. a losing session does not move the threshold, so the cost is confined to the daily budget.

sessions 4-7 - +$2,610 combined. completion reaches 71%, so size drops to three quarters and then half. no session exceeds the daily cap of roughly $2,000. the best day remains session 2 at $1,230 - about 18% of the eventual total, comfortably inside a 30% payout rule.

sessions 8-11 - +$1,480 combined. the final increment at half size, in four short sessions. the floor is recalculated each morning; on one morning the remaining buffer was below the planned per-trade risk, so the session was skipped entirely rather than traded at reduced size. that decision cost a day and preserved the evaluation.

completion. the target is reached on session 11 with the minimum day count satisfied. trading stops. the consistency ratio stands at roughly 18%, so the first payout request can be made as soon as the funded-phase conditions allow.

what the example shows: one session gave back $620 of unrealised profit, one session was skipped on a floor check, and the evaluation finished comfortably inside both the loss rules and the payout rule. none of that required a better market read than the plan already assumed.
most failures on a trailing model begin as an ordinary session that drifted past its budget.
six failure modes account for almost every reset on this type of structure.

the floor has already moved with the peak, so the retracement is measured from the peak rather than from the entry. this is the defining failure on any intraday trailing account, and it produces the specific experience of a green day that leaves the account more fragile than it started.

the instinct that fails trailing evaluations. progress shrinks the buffer, so the correct response is the opposite: reduce size as the target gets closer. a plan that holds constant size until the final session is taking its largest effective risk at the point of least room.

efficient at reaching a target and expensive twice over: it raises the threshold by the full unrealised peak and it concentrates profit so that a payout-stage consistency rule cannot be satisfied at the target. a $5,000 day on a $6,000 target is a passed evaluation waiting weeks for a withdrawal.

activity is not a requirement; the minimum day count is. on a trailing account every session either moves the floor or consumes budget, so a session with no specific plan costs something and gains nothing. four or five planned sessions a week produces a slower pass and a materially lower breach rate.

maximum contract counts and restricted trading windows are usually in the terms rather than on the evaluation page, and they are enforced by pattern detection rather than manual review. trading a permitted instrument at twice the permitted size is a breach, and it is one of the most common accidental ones.

traders who calculated their room once at the start of an evaluation and never recalculated it are consistently surprised in the final third. the check takes twenty seconds per session and it is the cheapest habit available on a trailing account.
the payout conditions govern the account long before the withdrawal request is made.
passing produces a funded account with its own conditions, and on futures accounts those conditions are usually the strictest part of the whole process.

the reassuring part is that trailing behaviour usually disappears at funding, replaced by a static level. the demanding part is that the payout conditions apply in sequence and independently: minimum days, profit threshold, consistency ratio, kyc, then processing. meeting four of the five produces nothing, which is why the funded-phase plan should list all five with a target date for each.

two habits make the difference in practice. complete kyc in the first week of the funded phase rather than when the threshold is reached, and plan the threshold and the minimum day count to complete on the same day so there is no idle period at target. traders who ignore both find the first withdrawal taking three to six weeks; traders who plan both find it taking days. the payout process guide covers the sequence, the three withdrawal methods and the delays that block first payouts.
futures firms differ far less on targets and splits than on how their failure thresholds behave, which is the axis that should drive the choice.

the single most valuable feature in that table is end-of-day trailing, because it removes the mechanic that punishes giving back an unrealised gain. where a firm offers both structures, the end-of-day version is generally the better assignment unless the intraday plan is dramatically cheaper - and the price gap is rarely large enough to justify the difference in difficulty.

a second comparison point that is often overlooked: consistency at payout is close to universal in futures, unlike in forex, where several major firms apply no consistency requirement at all. traders whose profit naturally concentrates - a small number of larger positions rather than many small ones - should weigh that carefully. for that style, a forex or cfd evaluation with a static drawdown and no consistency rule is frequently the easier route to a funded account, even though the instrument set is different.

smaller tiers are the sensible starting point for a trader new to trailing thresholds, for two reasons. first, the mechanic takes a few sessions to internalise, and learning it on a smaller account costs less in absolute terms when the lesson goes wrong. second, the fixed cost per contract is a larger drag on a small target, which discourages the very behaviour that fails trailing accounts - over-trading to reach a target quickly.

what smaller tiers do not do is change the rules. the plan, the ladder and the floor check are identical at every size; only the dollar figures move. a trader who size-mismanages a small account will size-mismanage a large one, which is why sequencing - pass one, trade it into a payout, then add a second - produces a funded portfolio faster than running several evaluations simultaneously and splitting attention across all of them.

everything in this guide can be executed by a disciplined trader working alone. the parts that a service adds are narrow and specific: the rulebook translation that identifies which of the two loss constraints binds today, the daily floor recalculation, and the discipline to cap a winning session and reduce size near the end - sustained for two to three weeks without the drift that comes from trading against a deadline.

pattern one: the strong monday. a trader opens the week with a large win, the floor jumps, and the remaining four sessions are spent defending a buffer too thin for their usual size. the account survives the week but ends it with less room than it started, and the following week begins with the trader already at their maximum size relative to available risk. the fix is a hard rule that a session worth more than 3% of target closes the day out.

pattern two: the recomputed floor. traders who plan against the starting threshold rather than the current one take on size that was appropriate on day one and is dangerous by day ten. the floor must be written down each morning before the first entry, not recalled from memory - the number changes precisely on the days a trader feels most confident, which is when recall is least reliable.

pattern three: the deadline drift. targets only bite when a trader has set a date for reaching them. as that date approaches, size creeps up and selectivity drops, and the account fails on a setup that would have been skipped a fortnight earlier. a calendar is the useful tool here, not as pressure but as evidence: if the plan needed more days than were available, the plan was wrong, not the market.

it follows your peak equity upward and never moves back down. the absolute distance from the peak to the threshold stays roughly constant, so any retracement from the peak is measured against a raised floor - which is why a profitable session can leave the account more fragile than it started.

eleven to sixteen trading days with disciplined pacing. faster passes are possible on a favourable rulebook but usually create a consistency problem that delays the first payout instead of arriving sooner.

a third of whichever constraint binds, with trading stopped once 80% of the daily budget is spent. on a trailing account the binding constraint is sometimes the daily limit and sometimes the remaining buffer to the threshold - calculate both each morning.

yes. full size to 40% of target, three quarters from 40% to 70%, half beyond 70%. this is mandatory on a trailing account rather than a preference, because progress reduces the room available for a normal losing sequence.
is a losing day or a winning day more expensive?

a winning day, on a trailing structure. a loss consumes part of the daily budget and does not move the floor. a win raises the floor permanently - and if part of that win was unrealised before a retracement, the floor rose by more than the amount banked.

the firm's reset and purchase options apply. where a passing service trades the evaluation, a reset on the same firm and size carries no additional service fee under the flat $220 arrangement, while the firm's own reset charge is separate.

yes. funded accounts usually require a minimum number of trading days plus a profit threshold before the first withdrawal, and firms process payout requests on a schedule rather than on demand. planning the threshold and the day count to land on the same date is the single biggest time saver.

the smallest tier you can trade without changing your approach, for two reasons: the trailing mechanic takes a few sessions to internalise, and a smaller target makes the fixed cost per contract a larger share of the goal, which discourages over-trading. the rules are identical at every size, so a smaller account teaches the same lesson more cheaply.

policies differ by firm and by plan, and holding into a gap adds a risk that a trailing threshold cannot absorb - the loss counts immediately while the floor has already moved. where the plan permits overnight positions, gap risk is budgeted explicitly; where it does not, the book is flat before the close.

continuing to trade after a strong session. the floor has moved, the consistency ratio has tightened, and the account has the least room and the least to gain. closing the session at the daily cap is the behaviour that separates passes from resets.
the first month on a funded take profit trader account

passing is the second-hardest part of a futures evaluation. the hardest is the first month on the funded account, where the trailing floor applies from day one, the payout conditions are live, and there is no target to aim at. traders who fail here usually fail by doing what worked during the evaluation at the wrong moment.

the first week after funding is not the time to press. the account has no buffer beyond its starting balance, the floor is at its closest, and the payout conditions probably require a minimum number of trading days anyway. a week of two or three small trades establishes the new routine and, more usefully, establishes a small profit cushion that widens the distance to the floor.

the counter-argument - that the account cost money and should be worked hard - is the reason many funded accounts never pay out. a funded account is not a race; it is a licence that remains valid as long as the rules are respected.

most funded programs require a profit threshold before the first withdrawal, so the objective in weeks two and three is to reach it without concentrating the result. that means a session cap: no day worth more than roughly a fifth of the required profit. the cap protects the consistency ratio later and prevents a single session from setting a best day that the rest of the account has to catch up with.

before any withdrawal request, compute the best day as a share of total profit. if the number is above the firm's threshold, the request will be refused, and the correct response is to add ordinary profit rather than to add size. the arithmetic is mechanical: required total profit equals best day divided by the consistency percentage.

once the threshold, the day count and the ratio are all satisfied, request the payout and keep trading at the same reduced size afterwards. the second cycle is easier than the first because the cushion is larger, and the third is easier again - which is why the first month is the one that decides whether a funded account becomes an income stream or a story about a firm that never pays.
take profit trader's trailing threshold is one of three structures a futures trader will encounter, and the differences are not academic - they change which strategies are viable.

the trailing structure is the strictest of the three and the one most sensitive to exit discipline. a strategy that relies on letting a winner run through a pullback is viable on a static account and expensive on a trailing one, not because the strategy is worse but because the structure charges for the pullback in a way the market does not.

the practical implication is to size down as the account progresses rather than to hold size constant. on a static account, constant size is fine; on a trailing account, the room available for a normal losing sequence shrinks with every new equity high, so constant size is an increasing risk over time even though nothing about the plan has changed.
what to do if the floor has already caught up

if a funded account is at a new high and the distance to the floor has narrowed to the point where two normal losses would end it, the answer is to stop, not to continue at a smaller size - because the position that recovers the account is the one taken with the least room. close the cycle, request the payout if eligible, and let the floor's relationship to balance reset with a banked profit rather than with hope.

that last point is worth restating because it inverts the instinct: on a trailing account, the moment a trader feels most capable is the moment the account is most fragile. the floor has followed the success, the buffer has shrunk, and the next ordinary losing sequence costs more room than the last one did. recognising that inversion is most of the skill the structure rewards.

a practical way to make the inversion visible is to write two figures at the top of each session: equity and distance to the floor. when the second number shrinks while the first grows, size comes down. traders who track both find the decision obvious; traders who track only equity find it surprising, usually on the day the account ends.

the same two figures answer a question traders ask constantly: when should i stop for the day? stop when the distance to the floor is less than three times the planned per-trade risk. at that point a normal losing sequence would end the account, and continuing is no longer trading a plan - it is trading the remainder of a plan.
written down, that rule turns a judgement call into arithmetic, which is the only form of discipline that survives a bad afternoon.

common thresholds are 30-50% of total profit from any single day.

a distribution of ordinary days passes more reliably than one oversized winner.

crypto fund trader is a crypto evaluator built on a evaluation for crypto pairs with a profit target and loss limit, with a plan-specific loss floor, a daily stop and one-off per attempt billing. the product is a reasonable fit for crypto traders who want an evaluation on digital assets. it is a poor fit for a trader whose strategy needs the opposite drawdown mechanic, or whose budget cannot absorb the billing rhythm across several attempts.

the crypto fund trader evaluation is best understood as a set of constraints that interact, not as a headline profit target with some footnotes. the target decides how much you have to make. the loss floor decides how much room you have to make it. the daily stop, if there is one, decides how quickly a bad session ends. the minimum-day rule decides how long the attempt takes even when the target is reached early. change any one of those and the same trading strategy produces a different outcome.

for crypto fund trader, the published structure is a evaluation for crypto pairs with a profit target and loss limit. the loss floor is firm-specific, the daily stop is yes, and the consistency condition is plan-specific. billing is one-off per attempt, payouts follow profit split on a fixed schedule, and the supported platforms are proprietary and mt5. those are the rows that matter. marketing pages tend to foreground the profit target and the profit split because both are easy to compare; neither tells you whether a given trade is survivable.

a static loss floor is the simplest rule in the crypto fund trader rulebook and the one traders most often misapply. the floor is anchored to the starting balance and does not move. on a $100,000 account with a 10% limit, the failure point stays at $90,000 from the first trade to the last, whatever the account does in between.

there is a second-order effect that matters on crypto accounts. the loss is measured on equity, which includes floating profit and loss, spread and commission. on a forex account, swap and commission are deducted from equity, so a position held overnight can reduce the cushion without a price move. a risk plan that ignores costs will drift into the floor more slowly than expected, then all at once.

the strengths are structural rather than promotional. crypto market access without posting full capital. 24/7 trading. simple evaluation structure. those are the features that show up in the trading experience, not just on the comparison table.

the cautions are equally structural. no session close means no natural reset point. volatility makes fixed-dollar stops harder to size. payout terms are firm-specific. none of them is a reason to avoid the firm automatically, but each has to be priced into the plan before the fee is paid.

the evaluation is the audition; the funded account is the job. crypto fund trader pays out on this rhythm: profit split on a fixed schedule. the split percentage is the number on the sales page, but the rhythm is the number that decides what the account is worth in the first year. a 90% split paid after ninety days is worth less than an 80% split paid in the first week if you need the cash flow, and a split with a consistency condition attached can be reduced after the fact.

step 2: choose the server-side option, not a chart line

a stop entered in the order ticket is sent to the server with the order and survives a disconnect. a horizontal line dragged onto the chart is a client-side object and does not. if the stop is added after entry, use the position's modify or stop loss command rather than a chart tool, and confirm the change in the order list.

the funded trading plus evaluation is best understood as a set of constraints that interact, not as a headline profit target with some footnotes. the target decides how much you have to make. the loss floor decides how much room you have to make it. the daily stop, if there is one, decides how quickly a bad session ends. the minimum-day rule decides how long the attempt takes even when the target is reached early. change any one of those and the same trading strategy produces a different outcome.

for funded trading plus, the published structure is a two-phase evaluation with a static floor. the loss floor is static, the daily stop is yes, and the consistency condition is yes. billing is one-off per attempt, payouts follow profit split on a fixed schedule, and the supported platforms are mt4, mt5, ctrader. those are the rows that matter. marketing pages tend to foreground the profit target and the profit split because both are easy to compare; neither tells you whether a given trade is survivable.

there is a test that separates a trader who understands a funded trading plus rulebook from one who has only read the sales page: ask what happens to the failure point after a winning trade. on a static floor the answer is "nothing". on a trailing threshold the answer is "it moves up, and it does not move back down". everything else in the risk plan follows from that answer.

a profit target is a distance, and the only useful question is how many trades it takes to cover that distance at a given risk-reward. on an illustrative $100,000 funded trading plus account with an 8% target, the account needs $8,000 of net profit. at a 1:2 risk-reward and 0.5% risk per trade, a winning trade makes $1,000 and a losing trade loses $500. a 50% win rate over 20 trades produces ten winners and ten losers: $10,000 gained, $5,000 lost, $5,000 net. that is short of the target. the same win rate over 32 trades produces $8,000 net, which is the target.

the cost of a funded trading plus attempt is not the entry fee. it is the entry fee multiplied by the expected number of attempts, plus the value of the time spent, plus the cost of the mistakes the attempt teaches. a $100 fee that takes four attempts costs $400; a $250 fee that takes one attempt costs $250. firms compete on the first number because it is visible at checkout, and traders compare on it because it is easy, but the second number is the one that leaves the bank account.

every number in this guide describes the published shape of the funded trading plus rulebook, not a guarantee of the terms on the day you buy. firms revise targets, loss limits and payout conditions between cohorts, and the dashboard you see after checkout is the only version that binds. the verification routine below takes ten minutes and is worth more than any comparison table, including this one.

the pass email is the midpoint, not the finish. between the pass and the first payout there is a verification step, a contract, a funded login and a compliance period. each has its own failure mode, and none of them is about trading skill. the first week after a funded trading plus pass is mostly administrative, and treating it that way prevents the most avoidable loss of the whole process.

the definition matters because the same word can mean different things at different firms. a "drawdown" can be static or trailing; a "daily loss" can be measured on balance or equity; a "consistency rule" can apply to the evaluation, the funded account or both. when a rule is ambiguous, the firm's own terms page is the definition, and a support reply in writing is the only useful clarification.

the table exposes the first trap: a 10% total loss allowance and a 1% risk unit allow ten consecutive losses, but the daily stop may end the day after five. the binding constraint is the smaller of the two, and it changes with the time of day. a trade that is acceptable at the open is not automatically acceptable after three losses in the same session.

the second trap is compounding. a 0.5% risk unit is 0.5% of the current balance, not of the starting balance, if the trader recalculates after each trade. after a 3% drawdown, the same percentage risks slightly less in dollars, which slows the recovery. after a 3% gain, it risks slightly more. most evaluation plans are simpler and safer with a fixed dollar risk, recalculated only when the account size changes.
the target is one distance; the loss allowance and daily stop are two separate limits.

read the loss-floor row before anything else. a loss floor measured from the starting balance is a fixed distance away for the whole attempt: profit does not move it, and an open position cannot pull it closer. a floor measured from peak equity behaves in the opposite way. it follows the high-water mark, so an open winner raises the failure point, and a retracement that gives back profit can end the account while the balance is still above where it started. those two mechanics require different stop placement, different position sizing and different answers to the question "how much can i risk on this trade?"

the daily stop row matters just as much for a different reason. a percentage daily stop measured on equity counts open positions, so it is not enough to check the realised balance at the end of the day. if a trade is $1,800 in profit and then reverses to a $3,200 loss on a $100,000 account with a 5% daily stop, the account can be closed by the swing even if the trader never intended to risk more than one percent. the stop is evaluated continuously, not at midnight.

finally, the minimum-day row sets the floor on elapsed time. a rulebook with no minimum can be passed in a session if the target is reached; one with a five- or ten-day minimum cannot. that matters for cost: on a subscription product, every extra required day is a day of billing, and on a one-off product it is a day of exposure with no additional fee. the same rule change alters the correct pace on the two billing models in opposite directions.

micro futures are the smallest exchange-traded contracts on the index, energy and metals products, and their tick values are a fixed fraction of the full-size contract. the arithmetic is simple, but the commission per contract is not proportional, which is why micros are easier to size and harder to trade profitably at high frequency. the consequence is a position size. once the stop distance and the instrument value are known, the calculation is exact, and an exact number is far easier to follow than an intention.

the calculation matters because it is the point where a rule becomes a trade. a risk percentage is an intention; a lot or contract count is an instruction. between the two sit the stop distance, the instrument's value per point or pip, and the account currency. get any of them wrong and the trade risks a different amount than the plan allows.

futures sizing starts with the contract specification. the e-mini s&p 500 (es) is $50 per index point; the micro e-mini (mes) is $5. the e-mini nasdaq (nq) is $20 per point; the micro nasdaq (mnq) is $2. gold (gc) is $100 per point with a 0.10 tick, so one tick is $10; the micro gold (mgc) is $10 per point and $1 per tick. those numbers, not the margin, determine the dollar risk of a stop.

the formula is: contracts = dollar risk ÷ (stop distance in points × value per point). on a $100,000 evaluation risking 0.5% ($500) with a 10-point stop on mes, each contract risks $50, so the position is ten contracts. the same $500 with a 40-point stop allows two contracts. the dollar risk is constant; the size moves with the stop.

commission changes the arithmetic at small sizes. a round turn on a micro typically costs a dollar or two per contract, so ten contracts cost $10-$20 before the trade moves. on a $500 risk budget that is 2-4% of the risk, and on a smaller budget it can be 10%. the commission has to be subtracted from the risk budget, not added to the target.

margin is a separate constraint. the exchange sets a maintenance margin and the broker sets an intraday margin, which can be lower. a trader who sizes to the intraday margin is using the maximum the platform will allow, which is almost always larger than the size the loss floor supports. the correct size is the smaller of the two calculations, and on an evaluation it is nearly always the loss-floor calculation.

a minimum deposit is the smallest amount a firm will accept before issuing an evaluation. it is separate from the evaluation fee and is usually held as trading capital, which changes the effective cost of the first attempt. the consequence is cumulative. fees, retries, data costs and payout timing add up to a total cost of reaching the first withdrawal, and that total is the number worth comparing across routes.

the total cost of reaching a first payout is the sum of those rows, not the first one. a $100 evaluation that takes three attempts, a $50 monthly data fee for three months and a $30 payout fee costs $430 before any profit. a $250 evaluation passed first time costs $280. the cheaper headline is the more expensive route in this example, which is why the comparison has to be made on the total.

the breakeven calculation is simple: divide the total cost by your expected net payout. if a funded account pays $1,600 net on a typical first withdrawal and the route costs $430, the first payout covers the cost and the second is profit. if the route costs $1,200, it takes most of a year of average payouts to break even. neither number is a reason to buy or avoid; they are the terms of the bet.

a prop evaluation is a leveraged bet on your own execution. the fee buys a chance at a funded account, not the account itself, and the expected value depends on the probability of a pass multiplied by the value of the funded account, minus the fee. that is the whole model, and most marketing avoids it because the probability is the hard input.

the probability can be estimated from your own record. if you have taken twenty trades at a fixed risk unit and a documented expectancy, you can simulate the pass probability for a given target and floor. if you have no record, the honest estimate is "unknown", and the correct first purchase is a small account or a demo, not the largest available evaluation.

the value of the funded account is the net payout you expect before the account fails or you stop trading it. that is usually a few months of average profit, not a year, because the same loss floor applies after the pass. a $10,000 account that pays $800 a month for four months is worth $3,200, not $9,600, and the fee should be compared with the former.
